snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The graph of a function f is shown in Figure 6. (a) Find the values of f(1) and f(5) . (b) What are the domain and range of f ? Solution (a) We see from Figure 6 that the point \left( {1,3} \right) lies on the graph of...
body_xml: Example 1 The graph of a function $$f$$ is shown in Figure 6. (a) Find the values of $$f(1)$$ and $$f(5)$$ . (b) What are the domain and range of $$f$$ ? Solution (a) We see from Figure 6 that the point $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ lies on the graph of $$f$$ , so the value of $$f$$ at $$1$$ is $$f(1) = 3$$ . (In other words, the point on the graph that lies above $$x = 1$$ is $$3$$ units above the $$x$$ -axis.) When $$x = 5$$ , the graph lies about $$0.7$$ units below the $$x$$ -axis, so we estimate that $$f(5) \approx - 0.7$$ . (b) We see that $$f(x)$$ is defined when $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 7$$ , so the domain of $$f$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,7} \right\rbrack$$ . Notice that $$f$$ takes on all values from $$- 2$$ to $$4$$ , so the range of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 4 \right\} = \lbrack - 2,4\rbrack$$ The notation for intervals is given in Appendix A.

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Sketch the graph and find the domain and range of each function. (a) f(x) = 2x - 1 (b) g(x) = x^{2} Solution (a) The equation of the graph is y = 2x - 1 , and we recognize this as being the equation of a line with...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Sketch the graph and find the domain and range of each function.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$g(x) = x^{2}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The equation of the graph is $$y = 2x - 1$$ , and we recognize this as being the equation of a line with slope $$2$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$- 1$$ . (Recall the slope-intercept form of the equation of a line: $$y = mx + b$$ . See Appendix B.) This enables us to sketch a portion of the graph of $$f$$ in Figure 7. The expression $$2x - 1$$ is defined for all real numbers, so the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers, which we denote by $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The graph shows that the range is also $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Figure 7 Details A line with positive slope is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The line labeled y = 2 x minus 1 enters the bottom left of the viewing window in the third quadrant, goes up and to the right, crosses the y axis at (0, negative 1), then crosses the x axis at (1/2, 0), and exits the top right of the viewing window in the first quadrant.</item>
      <item>(b) Since $$g(2) = 2^{2} = 4$$ and $$g\left( {- 1} \right) = \left( {- 1} \right)^{2} = 1$$ , we could plot the points $$(2,4)$$ and $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , together with a few other points on the graph, and join them to produce the graph (Figure 8). The equation of the graph is $$y = x^{2}$$ , which represents a parabola (see Appendix C). The domain of $$g$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The range of $$g$$ consists of all values of $$g(x)$$ , that is, all numbers of the form $$x^{2}$$ . But $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ for all numbers $$x$$ and any positive number $$y$$ is a square. So the range of $$g$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geqslant 0 \right\} = \lbrack 0,\infty)$$ . This can also be seen from Figure 8. Figure 8 Details An upward opening parabola, which is symmetric about the y axis, is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The parabola labeled y = x^2 enters the top left of the viewing window in the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, passes through the marked points (negative 2, 4), (negative 1, 1), (negative 0.5, 0.25), reaches its low point at (0, 0), then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant through the marked points (0.5, 0.25), (1, 1) and (2, 4).</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 If f(x) = 2x^{2} - 5x + 1 and h \neq 0 , evaluate \frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h} . Solution We first evaluate f\left( {a + h} \right) by replacing x by a + h in the expression for f(x) : \begin{array}{l}...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f(x) = 2x^{2} - 5x + 1$$ and $$h \neq 0$$ , evaluate $$\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We first evaluate $$f\left( {a + h} \right)$$ by replacing $$x$$ by $$a + h$$ in the expression for $$f(x)$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f{({a + h})}} = {2{({a + h})}^{2} - 5(a + h) + 1}} \\ {\phantom{f{({a + h})}} = {2(a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2}) - 5(a + h) + 1}} \\ {\phantom{f{({a + h})}} = {2a^{2} + 4ah + 2h^{2} - 5a - 5h + 1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then we substitute into the given expression and simplify:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h} = \frac{\left( {2a^{2} + 4ah + 2h^{2} - 5a - 5h + 1} \right) - \left( {2a^{2} - 5a + 1} \right)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}} = \frac{2a^{2} + 4ah + 2h^{2} - 5a - 5h + 1 - 2a^{2} + 5a - 1}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}} = {\frac{4ah + 2h^{2} - 5h}{h} = 4a + 2h - 5}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The expression</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>in Example 3 is called a difference quotient and occurs frequently in calculus. As we will see in Chapter 2, it represents the average rate of change of $$f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = a + h$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 When you turn on a hot-water faucet that is connected to a hot-water tank, the temperature T of the water depends on how long the water has been running. Draw a rough graph of T as a function of the time t that has...
body_xml: Example 4 When you turn on a hot-water faucet that is connected to a hot-water tank, the temperature $$T$$ of the water depends on how long the water has been running. Draw a rough graph of $$T$$ as a function of the time $$t$$ that has elapsed since the faucet was turned on. Solution The initial temperature of the running water is close to room temperature because the water has been sitting in the pipes. When the water from the hot-water tank starts flowing from the faucet, $$T$$ increases quickly. In the next phase, $$T$$ is constant at the temperature of the heated water in the tank. When the tank is drained, $$T$$ decreases to the temperature of the water supply. This enables us to make the rough sketch of $$T$$ as a function of $$t$$ shown in Figure 11.

unit_title: Four Ways to Represent a Function
title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 A rectangular storage container with an open top has a volume of 10m^{3} . The length of its base is twice its width. Material for the base costs $$\$ 10 per square meter; material for the sides costs \$ 6 per square...
body_xml: Example 5 A rectangular storage container with an open top has a volume of $$10m^{3}$$ . The length of its base is twice its width. Material for the base costs $$\$ 10$$ per square meter; material for the sides costs $$\$ 6$$ per square meter. Express the cost of materials as a function of the width of the base. Solution We draw a diagram as in Figure 12 and introduce notation by letting $$w$$ and $$2w$$ be the width and length of the base, respectively, and $$h$$ be the height. The area of the base is $$\left( {2w} \right)w = 2w^{2}$$ , so the cost, in dollars, of the material for the base is $$10{({2w^{2}})}$$ . Two of the sides have area $$wh$$ and the other two have area $$2wh$$ , so the cost of the material for the sides is $$6\left\lbrack 2(wh) + 2(2wh) \right\rbrack$$ . The total cost is therefore $$C = 10{({2w^{2}})} + 6\left\lbrack {2\left( {wh} \right) + 2\left( {2wh} \right)} \right\rbrack = 20w^{2} + 36wh$$ To express $$C$$ as a function of $$w$$ alone, we need to eliminate $$h$$ and we do so by using the fact that the volume is $$10m^{3}$$ . Thus $$w\left( {2w} \right)h = 10$$ which gives $$h = \frac{10}{2w^{2}} = \frac{5}{w^{2}}$$ In setting up applied functions as in Example 5, it may be useful to review the principles of problem solving at the end of this chapter, particularly Step 1: Understand the Problem. Substituting this into the expression for $$C$$ , we have $$C = 20w^{2} + 36w\left( \frac{5}{w^{2}} \right) = 20w^{2} + \frac{180}{w}$$ Therefore the equation $$C(w) = 20w^{2} + \frac{180}{w} w > 0$$ expresses $$C$$ as a function of $$w$$ .

snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the domain of each function. (a) f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2} (b) g(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - x} Solution (a) Because the square root of a negative number is not defined (as a real number), the domain of f consists of all...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the domain of each function.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2}$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$g(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - x}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Because the square root of a negative number is not defined (as a real number), the domain of $$f$$ consists of all values of $$x$$ such that $$x + 2 \geqslant 0$$ . This is equivalent to $$x \geqslant - 2$$ , so the domain is the interval $$\lbrack - 2,\infty)$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Since $$g(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - x} = \frac{1}{x\left( {x - 1} \right)}$$ and division by $$0$$ is not allowed, we see that $$g(x)$$ is not defined when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 1$$ . So the domain of $$g$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0,x \neq 1 \right\}$$ which could also be written in interval notation as $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right) \cup \left( {0,1} \right) \cup \left( {1,\infty} \right)$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">The Vertical Line Test</heading>
    <paragraph>A curve in the $$xy$$ -plane is the graph of a function of $$x$$ if and only if no vertical line intersects the curve more than once.</paragraph>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 A function f is defined by f(x) = \begin{cases} {1 - x} & {{if}x \leqslant - 1} \\ x^{2} & {{if}x > - 1} \end{cases} Evaluate f\left( {- 2} \right) , f\left( {- 1} \right) , and f(0) and sketch the graph. Solution...
body_xml: Example 7 A function $$f$$ is defined by $$f(x) = \begin{cases} {1 - x} & {{if}x \leqslant - 1} \\ x^{2} & {{if}x > - 1} \end{cases}$$ Evaluate $$f\left( {- 2} \right)$$ , $$f\left( {- 1} \right)$$ , and $$f(0)$$ and sketch the graph. Solution Remember that a function is a rule. For this particular function the rule is the following: First look at the value of the input $$x$$ . If it happens that $$x \leqslant - 1$$ , then the value of $$f(x)$$ is $$1 - x$$ . On the other hand, if $$x > - 1$$ , then the value of $$f(x)$$ is $$x^{2}$$ . Note that even though two different formulas are used, $$f$$ is one function, not two. $$\begin{array}{l} {{Since} - 2 \leqslant - 1,{we have}f( - 2) = 1 - ( - 2) = 3.} \\ {{Since} - 1 \leqslant - 1,{we have}f( - 1) = 1 - ( - 1) = 2.} \\ {{Since}0 > - 1,{we have}f(0) = 0^{2} = 0.} \end{array}$$ How do we draw the graph of $$f$$ ? We observe that if $$x \leqslant - 1$$ , then $$f(x) = 1 - x$$ , so the part of the graph of $$f$$ that lies to the left of the vertical line $$x = - 1$$ must coincide with the line $$y = 1 - x$$ , which has slope $$- 1$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$1$$ . If $$x > - 1$$ , then $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , so the part of the graph of $$f$$ that lies to the right of the line $$x = - 1$$ must coincide with the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ , which is a parabola. This enables us to sketch the graph in Figure 15. The solid dot indicates that the point $$\left( {- 1,2} \right)$$ is included on the graph; the open dot indicates that the point $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ is excluded from the graph.

body_xml: Example 8 Sketch the graph of the absolute value function $$f(x) = |x|$$ . Solution From the preceding discussion we know that $$|x| = \begin{cases} x & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \\ {- x} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$ Using the same method as in Example 7, we see that the graph of $$f$$ coincides with the line $$y = x$$ to the right of the $$y$$ -axis and coincides with the line $$y = - x$$ to the left of the $$y$$ -axis (see Figure 16).

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Find a formula for the function f graphed in Figure 17. Solution The line through \left( {0,0} \right) and \left( {1,1} \right) has slope m = 1 and y -intercept b = 0 , so its equation is y = x . Thus, for the part of...
body_xml: Example 9 Find a formula for the function $$f$$ graphed in Figure 17. Solution The line through $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ has slope $$m = 1$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$b = 0$$ , so its equation is $$y = x$$ . Thus, for the part of the graph of $$f$$ that joins $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ , we have $$f(x) = x {if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$$ The line through $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ has slope $$m = - 1$$ , so its point-slope form is $$y - 0 = \left( {- 1} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)$$ or $$y = 2 - x$$ So we have $$f(x) = 2 - x {if}1 < x \leqslant 2$$ We also see that the graph of $$f$$ coincides with the $$x$$ -axis for $$x > 2$$ . Putting this information together, we have the following three-piece formula for $$f$$ : $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1} \\ {2 - x} & {{if}1 < x \leqslant 2} \\ 0 & {{if}x > 2} \end{cases}$$ The point-slope form of the equation of a line is $$y - y_{1} = m\left( x - x_{1} \right)$$ . See Appendix B.

snippet: Example 11: Example 11 Determine whether each of the following functions is even, odd, or neither even nor odd. (a) f(x) = x^{5} + x (b) g(x) = 1 - x^{4} (c) h(x) = 2x - x^{2} Solution (a) \begin{array}{l} {{f( - x)} = {{( - x)}^{5} + ( -...
body_xml:
<example number="11">
    <heading level="4">Example 11</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine whether each of the following functions is even, odd, or neither even nor odd.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$f(x) = x^{5} + x$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$g(x) = 1 - x^{4}$$</item>
      <item>(c) $$h(x) = 2x - x^{2}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$\begin{array}{l} {{f( - x)} = {{( - x)}^{5} + ( - x) = {( - 1)}^{5}x^{5} + ( - x)}} \\ {\phantom{f( - x)} = {- x^{5} - x = - (x^{5} + x)}} \\ {\phantom{f( - x)} = {- f(x)}} \end{array}$$ Therefore $$f$$ is an odd function.</item>
      <item>(b) $$g\left( {- x} \right) = 1 - \left( {- x} \right)^{4} = 1 - x^{4} = g(x)$$ So $$g$$ is even.</item>
      <item>(c) $$h\left( {- x} \right) = 2\left( {- x} \right) - \left( {- x} \right)^{2} = - 2x - x^{2}$$ Since $$h\left( {- x} \right) \neq h(x)$$ and $$h\left( {- x} \right) \neq - h(x)$$ , we conclude that $$h$$ is neither even nor odd.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

unit_title: Mathematical Models: A Catalog of Essential Functions
title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 (a) As dry air moves upward, it expands and cools. If the ground temperature is 20{}_{}^{} and the temperature at a height of 1 km is 10{}_{}^{} , express the temperature T (in {}_{}^{}{} ) as a function of the height...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) As dry air moves upward, it expands and cools. If the ground temperature is $$20{}_{}^{}$$ and the temperature at a height of $$1$$ km is $$10{}_{}^{}$$ , express the temperature $$T$$ (in $${}_{}^{}{}$$ ) as a function of the height $$h$$ (in kilometers), assuming that a linear model is appropriate.</item>
      <item>(b) Draw the graph of the function in part (a). What does the slope represent?</item>
      <item>(c) What is the temperature at a height of $$2.5$$ km?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Because we are assuming that $$T$$ is a linear function of $$h$$ , we can write $$T = mh + b$$ We are given that $$T = 20$$ when $$h = 0$$ , so $$20 = m \cdot 0 + b = b$$ In other words, the $$y$$ -intercept is $$b = 20$$ . We are also given that $$T = 10$$ when $$h = 1$$ , so $$10 = m \cdot 1 + 20$$ The slope of the line is therefore $$m = 10 - 20 = - 10$$ and the required linear function is $$T = - 10h + 20$$</item>
      <item>(b) The graph is sketched in Figure 3. The slope is $$m = - 10{}_{}^{} \slash {km}$$ and this represents the rate of change of temperature with respect to height. Figure 3 Details A line with negative slope is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis labeled h is displayed from 0 to 5 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis labeled T is displayed from negative 10 to 25 in increments of 5 units. The line labeled T = negative 10 h + 20 begins at the point (0, 20), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and extends downward in the fourth quadrant.</item>
      <item>(c) At a height of $$h = 2.5$$ km, the temperature is $$T = - 10(2.5) + 20 = - 5{}_{}^{}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

unit_title: Mathematical Models: A Catalog of Essential Functions
title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Table 1 lists the average carbon dioxide level in the atmosphere, measured in parts per million at Mauna Loa Observatory from 1980 to 2016. Use the data in Table 1 to find a model for the carbon dioxide level. Table 1...
body_xml:
Example 2 Table 1 lists the average carbon dioxide level in the atmosphere, measured in parts per million at Mauna Loa Observatory from 1980 to 2016. Use the data in Table 1 to find a model for the carbon dioxide level. Table 1 Year $${CO}_{2}$$ level (in ppm) 1980 338.7 1984 344.4 1988 351.5 1992 356.3 1996 362.4 2000 369.4 2004 377.5 2008 385.6 2012 393.8 2016 404.2
Solution We use the data in Table 1 to make the scatter plot in Figure 4, where $$t$$ represents time (in years) and $$C$$ represents the $${CO}_{2}$$ level (in parts per million, ppm). Notice that the data points appear to lie close to a straight line, so it’s natural to choose a linear model in this case. But there are many possible lines that approximate these data points, so which one should we use? One possibility is the line that passes through the first and last data points. The slope of this line is $$\frac{404.2 - 338.7}{2016 - 1980} = \frac{65.5}{36} \approx 1.819$$ We write its equation as $$C - 338.7 = 1.819\left( {t - 1980} \right)$$ or $$C = 1.819t - 3262.92$$ Equation 1 gives one possible linear model for the carbon dioxide level; it is graphed in Figure 5. Notice that our model gives values higher than most of the actual $${CO}_{2}$$ levels. A better linear model is obtained by a procedure from statistics called linear regression. Many graphing calculators and computer software applications can determine the regression line for a set of data. One such calculator gives the slope and $$y$$ -intercept of the regression line for the data from Table 1 as $$m = 1.78242 b = - 3192.90$$ So our least squares model for the $${CO}_{2}$$ level is $$C = 1.78242t - 3192.90$$ In Figure 6 we graph the regression line as well as the data points. Comparing with Figure 5, we see that the regression line gives a better fit. A computer or graphing calculator finds the regression line by the method of least squares, which is to minimize the sum of the squares of the vertical distances between the data points and the line. The details are explained in Exercise 14.7.61.

unit_title: Mathematical Models: A Catalog of Essential Functions
title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use the linear model given by Equation 2 to estimate the average {CO}_{2} level for 1987 and to predict the level for the year 2025. According to this model, when will the {CO}_{2} level exceed 440 parts per million?...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the linear model given by Equation 2 to estimate the average $${CO}_{2}$$ level for 1987 and to predict the level for the year 2025. According to this model, when will the $${CO}_{2}$$ level exceed $$440$$ parts per million?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Using Equation 2 with $$t = 1987$$ , we estimate that the average $${CO}_{2}$$ level in 1987 was</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C(1987) = {1.78242(1987)} - 3192.90 \approx 348.77$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is an example of interpolation because we have estimated a value between observed values. (In fact, the Mauna Loa Observatory reported that the average $${CO}_{2}$$ level in 1987 was $$348.93$$ ppm, so our estimate is quite accurate.)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>With $$t = 2025$$ , we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C(2025) = {1.78242(2025)} - 3192.90 \approx 416.50$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So we predict that the average $${CO}_{2}$$ level in the year 2025 will be $$416.5$$ ppm. This is an example of extrapolation because we have predicted a value outside the time frame of observations. Consequently, we are far less certain about the accuracy of our prediction.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using Equation 2, we see that the $${CO}_{2}$$ level exceeds $$440$$ ppm when</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$1.78242t - 3192.90 > 440$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving this inequality, we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t > \frac{3632.9}{1.78242} \approx 2038.18$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We therefore predict that the $${CO}_{2}$$ level will exceed $$440$$ ppm by the year 2038. This prediction is risky because it involves a time quite remote from our observations. In fact, we see from Figure 6 that the trend has been for $${CO}_{2}$$ levels to increase rather more rapidly in recent years, so the level might exceed $$440$$ ppm well before 2038.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 A ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower, 450 m above the ground, and its height h above the ground is recorded at 1 -second intervals in Table 2. Find a model to fit the data and use the model...
body_xml:
Example 4 A ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower, $$450$$ m above the ground, and its height $$h$$ above the ground is recorded at $$1$$ -second intervals in Table 2. Find a model to fit the data and use the model to predict the time at which the ball hits the ground. Table 2 Time (seconds) Height (meters) 0 450 1 445 2 431 3 408 4 375 5 332 6 279 7 216 8 143 9 61
Solution We draw a scatter plot of the data in Figure 9 and observe that a linear model is inappropriate. But it looks as if the data points might lie on a parabola, so we try a quadratic model instead. Using a graphing calculator or computer algebra system (which uses the least squares method), we obtain the following quadratic model: $$h = 449.36 + 0.96t - 4.90t^{2}$$ In Figure 10 we plot the graph of Equation 3 together with the data points and see that the quadratic model gives a very good fit. The ball hits the ground when $$h = 0$$ , so we solve the quadratic equation $$- 4.90t^{2} + 0.96t + 449.36 = 0$$ The quadratic formula gives $$t = \frac{- 0.96 \pm \sqrt{(0.96)^{2} - 4( - 4.90)(449.36)}}{2( - 4.90)}$$ The positive root is $$t \approx 9.67$$ , so we predict that the ball will hit the ground after falling about $$9.7$$ seconds.

<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the domain of the function $$f(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 2\cos x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution This function is defined for all values of $$x$$ except for those that make the denominator $$0$$ . But</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. 1 - 2\cos x = 0 \Leftrightarrow \cos x = \frac{1}{2} \Leftrightarrow x = \frac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = \frac{5\pi}{3} + 2n\pi$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$n$$ is any integer (because the cosine function has period $$2\pi$$ ). So the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers except for the ones noted above.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 2 Sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{2} + 6x + 10$$ . <example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Sketch the graph of each function.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$y = \sin 2x$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$y = 1 - \sin x$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) We obtain the graph of $$y = \sin 2x$$ from that of $$y = \sin x$$ by compressing horizontally by a factor of $$2$$ . (See Figures 6 and 7.) Because the period of $$y = \sin x$$ is $$2\pi$$ , the period of $$y = \sin 2x$$ is $$2\pi \slash 2 = \pi$$ . Figure 6 Details A sine curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative pi to 2 pi in increments of pi/2. The y axis ranges from negative 1 to 1 in increments of 1 unit. The sine curve resembles a wave such that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each high point and low point. The curve, y = sin(x), enters the second quadrant from the left, falls to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), then falls below the x axis, reaches a low point at (negative pi/2, negative 1), then rises to the right through the origin, and reaches a high point in the first quadrant at (pi/2, 1). It then falls to the right, crosses the x axis at (pi, 0), reaches a low point at (3 pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (2 pi, 0). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right. Figure 7 Details A sine curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative pi to 2 pi in increments of pi/4. The y axis ranges from negative 1 to 1 in increments of 1 unit. The sine curve resembles a wave such that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each high point and low point. The curve, y = sin(2 x), enters the third quadrant at (negative 5 pi/4, negative 1), rises to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), reaches a high point at (negative 3 pi/4, 1), then falls to the right by crossing the x axis at (negative pi/2, 0), and reaches a low point in the fourth quadrant at (negative pi/4, negative 1). It then rises to the right through the origin, reaches its high point at (pi/4, 1), falls below the x axis through (pi/2, 0), reaches a low point at (3 pi/4, negative 1), and then rises to the right by crossing the x axis at (pi, 0). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right.</item>
      <item>(b) To obtain the graph of $$y = 1 - \sin x$$ , we again start with $$y = \sin x$$ . We reflect about the $$x$$ -axis to get the graph of $$y = - \sin x$$ and then we shift $$1$$ unit upward to get $$y = 1 - \sin x$$ . (See Figure 8.) Figure 8 Details A sine curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative 2 pi to 3 pi in increments of pi/2. The y axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. The sine curve resembles a wave such that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each high point and low point. The curve, y = 1 minus sin(x), enters the second quadrant at (negative 5 pi/2, 2), falls to the right, reaches a low point at (negative 3 pi/2, 0), then rises to the right to reach a high point at (negative pi/2, 2). It then falls to the right by crossing the y axis at (0, 1), reaches a low point at (pi/2, 0), then rises to the right to a high point at (3 pi/2, 2). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Figure 9 shows graphs of the number of hours of daylight as functions of the time of the year at several latitudes. Given that Philadelphia is located at approximately 40{}_{}^{} latitude, find a function that models...
body_xml: Example 4 Figure 9 shows graphs of the number of hours of daylight as functions of the time of the year at several latitudes. Given that Philadelphia is located at approximately $$40{}_{}^{}$$ latitude, find a function that models the length of daylight at Philadelphia. Solution Notice that each curve resembles a shifted and stretched sine function. By looking at the blue curve we see that, at the latitude of Philadelphia, daylight lasts about $$14.8$$ hours on June 21 and $$9.2$$ hours on December 21, so the amplitude of the curve (the factor by which we have to stretch the sine curve vertically) is $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {14.8 - 9.2} \right) = 2.8$$ . By what factor do we need to stretch the sine curve horizontally if we measure the time $$t$$ in days? Because there are about $$365$$ days in a year, the period of our model should be $$365$$ . But the period of $$y = \sin t$$ is $$2\pi$$ , so the horizontal stretching factor is $$2\pi \slash 365$$ . We also notice that the curve begins its cycle on March 21, the $$80$$ th day of the year, so we have to shift the curve $$80$$ units to the right. In addition, we shift it $$12$$ units upward. Therefore we model the length of daylight in Philadelphia on the $$t$$ th day of the year by the function $$L(t) = 12 + 2.8\sin\left\lbrack {\frac{2\pi}{365}\left( {t - 80} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$g(x) = x - 3$$ , find the composite functions $$f \circ g$$ and $$g \circ f$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} {\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)} & = & {f\left( {g(x)} \right) = f\left( {x - 3} \right) = \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}} \\ {\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x)} & = & {g(f(x)) = g(x^{2}) = x^{2} - 3} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note You can see from Example 6 that, in general, $$f \circ g \neq g \circ f$$ . Remember, the notation $$f \circ g$$ means that the function $$g$$ is applied first and then $$f$$ is applied second. In Example 6, $$f \circ g$$ is the function that first subtracts $$3$$ and then squares; $$g \circ f$$ is the function that first squares and then subtracts $$3$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 If f(x) = \sqrt{x} and g(x) = \sqrt{2 - x} , find each function and its domain. (a) f \circ g (b) g \circ f (c) f \circ f (d) g \circ g Solution (a) \left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) = f{(\sqrt{2 -...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{2 - x}$$ , find each function and its domain.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$f \circ g$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$g \circ f$$</item>
      <item>(c) $$f \circ f$$</item>
      <item>(d) $$g \circ g$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) = f{(\sqrt{2 - x})} = \sqrt{\sqrt{2 - x}} = \sqrt[4]{2 - x}$$ The domain of $$f \circ g$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| 2 - x \geqslant 0 \right\} = \left\{ x \middle| x \leqslant 2 \right\} = ( - \infty,2\rbrack$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) $$\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x) = g\left( {f(x)} \right) = g\left( \sqrt{x} \right) = \sqrt{2 - \sqrt{x}}$$ For $$\sqrt{x}$$ to be defined we must have $$x \geqslant 0$$ . For $$\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{x}}$$ to be defined we must have $$2 - \sqrt{x} \geqslant 0$$ , that is, $$\sqrt{x} \leqslant 2$$ , or $$x \leqslant 4$$ . Thus we have $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$$ , so the domain of $$g \circ f$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ . If $$0 \leqslant a \leqslant b$$ , then $$a^{2} \leqslant b^{2}$$ .</item>
      <item>(c) $$\left( {f \circ f} \right)(x) = f\left( {f(x)} \right) = f\left( \sqrt{x} \right) = \sqrt{\sqrt{x}} = \sqrt[4]{x}$$ The domain of $$f \circ f$$ is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .</item>
      <item>(d) $$\left( {g \circ g} \right)(x) = g\left( {g(x)} \right) = g{(\sqrt{2 - x})} = \sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2 - x}}$$ This expression is defined when both $$2 - x \geqslant 0$$ and $$2 - \sqrt{2 - x} \geqslant 0$$ . The first inequality means $$x \leqslant 2$$ , and the second is equivalent to $$\sqrt{2 - x} \leqslant 2$$ , or $$2 - x \leqslant 4$$ , or $$x \geqslant - 2$$ . Thus $$- 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2$$ , so the domain of $$g \circ g$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {- 2,2} \right\rbrack$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 2 Use a graphing calculator or computer to compare the exponential function $$f(x) = 2^{ x}$$ and the power function $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ . Which function grows more quickly when $$x$$ is large? Solution Figure 6 shows both functions graphed in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 2,6} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {0,40} \right\rbrack$$ . We see that the graphs intersect three times, but for $$x > 4$$ the graph of $$f(x) = 2^{ x}$$ stays above the graph of $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ . Figure 7 gives a more global view and shows that for large values of $$x$$ , the exponential function $$f(x) = 2^{ x}$$ grows far more rapidly than the power function $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ . Example 2 shows that $$y = 2^{ x}$$ increases more quickly than $$y = x^{2}$$ . To demonstrate just how quickly $$f(x) = 2^{ x}$$ increases, let’s perform the following thought experiment. Suppose we start with a piece of paper a thousandth of an inch thick and we fold it in half $$50$$ times. Each time we fold the paper in half, the thickness of the paper doubles, so the thickness of the resulting paper would be $$2^{50} \slash 1000$$ inches. How thick do you think that is? It works out to be more than $$17$$ million miles!

Example 3 Table 1 shows data for the population of the world in the 20th century and Figure 8 shows the corresponding scatter plot. Table 1 World Population $$t$$ (years since 1900) Population $$P$$ (millions) 0 1650 10 1750 20 1860 30 2070 40 2300 50 2560 60 3040 70 3710 80 4450 90 5280 100 6080 110 6870
The pattern of the data points in Figure 8 suggests exponential growth, so we use a graphing calculator (or computer) with exponential regression capability to apply the method of least squares and obtain the exponential model $$P(t) = {(1.43653 \times 10^{9})} \cdot (1.01395)^{t}$$ where $$t = 0$$ corresponds to 1900. Figure 9 shows the graph of this exponential function together with the original data points. We see that the exponential curve fits the data reasonably well. The period of relatively slow population growth is explained by the two world wars and the Great Depression of the 1930s.

body_xml:
Example 4 In 1995 a research article was published that detailed the effect of the protease inhibitor ABT-538 on the human immunodeficiency virus HIV-1.* Table 2 shows values of the plasma viral load $$V(t)$$ of patient 303, measured in RNA copies per mL, $$t$$ days after ABT-538 treatment was begun. The corresponding scatter plot is shown in Figure 10. D. Ho et al., “Rapid Turnover of Plasma Virions and CD4 Lymphocytes in HIV-1 Infection,” Nature 373 (1995): 123–26. Table 2 $$t$$ (days) $$V(t)$$ 1 76.0 4 53.0 8 18.0 11 9.4 15 5.2 22 3.6
The rather dramatic decline of the viral load that we see in Figure 10 reminds us of the graphs of the exponential function $$y = b^{ x}$$ in Figures 3 and 4(a) for the case where the base $$b$$ is less than $$1$$ . So let’s model the function $$V(t)$$ by an exponential function. Using a graphing calculator or computer to fit the data in Table 2 with an exponential function of the form $$y = a \cdot b^{ t}$$ , we obtain the model $$V = 96.39785 \cdot (0.818656)^{t}$$ In Figure 11 we graph this exponential function with the data points and observe that the model represents the viral load reasonably well for the first month of treatment.

body_xml: Example 6 Use a graphing calculator or computer to find the values of $$x$$ for which $$e^{ x} > 1,000,000$$ . Solution In Figure 17 we graph both the function $$y = e^{ x}$$ and the horizontal line $$y = 1,000,000$$ . We see that these curves intersect when $$x \approx 13.8$$ . So $$e^{ x} > 10^{6}$$ when $$x > 13.8$$ . It is perhaps surprising that the values of the exponential function have already surpassed a million when $$x$$ is only $$14$$ .

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A function f is called a one-to-one function if it never takes on the same value twice; that is, f(x_{1}) \neq f(x_{2}) {whenever}x_{1} \neq x_{2} In the language of inputs and outputs, Definition 1 says that f is...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ is called a one-to-one function if it never takes on the same value twice; that is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x_{1}) \neq f(x_{2}) {whenever}x_{1} \neq x_{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In the language of inputs and outputs, Definition 1 says that $$f$$ is one-to-one if each output corresponds to only one input.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Horizontal Line Test
snippet: Horizontal Line Test: Horizontal Line Test A function is one-to-one if and only if no horizontal line intersects its graph more than once.
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Horizontal Line Test" title="Horizontal Line Test">
    <heading level="4">Horizontal Line Test</heading>
    <paragraph>A function is one-to-one if and only if no horizontal line intersects its graph more than once.</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 1 Is the function $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ one-to-one? Solution 1 If $$x_{1} \neq x_{2}$$ , then $${x_{1}}^{3} \neq {x_{2}}^{3}$$ (two different numbers can’t have the same cube). Therefore, by Definition 1, $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ is one-to-one. Solution 2 From Figure 3 we see that no horizontal line intersects the graph of $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ more than once. Therefore, by the Horizontal Line Test, $$f$$ is one-to-one.

body_xml: Example 2 Is the function $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ one-to-one? Solution 1 This function is not one-to-one because, for instance, $$g(1) = 1 = g( - 1)$$ and so $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ have the same output. Solution 2 From Figure 4 we see that there are horizontal lines that intersect the graph of $$g$$ more than once. Therefore, by the Horizontal Line Test, $$g$$ is not one-to-one.

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition Let f be a one-to-one function with domain A and range B . Then its inverse function f^{- 1} has domain B and range A and is defined by \left. f^{- 1}(y) = x \Leftrightarrow f(x) = y \right. for any y in B .
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a one-to-one function with domain $$A$$ and range $$B$$ . Then its inverse function $$f^{- 1}$$ has domain $$B$$ and range $$A$$ and is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. f^{- 1}(y) = x \Leftrightarrow f(x) = y \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>for any $$y$$ in $$B$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the inverse function of $$f(x) = x^{3} + 2$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution According to (5) we first write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = x^{3} + 2$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then we solve this equation for $$x$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} x^{3} & = & {y - 2} \\ x & = & \sqrt[3]{y - 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Finally, we interchange $$x$$ and $$y$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \sqrt[3]{x - 2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore the inverse function is $$f^{- 1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 2}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In Example 4, notice how $$f^{- 1}$$ reverses the effect of $$f$$ . The function $$f$$ is the rule “Cube, then add $$2$$ ”; $$f^{- 1}$$ is the rule “Subtract $$2$$ , then take the cube root.”</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 5 Sketch the graphs of $$f(x) = \sqrt{- 1 - x}$$ and its inverse function using the same coordinate axes. Solution First we sketch the curve $$y = \sqrt{- 1 - x}$$ (the top half of the parabola $$y^{2} = - 1 - x$$ , or $$x = - y^{2} - 1$$ ) and then we reflect about the line $$y = x$$ to get the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ . (See Figure 10.) As a check on our graph, notice that the expression for $$f^{- 1}$$ is $$f^{- 1}(x) = - x^{2} - 1$$ , $$x \geqslant 0$$ . So the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ is the right half of the parabola $$y = - x^{2} - 1$$ and this seems reasonable from Figure 10.

title: Laws of Logarithms

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Laws of Logarithms" title="Laws of Logarithms">
    <heading level="4">Laws of Logarithms</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$x$$ and $$y$$ are positive numbers, then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\log_{b}\left( \mathit{xy} \right) = \log_{b}x + \log_{b}y$$</item>
      <item>$$\log_{b}\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) = \log_{b}x - \log_{b}y$$</item>
      <item>$${\log_{b}\left( x^{r} \right) = r\log_{b}x}$$ (where $$r$$ is any real number)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Use the laws of logarithms to evaluate \log_{2}80 - \log_{2}5 . Solution Using Law 2, we have \log_{2}80 - \log_{2}5 = \log_{2}\left( \frac{80}{5} \right) = \log_{2}16 = 4 because 2^{4} = 16 .

    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{2}80 - \log_{2}5 = \log_{2}\left( \frac{80}{5} \right) = \log_{2}16 = 4$$</paragraph>

    <heading level="4">Notation for Logarithms</heading>
    <paragraph>Most textbooks in calculus and the sciences, as well as calculators, use the notation $$\ln x$$ for the natural logarithm and $$\log x$$ for the “common logarithm,” $$\log_{10}x$$ . body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$x$$ if $$\ln x = 5$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1 From (8) we see that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\ln x = 5} {means} {e^{ 5} = x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore $$x = e^{ 5}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(If you have trouble working with the “ln” notation, just replace it by $$\log_{e}$$ . Then the equation becomes $$\log_{e}x = 5$$ ; so, by the definition of logarithm, $$e^{ 5} = x$$ .)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2 Start with the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\ln x = 5$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and apply the exponential function to both sides of the equation:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{\ln x} = e^{ 5}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>But the second cancellation equation in (9) says that $$e^{\ln x} = x$$ . Therefore $$x = e^{ 5}$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Solve the equation $$e^{5 - 3x} = 10$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We take natural logarithms of both sides of the equation and use (9):</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\ln(e^{5 - 3x})} & = & {\ln 10} \\ {5 - 3x} & = & {\ln 10} \\ {3x} & = & {5 - \ln 10} \\ x & = & {\frac{1}{3}(5 - \ln 10)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using a calculator, we can approximate the solution: to four decimal places, $$x \approx 0.8991$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 14
snippet: Example 14: Example 14 Simplify the expression \cos\left( \tan^{- 1}x \right) . Solution 1 Let y = \tan^{- 1}x . Then \tan y = x and - \pi/2 < y < \pi/2 . We want to find \cos y but, since \tan y is known, it is easier to find \sec y...
body_xml: Example 14 Simplify the expression $$\cos\left( \tan^{- 1}x \right)$$ . Solution 1 Let $$y = \tan^{- 1}x$$ . Then $$\tan y = x$$ and $$- \pi/2 < y < \pi/2$$ . We want to find $$\cos y$$ but, since $$\tan y$$ is known, it is easier to find $$\sec y$$ first: $$\begin{array}{lcl} {\sec^{2}y} & = & {{1 + \tan^{2}y} = {1 + x^{2}}} \\ {\sec y} & = & {\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} \left( {since}\sec y > 0{for} - \pi/2 < y < \pi/2 \right)} \end{array}$$ Thus $$\cos(\tan^{- 1}x) = \cos y = \frac{1}{\sec y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}$$ Solution 2 Instead of using trigonometric identities as in Solution 1, it is perhaps easier to use a diagram. If $$y = \tan^{- 1}x$$ , then $$\tan y = x$$ , and we can read from Figure 24 (which illustrates the case $$y > 0$$ ) that $$\cos(\tan^{- 1}x) = \cos y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola y = x^{2} at the point P(1,1) . Solution We will be able to find an equation of the tangent line \ell as soon as we know its slope m . The difficulty is that we know...
body_xml:
Example 1 Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the point $$P(1,1)$$ . Solution We will be able to find an equation of the tangent line $$\ell$$ as soon as we know its slope $$m$$ . The difficulty is that we know only one point, $$P$$ , on $$\ell$$ , whereas we need two points to compute the slope. But observe that we can compute an approximation to $$m$$ by choosing a nearby point $$Q(x,x^{2})$$ on the parabola (as in Figure 2) and computing the slope $$m_{PQ}$$ of the secant line $$PQ$$ . (A secant line, from the Latin word secans, meaning cutting, is a line that cuts [intersects] a curve more than once.) We choose $$x \neq 1$$ so that $$Q \neq P$$ . Then $$m_{PQ} = \frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}$$ For instance, for the point $$Q(1.5,2.25)$$ we have $$m_{PQ} = \frac{2.25 - 1}{1.5 - 1} = \frac{1.25}{0.5} = 2.5$$ The tables below show the values of $$m_{PQ}$$ for several values of $$x$$ close to $$1$$ . The closer $$Q$$ is to $$P$$ , the closer $$x$$ is to $$1$$ and, it appears from the tables, the closer $$m_{PQ}$$ is to $$2$$ . This suggests that the slope of the tangent line $$\ell$$ should be $$m = 2$$ . $$x$$ $$m_{PQ}$$ 2 3 1.5 2.5 1.1 2.1 1.01 2.01 1.001 2.001
$$x$$ $$m_{PQ}$$ 0 1 0.5 1.5 0.9 1.9 0.99 1.99 0.999 1.999
We say that the slope of the tangent line is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines, and we express this symbolically by writing $$\lim\limits_{Q\rightarrow P}m_{PQ} = m$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1} = 2$$ Assuming that the slope of the tangent line is indeed $$2$$ , we use the point-slope form of the equation of a line [ $$y - y_{1} = m({x - x_{1}})$$ , see Appendix B] to write the equation of the tangent line through $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ as $$y - 1 = 2(x - 1)$$ or $$y = 2x - 1$$

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 A pulse laser operates by storing charge on a capacitor and releasing it suddenly when the laser is fired. The data in the table describe the charge Q remaining on the capacitor (measured in coulombs) at time t...
body_xml:
Example 2 A pulse laser operates by storing charge on a capacitor and releasing it suddenly when the laser is fired. The data in the table describe the charge $$Q$$ remaining on the capacitor (measured in coulombs) at time $$t$$ (measured in seconds after the laser is fired). Use the data to draw the graph of this function and estimate the slope of the tangent line at the point where $$t = 0.04$$ . (Note: The slope of the tangent line represents the electric current flowing from the capacitor to the laser [measured in amperes].) $$t$$ $$Q$$ 0 10 0.02 8.187 0.04 6.703 0.06 5.488 0.08 4.493 0.1 3.676
Solution In Figure 4 we plot the given data and use these points to sketch a curve that approximates the graph of the function. Given the points $$P(0.04,6.703)$$ and $$R(0,10)$$ on the graph, we find that the slope of the secant line $$PR$$ is $$m_{PR} = \frac{10 - 6.703}{0 - 0.04} = - 82.425$$ The table below shows the results of similar calculations for the slopes of other secant lines. From this table we would expect the slope of the tangent line at $$t = 0.04$$ to lie somewhere between $$- 74.20$$ and $$- 60.75$$ . In fact, the average of the slopes of the two closest secant lines is $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {- 74.20 - 60.75} \right) = - 67.475$$ $$R$$ $$m_{PR}$$ (0, 10) −82.425 (0.02, 8.187) −74.200 (0.06, 5.488) −60.750 (0.08, 4.493) −55.250 (0.1, 3.676) −50.450
So, by this method, we estimate the slope of the tangent line to be about $$- 67.5$$ . Another method is to draw an approximation to the tangent line at $$P$$ and measure the sides of the triangle $$ABC$$ , as in Figure 5. This gives an estimate of the slope of the tangent line as $$- \frac{\left| {AB} \right|}{\left| {BC} \right|} \approx - \frac{8.0 - 5.4}{0.06 - 0.02} = - 65.0$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Suppose that a ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower in Toronto, 450 m above the ground. Find the velocity of the ball after 5 seconds. Solution The difficulty in finding the instantaneous...
body_xml:
Example 3 Suppose that a ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower in Toronto, $$450$$ m above the ground. Find the velocity of the ball after $$5$$ seconds. Solution The difficulty in finding the instantaneous velocity at $$5$$ seconds is that we are dealing with a single instant of time $$(t = 5)$$ , so no time interval is involved. However, we can approximate the desired quantity by computing the average velocity over the brief time interval of a tenth of a second from $$t = 5$$ to $$t = 5.1$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {{average velocity} = \frac{change in position}{time elapsed}} \\ {\phantom{average velocity} = \frac{s(5.1) - s(5)}{0.1}} \\ {\phantom{average velocity} = \frac{4.9{(5.1)}^{2} - 4.9{(5)}^{2}}{0.1} = {49.49m \slash s}} \end{array}$$ The following table shows the results of similar calculations of the average velocity over successively smaller time periods. Time interval Average velocity $$(m \slash s)$$ $$5 \leqslant t \leqslant 5.1$$ 49.49 $$5 \leqslant t \leqslant 5.05$$ 49.245 $$5 \leqslant t \leqslant 5.01$$ 49.049 $$5 \leqslant t \leqslant 5.001$$ 49.0049
It appears that as we shorten the time period, the average velocity is becoming closer to $$49m \slash s$$ . The instantaneous velocity when $$t = 5$$ is defined to be the limiting value of these average velocities over shorter and shorter time periods that start at $$t = 5$$ . Thus it appears that the (instantaneous) velocity after $$5$$ seconds is $$49m \slash s$$ .

<note type="theorem" source_type="Intuitive Definition of a Limit" title="Intuitive Definition of a Limit">
    <heading level="4">Intuitive Definition of a Limit</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose $$f(x)$$ is defined when $$x$$ is near the number $$a$$ . (This means that $$f$$ is defined on some open interval that contains $$a$$ , except possibly at $$a$$ itself.) Then we write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and say</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>“the limit of $$f(x)$$ , as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , equals $$L$$ ”</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>if we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ arbitrarily close to $$L$$ (as close to $$L$$ as we like) by restricting $$x$$ to be sufficiently close to $$a$$ (on either side of $$a$$ ) but not equal to $$a$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 4 The graph of a function $$g$$ is shown in Figure 7. Use the graph to state the values (if they exist) of the following: (a) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}g(x)$$ (b) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}g(x)$$ (c) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)$$ (d) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5^{-}}g(x)$$ (e) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5^{+}}g(x)$$ (f) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}g(x)$$ Solution Looking at the graph we see that the values of $$g(x)$$ approach $$3$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the left, but they approach $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the right. Therefore (a) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}g(x) = 3$$ and (b) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}g(x) = 1$$ (c) Since the left and right limits are different, we conclude from (3) that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)$$ does not exist. The graph also shows that (d) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5^{-}}g(x) = 2$$ and (e) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5^{+}}g(x) = 2$$ (f) This time the left and right limits are the same and so, by (3), we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}g(x) = 2$$ Despite this fact, notice that $$g(5) \neq 2$$ .

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Investigate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin\frac{\pi}{x} . Solution Notice that the function f(x) = \sin(\pi \slash x) is undefined at 0 . Evaluating the function for some small values of x , we get \begin{matrix}...
body_xml: Example 5 Investigate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin\frac{\pi}{x}$$ . Solution Notice that the function $$f(x) = \sin(\pi \slash x)$$ is undefined at $$0$$ . Evaluating the function for some small values of $$x$$ , we get $$\begin{matrix} {f(1) = \sin\pi = 0} & {f\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = \sin 2\pi = 0} \\ {f\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \sin 3\pi = 0} & {f\left( \frac{1}{4} \right) = \sin 4\pi = 0} \\ { f(0.1) = \sin 10\pi = 0} & {{f(0.01) = \sin 100\pi = 0}} \end{matrix}$$ Similarly, $$f(0.001) = f(0.0001) = 0$$ . On the basis of this information we might be tempted to guess that the limit is $$0$$ , but this time our guess is wrong. Note that although $$f(1 \slash n) = \sin n\pi = 0$$ for any integer $$n$$ , it is also true that $$f(x) = 1$$ for infinitely many values of $$x$$ (such as $$2 \slash 5$$ or $$2 \slash 101$$ ) that approach $$0$$ . You can see this from the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 8. The dashed lines near the $$y$$ -axis indicate that the values of $$\sin(\pi \slash x)$$ oscillate between $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ infinitely often as $$x$$ approaches $$0$$ . Since the values of $$f(x)$$ do not approach a fixed number as $$x$$ approaches $$0$$ , $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin\frac{\pi}{x}{does not exist}$$

Solution As $$x$$ becomes close to $$0$$ , $$x^{2}$$ also becomes close to $$0$$ , and $$1 \slash x^{2}$$ becomes very large. (See the following table.) In fact, it appears from the graph of the function $$f(x) = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ shown in Figure 9 that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily large by taking $$x$$ close enough to $$0$$ . Thus the values of $$f(x)$$ do not approach a number, so $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( {1 \slash x^{2}} \right)$$ does not exist. $$x$$ $$\frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ ±1 1 ±0.5 4 ±0.2 25 ±0.1 100 ±0.05 400 ±0.01 10,000 ±0.001 1,000,000

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Does the curve y = \frac{2x}{x - 3} have a vertical asymptote? Solution There is a potential vertical asymptote where the denominator is 0 , that is, at x = 3 , so we investigate the one-sided limits there. If x is...
body_xml: Example 7 Does the curve $$y = \frac{2x}{x - 3}$$ have a vertical asymptote? Solution There is a potential vertical asymptote where the denominator is $$0$$ , that is, at $$x = 3$$ , so we investigate the one-sided limits there. If $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ but larger than $$3$$ , then the denominator $$x - 3$$ is a small positive number and $$2x$$ is close to $$6$$ . So the quotient $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is a large positive number. [For instance, if $$x = 3.01$$ then $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right) = 6.02 \slash 0.01 = 602$$ .] Thus, intuitively, we see that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}\frac{2x}{x - 3} = \infty$$ Likewise, if $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ but smaller than $$3$$ , then $$x - 3$$ is a small negative number but $$2x$$ is still a positive number (close to $$6$$ ). So $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is a numerically large negative number. Thus $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}\frac{2x}{x - 3} = - \infty$$ The graph of the curve $$y = 2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is given in Figure 13. According to Definition 6, the line $$x = 3$$ is a vertical asymptote.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find the vertical asymptotes of f(x) = \tan x . Solution Because \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} there are potential vertical asymptotes where \cos x = 0 . In fact, since \left. \cos x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right. as \left....
body_xml: Example 8 Find the vertical asymptotes of $$f(x) = \tan x$$ . Solution Because $$\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$$ there are potential vertical asymptotes where $$\cos x = 0$$ . In fact, since $$\left. \cos x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right)^{-} \right.$$ and $$\left. \cos x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right)^{+} \right.$$ , whereas $$\sin x$$ is positive (near $$1$$ ) when $$x$$ is near $$\pi \slash 2$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{(\pi \slash 2)}^{-}}\tan x = \infty$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{(\pi \slash 2)}^{+}}\tan x = - \infty$$ This shows that the line $$x = \pi \slash 2$$ is a vertical asymptote. Similar reasoning shows that the lines $$x = \pi \slash 2 + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer, are all vertical asymptotes of $$f(x) = \tan x$$ . The graph in Figure 14 confirms this.

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Limit Laws" title="Limit Laws">
    <heading level="4">Limit Laws</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that $$c$$ is a constant and the limits</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>exist. Then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\lbrack f(x) + g(x)\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\lbrack f(x) - g(x)\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\lbrack cf(x)\rbrack = c\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f{(x)}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g{(x)}}{if}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g{(x)} \neq 0$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Use the Limit Laws and the graphs of f and g in Figure 1 to evaluate the following limits, if they exist. (a) \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {f(x) + 5g(x)} \right\rbrack (b) \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow...
body_xml: Example 1 Use the Limit Laws and the graphs of $$f$$ and $$g$$ in Figure 1 to evaluate the following limits, if they exist. (a) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {f(x) + 5g(x)} \right\rbrack$$ (b) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack$$ (c) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$ Solution (a) From the graphs of $$f$$ and $$g$$ we see that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}f(x) = 1$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}g(x) = - 1$$ Therefore we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {f(x) + 5g(x)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}f(x) + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {5g(x)} \right\rbrack \left( {{by Limit Law}1} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {f(x) + 5g(x)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}f(x) + 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}g(x) \left( {{by Limit Law}3} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\left\lbrack {f(x) + 5g(x)} \right\rbrack} = {1 + 5( - 1) = - 4}} \end{array}$$ (b) We see that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 1}f(x) = 2$$ . But $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 1}g(x)$$ does not exist because the left and right limits are different: $${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}g(x) = - 2} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}g(x) = - 1}$$ So we can’t use Law 4 for the desired limit. But we can use Law 4 for the one-sided limits: $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}f(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}g(x)} = {2 \cdot ( - 2)} = {- 4}} \\ {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}f(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}g(x)} = {2 \cdot ( - 1)} = {- 2}} \end{array}$$ The left and right limits aren’t equal, so $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 1}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack$$ does not exist. (c) The graphs show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}f(x) \approx 1.4$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}g(x) = 0$$ Because the limit of the denominator is $$0$$ , we can’t use Law 5. The given limit does not exist because the denominator approaches $$0$$ while the numerator approaches a nonzero number.

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate the following limits and justify each step.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}{({2x^{2} - 3x + 4})}$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(2x^{2} - 3x + 4)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(2x^{2}) - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(3x) + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}4 {({by Laws}2{and}1)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(2x^{2} - 3x + 4)} = {2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}x^{2} - 3\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}x + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}4 {({by}3)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(2x^{2} - 3x + 4)} = {2(5^{2}) - 3(5) + 4 {({by}10,9,{and}8)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}(2x^{2} - 3x + 4)} = 39} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) We start by using Law 5, but its use is fully justified only at the final stage when we see that the limits of the numerator and denominator exist and the limit of the denominator is not $$0$$ . $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}(x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}(5 - 3x)} \left( {{by Law}5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}x^{3} + 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}x^{2} - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}1}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}5 - 3\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}x} \left( {{by}1,2,{and}3} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {\frac{( - 2)^{3} + 2( - 2)^{2} - 1}{5 - 3( - 2)} \left( {{by}10,9,{and}8} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {- \frac{1}{11}}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Let $$f{(x)} = {({x^{2} - 1})} \slash {({x - 1})}$$ . We can’t find the limit by substituting $$x = 1$$ because $$f(1)$$ isn’t defined. Nor can we apply the Quotient Law, because the limit of the denominator is $$0$$ . Instead, we need to do some preliminary algebra. We factor the numerator as a difference of squares:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1} = \frac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{x - 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The numerator and denominator have a common factor of $$x - 1$$ . When we take the limit as $$x$$ approaches $$1$$ , we have $$x \neq 1$$ and so $$x - 1 \neq 0$$ . Therefore we can cancel the common factor, $$x - 1$$ , and then compute the limit by direct substitution as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{x - 1}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}(x + 1)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}} = {1 + 1 = 2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The limit in this example arose in Example 2.1.1 in finding the tangent to the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the point $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that in Example 3 we do not have an infinite limit even though the denominator approaches $$0$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 1 \right.$$ . When both numerator and denominator approach $$0$$ , the limit may be infinite or it may be some finite value.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {3 + h} \right)^{2} - 9}{h}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If we define</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$F(h) = \frac{\left( {3 + h} \right)^{2} - 9}{h}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>then, as in Example 3, we can’t compute $$\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}F(h)$$ by letting $$h = 0$$ because $$F(0)$$ is undefined. But if we simplify $$F(h)$$ algebraically, we find that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {F(h) = \frac{\left( 9 + 6h + h^{2} \right) - 9}{h} = \frac{6h + h^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{F(h)} = \frac{h(6 + h)}{h} = 6 + h} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(Recall that we consider only $$h \neq 0$$ when letting $$h$$ approach $$0$$ .) Thus</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {3 + h} \right)^{2} - 9}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {6 + h} \right) = 6$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We can’t apply the Quotient Law immediately because the limit of the denominator is $$0$$ . Here the preliminary algebra consists of rationalizing the numerator:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} + 3}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} + 3}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{(t^{2} + 9) - 9}{t^{2}(\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} + 3)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{t^{2}}{t^{2}(\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} + 3)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} + 3}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}(t^{2} + 9)} + 3} {( \text{Here we use several properties of limits:} 5,1,7,8,10.)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}} = {\frac{1}{3 + 3} = \frac{1}{6}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This calculation confirms the guess that we made in Example 2.2.1.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 7 Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}|x| = 0$$ . Solution Recall that $$|x| = \begin{cases} x & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \\ {- x} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$ Since $$|x| = x$$ for $$x > 0$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}|x| = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x = 0$$ For $$x < 0$$ we have $$|x| = - x$$ and so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}|x| = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}( - x) = 0$$ Therefore, by Theorem 1, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}|x| = 0$$ The result of Example 7 looks plausible from Figure 3.

body_xml: Example 8 Prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{|x|}{x}$$ does not exist. Solution Using the facts that $$|x| = x$$ when $$x > 0$$ and $$|x| = - x$$ when $$x < 0$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{|x|}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{x}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}1 = 1} \\ {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{|x|}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{- x}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}( - 1) = - 1} \end{array}$$ Since the right- and left-hand limits are different, it follows from Theorem 1 that $$\left. \lim_{x\rightarrow 0} \middle| x \middle| \slash x \right.$$ does not exist. The graph of the function $$f(x) = |x| \slash x$$ is shown in Figure 4 and supports the one-sided limits that we found.

body_xml: Example 9 If $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{x - 4} & {{if}x > 4} \\ {8 - 2x} & {{if}x < 4} \end{cases}$$ determine whether $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 4}f(x)$$ exists. Solution Since $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}$$ for $$x > 4$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4^{+}}\sqrt{x - 4} = \sqrt{4 - 4} = 0$$ It is shown in Example 2.4.4 that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ . Since $$f(x) = 8 - 2x$$ for $$x < 4$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4^{-}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4^{-}}\left( {8 - 2x} \right) = 8 - 2 \cdot 4 = 0$$ The right- and left-hand limits are equal. Thus the limit exists and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}f(x) = 0$$ The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure 5.

body_xml: Example 10 The greatest integer function is defined by $$〚x〛 = \text{the largest integer}$$ that is less than or equal to $$x$$ . (For instance, $${〚4〛} = 4$$ , $${〚4.8〛} = 4$$ , $${〚\pi 〛} = 3$$ , $${〚\sqrt{2}〛} = 1$$ , $${〚{- \frac{1}{2}}〛} = - 1$$ .) Show that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}{〚x〛}$$ does not exist. Solution The graph of the greatest integer function is shown in Figure 6. Since $${〚x〛} = 3$$ for $$3 \leqslant x < 4$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{〚x〛} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}3 = 3$$ Since $${〚x〛} = 2$$ for $$2 \leqslant x < 3$$ , we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{〚x〛} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}2 = 2$$ Because these one-sided limits are not equal, $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}{〚x〛}$$ does not exist by Theorem 1. Other notations for $$〚x〛$$ are $$\lbrack x\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lfloor x \right\rfloor$$ . The greatest integer function is sometimes called the floor function.

snippet: Example 11: Example 11 Show that \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x} = 0 . Solution First note that we cannot rewrite the limit as the product of the limits \lim_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2} and \lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin(1/x) because...
body_xml: Example 11 Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ . Solution First note that we cannot rewrite the limit as the product of the limits $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2}$$ and $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin(1/x)$$ because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin(1/x)$$ does not exist (see Example 2.2.5). We can find the limit by using the Squeeze Theorem. To apply the Squeeze Theorem we need to find a function $$f$$ smaller than $$g(x) = x^{2}\sin{({1 \slash x})}$$ and a function $$h$$ bigger than $$g$$ such that both $$f(x)$$ and $$h(x)$$ approach $$0$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . To do this we use our knowledge of the sine function. Because the sine of any number lies between $$- 1$$ and $$1$$ , we can write $$- 1 \leqslant \sin\frac{1}{x} \leqslant 1$$ Any inequality remains true when multiplied by a positive number. We know that $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ and so, multiplying each side of the inequalities in (4) by $$x^{2}$$ , we get $$- x^{2} \leqslant x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x} \leqslant x^{2}$$ as illustrated by Figure 8. We know that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2} = 0$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}{({- x^{2}})} = 0$$ Taking $$f(x) = - x^{2}$$ , $$g(x) = x^{2}\sin\left( {1 \slash x} \right)$$ , and $$h(x) = x^{2}$$ in the Squeeze Theorem, we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x} = 0$$

snippet: Precise Definition of a Limit: Precise Definition of a Limit Let f be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number a , except possibly at a itself. Then we say that the limit of \mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right) as...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Precise Definition of a Limit" title="Precise Definition of a Limit">
    <heading level="4">Precise Definition of a Limit</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number $$a$$ , except possibly at $$a$$ itself. Then we say that the limit of $$\mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)$$ as $$\mathbf{x}$$ approaches $$\mathbf{a}$$ is $$\mathbf{L}$$ , and we write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every number $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there is a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - a \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| f(x) - L \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Since f(x) = x^{3} - 5x + 6 is a polynomial, we know from the Direct Substitution Property that \lim_{x\rightarrow 1}f(x) = f(1) = 1^{3} - 5(1) + 6 = 2 . Use a graph to find a number \delta such that if x is within...
body_xml: Example 1 Since $$f(x) = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ is a polynomial, we know from the Direct Substitution Property that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 1}f(x) = f(1) = 1^{3} - 5(1) + 6 = 2$$ . Use a graph to find a number $$\delta$$ such that if $$x$$ is within $$\delta$$ of $$1$$ , then $$y$$ is within $$0.2$$ of $$2$$ , that is, $$\left. {if} \middle| x - 1 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| {({x^{3} - 5x + 6})} - 2 \middle| < 0.2 \right.$$ In other words, find a number $$\delta$$ that corresponds to $$\varepsilon = 0.2$$ in the definition of a limit for the function $$f(x) = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ with $$a = 1$$ and $$L = 2$$ . Solution A graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure 7; we are interested in the region near the point $$(1,2)$$ . Notice that we can rewrite the inequality $$\left| {({x^{3} - 5x + 6})} - 2 \middle| < 0.2 \right.$$ as $$- 0.2 < {({x^{3} - 5x + 6})} - 2 < 0.2$$ or equivalently $$1.8 < x^{3} - 5x + 6 < 2.2$$ So we need to determine the values of $$x$$ for which the curve $$y = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ lies between the horizontal lines $$y = 1.8$$ and $$y = 2.2$$ . Therefore we graph the curves $$y = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ , $$y = 1.8$$ , and $$y = 2.2$$ near the point $$(1,2)$$ in Figure 8. We estimate that the $$x$$ -coordinate of the point of intersection of the line $$y = 2.2$$ and the curve $$y = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ is about $$0.911$$ . Similarly, $$y = x^{3} - 5x + 6$$ intersects the line $$y = 1.8$$ when $$x \approx 1.124$$ . So, rounding toward $$1$$ to be safe, we can say that $${{if} 0.92 < x < 1.12} {then} {1.8 < x^{3} - 5x + 6 < 2.2}$$ This interval $$(0.92,1.12)$$ is not symmetric about $$x = 1$$ . The distance from $$x = 1$$ to the left endpoint is $$1 - 0.92 = 0.08$$ and the distance to the right endpoint is $$0.12$$ . We can choose $$\delta$$ to be the smaller of these numbers, that is, $$\delta = 0.08$$ . Then we can rewrite our inequalities in terms of distances as follows: $$\left. {if} \middle| x - 1 \middle| < 0.08 \right. {then} \left| {({x^{3} - 5x + 6})} - 2 \middle| < 0.2 \right.$$ This just says that by keeping $$x$$ within $$0.08$$ of $$1$$ , we are able to keep $$f(x)$$ within $$0.2$$ of $$2$$ . Although we chose $$\delta = 0.08$$ , any smaller positive value of $$\delta$$ would also have worked.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Prove that \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\left( {4x - 5} \right) = 7 . Solution Preliminary analysis of the problem (guessing a value for \delta ). Let \varepsilon be a given positive number. We want to find a number...
body_xml: Example 2 Prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\left( {4x - 5} \right) = 7$$ . Solution Preliminary analysis of the problem (guessing a value for $$\delta$$ ). Let $$\varepsilon$$ be a given positive number. We want to find a number $$\delta$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| \left( {4x - 5} \right) - 7 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ But $$\left| (4x - 5) - 7 \middle| = \middle| 4x - 12 \middle| = \middle| 4(x - 3) \middle| = 4 \middle| x - 3 \right|$$ . Therefore we want $$\delta$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left. 4 \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ that is, $${{if} 0 < |x - 3| < \delta} {then} {|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{4}}$$ This suggests that we should choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash 4$$ . Proof (showing that this $$\delta$$ works). Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash 4$$ . If $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right.$$ , then $$|(4x - 5) - 7| = |4x - 12| = 4|x - 3| < 4\delta = 4\left( \frac{\varepsilon}{4} \right) = \varepsilon$$ Thus $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| \left( {4x - 5} \right) - 7 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ Therefore, by the definition of a limit, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\left( {4x - 5} \right) = 7$$ This example is illustrated by Figure 9.
