snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Prove that \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{2} = 9 . Solution Guessing a value for \delta . Let \varepsilon > 0 be given. We have to find a number \delta > 0 such that \left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{2} = 9$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Guessing a value for $$\delta$$ . Let $$\varepsilon > 0$$ be given. We have to find a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| x^{2} - 9 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ To connect $$\left| x^{2} - 9 \right|$$ with $$|x - 3|$$ we write $$\left| x^{2} - 9 \middle| = \middle| \left( {x + 3} \right)\left( {x - 3} \right) \right|$$ . Then we want $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| x + 3 \middle| \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ Notice that if we can find a positive constant $$C$$ such that $$\left| x + 3 \middle| < C \right.$$ , then $$\left| x + 3 \middle| \middle| x - 3 \middle| < C \middle| x - 3 \right|$$ and we can make $$\left. C \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ by taking $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \slash C \right.$$ , so we could choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash C$$ . We can find such a number $$C$$ if we restrict $$x$$ to lie in some interval centered at $$3$$ . In fact, since we are interested only in values of $$x$$ that are close to $$3$$ , it is reasonable to assume that $$x$$ is within a distance $$1$$ from $$3$$ , that is, $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1 \right.$$ . Then $$2 < x < 4$$ , so $$5 < x + 3 < 7$$ . Thus we have $$\left| x + 3 \middle| < 7 \right.$$ , and so $$C = 7$$ is a suitable choice for the constant. But now there are two restrictions on $$|x - 3|$$ , namely $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1 \right.$$ and $$|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{C} = \frac{\varepsilon}{7}$$ To make sure that both of these inequalities are satisfied, we take $$\delta$$ to be the smaller of the two numbers $$1$$ and $$\varepsilon \slash 7$$ . The notation for this is $$\delta = \min\left\{ {1,\varepsilon \slash 7} \right\}$$ .</item>
      <item>Showing that this $$\delta$$ works. Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , let $$\delta = \min\left\{ {1,\varepsilon \slash 7} \right\}$$ . If $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right.$$ , then $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1\Rightarrow 2 < x < 4\Rightarrow \middle| x + 3 \middle| < 7 \right.$$ (as in part 1). We also have $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \slash 7 \right.$$ , so $$|x^{2} - 9| = |x + 3||x - 3| < 7 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{7} = \varepsilon$$ This shows that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{2} = 9$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Definition 4 to prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Guessing a value for $$\delta$$ . Let $$\varepsilon$$ be a given positive number. Here $$a = 0$$ and $$L = 0$$ , so we want to find a number $$\delta$$ such that $${{if} 0 < x < \delta} {then} \left| \sqrt{x} - 0 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ that is, $${{if} 0 < x < \delta} {then} {\sqrt{x} < \varepsilon}$$ or, squaring both sides of the inequality $$\sqrt{x} < \varepsilon$$ , we get $${{if} 0 < x < \delta} {then} {x < \varepsilon^{2}}$$ This suggests that we should choose $$\delta = \varepsilon^{2}$$ .</item>
      <item>Showing that this $$\delta$$ works. Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , let $$\delta = \varepsilon^{2}$$ . If $$0 < x < \delta$$ , then $$\sqrt{x} < \sqrt{\delta} = \sqrt{\varepsilon^{2}} = \varepsilon$$ so $$\left| \sqrt{x} - 0 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ According to Definition 4, this shows that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">Precise Definition of an Infinite Limit</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number $$a$$ , except possibly at $$a$$ itself. Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>means that for every positive number $$M$$ there is a positive number $$\delta$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - a \middle| < \delta \right. {then} {f(x) > M}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Definition 6 to prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}} = \infty$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Let $$M$$ be a given positive number. We want to find a number $$\delta$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x \middle| < \delta \right. {then} {1 \slash x^{2} > M}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>But</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. {\frac{1}{x^{2}} > M} \Leftrightarrow {x^{2} < \frac{1}{M}} \Leftrightarrow {\sqrt{x^{2}} < \sqrt{\frac{1}{M}}} \Leftrightarrow {|x| < \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}} \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So if we choose $$\delta = 1 \slash \sqrt{M}$$ and $$\left. 0 < \middle| x \middle| < \delta = 1 \slash \sqrt{M} \right.$$ , then $$1 \slash x^{2} > M$$ . This shows that $$\left. 1 \slash x^{2}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Figure 2 shows the graph of a function f . At which numbers is f discontinuous? Why? Solution It looks as if there is a discontinuity when a = 1 because the graph has a break there. The official reason that f is...
body_xml: Example 1 Figure 2 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ . At which numbers is $$f$$ discontinuous? Why? Solution It looks as if there is a discontinuity when $$a = 1$$ because the graph has a break there. The official reason that $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$1$$ is that $$f(1)$$ is not defined. The graph also has a break when $$a = 3$$ , but the reason for the discontinuity is different. Here, $$f(3)$$ is defined, but $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}f(x)$$ does not exist (because the left and right limits are different). So $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$3$$ . What about $$a = 5$$ ? Here, $$f(5)$$ is defined and $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 5}f(x)$$ exists (because the left and right limits are the same). But $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 5}f(x) \neq f(5)$$ So $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$5$$ .

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Where are each of the following functions discontinuous? (a) f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{x - 2} (b) f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{x - 2} & {{if}{x \neq 2}} \\ 1 & {{if}{x = 2}} \end{cases} (c) f(x) =...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Where are each of the following functions discontinuous?</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{x - 2}$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{x - 2} & {{if}{x \neq 2}} \\ 1 & {{if}{x = 2}} \end{cases}$$</item>
      <item>(c) $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x^{2}} & {{if}{x \neq 0}} \\ 1 & {{if}{x = 0}} \end{cases}$$</item>
      <item>(d) $$f(x) = {〚x〛}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Notice that $$f(2)$$ is not defined, so $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$2$$ . Later we’ll see why $$f$$ is continuous at all other numbers.</item>
      <item>(b) Here $$f(2) = 1$$ is defined and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{x^{2} - x - 2}{x - 2} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}{x - 2} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {x + 1} \right) = 3$$ exists. But $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}f(x) \neq f(2)$$ so $$f$$ is not continuous at $$2$$ .</item>
      <item>(c) Here $$f(0) = 1$$ is defined but $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ does not exist. (See Example 2.2.6.) So $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$0$$ .</item>
      <item>(d) The greatest integer function $$f(x) = 〚x〛$$ has discontinuities at all of the integers because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow n}{〚x〛}$$ does not exist if $$n$$ is an integer. (See Example 2.3.10 and Exercise 2.3.55.)</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Show that the function f(x) = 1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{2}} is continuous on the interval \left\lbrack {- 1,1} \right\rbrack . Solution If - 1 < a < 1 , then using the Limit Laws from Section 2.3, we have \begin{array}{l}...
body_xml: Example 4 Show that the function $$f(x) = 1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ is continuous on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,1} \right\rbrack$$ . Solution If $$- 1 < a < 1$$ , then using the Limit Laws from Section 2.3, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left( {1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {1 - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \left( {{by Laws}2{and}8} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {1 - \sqrt{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)} \left( {{by}7} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {1 - \sqrt{1 - a^{2}}} \left( {{by}2,8,{and}10} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {f(a)}} \end{array}$$ Thus, by Definition 1, $$f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ if $$- 1 < a < 1$$ . Similar calculations show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1^{+}}f(x) = 1 = f\left( {- 1} \right)$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}f(x) = 1 = f(1)$$ so $$f$$ is continuous from the right at $$- 1$$ and continuous from the left at $$1$$ . Therefore, according to Definition 3, $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {- 1,1} \right\rbrack$$ . The graph of $$f$$ is sketched in Figure 4. It is the lower half of the circle $$x^{2} + \left( {y - 1} \right)^{2} = 1$$

title: Theorem
snippet: Theorem: Theorem If f and g are continuous at a and c is a constant, then the following functions are also continuous at a : f + g f - g cf fg \frac{f}{g} {{if}g(a) \neq 0}
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem" title="Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous at $$a$$ and $$c$$ is a constant, then the following functions are also continuous at $$a$$ :</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f + g$$</item>
      <item>$$f - g$$</item>
      <item>$$cf$$</item>
      <item>$$fg$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{f}{g} {{if}g(a) \neq 0}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Theorem: Theorem (a) Any polynomial is continuous everywhere; that is, it is continuous on {\mathbb{R}} = ( - \infty,\infty) . (a) Any rational function is continuous wherever it is defined; that is, it is continuous on its domain.

<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is rational, so by Theorem 5 it is continuous on its domain, which is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq \frac{5}{3} \right\}$$ . Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}f{(x)} = f{({- 2})}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 2}\frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 1}{5 - 3x}} = {\frac{\left( {- 2} \right)^{3} + 2\left( {- 2} \right)^{2} - 1}{5 - 3\left( {- 2} \right)} = - \frac{1}{11}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Where is the function f(x) = \frac{\ln x + \tan^{- 1}x}{x^{2} - 1} continuous? Solution We know from Theorem 7 that the function y = \ln x is continuous for x > 0 and y = \tan^{- 1}x is continuous on \mathbb{R} . Thus,...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Where is the function $$f(x) = \frac{\ln x + \tan^{- 1}x}{x^{2} - 1}$$ continuous?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We know from Theorem 7 that the function $$y = \ln x$$ is continuous for $$x > 0$$ and $$y = \tan^{- 1}x$$ is continuous on $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Thus, by part 1 of Theorem 4, $$y = \ln x + \tan^{- 1}x$$ is continuous on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . The denominator, $$y = x^{2} - 1$$ , is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere. Therefore, by part 5 of Theorem 4, $$f$$ is continuous at all positive numbers $$x$$ except where $$\left. x^{2} - 1 = 0\Leftrightarrow x = \pm 1 \right.$$ . So $$f$$ is continuous on the intervals $$(0,1)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Evaluate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi}\frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x} . Solution Theorem 7 tells us that y = \sin x is continuous. The function in the denominator, y = 2 + \cos x , is the sum of two continuous functions and...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi}\frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Theorem 7 tells us that $$y = \sin x$$ is continuous. The function in the denominator, $$y = 2 + \cos x$$ , is the sum of two continuous functions and is therefore continuous. Notice that this function is never $$0$$ because $$\cos x \geq - 1$$ for all $$x$$ and so $$2 + \cos x > 0$$ everywhere. Thus the ratio</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is continuous everywhere. Hence, by the definition of a continuous function,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi}\frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi}f(x) = f(\pi) = \frac{\sin\pi}{2 + \cos\pi} = \frac{0}{2 - 1} = 0$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Where are the following functions continuous? (a) h{(x)} = \sin{(x^{2})} (b) F(x) = \ln\left( {1 + \cos x} \right) Solution (a) We have h(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) , where g(x) = x^{2} and f(x) = \sin x We know that...
body_xml:
<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Where are the following functions continuous?</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$h{(x)} = \sin{(x^{2})}$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$F(x) = \ln\left( {1 + \cos x} \right)$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) We have $$h(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ , where $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$f(x) = \sin x$$ We know that $$g$$ is continuous on $$\mathbb{R}$$ since it is a polynomial, and $$f$$ is also continuous everywhere. Thus $$h = f \circ g$$ is continuous on $$\mathbb{R}$$ by Theorem 9.</item>
      <item>(b) We know from Theorem 7 that $$f(x) = \ln x$$ is continuous and $$g(x) = 1 + \cos x$$ is continuous (because both $$y = 1$$ and $$y = \cos x$$ are continuous). Therefore, by Theorem 9, $$F(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ is continuous wherever it is defined. The expression $$\ln\left( {1 + \cos x} \right)$$ is defined when $$1 + \cos x > 0$$ , so it is undefined when $$\cos x = - 1$$ , and this happens when $$x = \pm \pi, \pm 3\pi,\ldots$$ . Thus $$F$$ has discontinuities when $$x$$ is an odd multiple of $$\pi$$ and is continuous on the intervals between these values (see Figure 7). Figure 7 Details A function is graphed on the graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 10 to 10 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from negative 6 to 2 in increments of 2 units. The parts of the curve resemble an inverted U-shape. The first part enters the third quadrant from the bottom to the right of x = negative 10, goes up and to the right, crosses the negative x axis at (negative 5 pi/2, 0), reaches its high point at approximately (negative 2 pi, 0.7), then goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at (negative 3 pi/2, 0), and exits the fourth quadrant to the left of x = negative 3. The second part follows exactly the same movement, located between x = negative 3 and x = 3, goes up and to the right by crossing the negative x axis at (negative pi/2, 0), reaches its high point at approximately (0, 0.7), again goes down and to the right by crossing the positive x axis at (pi/2, 0). The third part is located between x = 3 and x = 10, and reaches a high point at approximately (2 pi, 0.7). $$y = \ln\left( 1 + \cos x \right)$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that there is a solution of the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$4x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 3x - 2 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>between $$1$$ and $$2$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Let $$f(x) = 4x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 3x - 2$$ . We are looking for a solution of the given equation, that is, a number $$c$$ between $$1$$ and $$2$$ such that $$f(c) = 0$$ . Therefore we take $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , and $$N = 0$$ in Theorem 10. We have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(1) = 4 - 6 + 3 - 2 = - 1 < 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(2) = 32 - 24 + 6 - 2 = 12 > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$f(1) < 0 < f(2)$$ ; that is, $$N = 0$$ is a number between $$f(1)$$ and $$f(2)$$ . The function $$f$$ is continuous since it is a polynomial, so the Intermediate Value Theorem says there is a number $$c$$ between $$1$$ and $$2$$ such that $$f(c) = 0$$ . In other words, the equation $$4x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 3x - 2 = 0$$ has at least one solution $$c$$ in the interval $$(1,2)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In fact, we can locate a solution more precisely by using the Intermediate Value Theorem again. Since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(1.2) = - 0.128 < 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(1.3) = 0.548 > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>a solution must lie between $$1.2$$ and $$1.3$$ . A calculator gives, by trial and error,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(1.22) = - 0.007008 < 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(1.23) = 0.056068 > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so a solution lies in the interval $$(1.22,1.23)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the infinite limits, limits at infinity, and asymptotes for the function f whose graph is shown in Figure 5. Solution We see that the values of f(x) become large as \left. x\rightarrow - 1 \right. from both sides,...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the infinite limits, limits at infinity, and asymptotes for the function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 5. Solution We see that the values of $$f(x)$$ become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow - 1 \right.$$ from both sides, so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1}f(x) = \infty$$ Notice that $$f(x)$$ becomes large negative as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the left, but large positive as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ from the right. So $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}f(x) = - \infty$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}f(x) = \infty$$ Thus both of the lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ are vertical asymptotes. As $$x$$ becomes large, it appears that $$f(x)$$ approaches $$4$$ . But as $$x$$ decreases through negative values, $$f(x)$$ approaches $$2$$ . So $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = 4$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = 2$$ This means that both $$y = 4$$ and $$y = 2$$ are horizontal asymptotes.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} and \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x} . Solution Observe that when x is large, 1 \slash x is small. For instance, {\frac{1}{100} = 0.01} {\frac{1}{10,000} =...
body_xml: Example 2 Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x}$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x}$$ . Solution Observe that when $$x$$ is large, $$1 \slash x$$ is small. For instance, $${\frac{1}{100} = 0.01} {\frac{1}{10,000} = 0.0001} {\frac{1}{1,000,000} = 0.000001}$$ In fact, by taking $$x$$ large enough, we can make $$1 \slash x$$ as close to $$0$$ as we please. Therefore, according to Definition 1, we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ Similar reasoning shows that when $$x$$ is large negative, $$1 \slash x$$ is small negative, so we also have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ It follows that the line $$y = 0$$ (the $$x$$ -axis) is a horizontal asymptote of the curve $$y = 1 \slash x$$ . (This is a hyperbola; see Figure 6.)

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate the following limit and indicate which properties of limits are used at each stage. \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1} Solution As x becomes large, both numerator and...
body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate the following limit and indicate which properties of limits are used at each stage. $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}$$ Solution As $$x$$ becomes large, both numerator and denominator become large, so it isn’t obvious what happens to their ratio. We need to do some preliminary algebra. To evaluate the limit at infinity of any rational function, we first divide both the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ that occurs in the denominator. (We may assume that $$x \neq 0$$ , since we are interested only in large values of $$x$$ .) In this case the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator is $$x^{2}$$ , so we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{x^{2}}}{\frac{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}{x^{2}}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3 - \frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{x^{2}}}{5 + \frac{4}{x} + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {3 - \frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{x^{2}}} \right)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {5 + \frac{4}{x} + \frac{1}{x^{2}}} \right)} \left( {{by Limit Law}5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}3 - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} - 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}5 + 4\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}} \left( {{by}1,2,{and}3} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = {\frac{3 - 0 - 0}{5 + 0 + 0} \left( {{by}8{and Theorem}5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1}} = \frac{3}{5}} \end{array}$$ A similar calculation shows that the limit as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ is also $$\frac{3}{5}$$ . Figure 7 illustrates the results of these calculations by showing how the graph of the given rational function approaches the horizontal asymptote $$y = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the horizontal asymptotes of the graph of the function f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5} Solution Dividing both numerator and denominator by x (which is the highest power of x in the denominator) and using...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the horizontal asymptotes of the graph of the function $$f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5}$$ Solution Dividing both numerator and denominator by $$x$$ (which is the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator) and using the properties of limits, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{x}}{\frac{3x - 5}{x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x^{2}}}}{\frac{3x - 5}{x}} {({since}\sqrt{x^{2}} = x{for}x > 0)}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5}} = {\frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {3 - \frac{5}{x}} \right)} = \frac{\sqrt{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}2 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}3 - 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x}} = \frac{\sqrt{2 + 0}}{3 - 5 \cdot 0} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore the line $$y = \sqrt{2} \slash 3$$ is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ . In computing the limit as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , we must remember that for $$x < 0$$ , we have $$\sqrt{x^{2}} = |x| = - x$$ . So when we divide the numerator by $$x$$ , for $$x < 0$$ we get $$\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{- \sqrt{x^{2}}} = - \sqrt{\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x^{2}}} = - \sqrt{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}$$ Therefore $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 1}}{3x - 5} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{- \sqrt{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{3 - \frac{5}{x}} = \frac{- \sqrt{2 + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}}{3 - 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{x}} = - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$$ Thus the line $$y = - \sqrt{2} \slash 3$$ is also a horizontal asymptote. See Figure 8.

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Compute \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})} . Solution Because both \sqrt{x^{2} + 1} and x are large when x is large, it’s difficult to see what happens to their difference, so we use algebra to...
body_xml: Example 5 Compute $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}$$ . Solution Because both $$\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ and $$x$$ are large when $$x$$ is large, it’s difficult to see what happens to their difference, so we use algebra to rewrite the function. We first multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate radical: $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}{({\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x})}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(x^{2} + 1) - x^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}}} \end{array}$$ We can think of the given function as having a denominator of $$1$$ . Notice that the denominator of this last expression $$(\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x)$$ becomes large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (it’s bigger than $$x$$ ). So $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}(\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} - x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x} = 0$$ Figure 9 illustrates this result.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Evaluate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\arctan\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right) . Solution If we let t = 1 \slash \left( {x - 2} \right) , we know that \left. t\rightarrow\infty \right. as \left. x\rightarrow 2^{+}...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\arctan\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If we let $$t = 1 \slash \left( {x - 2} \right)$$ , we know that $$\left. t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 2^{+} \right.$$ . Therefore, by the second equation in (4), we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\arctan\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\arctan t = \frac{\pi}{2}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Evaluate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}e^{1 \slash x} . The problem-solving strategy for Examples 6 and 7 is introducing something extra (see Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1). Here, the something...

    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>

    <paragraph>The problem-solving strategy for Examples 6 and 7 is introducing something extra (see Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1). Here, the something extra, the auxiliary aid, is the new variable $$t$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If we let $$t = 1 \slash x$$ , we know that $$\left. t\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ . Therefore, by (6),</paragraph>

    <paragraph>(See Exercise 81.)</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Evaluate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sin x . Solution As x increases, the values of \sin x oscillate between 1 and - 1 infinitely often and so they don’t approach any definite number. Thus...
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sin x$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution As $$x$$ increases, the values of $$\sin x$$ oscillate between $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ infinitely often and so they don’t approach any definite number. Thus $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sin x$$ does not exist.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{3} and \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}x^{3} . Solution When x becomes large, x^{3} also becomes large. For instance, {10^{3} = 1000} {100^{3} = 1,000,000} {1000^{3} =...
body_xml: Example 9 Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{3}$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}x^{3}$$ . Solution When $$x$$ becomes large, $$x^{3}$$ also becomes large. For instance, $${10^{3} = 1000} {100^{3} = 1,000,000} {1000^{3} = 1,000,000,000}$$ In fact, we can make $$x^{3}$$ as big as we like by requiring $$x$$ to be large enough. Therefore we can write $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{3} = \infty$$ Similarly, when $$x$$ is large negative, so is $$x^{3}$$ . Thus $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}x^{3} = - \infty$$ These limit statements can also be seen from the graph of $$y = x^{3}$$ in Figure 11.

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {x^{2} - x} \right) . Solution Limit Law 2 says that the limit of a difference is the difference of the limits, provided that these limits exist. We cannot use Law 2 here...
body_xml:
<example number="10">
    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {x^{2} - x} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Limit Law 2 says that the limit of a difference is the difference of the limits, provided that these limits exist. We cannot use Law 2 here because</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{2} = \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x = \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In general, the Limit Laws can’t be applied to infinite limits because $$\infty$$ is not a number ( $$\infty - \infty$$ can’t be defined). However, we can write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}(x^{2} - x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x(x - 1) = \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>because both $$x$$ and $$x - 1$$ become arbitrarily large and so their product does too.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 11
snippet: Example 11: Example 11 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} + x}{3 - x} . Solution As in Example 3, we divide the numerator and denominator by the highest power of x in the denominator, which is simply x :...
body_xml:
<example number="11">
    <heading level="4">Example 11</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} + x}{3 - x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution As in Example 3, we divide the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ in the denominator, which is simply $$x$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} + x}{3 - x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x + 1}{\frac{3}{x} - 1} = - \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>because $$\left. x + 1\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. 3 \slash x - 1\rightarrow 0 - 1 = - 1 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 12
snippet: Example 12: Example 12 Sketch the graph of y = \left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) by finding its intercepts and its limits as \left. x\rightarrow\infty \right. and as \left. x\rightarrow - \infty...
body_xml: Example 12 Sketch the graph of $$y = \left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ by finding its intercepts and its limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and as $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ . Solution The $$y$$ -intercept is $$f(0) = ( - 2)^{4}(1)^{3}( - 1) = - 16$$ and the $$x$$ -intercepts are found by setting $$y = 0$$ : $$x = 2, - 1,1$$ . Notice that since $$\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}$$ is never negative, the function doesn’t change sign at $$2$$ ; thus the graph doesn’t cross the $$x$$ -axis at $$2$$ . The graph crosses the axis at $$- 1$$ and $$1$$ . When $$x$$ is large positive, all three factors are large, so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) = \infty$$ When $$x$$ is large negative, the first factor is large positive and the second and third factors are both large negative, so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {x - 2} \right)^{4}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) = \infty$$ Combining this information, we give a rough sketch of the graph in Figure 13.

snippet: Example 13: Example 13 Use a graph to find a number N such that {{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1} - 0.6} \right| < 0.1} Solution We rewrite the given inequality as 0.5 < \frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x +...
body_xml: Example 13 Use a graph to find a number $$N$$ such that $${{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1} - 0.6} \right| < 0.1}$$ Solution We rewrite the given inequality as $$0.5 < \frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1} < 0.7$$ We need to determine the values of $$x$$ for which the given curve lies between the horizontal lines $$y = 0.5$$ and $$y = 0.7$$ . So we graph the curve and these lines in Figure 17. Then we use the graph to estimate that the curve crosses the line $$y = 0.5$$ when $$x \approx 6.7$$ . To the right of this number it seems that the curve stays between the lines $$y = 0.5$$ and $$y = 0.7$$ . Rounding up to be safe, we can say that $${{if} x > 7} {then} {\left| {\frac{3x^{2} - x - 2}{5x^{2} + 4x + 1} - 0.6} \right| < 0.1}$$ In other words, for $$\varepsilon = 0.1$$ we can choose $$N = 7$$ (or any larger number) in Definition 7.

title: Example 14
snippet: Example 14: Example 14 Use Definition 7 to prove that \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0 . Solution Given \varepsilon > 0 , we want to find N such that {{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {\frac{1}{x} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon} In...
body_xml: Example 14 Use Definition 7 to prove that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ . Solution Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , we want to find $$N$$ such that $${{if} x > N} {then} {\left| {\frac{1}{x} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon}$$ In computing the limit we may assume that $$x > 0$$ . Then $$\left. 1 \slash x < \varepsilon\Leftrightarrow x > 1 \slash \varepsilon \right.$$ . Let’s choose $$N = 1 \slash \varepsilon$$ . So $${{if} x > N = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}} {then} {\left| {\frac{1}{x} - 0} \right| = \frac{1}{x} < \varepsilon}$$ Therefore, by Definition 7, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$$ Figure 18 illustrates the proof by showing some values of $$\varepsilon$$ and the corresponding values of $$N$$ .

    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some interval $$(a,\infty)$$ . Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>means that for every positive number $$M$$ there is a corresponding positive number $$N$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${{if} x > N} {then} {f(x) > M}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the point $$P\left( {1,1} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Here we have $$a = 1$$ and $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , so the slope is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{f(x) - f(1)}{x - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}{x - 1}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\left( {x + 1} \right) = 1 + 1 = 2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using the point-slope form of the equation of a line, we find that an equation of the tangent line at $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y - 1 = 2(x - 1)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = 2x - 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Point-slope form for a line through the point $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ with slope $$m$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y - y_{1} = m\left( x - x_{1} \right)$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find an equation of the tangent line to the hyperbola y = 3 \slash x at the point \left( {3,1} \right) . Solution Let f(x) = 3 \slash x . Then, by Equation 2, the slope of the tangent at \left( {3,1} \right) is...
body_xml: Example 2 Find an equation of the tangent line to the hyperbola $$y = 3 \slash x$$ at the point $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ . Solution Let $$f(x) = 3 \slash x$$ . Then, by Equation 2, the slope of the tangent at $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({3 + h})} - f{(3)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{3}{3 + h} - 1}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{3 - {({3 + h})}}{3 + h}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- h}{h{({3 + h})}} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0} - \frac{1}{3 + h} = - \frac{1}{3}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore an equation of the tangent at the point $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ is $$y - 1 = - \frac{1}{3}\left( {x - 3} \right)$$ which simplifies to $$x + 3y - 6 = 0$$ The hyperbola and its tangent are shown in Figure 4.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Suppose that a ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower, 450 m above the ground. (a) What is the velocity of the ball after 5 seconds? (b) How fast is the ball traveling when it hits the ground?...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that a ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower, $$450$$ m above the ground.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) What is the velocity of the ball after $$5$$ seconds?</item>
      <item>(b) How fast is the ball traveling when it hits the ground?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution Since two different velocities are requested, it’s efficient to start by finding the velocity at a general time $$t = a$$ . Using the equation of motion $$s = f(t) = 4.9t^{2}$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({a + h})} - f{(a)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({a + h})}^{2} - 4.9a^{2}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} - a^{2}})}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({2ah + h^{2}})}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9h{({2a + h})}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}4.9{({2a + h})} = 9.8a}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The velocity after $$5$$ seconds is $$\upsilon(5) = (9.8)(5) = 49m \slash s$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Since the observation deck is $$450$$ m above the ground, the ball will hit the ground at the time $$t$$ when $$s(t) = 450$$ , that is, $$4.9t^{2} = 450$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>This gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t^{2} = \frac{450}{4.9}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t = \sqrt{\frac{450}{4.9}} \approx 9.6s$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The velocity of the ball as it hits the ground is therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\upsilon\left( \sqrt{\frac{450}{4.9}} \right) = 9.8\sqrt{\frac{450}{4.9}} \approx 94m \slash s$$</paragraph>
  </example>

    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(a) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$</paragraph>

body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Definition 4 to find the derivative of the function $$f(x) = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the number (a) $$2$$ and (b) $$a$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) From Definition 4 we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({2 + h})} - f{(2)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{{({2 + h})}^{2} - 8{({2 + h})} + 9} - ( - 3)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4 + 4h + h^{2} - 16 - 8h + 9 + 3}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h^{2} - 4h}{h} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h(h - 4)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{(h - 4) = - 4}}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({a + h})} - f{(a)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{{({a + h})}^{2} - 8{({a + h})} + 9}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{a^{2} - 8a + 9}\rbrack}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} - 8a - 8h + 9 - a^{2} + 8a - 9}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{2ah + h^{2} - 8h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({2a + h - 8}) = {2a - 8}}}} \end{array}$$ As a check on our work in part (a), notice that if we let $$a = 2$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(2) = 2(2) - 8 = - 4$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Definitions 4 and 5 are equivalent, so we can use either one to compute the derivative. In practice, Definition 4 often leads to simpler computations.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Equation 5 to find the derivative of the function $$f(x) = 1/\sqrt{x}$$ at the number $$a(a > 0)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution From Equation 5 we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f{(x)} - f{(a)}}{x - a}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}}{x - a} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}}{x - a} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{a}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{- (x - a)}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x} \right)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{- 1}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \frac{- 1}{\sqrt{a^{2}}\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{a} \right)} = \frac{- 1}{a \cdot 2\sqrt{a}} = - \frac{1}{2a^{3/2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>You can verify that using Definition 4 gives the same result.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola y = x^{2} - 8x + 9 at the point \left( {3, - 6} \right) . Solution From Example 4(b) we know that the derivative of f(x) = x^{2} - 8x + 9 at the number a is...
body_xml: Example 6 Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola $$y = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the point $$\left( {3, - 6} \right)$$ . Solution From Example 4(b) we know that the derivative of $$f(x) = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the number $$a$$ is $$f^{\prime}(a) = 2a - 8$$ . Therefore the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {3, - 6} \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(3) = 2(3) - 8 = - 2$$ . Thus an equation of the tangent line, shown in Figure 7, is $$y - \left( {- 6} \right) = \left( {- 2} \right)\left( {x - 3} \right)$$ or $$y = - 2x$$

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 A manufacturer produces bolts of a fabric with a fixed width. The cost of producing x yards of this fabric is C = f(x) dollars. (a) What is the meaning of the derivative f^{\prime}(x) ? What are its units? (b) In...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>A manufacturer produces bolts of a fabric with a fixed width. The cost of producing $$x$$ yards of this fabric is $$C = f(x)$$ dollars.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) What is the meaning of the derivative $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ ? What are its units?</item>
      <item>(b) In practical terms, what does it mean to say that $$f^{\prime}(1000) = 9$$ ?</item>
      <item>(c) Which do you think is greater, $$f^{\prime}(50)$$ or $$f^{\prime}(500)$$ ? What about $$f^{\prime}(5000)$$ ?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The derivative $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of $$C$$ with respect to $$x$$ ; that is, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ means the rate of change of the production cost with respect to the number of yards produced. (Economists call this rate of change the marginal cost. This idea is discussed in more detail in Sections 3.7 and 4.7.) Because $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x}$$ the units for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ are the same as the units for the difference quotient $$\Delta C \slash \Delta x$$ . Since $$\Delta C$$ is measured in dollars and $$\Delta x$$ in yards, it follows that the units for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ are dollars per yard.</item>
      <item>(b) The statement that $$f^{\prime}(1000) = 9$$ means that, after $$1000$$ yards of fabric have been manufactured, the rate at which the production cost is increasing is $$\$ 9 \slash {yard}$$ . (When $$x = 1000$$ , $$C$$ is increasing $$9$$ times as fast as $$x$$ .) Since $$\Delta x = 1$$ is small compared with $$x = 1000$$ , we could use the approximation $$f^{\prime}(1000) \approx \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta C}{1} = \Delta C$$ and say that the cost of manufacturing the $$1000$$ th yard (or the $$1001$$ st) is about $$\$ 9$$ . Here we are assuming that the cost function is well behaved; in other words, $$C(x)$$ doesn’t oscillate rapidly near $$x = 1000$$ .</item>
      <item>(c) The rate at which the production cost is increasing (per yard) is probably lower when $$x = 500$$ than when $$x = 50$$ (the cost of making the $$500$$ th yard is less than the cost of the $$50$$ th yard) because of economies of scale. (The manufacturer makes more efficient use of the fixed costs of production.) So $$f^{\prime}(50) > f^{\prime}(500)$$ But, as production expands, the resulting large-scale operation might become inefficient and there might be overtime costs. Thus it is possible that the rate of increase of costs will eventually start to rise. So it may happen that $$f^{\prime}(5000) > f^{\prime}(500)$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Let D(t) be the US national debt at time t . The table below gives approximate values of this function by providing end of year estimates, in billions of dollars, from 2000 to 2016. Interpret and estimate the value of...
body_xml:
Example 8 Let $$D(t)$$ be the US national debt at time $$t$$ . The table below gives approximate values of this function by providing end of year estimates, in billions of dollars, from 2000 to 2016. Interpret and estimate the value of $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ . $$t$$ $$D(t)$$ 2000 5662.2 2004 7596.1 2008 10,699.8 2012 16,432.7 2016 19,976.8
Solution The derivative $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ means the rate of change of $$D$$ with respect to $$t$$ when $$t = 2008$$ , that is, the rate of increase of the national debt in $$2008$$ . According to Equation 5, $$D^{\prime}(2008) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2008}\frac{D(t) - D(2008)}{t - 2008}$$ One way we can estimate this value is to compare average rates of change over different time intervals by computing difference quotients, as compiled in the following table. $$t$$ Time interval $${Average rate of change} =$$ $$\frac{D(t) - D(2008)}{t - 2008}$$ 2000 [2000, 2008] 629.7 2004 [2004, 2008] 775.93 2012 [2008, 2012] 1433.23 2016 [2008, 2016] 1159.63
From this table we see that $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ lies somewhere between $$775.93$$ and $$1433.23$$ billion dollars per year. [Here we are making the reasonable assumption that the debt didn’t fluctuate wildly between 2004 and 2012.] A good estimate for the rate of increase of the US national debt in 2008 would be the average of these two numbers, namely $$D^{\prime}(2008) \approx 1105{billion dollars}{per year}$$ Another method would be to plot the debt function and estimate the slope of the tangent line when $$t = 2008$$ . A Note on Units The units for the average rate of change $$\Delta D \slash \Delta t$$ are the units for $$\Delta D$$ divided by the units for $$\Delta t$$ , namely billions of dollars per year. The instantaneous rate of change is the limit of the average rates of change, so it is measured in the same units: billions of dollars per year.

body_xml: Example 1 The graph of a function $$f$$ is given in Figure 1. Use it to sketch the graph of the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ . Solution We can estimate the value of the derivative at any value of $$x$$ by drawing the tangent at the point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and estimating its slope. For instance, for $$x = 3$$ we draw a tangent at $$P$$ in Figure 2 and estimate its slope to be about $$- \frac{2}{3}$$ . (We have drawn a triangle to help estimate the slope.) Thus $$f^{\prime}(3) \approx - \frac{2}{3} \approx - 0.67$$ and this allows us to plot the point $$P^{\prime}(3, - 0.67)$$ on the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ directly beneath $$P$$ . (The slope of the graph of $$f$$ becomes the $$y$$ -value on the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ .) The slope of the tangent drawn at $$A$$ appears to be about $$- 1$$ , so we plot the point $$A^{\prime}$$ with a $$y$$ -value of $$- 1$$ on the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ (directly beneath $$A$$ ). The tangents at $$B$$ and $$D$$ are horizontal, so the derivative is $$0$$ there and the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ crosses the $$x$$ -axis (where $$y = 0$$ ) at the points $$B^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{\prime}$$ , directly beneath $$B$$ and $$D$$ . Between $$B$$ and $$D$$ , the graph of $$f$$ is steepest at $$C$$ and the tangent line there appears to have slope $$1$$ , so the largest value of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ between $$B^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{\prime}$$ is $$1$$ (at $$C^{\prime}$$ ). Notice that between $$B$$ and $$D$$ the tangents have positive slope, so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive there. (The graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ is above the $$x$$ -axis.) But to the right of $$D$$ the tangents have negative slope, so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative there. (The graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ is below the $$x$$ -axis.)

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 (a) If f(x) = x^{3} - x , find a formula for f^{\prime}(x) . (b) Illustrate this formula by comparing the graphs of f and f^{\prime} . Solution (a) When using Equation 2 to compute a derivative, we must remember that...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) If $$f(x) = x^{3} - x$$ , find a formula for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Illustrate this formula by comparing the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) When using Equation 2 to compute a derivative, we must remember that the variable is $$h$$ and that $$x$$ is temporarily regarded as a constant during the calculation of the limit. $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{{({x + h})}^{3} - {({x + h})}}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{x^{3} - x}\rbrack}}{h}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{x^{3} + 3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3} - x - h - x^{3} + x}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3} - h}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({3x^{2} + 3xh + h^{2} - 1})} = 3x^{2} - 1}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) We use a calculator to graph $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 3. Notice that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$f$$ has horizontal tangents and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive when the tangents have positive slope. So these graphs serve as a check on our work in part (a). Figure 3 Details Two graphing calculator screens display two curves on a coordinate plane. In both the graphs, the x and the y axes are displayed from negative 2 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. In the first graph, the curve labeled f enters the viewing window in the third quadrant at approximately (negative 1.5, negative 2), goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the x axis at (negative 1, 0), reaches its high point in the second quadrant at approximately (negative 0.5, 0.4), then goes down and to the right through the origin. It then enters into the fourth quadrant, now becoming concave up, reaches its low point in the fourth quadrant at approximately (0.5, negative 0.4), and then goes up and to the right through the point (1, 0), and exits the viewing window in the first quadrant at (1.5, 2). In the second graph, the curve labeled f prime enters the viewing window at (negative 1, 2), goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at approximately (negative 0.6, 0), concave up, reaches its low point on the vertical axis at (0, negative 1), then goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at approximately (0.6, 0), and exits the viewing window at (1, 2).</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ , find the derivative of $$f$$ . State the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}} \right) {({{Rationalize the numerator}.})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{{({x + h})} - x}{h({\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}})} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h}{h({\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}})}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ exists if $$x > 0$$ , so the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . This is slightly smaller than the domain of $$f$$ , which is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$f^{\prime}$$ if $$f(x) = \frac{1 - x}{2 + x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{\frac{1 - {({x + h})}}{2 + {({x + h})}} - \frac{1 - x}{2 + x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{{({1 - x - h})}{({2 + x})} - {({1 - x})}{({2 + x + h})}}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{{({2 - x - 2h - x^{2} - xh})} - {({2 - x + h - x^{2} - xh})}}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{- 3h}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{- 3}{({2 + x + h}){({2 + x})}} = - \frac{3}{{({2 + x})}^{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\frac{a}{b} - \frac{c}{d}}{e} = \frac{ad - bc}{bd} \cdot \frac{1}{e}$$</paragraph>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Where is the function \left. f(x) = \middle| x \right| differentiable? Solution If x > 0 , then \left| x \middle| = x \right. and we can choose h small enough that x + h > 0 and hence \left| x + h \middle| = x + h...
body_xml: Example 5 Where is the function $$\left. f(x) = \middle| x \right|$$ differentiable? Solution If $$x > 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = x \right.$$ and we can choose $$h$$ small enough that $$x + h > 0$$ and hence $$\left| x + h \middle| = x + h \right.$$ . Therefore, for $$x > 0$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| x + h \middle| - \middle| x \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {x + h} \right) - x}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}1 = 1}} \end{array}$$ and so $$f$$ is differentiable for any $$x > 0$$ . Similarly, for $$x < 0$$ we have $$\left| x \middle| = - x \right.$$ and $$h$$ can be chosen small enough that $$x + h < 0$$ and so $$\left| x + h \middle| = - \left( {x + h} \right) \right.$$ . Therefore, for $$x < 0$$ , $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| x + h \middle| - \middle| x \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- \left( {x + h} \right) - \left( {- x} \right)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {- 1} \right) = - 1}} \end{array}$$ and so $$f$$ is differentiable for any $$x < 0$$ . For $$x = 0$$ we have to investigate $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(0)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {0 + h} \right) - f(0)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(0)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| 0 + h \middle| - \middle| 0 \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{|h|}{h} ({if it exists})}} \end{array}$$ Let’s compute the left and right limits separately: $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{|h|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}1 = 1$$ and $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{|h|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{- h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\left( {- 1} \right) = - 1$$ Since these limits are different, $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ does not exist. Thus $$f$$ is differentiable at all $$x$$ except $$0$$ . A formula for $$f^{\prime}$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & {{if}x > 0} \\ {- 1} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$ and its graph is shown in Figure 5(b). The fact that $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ does not exist is reflected geometrically in the fact that the curve $$\left. y = \middle| x \right|$$ does not have a tangent line at $$(0,0)$$ . [See Figure 5(a).]

body_xml: Example 6 If $$f(x) = x^{3} - x$$ , find and interpret $$f^{''}(x)$$ . Solution In Example 2 we found that the first derivative is $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 1$$ . So the second derivative is $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x + h) - f^{\prime}(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{3{({x + h})}^{2} - 1}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{3x^{2} - 1}\rbrack}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3x^{2} + 6xh + 3h^{2} - 1 - 3x^{2} + 1}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({6x + 3h})} = 6x}} \end{array}$$ The graphs of $$f$$ , $$f^{\prime}$$ , and $$f^{''}$$ are shown in Figure 10. We can interpret $$f^{''}(x)$$ as the slope of the curve $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f^{\prime}(x)} \right)$$ . In other words, it is the rate of change of the slope of the original curve $$y = f(x)$$ . Notice from Figure 10 that $$f^{''}(x)$$ is negative when $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ has negative slope and positive when $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ has positive slope. So the graphs serve as a check on our calculations.

    <paragraph>Solution In Example 6 we found that $$f^{''}(x) = 6x$$ . The graph of the second derivative has equation $$y = 6x$$ and so it is a straight line with slope $$6$$ . Since the derivative $$f^{'''}(x)$$ is the slope of $$f^{''}(x)$$ , we have</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 3 Find equations of the tangent line and normal line to the curve $$y = x\sqrt{x}$$ at the point $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ . Illustrate by graphing the curve and these lines. Solution The derivative of $$f(x) = x\sqrt{x} = xx^{1 \slash 2} = x^{3 \slash 2}$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{3}{2}x^{(3 \slash 2) - 1} = \frac{3}{2}x^{1 \slash 2} = \frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}$$ So the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(1) = \frac{3}{2}$$ . Therefore an equation of the tangent line is $$y - 1 = \frac{3}{2}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ or $$y = \frac{3}{2}x - \frac{1}{2}$$ The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent line, so its slope is the negative reciprocal of $$\frac{3}{2}$$ , that is, $$- \frac{2}{3}$$ . Thus an equation of the normal line is $$y - 1 = - \frac{2}{3}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ or $$y = - \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{5}{3}$$ We graph the curve and its tangent line and normal line in Figure 4.

body_xml: Example 6 Find the points on the curve $$y = x^{4} - 6x^{2} + 4$$ where the tangent line is horizontal. Solution Horizontal tangents occur where the derivative is zero. We have $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{4})} - 6\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{2})} + \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(4)}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {4x^{3} - 12x + 0 = 4x{({x^{2} - 3})}}} \end{array}$$ Thus $$dy \slash dx = 0$$ if $$x = 0$$ or $$x^{2} - 3 = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \pm \sqrt{3^{}}$$ . So the given curve has horizontal tangents when $$x = 0$$ , $$\sqrt{3^{}}$$ , and $$- \sqrt{3^{}}$$ . The corresponding points are $$\left( {0,4} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\sqrt{3^{}}, - 5} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {- \sqrt{3^{}}, - 5} \right)$$ . (See Figure 5.)

body_xml: Example 8 If $$f(x) = e^{ x} - x$$ , find $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ . Compare the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ . Solution Using the Difference Rule, we have $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {e^{ x} - x} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x) = e^{ x} - 1$$ In Section 2.8 we defined the second derivative as the derivative of $$f^{\prime}$$ , so $$f^{''}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {e^{ x} - 1} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(1) = e^{ x}$$ The function $$f$$ and its derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ are graphed in Figure 8. Notice that $$f$$ has a horizontal tangent when $$x = 0$$ ; this corresponds to the fact that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . Notice also that, for $$x > 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive and $$f$$ is increasing. When $$x < 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative and $$f$$ is decreasing.

body_xml: Example 9 At what point on the curve $$y = e^{ x}$$ is the tangent line parallel to the line $$y = 2x$$ ? Solution Since $$y = e^{ x}$$ , we have $$y^{\prime} = e^{ x}$$ . Let the $$x$$ -coordinate of the point in question be $$a$$ . Then the slope of the tangent line at that point is $$e^{ a}$$ . This tangent line will be parallel to the line $$y = 2x$$ if it has the same slope, that is, $$2$$ . Equating slopes, we get $${e^{ a} = 2}{ a = \ln 2}$$ Therefore the required point is $$\left( {a,e^{ a}} \right) = \left( {\ln 2,2} \right)$$ . (See Figure 9.)

      <item>(b) Find the $$n$$ th derivative, $$f^{(n)}(x)$$ .</item>

    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) By the Product Rule, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {xe^{ x}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) + e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {xe^{ x} + e^{ x} \cdot 1 = \left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) Using the Product Rule a second time, we get $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{''}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {\left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{f^{''}(x)} = {\left( {x + 1} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) + e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x + 1} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{''}(x)} = {\left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x} + e^{ x} \cdot 1 = \left( {x + 2} \right)e^{ x}}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Further applications of the Product Rule give</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f^{'''}(x) = \left( {x + 3} \right)e^{ x}} {f^{(4)}(x) = \left( {x + 4} \right)e^{ x}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In fact, each successive differentiation adds another term $$e^{ x}$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{(n)}(x) = \left( {x + n} \right)e^{ x}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="2">

    <paragraph>Differentiate the function $$f(t) = \sqrt{t}\left( {a + bt} \right)$$ .</paragraph>

    <paragraph>In Example 2, $$a$$ and $$b$$ are constants. It is customary in mathematics to use letters near the beginning of the alphabet to represent constants and letters near the end of the alphabet to represent variables.</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 5 Find an equation of the tangent line to the curve $$y = e^{ x} \slash \left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)$$ at the point $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ . Solution According to the Quotient Rule, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\frac{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)e^{ x} - e^{ x}\left( {2x} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}} = \frac{e^{ x}\left( {1 - 2x + x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{e^{ x}\left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$ So the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ is $$\left. \frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} \right|_{x = 1} = 0$$ This means that the tangent line at $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ is horizontal and its equation is $$y = \frac{1}{2}e$$ . (See Figure 4.)

body_xml: Example 2 Differentiate $$f(x) = \frac{\sec x}{1 + \tan x}$$ . For what values of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f$$ have a horizontal tangent? Solution The Quotient Rule gives $$\begin{array}{lc} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sec x} \right) - \sec x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)\sec x\tan x - \sec x \cdot \sec^{2}x}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\sec x\left( {\tan x + \tan^{2}x - \sec^{2}x} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\sec x\left( {\tan x - 1} \right)}{\left( {1 + \tan x} \right)^{2}}} & { \left( \sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x + 1 \right)} \end{array}$$ Because $$\sec x$$ is never $$0$$ , we see that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\tan x = 1$$ , and this occurs when $$x = \pi \slash 4 + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer (see Figure 3).

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 An object fastened to the end of a vertical spring is stretched 4 cm beyond its rest position and released at time t = 0 . (See Figure 4 and note that the downward direction is positive.) Its position at time t is s =...
body_xml: Example 3 An object fastened to the end of a vertical spring is stretched $$4$$ cm beyond its rest position and released at time $$t = 0$$ . (See Figure 4 and note that the downward direction is positive.) Its position at time $$t$$ is $$s = f(t) = 4\cos t$$ Find the velocity and acceleration at time $$t$$ and use them to analyze the motion of the object. Solution The velocity and acceleration are $$\begin{array}{lll} \upsilon & = & {\frac{ds}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left( {4\cos t} \right) = 4\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\cos t} \right) = - 4\sin t} \\ a & = & {\frac{\mathit{dv}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left( {- 4\sin t} \right) = - 4\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\sin t} \right) = - 4\cos t} \end{array}$$ The object oscillates from the lowest point $$\left( {s = 4{cm}} \right)$$ to the highest point $$\left( {s = - 4{cm}} \right)$$ . The period of the oscillation is $$2\pi$$ , the period of $$\cos t$$ . The speed is $$|\upsilon| = 4\left| {\sin t} \right|$$ , which is greatest when $$\left| {\sin t} \right| = 1$$ , that is, when $$\cos t = 0$$ . So the object moves fastest as it passes through its equilibrium position $$\left( {s = 0} \right)$$ . Its speed is $$0$$ when $$\sin t = 0$$ , that is, at the highest and lowest points. The acceleration $$a = - 4\cos t = 0$$ when $$s = 0$$ . It has greatest magnitude at the highest and lowest points. See the graphs in Figure 5.

body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the $$27$$ th derivative of $$\cos x$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The first few derivatives of $$f(x) = \cos x$$ are as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Look for a pattern.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {f^{\prime}{(x)}} & = & {- \sin x} \\ {f^{''}{(x)}} & = & {- \cos x} \\ {f^{'''}{(x)}} & = & {\sin x} \\ {f^{(4)}{(x)}} & = & {\cos x} \\ {f^{(5)}{(x)}} & = & {- \sin x} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We see that the successive derivatives occur in a cycle of length $$4$$ and, in particular, $$f^{(n)}(x) = \cos x$$ whenever $$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$ . Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{(24)}(x) = \cos x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and, differentiating three more times, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{(27)}(x) = \sin x$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: The Chain Rule
snippet: The Chain Rule: The Chain Rule If g is differentiable at x and f is differentiable at g(x) , then the composite function F = f \circ g defined by {F(x)} = {f({g(x)})} is differentiable at x and F^{\prime} is given by the product...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The Chain Rule" title="The Chain Rule">
    <heading level="4">The Chain Rule</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$g$$ is differentiable at $$x$$ and $$f$$ is differentiable at $$g(x)$$ , then the composite function $$F = f \circ g$$ defined by $${F(x)} = {f({g(x)})}$$ is differentiable at $$x$$ and $$F^{\prime}$$ is given by the product</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${F^{\prime}(x)} = {f^{\prime}({g(x)})} \cdot {g^{\prime}(x)}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In Leibniz notation, if $$y = {f(u)}$$ and $$u = {g(x)}$$ are both differentiable functions, then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Comments on the Proof of the Chain Rule
source_type: Comments on the Proof of the Chain Rule
snippet: Comments on the Proof of the Chain Rule: Comments on the Proof of the Chain Rule Let \Delta u be the change in u corresponding to a change of \Delta x in x , that is, \Delta u = {g({x + \Delta x})} - {g(x)} Then the corresponding change in...
body_xml:
Comments on the Proof of the Chain Rule Let $$\Delta u$$ be the change in $$u$$ corresponding to a change of $$\Delta x$$ in $$x$$ , that is, $$\Delta u = {g({x + \Delta x})} - {g(x)}$$ Then the corresponding change in $$y$$ is $$\Delta y = {f({u + \Delta u})} - {f(u)}$$ It is tempting to write $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}}$$ $$\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \cdot \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}}$$ $$\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \cdot \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}}$$ $$\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\lim\limits_{\Delta u\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \cdot \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} \left. ({Note that}\Delta u\rightarrow 0{as}\Delta x\rightarrow 0{because}g{is continuous.}) \right.}$$ $$\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}}$$
The only flaw in this reasoning is that in (3) it might happen that $$\Delta u = 0$$ (even when $$\Delta x \neq 0$$ ) and, of course, we can’t divide by $$0$$ . Nonetheless, this reasoning does at least suggest that the Chain Rule is true. A full proof of the Chain Rule is given at the end of this section.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find F^{\prime}(x) if {F(x)} = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1} . Solution 1 (using Formula 1): At the beginning of this section we expressed F as {F(x)} = {({f \circ g})}{(x)} = {f({g(x)})} where {f(u)} = \sqrt{u} and {g(x)} = x^{2}...

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$F^{\prime}(x)$$ if $${F(x)} = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1 (using Formula 1): At the beginning of this section we expressed $$F$$ as $${F(x)} = {({f \circ g})}{(x)} = {f({g(x)})}$$ where $${f(u)} = \sqrt{u}$$ and $${g(x)} = x^{2} + 1$$ . Since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f^{\prime}(u)} = \frac{1}{2}u^{- 1 \slash 2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${g^{\prime}(x)} = 2x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{F^{\prime}(x)} = {{f^{\prime}({g(x)})} \cdot {g^{\prime}(x)}}} \\ {\phantom{F^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \cdot 2x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2 (using Formula 2): If we let $$u = x^{2} + 1$$ and $$y = \sqrt{u}$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${F^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}{({2x})} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}{({2x})} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Differentiate (a) y = \sin{(x^{2})} and (b) y = \sin^{2}x . Solution (a) If y = \sin{(x^{2})} , then the outer function is the sine function and the inner function is the squaring function, so the Chain Rule gives...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiate</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$y = \sin{(x^{2})}$$ and</item>
      <item>(b) $$y = \sin^{2}x$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) If $$y = \sin{(x^{2})}$$ , then the outer function is the sine function and the inner function is the squaring function, so the Chain Rule gives $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\underset{\begin{matrix} {outer} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\sin\limits_{︸}}\underset{\begin{matrix} {evaluated} \\ {at inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{(x^{2})}} = \underset{\begin{matrix} {derivative} \\ {of outer} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\cos\limits_{︸}}\underset{\begin{matrix} {evaluated} \\ {at inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{(x^{2})}} \cdot \underset{\begin{matrix} {derivative} \\ {of inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{2x}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {2x\cos{(x^{2})}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) Note that $$\sin^{2}x = {({\sin x})}^{2}$$ . Here the outer function is the squaring function and the inner function is the sine function. So $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{\underset{\begin{matrix} {inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{({\sin x})}}}^{2} = \underset{\begin{matrix} {derivative} \\ {of outer} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{2 \cdot}}\underset{\begin{matrix} {evaluated} \\ {at inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{({\sin x})}} \cdot \underset{\begin{matrix} {derivative} \\ {of inner} \\ {function} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{\cos x}}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>The answer can be left as $$2\sin x\cos x$$ or written as $$\sin 2x$$ (by a trigonometric identity known as the double-angle formula).</paragraph>
    <paragraph>See The Area Problem or Appendix D.</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="theorem" source_type="The Power Rule Combined with the Chain Rule" title="The Power Rule Combined with the Chain Rule">
    <heading level="4">The Power Rule Combined with the Chain Rule</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$n$$ is any real number and $$u = {g(x)}$$ is differentiable, then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(u^{n})} = nu^{n - 1}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Alternatively,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{\lbrack g(x)\rbrack}^{n} = n{\lbrack g(x)\rbrack}^{n - 1} \cdot g^{\prime}(x)$$</paragraph>
  </note>

Solution In this example we must use the Product Rule before using the Chain Rule: $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = {{({2x + 1})}^{5}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{4} + {({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{4}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({2x + 1})}^{5}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {{({2x + 1})}^{5} \cdot 4{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{3}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({x^{3} - x + 1})} + {({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{4} \cdot 5{({2x + 1})}^{4}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({2x + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {4{({2x + 1})}^{5}{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{3}{({3x^{2} - 1})} + 5{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{4}{({2x + 1})}^{4} \cdot 2}} \end{array}$$ Noticing that each term has the common factor $$2{({2x + 1})}^{4}{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{3}$$ , we could factor it out and write the answer as $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 2{({2x + 1})}^{4}{({x^{3} - x + 1})}^{3}{({17x^{3} + 6x^{2} - 9x + 3})}$$ The graphs of the functions $$y$$ and $$y^{\prime}$$ in Example 6 are shown in Figure 1. Notice that $$y^{\prime}$$ is large when $$y$$ increases rapidly and $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ when $$y$$ has a horizontal tangent. So our answer appears to be reasonable.
