<example number="10">
    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the derivative of each of the functions.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$g(x) = 2^{x}$$</item>
      <item>$$h(x) = 5^{x^{2}}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>We use Formula 5 with $$b = 2$$ : $$g^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(2^{x}) = 2^{x}\ln 2$$ This is consistent with the estimate $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(2^{x}) \approx (0.693)2^{x}$$ we gave in Section 3.1 because $$\ln 2 \approx 0.693147$$ .</item>
      <item>The outer function is an exponential function and the inner function is the squaring function, so we use Formula 5 and the Chain Rule to get $$h^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(5^{x^{2}}) = 5x^{2}\ln 5 \cdot \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{2}) = 2x \cdot 5^{x^{2}}\ln 5$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <paragraph>The first person to formulate the Chain Rule was the Scottish mathematician James Gregory (1638–1675), who also designed the first practical reflecting telescope. Gregory discovered the basic ideas of calculus at about the same time as Newton. He became the first Professor of Mathematics at the University of St. Andrews and later held the same position at the University of Edinburgh. But one year after accepting that position, he died at the age of 36.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 If x^{2} + y^{2} = 25 , find \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} . Then find an equation of the tangent to the circle x^{2} + y^{2} = 25 at the point \left( {3,4} \right) . Solution 1 Differentiate both sides of the...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$$ , find $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$ . Then find an equation of the tangent to the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$$ at the point $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Differentiate both sides of the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}} & = & {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(25)}} \\ {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{2})} + \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(y^{2})}} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Remembering that $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ and using the Chain Rule, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(y^{2})} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dy}}{(y^{2})}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2x + 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now we solve this equation for $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \frac{x}{y}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At the point $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ we have $$x = 3$$ and $$y = 4$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \frac{3}{4}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>An equation of the tangent to the circle at $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ is therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y - 4 = - \frac{3}{4}(x - 3)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$3x + 4y = 25$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$$ for $$y$$ , we get $$y = \pm \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}$$ . The point $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ lies on the upper semicircle $$y = \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}$$ and so we consider the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}$$ . Differentiating $$f$$ using the Chain Rule, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\frac{1}{2}{({25 - x^{2}})}^{- 1 \slash 2}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({25 - x^{2}})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\frac{1}{2}{({25 - x^{2}})}^{- 1 \slash 2}{({- 2x})} = - \frac{x}{\sqrt{25 - x^{2}}}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At the point ( $$3$$ , $$4$$ ) we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(3) = - \frac{3}{\sqrt{25 - 3^{2}}} = - \frac{3}{4}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and, as in Solution 1, an equation of the tangent is $$3x + 4y = 25$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Example 1 illustrates that even when it is possible to solve an equation explicitly for $$y$$ in terms of $$x$$ , it may be easier to use implicit differentiation.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 (a) Find y^{\prime} if x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy . (b) Find the tangent to the folium of Descartes x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy at the point \left( {3,3} \right) . (c) At what point in the first quadrant is the tangent line...
body_xml: Example 2 (a) Find $$y^{\prime}$$ if $$x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy$$ . (b) Find the tangent to the folium of Descartes $$x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy$$ at the point $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ . (c) At what point in the first quadrant is the tangent line horizontal? Solution We can use either of the notations $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ or $$y^{\prime}$$ for the derivative of $$y$$ with respect to $$x$$ . (a) Differentiating both sides of $$x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy$$ with respect to $$x$$ , regarding $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ , and using the Chain Rule on the term $$y^{3}$$ and the Product Rule on the term $$6xy$$ , we get $$3x^{2} + 3y^{2}y^{\prime} = 6xy^{\prime} + 6y$$ or $$x^{2} + y^{2}y^{\prime} = 2xy^{\prime} + 2y$$ We now solve for $$y^{\prime}$$ : $$\begin{array}{rll} {y^{2}y^{\prime} - 2xy^{\prime}} & = & {2y - x^{2}} \\ {{({y^{2} - 2x})}y^{\prime}} & = & {2y - x^{2}} \\ y^{\prime} & = & \frac{2y - x^{2}}{y^{2} - 2x} \end{array}$$ (b) When $$x = y = 3$$ , $$y^{\prime} = \frac{2 \cdot 3 - 3^{2}}{3^{2} - 2 \cdot 3} = - 1$$ and a glance at Figure 4 confirms that this is a reasonable value for the slope at $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ . So an equation of the tangent to the folium at $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ is $$y - 3 = - 1\left( {x - 3} \right)$$ or $$x + y = 6$$ Figure 4 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at the origin, then goes up and to the right until the point (3, 3) in the first quadrant. From point (3, 3), the curve then goes down and to the right, concave down so that it forms a loop in the first quadrant, reaches its leftmost point at the origin, and then goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant, now concave up. A tangent line with a negative slope is drawn above the loop in the first quadrant such that the tangent touches the curve exactly once at the marked point (3, 3). (c) The tangent line is horizontal if $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ . Using the expression for $$y^{\prime}$$ from part (a), we see that $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ when $$2y - x^{2} = 0$$ (provided that $$y^{2} - 2x \neq 0$$ ). Substituting $$y = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}$$ in the equation of the curve, we get $$x^{3} + \left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right)^{3} = 6x\left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right)$$ which simplifies to $$x^{6} = 16x^{3}$$ . Since $$x \neq 0$$ in the first quadrant, we have $$x^{3} = 16$$ . If $$x = 16^{1 \slash 3} = 2^{4 \slash 3}$$ , then $$y = \frac{1}{2}{(2^{8 \slash 3})} = 2^{5 \slash 3}$$ . Thus the tangent is horizontal at $$({2^{4 \slash 3},2^{5 \slash 3}})$$ , which is approximately $$(2.5198,3.1748)$$ . Looking at Figure 5, we see that our answer is reasonable.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find y^{\prime} if \sin\left( {x + y} \right) = y^{2}\cos x . Solution Differentiating implicitly with respect to x and remembering that y is a function of x , we get \cos(x + y) \cdot (1 + y^{\prime}) = y^{2}( - \sin...
body_xml: Example 3 Find $$y^{\prime}$$ if $$\sin\left( {x + y} \right) = y^{2}\cos x$$ . Solution Differentiating implicitly with respect to $$x$$ and remembering that $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ , we get $$\cos(x + y) \cdot (1 + y^{\prime}) = y^{2}( - \sin x) + (\cos x)(2yy^{\prime})$$ (Note that we have used the Chain Rule on the left side and the Product Rule and Chain Rule on the right side.) If we collect the terms that involve $$y^{\prime}$$ , we get $$\cos\left( {x + y} \right) + y^{2}\sin x = \left( {2y\cos x} \right)y^{\prime} - \cos\left( {x + y} \right) \cdot y^{\prime}$$ So $$y^{\prime} = \frac{y^{2}\sin x + \cos\left( {x + y} \right)}{2y\cos x - \cos\left( {x + y} \right)}$$ Figure 6, drawn by a computer, shows part of the curve $$\sin\left( {x + y} \right) = y^{2}\cos x$$ . As a check on our calculation, notice that $$y^{\prime} = - 1$$ when $$x = y = 0$$ and it appears from the graph that the slope is approximately $$- 1$$ at the origin.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find y^{''} if x^{4} + y^{4} = 16 . Solution Differentiating the equation implicitly with respect to x , we get 4x^{3} + 4y^{3}y^{\prime} = 0 Solving for y^{\prime} gives y^{\prime} = - \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}} To find...
body_xml: Example 4 Find $$y^{''}$$ if $$x^{4} + y^{4} = 16$$ . Solution Differentiating the equation implicitly with respect to $$x$$ , we get $$4x^{3} + 4y^{3}y^{\prime} = 0$$ Solving for $$y^{\prime}$$ gives $$y^{\prime} = - \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}}$$ To find $$y^{''}$$ we differentiate this expression for $$y^{\prime}$$ using the Quotient Rule and remembering that $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {{y^{''} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {- \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}}} \right)} = {- \frac{y^{3}{({d \slash \mathit{dx}})}{(x^{3})} - x^{3}{({d \slash \mathit{dx}})}{(y^{3})}}{{(y^{3})}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {- \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}}} \right)} = {- \frac{y^{3} \cdot 3x^{2} - x^{3}{({3y^{2}y^{\prime}})}}{y^{6}}}} \end{array}$$ If we now substitute Equation 3 into this expression, we get $$\begin{array}{l} {y^{''} = {- \frac{3x^{2}y^{3} - 3x^{3}y^{2}\left( {- \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}}} \right)}{y^{6}}}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''}} = {- \frac{3{({x^{2}y^{4} + x^{6}})}}{y^{7}} = - \frac{3x^{2}{({y^{4} + x^{4}})}}{y^{7}}}} \end{array}$$ But the values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ must satisfy the original equation $$x^{4} + y^{4} = 16$$ . So the answer simplifies to $$y^{''} = - \frac{3x^{2}(16)}{y^{7}} = - 48\frac{x^{2}}{y^{7}}$$ Figure 10 shows the graph of the curve $$x^{4} + y^{4} = 16$$ of Example 4. Notice that it’s a stretched and flattened version of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ . For this reason it’s sometimes called a fat circle. It starts out very steep on the left but quickly becomes very flat. This can be seen from the expression $$y^{\prime} = - \frac{x^{3}}{y^{3}} = - \left( \frac{x}{y} \right)^{3}$$

<note type="theorem" source_type="Abel and Galois" title="Abel and Galois">
    <heading level="4">Abel and Galois</heading>
    <paragraph>The Norwegian mathematician Niels Abel proved in 1824 that no general formula in terms of radicals can be given for the solutions of the equation $$p(x) = 0$$ , where $$p$$ is a polynomial of degree $$5$$ with integer coefficients. Later the French mathematician Evariste Galois proved that it is impossible to find a general formula in terms of radicals for the solutions of an equation $$p(x) = 0$$ , where $$p$$ is a polynomial of degree $$n \geqslant 5$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 5 Find $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}$$ . Solution 1 $$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\frac{1}{\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\frac{\sqrt{x - 2}}{x + 1}\frac{\sqrt{x - 2} \cdot 1 - \left( {x + 1} \right)\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)^{- 1 \slash 2}}{x - 2}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = \frac{x - 2 - \frac{1}{2}\left( {x + 1} \right)}{\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = \frac{x - 5}{2\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)}} \end{array}$$ Solution 2 If we first expand the given function using the laws of logarithms, then the differentiation becomes easier: $$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{\lbrack{\ln\left( {x + 1} \right) - \frac{1}{2}\ln\left( {x - 2} \right)}\rbrack}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\frac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{1}{x - 2} \right)}} \end{array}$$ (This answer can be left as written, but if we used a common denominator we would see that it gives the same answer as in Solution 1.) Figure 1 shows the graph of the function $$f$$ of Example 5 together with the graph of its derivative. It gives a visual check on our calculation. Notice that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is large negative when $$f$$ is decreasing rapidly.

body_xml: Example 6 Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ if $$f(x) = \ln|x|$$ . Solution Since $$f(x) = \begin{cases} {\ln x} & {{if}x > 0} \\ {\ln( - x)} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$ it follows that $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x} & {{if}x > 0} \\ {\frac{1}{- x}( - 1) = \frac{1}{x}} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$ Thus $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 \slash x$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ . Figure 2 shows the graph of the function $$f(x) = \ln|x|$$ in Example 6 and its derivative $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 \slash x$$ . Notice that when $$x$$ is small, the graph of $$y = \ln|x|$$ is steep and so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is large (positive or negative).

snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Differentiate y = \frac{x^{3 \slash 4}\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}{\left( {3x + 2} \right)^{5}} . Solution We take logarithms of both sides of the equation and use the Laws of Logarithms to simplify: \ln y = \frac{3}{4}\ln x +...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiate $$y = \frac{x^{3 \slash 4}\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}{\left( {3x + 2} \right)^{5}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We take logarithms of both sides of the equation and use the Laws of Logarithms to simplify:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\ln y = \frac{3}{4}\ln x + \frac{1}{2}\ln{({x^{2} + 1})} - 5\ln\left( {3x + 2} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Differentiating implicitly with respect to $$x$$ gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{1}{y}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 1} - 5 \cdot \frac{3}{3x + 2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving for $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ , we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = y\left( {\frac{3}{4x} + \frac{x}{x^{2} + 1} - \frac{15}{3x + 2}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Because we have an explicit expression for $$y$$ , we can substitute and write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{x^{3 \slash 4}\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}{\left( {3x + 2} \right)^{5}}\left( {\frac{3}{4x} + \frac{x}{x^{2} + 1} - \frac{15}{3x + 2}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we hadn’t used logarithmic differentiation in Example 7, we would have had to use both the Quotient Rule and the Product Rule. The resulting calculation would have been horrendous.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Proof of the Power Rule (General Version)" title="Proof of the Power Rule (General Version)">
    <heading level="4">Proof of the Power Rule (General Version)</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$y = x^{n}$$ and use logarithmic differentiation:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\ln|y| = \ln|x|^{n} = n\ln|x| x \neq 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{y^{\prime}}{y} = \frac{n}{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Hence</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = n\frac{y}{x} = n\frac{x^{n}}{x} = nx^{n - 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If $$x = 0$$ , we can show that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ for $$n > 1$$ directly from the definition of a derivative.</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
Example 8 Differentiate $$y = x^{\sqrt{x}}$$ . Solution 1 Since both the base and the exponent are variable, we use logarithmic differentiation: $$\begin{array}{rll} {\ln y} & = & {\ln x^{\sqrt{x}} = \sqrt{x}\ln x} \\ \frac{y^{\prime}}{y} & = & {\sqrt{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \left( {\ln x} \right)\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}} \\ y^{\prime} & = & {y\left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + \frac{\ln x}{2\sqrt{x}}} \right) = x^{\sqrt{x}}\left( \frac{2 + \ln x}{2\sqrt{x}} \right)} \end{array}$$ Solution 2 Another method is to use Equation 1.5.10 to write $$x^{\sqrt{x}} = {(e^{\ln x})}^{\sqrt{x}}$$ : $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{\sqrt{x}})}$$ $$= {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(e^{\sqrt{x}\ln x})} = e^{\sqrt{x}\ln x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({\sqrt{x}\ln x})}}$$ $$= {x^{\sqrt{x}}{\left( \frac{2 + \ln x}{2\sqrt{x}} \right) }}$$ (as in Solution 1 )
Figure 3 illustrates Example 8 by showing the graphs of $$f(x) = x^{\sqrt{x}}$$ and its derivative.

unit_title: Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The position of a particle is given by the equation s = f(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 9t where t is measured in seconds and s in meters. (a) Find the velocity at time t . (b) What is the velocity after 2 s? After 4 s? (c)...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>The position of a particle is given by the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$s = f(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 9t$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$t$$ is measured in seconds and $$s$$ in meters.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Find the velocity at time $$t$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) What is the velocity after $$2$$ s? After $$4$$ s?</item>
      <item>(c) When is the particle at rest?</item>
      <item>(d) When is the particle moving forward (that is, in the positive direction)?</item>
      <item>(e) Draw a diagram to represent the motion of the particle.</item>
      <item>(f) Find the total distance traveled by the particle during the first five seconds.</item>
      <item>(g) Find the acceleration at time $$t$$ and after $$4$$ s.</item>
      <item>(h) Graph the position, velocity, and acceleration functions for $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 5$$ .</item>
      <item>(i) When is the particle speeding up? When is it slowing down?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The velocity function is the derivative of the position function: $$\begin{array}{cll} s & = & {f(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 9t} \\ {\upsilon(t)} & = & {\frac{ds}{\mathit{dt}} = 3t^{2} - 12t + 9} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) The velocity after $$2$$ s means the instantaneous velocity when $$t = 2$$ , that is, $$\upsilon(2) = \left. \frac{\mathit{ds}}{\mathit{dt}} \right|_{t = 2} = 3(2)^{2} - 12(2) + 9 = - 3m \slash s$$ The velocity after $$4$$ s is $$\upsilon(4) = 3{(4)}^{2} - 12(4) + 9 = 9m \slash s$$</item>
      <item>(c) The particle is at rest when $$\upsilon(t) = 0$$ , that is, $$3t^{2} - 12t + 9 = 3({t^{2} - 4t + 3}) = 3({t - 1})({t - 3}) = 0$$ and this is true when $$t = 1$$ or $$t = 3$$ . Thus the particle is at rest after $$1$$ s and after $$3$$ s.</item>
      <item>(d) The particle moves in the positive direction when $$\upsilon(t) > 0$$ , that is, $$3t^{2} - 12t + 9 = 3({t - 1})({t - 3}) > 0$$ This inequality is true when both factors are positive $$\left( {t > 3} \right)$$ or when both factors are negative $$\left( {t < 1} \right)$$ . Thus the particle moves in the positive direction in the time intervals $$t < 1$$ and $$t > 3$$ . It moves backward (in the negative direction) when $$1 < t < 3$$ .</item>
      <item>(e) Using the information from part (d) we make a schematic sketch in Figure 2 of the motion of the particle back and forth along a line (the $$s$$ -axis). Figure 2 Details A horizontal line labeled s has two marked points: the first point on the left is labeled t = 0, s = 0; the second point on the right is labeled t = 1, s = 4. Above the line, an arrow begins at the first marked point, runs horizontally rightward, then turns at another marked point labeled t = 1, s = 4, running horizontally leftward, then turns directly above the initial point. This turning point is labeled t = 3, s = 0. It then runs horizontally rightward.</item>
      <item>(f) Because of what we learned in parts (d) and (e), we need to calculate the distances traveled during the time intervals $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack 1,3\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack 3,5\rbrack$$ separately. The distance traveled in the first second is $$\left| f(1) - f(0) \middle| = \middle| 4 - 0 \middle| = 4m \right.$$ From $$t = 1$$ to $$t = 3$$ the distance traveled is $$\left| f(3) - f(1) \middle| = \middle| 0 - 4 \middle| = 4m \right.$$ From $$t = 3$$ to $$t = 5$$ the distance traveled is $$\left| f(5) - f(3) \middle| = \middle| 20 - 0 \middle| = 20m \right.$$ The total distance is $$4 + 4 + 20 = 28m$$ .</item>
      <item>(g) The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity function: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {a(t)} & = & {\frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}} = \frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dt}} = 6t - 12} \\ {a(4)} & = & {6(4) - 12 = 12{m \slash s}^{2}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(h) Figure 3 shows the graphs of $$s$$ , $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ . Figure 3 Details Three curves are graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from 0 to 5 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from negative 12 to 25. The curve labeled s begins at the origin, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (1.2, 4), goes down and to the right, now concave up, crosses the x axis at approximately (2.5, 0), reaches its low point at (3, negative 1), again goes up and to the right, and exits the first quadrant at approximately (5, 19). The curve labeled v begins on the vertical axis at (0, 8), goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the x axis at approximately (1, 0), reaches its low point in the fourth quadrant at (2, negative 4), then goes up and to the right by passing through (3, 0), and exits the viewing window to the left of curve s at approximately (5, 23). The curve labeled a enters the viewing window at (0, negative 12), goes up and to the right, almost follows a linear path, crossing the x axis at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window at approximately (5, 17) by intersecting the previous two curves.</item>
      <item>(i) The particle speeds up when the velocity is positive and increasing ( $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ are both positive) and also when the velocity is negative and decreasing ( $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ are both negative). In other words, the particle speeds up when the velocity and acceleration have the same sign. (The particle is pushed in the same direction it is moving.) From Figure 3 we see that this happens when $$1 < t < 2$$ and when $$t > 3$$ . The particle slows down when $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ have opposite signs, that is, when $$0 \leqslant t < 1$$ and when $$2 < t < 3$$ . Figure 4 summarizes the motion of the particle. Figure 4 Details Three curves are graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis t is displayed from 0 to beyond 4 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from below negative 10 to 20. The curve labeled s begins at the origin, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (1.2, 4), goes down and to the right, now concave up, appears to reach its low point at (3, 0), again goes up and to the right, and exits the first quadrant at approximately (5, 19). The curve labeled v begins on the vertical axis at approximately (0, 8), goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), reaches its low point in the fourth quadrant at (2, negative 4), then goes up and to the right by passing through (3, 0), and exits the viewing window to the left of curve s at approximately (5, 23). The curve labeled a enters at (0, negative 12), goes up and to the right, almost follows a linear path, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window at (5, 17) by intersecting the two previous curves. The movement of the particle is described as follows: from t = 0 to t = 1, forward; from t = 1 to t = 3, backward; and for t > 3, forward. The speed of the particle is described as follows: from t = 0 to t = 1, slows down; from t = 1 to t = 2, speeds up; from t = 2 to t = 3, slows down; and for t > 3, speeds up.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 If a rod or piece of wire is homogeneous, then its linear density is uniform and is defined as the mass per unit length \left( {\rho = m \slash l} \right) and measured in kilograms per meter. Suppose, however, that the...
body_xml: Example 2 If a rod or piece of wire is homogeneous, then its linear density is uniform and is defined as the mass per unit length $$\left( {\rho = m \slash l} \right)$$ and measured in kilograms per meter. Suppose, however, that the rod is not homogeneous but that its mass measured from its left end to a point $$x$$ is $$m = f(x)$$ , as shown in Figure 5. The mass of the part of the rod that lies between $$x = x_{1}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is given by $$\Delta m = f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})$$ , so the average density of that part of the rod is $${average density} = \frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ If we now let $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ (that is, $$\left. x_{2}\rightarrow x_{1} \right.$$ ), we are computing the average density over smaller and smaller intervals. The linear density $$\rho$$ at $$x_{1}$$ is the limit of these average densities as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ ; that is, the linear density is the rate of change of mass with respect to length. Symbolically, $$\rho = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{\mathit{dm}}{\mathit{dx}}$$ Thus the linear density of the rod is the derivative of mass with respect to length. For instance, if $$m = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ , where $$x$$ is measured in meters and $$m$$ in kilograms, then the average density of the part of the rod given by $$1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1.2$$ is $$\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(1.2) - f(1)}{1.2 - 1} = \frac{\sqrt{1.2} - 1}{0.2} \approx 0.48{kg} \slash m$$ while the density right at $$x = 1$$ is $$\left. \rho = \frac{\mathit{dm}}{\mathit{dx}} \right|_{x = 1}\left. = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \right|_{x = 1} = 0.50{kg} \slash m$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 A current exists whenever electric charges move. Figure 6 shows part of a wire and electrons moving through a plane surface, shaded red. If \Delta Q is the net charge that passes through this surface during a time...
body_xml: Example 3 A current exists whenever electric charges move. Figure 6 shows part of a wire and electrons moving through a plane surface, shaded red. If $$\Delta Q$$ is the net charge that passes through this surface during a time period $$\Delta t$$ , then the average current during this time interval is defined as $${average current} = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{Q_{2} - Q_{1}}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$ If we take the limit of this average current over smaller and smaller time intervals, we get what is called the current $$I$$ at a given time $$t_{1}$$ : $$I = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{dQ}{\mathit{dt}}$$ Thus the current is the rate at which charge flows through a surface. It is measured in units of charge per unit time (often coulombs per second, called amperes).

unit_title: Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 A chemical reaction results in the formation of one or more substances (called products) from one or more starting materials (called reactants). For instance, the “equation” \left. 2H_{2} + O_{2}\rightarrow 2H_{2}O...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>A chemical reaction results in the formation of one or more substances (called products) from one or more starting materials (called reactants). For instance, the “equation”</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. 2H_{2} + O_{2}\rightarrow 2H_{2}O \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>indicates that two molecules of hydrogen and one molecule of oxygen form two molecules of water. Let’s consider the reaction</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. A + B\rightarrow C \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$A$$ and $$B$$ are the reactants and $$C$$ is the product. The concentration of a reactant $$A$$ is the number of moles $$\left( 1{mole} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}{molecules} \right)$$ per liter and is denoted by $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ . The concentration varies during a reaction, so $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack B\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack C\rbrack$$ are all functions of time $$(t)$$ . The average rate of reaction of the product $$C$$ over a time interval $$t_{1} \leqslant t \leqslant t_{2}$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\Delta\lbrack C\rbrack}{\Delta t} = \frac{\lbrack C\rbrack\left( t_{2} \right) - \lbrack C\rbrack\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>But chemists are interested in the instantaneous rate of reaction because it gives information about the mechanism of the chemical reaction. The instantaneous rate of reaction is obtained by taking the limit of the average rate of reaction as the time interval $$\Delta t$$ approaches $$0$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${rate of reaction} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\lbrack C\rbrack}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since the concentration of the product increases as the reaction proceeds, the derivative $$d\lbrack C\rbrack \slash dt$$ will be positive, and so the rate of reaction of $$C$$ is positive. The concentrations of the reactants, however, decrease during the reaction, so, to make the rates of reaction of $$A$$ and $$B$$ positive numbers, we put minus signs in front of the derivatives $$d\lbrack A\rbrack \slash dt$$ and $$d\lbrack B\rbrack \slash dt$$ . Since $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ and $$\lbrack B\rbrack$$ each decrease at the same rate that $$\lbrack C\rbrack$$ increases, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${rate of reaction} = \frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{d\lbrack A\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{d\lbrack B\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>More generally, it turns out that for a reaction of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. aA + bB\rightarrow cC + dD \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{1}{a}\frac{d\lbrack A\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{1}{b}\frac{d\lbrack B\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{d\lbrack D\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rate of reaction can be determined from data and graphical methods. In some cases there are explicit formulas for the concentrations as functions of time that enable us to compute the rate of reaction (see Exercise 26).</paragraph>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 One of the quantities of interest in thermodynamics is compressibility. If a given substance is kept at a constant temperature, then its volume V depends on its pressure P . We can consider the rate of change of volume...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>One of the quantities of interest in thermodynamics is compressibility. If a given substance is kept at a constant temperature, then its volume $$V$$ depends on its pressure $$P$$ . We can consider the rate of change of volume with respect to pressure—namely, the derivative $$dV \slash dP$$ . As $$P$$ increases, $$V$$ decreases, so $$dV \slash dP < 0$$ . The compressibility is defined by introducing a minus sign and dividing this derivative by the volume $$V$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${isothermal compressibility} = \beta = - \frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dP}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$\beta$$ measures how fast, per unit volume, the volume of a substance decreases as the pressure on it increases at constant temperature.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For instance, the volume $$V$$ (in cubic meters) of a sample of air at $$25{}_{}^{}$$ was found to be related to the pressure $$V$$ (in kilopascals) by the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$V = \frac{5.3}{P}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rate of change of $$V$$ with respect to $$P$$ when $$P = 50{kPa}$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50} = \left. {- \frac{5.3}{P^{2}}} \right|_{P = 50}} \\ {\phantom{\left. \frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50}} = {- \frac{5.3}{2500} = - 0.00212m^{3} \slash {kPa}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The compressibility at that pressure is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \beta = - \frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50} = \frac{0.00212}{\frac{5.3}{50}} = 0.02({m^{3} \slash {kPa}}){\slash m}^{3}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Let n = f(t) be the number of individuals in an animal or plant population at time t . The change in the population size between the times t = t_{1} and t = t_{2} is \Delta n = f(t_{2}) - f(t_{1}) , and so the average...
body_xml: Example 6 Let $$n = f(t)$$ be the number of individuals in an animal or plant population at time $$t$$ . The change in the population size between the times $$t = t_{1}$$ and $$t = t_{2}$$ is $$\Delta n = f(t_{2}) - f(t_{1})$$ , and so the average rate of growth during the time period $$t_{1} \leqslant t \leqslant t_{2}$$ is $${average rate of growth} = \frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t} = \frac{f(t_{2}) - f(t_{1})}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$ The instantaneous rate of growth is obtained from this average rate of growth by letting the time period $$\Delta t$$ approach $$0$$ : $${growth rate} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t} = \frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}}$$ Strictly speaking, this is not quite accurate because the actual graph of a population function $$n = f(t)$$ would be a step function that is discontinuous whenever a birth or death occurs and therefore not differentiable. However, for a large animal or plant population, we can replace the graph by a smooth approximating curve as in Figure 7. To be more specific, consider a population of bacteria in a homogeneous nutrient medium. Suppose that by sampling the population at certain intervals it is determined that the population doubles every hour. If the initial population is $$n_{0}$$ and the time $$t$$ is measured in hours, then $$\begin{matrix} {f(1) = 2f(0) = 2n_{0}} \\ {f(2) = 2f(1) = 2^{2}n_{0}} \\ {f(3) = 2f(2) = 2^{3}n_{0}} \end{matrix}$$ and, in general, $$f(t) = 2^{t}n_{0}$$ The population function is $$n = n_{0}2^{t}$$ . In Section 3.4 we showed that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( b^{ x} \right) = b^{ x}\ln b$$ So the rate of growth of the bacteria population at time $$t$$ is $$\frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}{({n_{0}2^{t}})} = n_{0}2^{t}\ln 2$$ For example, suppose that we start with an initial population of $$n_{0} = 100{bacteria}$$ . Then the rate of growth after $$4$$ hours is $$\left. \frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}} \right|_{t = 4} = 100 \cdot 2^{4}\ln 2 = 1600\ln 2 \approx 1109$$ This means that, after $$4$$ hours, the bacteria population is growing at a rate of about $$1109$$ bacteria per hour.

unit_title: Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 When we consider the flow of blood through a blood vessel, such as a vein or artery, we can model the shape of the blood vessel by a cylindrical tube with radius R and length l as illustrated in Figure 8. Because of...
body_xml: Example 7 When we consider the flow of blood through a blood vessel, such as a vein or artery, we can model the shape of the blood vessel by a cylindrical tube with radius $$R$$ and length $$l$$ as illustrated in Figure 8. Because of friction at the walls of the tube, the velocity $$\upsilon$$ of the blood is greatest along the central axis of the tube and decreases as the distance $$r$$ from the axis increases until $$\upsilon$$ becomes $$0$$ at the wall. The relationship between $$\upsilon$$ and $$r$$ is given by the law of laminar flow, which was experimentally derived by the French physicist Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille in 1838. This law states that $$v = \frac{P}{4\eta l}{({R^{2} - r^{2}})}$$ where $$\eta$$ is the viscosity of the blood and $$P$$ is the pressure difference between the ends of the tube. If $$P$$ and $$l$$ are constant, then $$\upsilon$$ is a function of $$r$$ with domain $$\left\lbrack {0,R} \right\rbrack$$ . For more detailed information, see W. Nichols, M. O’Rourke, and C. Vlachopoulos (eds.), McDonald’s Blood Flow in Arteries: Theoretical, Experimental, and Clinical Principles, 6th ed. (Boca Raton, FL, 2011). The average rate of change of the velocity as we move from $$r = r_{1}$$ outward to $$r = r_{2}$$ is given by $$\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta r} = \frac{v\left( r_{2} \right) - v\left( r_{1} \right)}{r_{2} - r_{1}}$$ and if we let $$\left. \Delta r\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we obtain the velocity gradient, that is, the instantaneous rate of change of velocity with respect to $$r$$ : $${velocity gradient} = \lim\limits_{\Delta r\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta r} = \frac{dv}{\mathit{dr}}$$ Using Equation 1, we obtain $$\frac{dv}{\mathit{dr}} = \frac{P}{4\eta l}\left( {0 - 2r} \right) = - \frac{Pr}{2\eta l}$$ For one of the smaller human arteries we can take $$\eta = 0.027$$ , $$R = 0.008{cm}$$ , $$l = 2{cm}$$ , and $$P = 4000{{dynes} \slash {cm}}^{2}$$ , which gives $$\begin{array}{l} {\upsilon = {\frac{4000}{4(0.027)2}{({0.000064 - r^{2}})}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon} \approx {1.85 \times 10^{4}({6.4 \times 10^{- 5} - r^{2}})}} \end{array}$$ At $$r = 0.002{cm}$$ the blood is flowing at a speed of $$\begin{array}{l} {{\upsilon(0.002)} \approx {1.85 \times 10^{4}({64 \times 10^{- 6} - 4 \times 10^{- 6}})}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon(0.002)} = {1.11{cm} \slash s}} \end{array}$$ and the velocity gradient at that point is $$\left. \frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dr}} \right|_{r = 0.002} = - \frac{4000(0.002)}{2(0.027)2} \approx - 74({{cm} \slash s}) \slash {cm}$$ To get a feeling for what this statement means, let’s change our units from centimeters to micrometers $$(1{cm} = 10,000{\mu m})$$ . Then the radius of the artery is $$80$$ μm. The velocity at the central axis is $$\left. 11,850\mu m\slash s \right.$$ , which decreases to $$\left. 11,110\mu m\slash s \right.$$ at a distance of $$r = 20{\mu m}$$ . The fact that $$\left. dv\slash dr = - 74\left( {\mu m}\slash s \right)\slash\mu m \right.$$ means that, when $$r = 20{\mu m}$$ , the velocity is decreasing at a rate of about $$\left. 74{\mu m}\slash s \right.$$ for each micrometer that we proceed away from the center.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Suppose C(x) is the total cost that a company incurs in producing x units of a certain commodity. The function C is called a cost function. If the number of items produced is increased from x_{1} to x_{2} , then the...
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose $$C(x)$$ is the total cost that a company incurs in producing $$x$$ units of a certain commodity. The function $$C$$ is called a cost function. If the number of items produced is increased from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ , then the additional cost is $$\Delta C = C\left( x_{2} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)$$ , and the average rate of change of the cost is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{C\left( x_{2} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)}{x_{2} - x_{1}} = \frac{C\left( {x_{1} + \Delta x} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)}{\Delta x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The limit of this quantity as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , that is, the instantaneous rate of change of cost with respect to the number of items produced, is called the marginal cost by economists:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${marginal cost} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{dC}{\mathit{dx}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>[Since $$x$$ often takes on only integer values, it may not make literal sense to let $$\Delta x$$ approach $$0$$ , but we can always replace $$C(x)$$ by a smooth approximating function as in Example 6.]</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Taking $$\Delta x = 1$$ and $$n$$ large (so that $$\Delta x$$ is small compared to $$n$$ ), we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C^{\prime}(n) \approx C\left( {n + 1} \right) - C(n)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus the marginal cost of producing $$n$$ units is approximately equal to the cost of producing one more unit [the $$(n + 1)$$ st unit].</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It is often appropriate to represent a total cost function by a polynomial</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C(x) = a + bx + cx^{2} + dx^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$a$$ represents the overhead cost (rent, heat, maintenance) and the other terms represent the cost of raw materials, labor, and so on. (The cost of raw materials may be proportional to $$x$$ , but labor costs might depend partly on higher powers of $$x$$ because of overtime costs and inefficiencies involved in large-scale operations.)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For instance, suppose a company has estimated that the cost (in dollars) of producing $$x$$ items is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C(x) = 10,000 + 5x + 0.01x^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then the marginal cost function is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C^{\prime}(x) = 5 + 0.02x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The marginal cost at the production level of $$500$$ items is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C^{\prime}(500) = 5 + 0.02(500) = \$ 15 \slash {item}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This gives the rate at which costs are increasing with respect to the production level when $$x = 500$$ and predicts the cost of the $$501$$ st item.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The actual cost of producing the $$501$$ st item is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{C(501) - C(500)} = {\lbrack{10,000 + 5(501) + 0.01{(501)}^{2}}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{10,000 + 5(500) + 0.01{(500)}^{2}}\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{C(501) - C(500)} = {\$ 15.01}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that $$C^{\prime}(500) \approx C(501) - C(500)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Theorem
snippet: Theorem: Theorem The only solutions of the differential equation {\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dt}} = ky are the exponential functions y(t) = y(0)e^{\mathit{kt}}
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem" title="Theorem">
    <heading level="3">Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>The only solutions of the differential equation $${\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dt}} = ky$$ are the exponential functions</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y(t) = y(0)e^{\mathit{kt}}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Use the fact that the world population was 2560 million in 1950 and 3040 million in 1960 to model the population of the world in the second half of the 20 th century. (Assume that the growth rate is proportional to the...
body_xml: Example 1 Use the fact that the world population was $$2560$$ million in 1950 and $$3040$$ million in 1960 to model the population of the world in the second half of the $$20$$ th century. (Assume that the growth rate is proportional to the population size.) What is the relative growth rate? Use the model to estimate the world population in 1993 and to predict the population in the year 2025. Solution We measure the time $$t$$ in years and let $$t = 0$$ in the year 1950. We measure the population $$P(t)$$ in millions of people. Then $$P(0) = 2560$$ and $$P(10) = 3040$$ . Since we are assuming that $$dP \slash dt = kP$$ , Theorem 2 gives $$\begin{array}{rll} {P(t)} & = & {P(0)e^{\mathit{kt}} = 2560e^{\mathit{kt}}} \\ {P(10)} & = & {2560e^{10k} = 3040} \\ k & = & {\frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{3040}{2560} \approx 0.017185} \end{array}$$ The relative growth rate is about $$1.7\%$$ per year and the model is $$P(t) = 2560e^{0.017185t}$$ We estimate that the world population in 1993 was $$P{(43)} = 2560e^{0.017185{(43)}} \approx 5360{million}$$ The model predicts that the population in 2025 will be $$P{(75)} = 2560e^{0.017185{(75)}} \approx 9289{million}$$ The graph in Figure 1 shows that the model is fairly accurate to the end of the $$20$$ th century (the dots represent the actual population), so the estimate for 1993 is quite reliable. But the prediction for 2025 may not be so accurate.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 The half-life of radium- 226 is 1590 years. (a) A sample of radium- 226 has mass 100 mg. Find a formula for the mass of the sample that remains after t years. (b) Find the mass remaining after 1000 years correct to the...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>The half-life of radium- $$226$$ is 1590 years.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) A sample of radium- $$226$$ has mass $$100$$ mg. Find a formula for the mass of the sample that remains after $$t$$ years.</item>
      <item>(b) Find the mass remaining after $$1000$$ years correct to the nearest milligram.</item>
      <item>(c) When will the mass be reduced to $$30$$ mg?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Let $$m(t)$$ be the mass of radium- $$226$$ (in milligrams) that remains after $$t$$ years. Then $$\mathit{dm} \slash dt = km$$ and $$m(0) = 100$$ , so Theorem 2 gives $$m(t) = m(0)e^{\mathit{kt}} = 100e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ In order to determine the value of $$k$$ , we use the fact that $$m(1590) = \frac{1}{2}(100)$$ . Thus $$100e^{1590k} = 50$$ so $$e^{1590k} = \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$\begin{array}{cll} {1590k} & = & {\ln\frac{1}{2} = - \ln 2} \\ k & = & {- \frac{\ln 2}{1590}} \end{array}$$ Therefore $$m(t) = 100e^{- {({\ln 2})}t \slash 1590}$$ We could use the fact that $$e^{\ln 2} = 2$$ to write the expression for $$m(t)$$ in the alternative form $$m(t) = 100 \times 2^{- t \slash 1590}$$</item>
      <item>(b) The mass remaining after $$1000$$ years is $$m{(1000)} = 100e^{- {({\ln 2})}1000 \slash 1590} \approx 65{mg}$$</item>
      <item>(c) We want to find the value of $$t$$ such that $$m(t) = 30$$ , that is, $$100e^{- {({\ln 2})}t \slash 1590} = 30$$ or $$e^{- {({\ln 2})}t \slash 1590} = 0.3$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>We solve this equation for $$t$$ by taking the natural logarithm of both sides:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{\ln 2}{1590}t = \ln 0.3$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t = - 1590\frac{\ln 0.3}{\ln 2} \approx 2762{years}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 A bottle of iced tea at room temperature \left( 72{}_{}^{} \right) is placed in a refrigerator where the temperature is 44{}_{}^{} . After half an hour the tea has cooled to 61{}_{}^{} . (a) What is the temperature of...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>A bottle of iced tea at room temperature $$\left( 72{}_{}^{} \right)$$ is placed in a refrigerator where the temperature is $$44{}_{}^{}$$ . After half an hour the tea has cooled to $$61{}_{}^{}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) What is the temperature of the tea after another half hour?</item>
      <item>(b) How long does it take for the tea to cool to $$50{}_{}^{}$$ ?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Let $$T(t)$$ be the temperature of the tea after $$t$$ minutes. The surrounding temperature is $$T_{s} = 44{}_{}^{}$$ , so Newton’s Law of Cooling states that $$\frac{dT}{\mathit{dt}} = k\left( {T - 44} \right)$$ If we let $$y = T - 44$$ , then $$y(0) = T(0) - 44 = 72 - 44 = 28$$ , so $$y$$ satisfies $${\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = ky} {y(0) = 28}$$ and by (2) we have $$y(t) = y(0)e^{\mathit{kt}} = 28e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ We are given that $$T(30) = 61$$ , so $$y(30) = 61 - 44 = 17$$ and $${28e^{ 30k} = 17} {e^{ 30k} = \frac{17}{28}}$$ Taking logarithms, we have $$k = \frac{\ln\left( \frac{17}{28} \right)}{30} \approx - 0.01663$$ Thus $$\begin{array}{rll} {y(t)} & = & {28e^{- 0.01663t}} \\ {T(t)} & = & {44 + 28e^{- 0.01663t}} \\ {T(60)} & = & {44 + 28e^{- 0.01663{(60)}} \approx 54.3} \end{array}$$ So after another half hour the tea has cooled to about $$54{}_{}^{}$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) We have $$T(t) = 50$$ when $$\begin{array}{rll} {44 + 28e^{- 0.01663t}} & = & 50 \\ e^{- 0.01663t} & = & \frac{6}{28} \\ t & = & {\frac{\ln\left( \frac{6}{28} \right)}{- 0.01663} \approx 92.6} \end{array}$$ The tea cools to $$50{}_{}^{}$$ after about $$1$$ hour $$33$$ minutes.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 If $$\$ 5000 is invested at 2\% interest, compounded annually, then after 1 year the investment is worth \$ 5000(1.02) = \$ 5100.00 , after 2 years it’s worth \left\lbrack {\$ 5000(1.02)} \right\rbrack(1.02) = \$...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$\$ 5000$$ is invested at $$2\%$$ interest, compounded annually, then after $$1$$ year the investment is worth $$\$ 5000(1.02) = \$ 5100.00$$ , after $$2$$ years it’s worth $$\left\lbrack {\$ 5000(1.02)} \right\rbrack(1.02) = \$ 5202.00$$ , and after $$t$$ years it’s worth $$\$ 5000(1.02)^{t}$$ . In general, if an amount $$A_{0}$$ is invested at an interest rate $$r\left( {r = 0.02{in this example}} \right)$$ , then after $$t$$ years it’s worth $$A_{0}\left( {1 + r} \right)^{t}$$ . Usually, however, interest is compounded more frequently, say, $$n$$ times a year. Then in each compounding period the interest rate is $$r \slash n$$ and there are $$nt$$ compounding periods in $$t$$ years, so the value of the investment is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A = A_{0}\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For instance, after $$3$$ years at $$2\%$$ interest a $$\$ 5000$$ investment will be worth</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {\$ 5000(1.02)^{3}} & = & {\$ 5306.04{with annual compounding}} \\ {\$ 5000(1.01)^{6}} & = & {\$ 5307.60{with semiannual compounding}} \\ {\$ 5000(1.005)^{12}} & = & {\$ 5308.39{with quarterly compounding}} \\ {\$ 5000\left( {1 + \frac{0.02}{12}} \right)^{36}} & = & {\$ 5308.92{with monthly compounding}} \\ {\$ 5000\left( {1 + \frac{0.02}{365}} \right)^{365 \cdot 3}} & = & {\$ 5309.17{with daily compounding}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>You can see that the interest paid increases as the number of compounding periods $$(n)$$ increases. If we let $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , then we will be compounding the interest continuously and the value of the investment will be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{A(t)} = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}A_{0}\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}}} \\ {\phantom{A(t)} = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}A_{0}\left\lbrack \left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n \slash r} \right\rbrack^{rt}}} \\ {\phantom{A(t)} = {A_{0}\left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n \slash r}} \right\rbrack^{rt}}} \\ {\phantom{A(t)} = {A_{0}\left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{m\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{m}} \right)^{m}} \right\rbrack^{rt} \left( {{where}m = {n \slash r}} \right)}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Equation 3.6.6:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{n}} \right)^{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>But the limit in this expression is equal to the number $$e$$ (see Equation 3.6.6). So with continuous compounding of interest at interest rate $$r$$ , the amount after $$t$$ years is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A(t) = A_{0}e^{ rt}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we differentiate this equation, we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dA}{\mathit{dt}} = rA_{0}e^{ rt} = rA(t)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which says that, with continuous compounding of interest, the rate of increase of an investment is proportional to its size.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Returning to the example of $$\$ 5000$$ invested for $$3$$ years at $$2\%$$ interest, we see that with continuously compounding of interest the value of the investment will be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A(3) = \$ 5000e^{{(0.02)}3} = \$ 5309.18$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice how close this is to the amount we calculated for daily compounding, $$\$ 5309.17$$ . But the amount is easier to compute if we use continuous compounding.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Air is being pumped into a spherical balloon so that its volume increases at a rate of 100{{cm}^{3} \slash s} . How fast is the radius of the balloon increasing when the diameter is 50 cm? According to the Principles...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="3">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Air is being pumped into a spherical balloon so that its volume increases at a rate of $$100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}$$ . How fast is the radius of the balloon increasing when the diameter is $$50$$ cm?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>According to the Principles of Problem Solving discussed following Chapter 1, the first step is to understand the problem. This includes reading the problem carefully, identifying the given and the unknown, and introducing suitable notation.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We start by identifying two things:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>the given information:</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the rate of increase of the volume of air is $$100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>and the unknown:</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the rate of increase of the radius when the diameter is $$50$$ cm</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>In order to express these quantities mathematically, we introduce some suggestive notation:</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Let $$V$$ be the volume of the balloon and let $$r$$ be its radius.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>The key thing to remember is that rates of change are derivatives. In this problem, the volume and the radius are both functions of the time $$t$$ . The rate of increase of the volume with respect to time is the derivative $$dV \slash dt$$ , and the rate of increase of the radius is $$dr \slash dt$$ . We can therefore restate the given and the unknown as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\mathit{Given}:} & { \frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = 100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}} \\ {\mathit{Unknown}:} & { \frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} {when}r = 25{cm}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The second stage of problem solving is to think of a plan for connecting the given and the unknown.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In order to connect $$dV \slash dt$$ and $$dr \slash dt$$ , we first relate $$V$$ and $$r$$ by a formula—in this case, the formula for the volume of a sphere:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In order to use the given information, we differentiate each side of this equation with respect to $$t$$ . To differentiate the right side, we need to use the Chain Rule:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{dV}{\mathit{dr}}\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = 4\pi r^{2}\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now we solve for the unknown quantity:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{4\pi r^{2}}\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we put $$r = 25$$ and $$dV \slash dt = 100$$ in this equation, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{4\pi(25)^{2}}100 = \frac{1}{25\pi}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The radius of the balloon is increasing at the rate of $$1 \slash \left( {25\pi} \right) \approx 0.0127{{cm} \slash s}$$ when the diameter is $$50{cm}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that, although $${dV} \slash \mathit{dt}$$ is constant, $$\mathit{dr} \slash \mathit{dt}$$ is not constant.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 A ladder 10 ft long rests against a vertical wall. If the bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a rate of 4{{ft} \slash s} , how fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the bottom of the...
body_xml: Example 2 A ladder $$10$$ ft long rests against a vertical wall. If the bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a rate of $$4{{ft} \slash s}$$ , how fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the bottom of the ladder is $$6$$ ft from the wall? Solution We first draw a diagram and label it as in Figure 1. Let $$x$$ feet be the distance from the bottom of the ladder to the wall and $$y$$ feet the distance from the top of the ladder to the ground. Note that $$x$$ and $$y$$ are both functions of $$t$$ (time, measured in seconds). We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4{{ft} \slash s}$$ and we are asked to find $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt$$ when $$x = 6$$ ft (see Figure 2). In this problem, the relationship between $$x$$ and $$y$$ is given by the Pythagorean Theorem: $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 100$$ Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ using the Chain Rule, we have $$2x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = 0$$ Solving this equation for the desired rate, we obtain $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{x}{y}\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}$$ When $$x = 6$$ , the Pythagorean Theorem gives $$y = 8$$ and so, substituting these values and $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4$$ , we have $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{6}{8}(4) = - 3{ft} \slash s$$ The fact that $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt$$ is negative means that the distance from the top of the ladder to the ground is decreasing at a rate of $$3{{ft} \slash s}$$ . In other words, the top of the ladder is sliding down the wall at a rate of $$3{{ft} \slash s}$$ .

title: Problem Solving Strategy
snippet: Problem Solving Strategy: Problem Solving Strategy Look back: What have we learned from Examples 1 and 2 that will help us solve future problems? It is useful to recall some of the problem-solving principles and adapt them to related rates...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem Solving Strategy" title="Problem Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="3">Problem Solving Strategy</heading>
    <paragraph>Look back: What have we learned from Examples 1 and 2 that will help us solve future problems?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It is useful to recall some of the problem-solving principles and adapt them to related rates in light of our experience in Examples 1 and 2:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Read the problem carefully.</item>
      <item>Draw a diagram if possible.</item>
      <item>Introduce notation. Assign symbols to all quantities that are functions of time.</item>
      <item>Express the given information and the required rate in terms of derivatives.</item>
      <item>Write an equation that relates the various quantities of the problem. If necessary, use the geometry of the situation to eliminate one of the variables by substitution (see Example 3).</item>
      <item>Use the Chain Rule to differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $$t$$ .</item>
      <item>Substitute the given information into the resulting equation and solve for the unknown rate.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>See also Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 A water tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with base radius 2 m and height 4 m. If water is being pumped into the tank at a rate of 2{m^{3} \slash \min} , find the rate at which the water level is rising...
body_xml: Example 3 A water tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with base radius $$2$$ m and height $$4$$ m. If water is being pumped into the tank at a rate of $$2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ , find the rate at which the water level is rising when the water is $$3$$ m deep. Solution We first sketch the cone and label it as in Figure 3. Let $$V$$ , $$r$$ , and $$h$$ be the volume of the water, the radius of the surface, and the height of the water at time $$t$$ , where $$t$$ is measured in minutes. We are given that $$dV \slash dt = 2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ and we are asked to find $$dh \slash dt$$ when $$h$$ is $$3$$ m. The quantities $$V$$ and $$h$$ are related by the equation $$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h$$ but it is very useful to express $$V$$ as a function of $$h$$ alone. In order to eliminate $$r$$ , we use the similar triangles in Figure 3 to write $${\frac{r}{h} = \frac{2}{4}} {r = \frac{h}{2}}$$ and the expression for $$V$$ becomes $$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi\left( \frac{h}{2} \right)^{2}h = \frac{\pi}{12}h^{3}$$ Now we can differentiate each side with respect to $$t$$ : $$\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{\pi}{4}h^{2}\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}}$$ so $$\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{4}{\pi h^{2}}\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}}$$ Substituting $$h = 3$$ m and $$dV \slash dt = 2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ , we have $$\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{4}{\pi(3)^{2}} \cdot 2 = \frac{8}{9\pi}$$ The water level is rising at a rate of $$8 \slash \left( {9\pi} \right) \approx 0.28{m \slash \min}$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Car A is traveling west at 50{{mi} \slash h} and car B is traveling north at 60{{mi} \slash h} . Both are headed for the intersection of the two roads. At what rate are the cars approaching each other when car A is 0.3...
body_xml: Example 4 Car A is traveling west at $$50{{mi} \slash h}$$ and car B is traveling north at $$60{{mi} \slash h}$$ . Both are headed for the intersection of the two roads. At what rate are the cars approaching each other when car A is $$0.3$$ mi and car B is $$0.4$$ mi from the intersection? Solution We draw Figure 4, where $$C$$ is the intersection of the roads. At a given time $$t$$ , let $$x$$ be the distance from car $$A$$ to $$C$$ , let $$y$$ be the distance from car $$B$$ to $$C$$ , and let $$z$$ be the distance between the cars, where $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ are measured in miles. We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = - 50{{mi} \slash h}$$ and $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt = - 60{{mi} \slash h}$$ . (The derivatives are negative because $$x$$ and $$y$$ are decreasing.) We are asked to find $$dz \slash dt$$ . The equation that relates $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ is given by the Pythagorean Theorem: $$z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{rll} {2z\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}}} & = & {2x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}} \\ \frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}} & = & {\frac{1}{z}\left( {x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}} \right)} \end{array}$$ When $$x = 0.3$$ mi and $$y = 0.4$$ mi, the Pythagorean Theorem gives $$z = 0.5$$ mi, so $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}} = {\frac{1}{0.5}\left\lbrack {0.3\left( {- 50} \right) + 0.4\left( {- 60} \right)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}}} = {- 78{mi} \slash h}} \end{array}$$ The cars are approaching each other at a rate of $$78{mi} \slash h$$ .

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 A man walks along a straight path at a speed of 4{{ft} \slash s} . A spotlight is located on the ground 20 ft from the path and is kept focused on the man. At what rate is the spotlight rotating when the man is 15 ft...
body_xml: Example 5 A man walks along a straight path at a speed of $$4{{ft} \slash s}$$ . A spotlight is located on the ground $$20$$ ft from the path and is kept focused on the man. At what rate is the spotlight rotating when the man is $$15$$ ft from the point on the path closest to the light? Solution We draw Figure 5 and let $$x$$ be the distance from the man to the point on the path closest to the spotlight. We let $$\theta$$ be the angle between the beam of the light and the perpendicular to the path. We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4{{ft} \slash s}$$ and are asked to find $$d\theta \slash dt$$ when $$x = 15$$ . The equation that relates $$x$$ and $$\theta$$ can be written from Figure 5: $${\frac{x}{20} = \tan\theta} {x = 20\tan\theta}$$ Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ , we get $$\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} = 20\sec^{2}\theta\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}}$$ so $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}} = {\frac{1}{20}\cos^{2}\theta\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}}} = {\frac{1}{20}\cos^{2}\theta(4) = \frac{1}{5}\cos^{2}\theta}} \end{array}$$ When $$x = 15$$ , the length of the beam is $$25$$ , so $$\cos\theta = \frac{20}{25} = \frac{4}{5}$$ and $$\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{5}\left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{2} = \frac{16}{125} = 0.128$$ The spotlight is rotating at a rate of $$0.128{{rad} \slash s}$$ . $$0.128\frac{rad}{s} \times \frac{1{rotation}}{2\pi{rad}} \times \frac{60s}{1\min} \approx 1.22{rotations per min}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the linearization of the function f(x) = \sqrt{x + 3} at a = 1 and use it to approximate the numbers \sqrt{3.98} and \sqrt{4.05} . Are these approximations overestimates or underestimates? Solution The derivative...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the linearization of the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}$$ at $$a = 1$$ and use it to approximate the numbers $$\sqrt{3.98}$$ and $$\sqrt{4.05}$$ . Are these approximations overestimates or underestimates? Solution The derivative of $$f(x) = \left( {x + 3} \right)^{1 \slash 2}$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left( {x + 3} \right)^{- 1 \slash 2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x + 3}}$$ and so we have $$f(1) = 2$$ and $$f^{\prime}(1) = \frac{1}{4}$$ . Putting these values into Equation 1, we see that the linearization is $$L(x) = f(1) + f^{\prime}(1)\left( {x - 1} \right) = 2 + \frac{1}{4}\left( {x - 1} \right) = \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4}$$ The corresponding linear approximation (2) is $$\sqrt{x + 3} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4} \left( {{when}x{is near}1} \right)$$ In particular, we have $$\sqrt{3.98} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{0.98}{4} = 1.995$$ and $$\sqrt{4.05} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{1.05}{4} = 2.0125$$ The linear approximation is illustrated in Figure 2. We see that, indeed, the tangent line approximation is a good approximation to the given function when $$x$$ is near $$1$$ . We also see that our approximations are overestimates because the tangent line lies above the curve. Of course, a calculator could give us approximations for $$\sqrt{3.98}$$ and $$\sqrt{4.05}$$ , but the linear approximation gives an approximation over an entire interval.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 For what values of x is the linear approximation \sqrt{x + 3} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4} accurate to within 0.5 ? What about accuracy to within 0.1 ? Solution Accuracy to within 0.5 means that the functions...
body_xml: Example 2 For what values of $$x$$ is the linear approximation $$\sqrt{x + 3} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4}$$ accurate to within $$0.5$$ ? What about accuracy to within $$0.1$$ ? Solution Accuracy to within $$0.5$$ means that the functions should differ by less than $$0.5$$ : $$\left| {\sqrt{x + 3} - \left( {\frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4}} \right)} \right| < 0.5$$ Equivalently, we could write $$\sqrt{x + 3} - 0.5 < \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4} < \sqrt{x + 3} + 0.5$$ This says that the linear approximation should lie between the curves obtained by shifting the curve $$y = \sqrt{x + 3}$$ upward and downward by an amount $$0.5$$ . Figure 3 shows the tangent line $$y = \left( {7 + x} \right) \slash 4$$ intersecting the upper curve $$y = \sqrt{x + 3} + 0.5$$ at $$P$$ and $$Q$$ . We estimate that the $$x$$ -coordinate of $$P$$ is about $$- 2.66$$ and the $$x$$ -coordinate of $$Q$$ is about $$8.66$$ . Thus we see from the graph that the approximation $$\sqrt{x + 3} \approx \frac{7}{4} + \frac{x}{4}$$ is accurate to within $$0.5$$ when $$- 2.6 < x < 8.6$$ . (We have rounded the smaller value up and the larger value down.) Similarly, from Figure 4 we see that the approximation is accurate to within $$0.1$$ when $$- 1.1 < x < 3.9$$ .

body_xml: Example 3 Compare the values of $$\Delta y$$ and $$\mathit{dy}$$ if $$y = f(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} - 2x + 1$$ and $$x$$ changes (a) from $$2$$ to $$2.05$$ and (b) from $$2$$ to $$2.01$$ . Solution (a) We have $$\begin{array}{rll} {f(2)} & = & {2^{3} + 2^{2} - 2(2) + 1 = 9} \\ {f(2.05)} & = & {(2.05)^{3} + (2.05)^{2} - 2(2.05) + 1 = 9.717625} \\ {\Delta y} & = & {f(2.05) - f(2) = 0.717625} \end{array}$$ In general, $$\mathit{dy} = f^{\prime}{(x)}\mathit{dx} = {({3x^{2} + 2x - 2})}\mathit{dx}$$ When $$x = 2$$ and $$\mathit{dx} = \Delta x = 0.05$$ , this becomes $$\mathit{dy} = {\lbrack{3(2)^{2} + 2(2) - 2}\rbrack}0.05 = 0.7$$ (b) $$\begin{array}{rll} {f(2.01)} & = & {(2.01)^{3} + (2.01)^{2} - 2(2.01) + 1 = 9.140701} \\ {\Delta y} & = & {f(2.01) - f(2) = 0.140701} \end{array}$$ When $$\mathit{dx} = \Delta x = 0.01$$ , $$\mathit{dy} = {\lbrack{3(2)^{2} + 2(2) - 2}\rbrack}0.01 = 0.14$$ Figure 6 shows the function in Example 3 and a comparison of $$\mathit{dy}$$ and $$\Delta y$$ when $$a = 2$$ . The viewing rectangle is $$\left\lbrack {1.8,2.5} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {6,18} \right\rbrack$$ .

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>The radius of a sphere was measured and found to be $$21$$ cm with a possible error in measurement of at most $$0.05$$ cm. What is the maximum error in using this value of the radius to compute the volume of the sphere?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If the radius of the sphere is $$r$$ , then its volume is $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$ . If the error in the measured value of $$r$$ is denoted by $$dr = \Delta r$$ , then the corresponding error in the calculated value of $$V$$ is $$\Delta V$$ , which can be approximated by the differential</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$dV = 4\pi r^{2}dr$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>When $$r = 21$$ and $$dr = 0.05$$ , this becomes</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$dV = 4\pi(21)^{2}0.05 \approx 277$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The maximum error in the calculated volume is about $$277{cm}^{3}$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that $$\sinh^{- 1}x = \ln{({x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}})}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Let $$y = \sinh^{- 1}x$$ . Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = \sinh y = \frac{e^{ y} - e^{- y}}{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{ y} - 2x - e^{- y} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or, multiplying by $$e^{ y}$$ ,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{2y} - 2xe^{ y} - 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is really a quadratic equation in $$e^{ y}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( e^{ y} \right)^{2} - 2x\left( e^{ y} \right) - 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving by the quadratic formula, we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{ y} = \frac{2x \pm \sqrt{4x^{2} + 4}}{2} = x \pm \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that $$e^{ y} > 0$$ , but $$x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 1} < 0$$ (because $$x < \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ ). Thus the minus sign is inadmissible and we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{ y} = x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \ln{(e^{ y})} = \ln\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This shows that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sinh^{- 1}x = \ln\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(See Exercise 29 for another method.)</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Prove that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh^{- 1}x} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1 Let $$y = \sinh^{- 1}x$$ . Then $$\sinh y = x$$ . If we differentiate this equation implicitly with respect to $$x$$ , we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\cosh y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$\cosh^{2}y - \sinh^{2}y = 1$$ and $$\cosh y \geqslant 0$$ , we have $$\cosh y = \sqrt{1 + \sinh^{2}y}$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{\cosh y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \sinh^{2}y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2 From Equation 3 (proved in Example 3), we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({\sinh^{- 1}x})}} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\ln\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh^{- 1}x} \right)} = {\frac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh^{- 1}x} \right)} = {\frac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}\left( {1 + \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh^{- 1}x} \right)} = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + x}{\left( x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1} \right)\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh^{- 1}x} \right)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="5">

title: Definition

body_xml: Example 5 If $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . But $$f$$ has no maximum or minimum at $$0$$ , as you can see from its graph in Figure 12. (Or observe that $$x^{3} > 0$$ for $$x > 0$$ but $$x^{3} < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ .) The fact that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ simply means that the curve $$y = x^{3}$$ has a horizontal tangent at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Instead of having a maximum or minimum at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , the curve crosses its horizontal tangent there.
