title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A critical number of a function f is a number c in the domain of f such that either f^{\prime}(c) = 0 or f^{\prime}(c) does not exist.
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A critical number of a function $$f$$ is a number $$c$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that either $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Find the critical numbers of f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1 and f(x) = x^{3 \slash 5}\left( {4 - x} \right) . Solution The derivative of f is f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 6x = 3x(x - 2) . Since f^{\prime}(x) exists for all x ,...
body_xml: Example 7 Find the critical numbers of $$f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1$$ and $$f(x) = x^{3 \slash 5}\left( {4 - x} \right)$$ . Solution The derivative of $$f$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 6x = 3x(x - 2)$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ exists for all $$x$$ , the only critical numbers of $$f$$ occur when $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , that is, when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 2$$ . First note that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The Product Rule gives $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {x^{3 \slash 5}\left( {- 1} \right) + \left( {4 - x} \right)\left( {\frac{3}{5}x^{- 2 \slash 5}} \right) = - x^{3 \slash 5} + \frac{3\left( {4 - x} \right)}{5x^{2 \slash 5}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{- 5x + 3\left( {4 - x} \right)}{5x^{2 \slash 5}} = \frac{12 - 8x}{5x^{2 \slash 5}}}} \end{array}$$ [The same result could be obtained by first writing $$f(x) = 4x^{3 \slash 5} - x^{8 \slash 5}$$ .] Therefore $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ if $$12 - 8x = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \frac{3}{2}$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist when $$x = 0$$ . Thus the critical numbers are $$\frac{3}{2}$$ and $$0$$ . Figure 14 shows a graph of the function $$f$$ in Example 7(b). It supports our answer because there is a horizontal tangent when $$x = 1.5$$ [where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ ] and a vertical tangent when $$x = 0$$ [where $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is undefined].

title: The Closed Interval Method
snippet: The Closed Interval Method: The Closed Interval Method To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function f on a closed interval \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack : Find the values of f at the critical numbers of f in...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="The Closed Interval Method" title="The Closed Interval Method">
    <heading level="4">The Closed Interval Method</heading>
    <paragraph>To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function $$f$$ on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ :</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find the values of $$f$$ at the critical numbers of $$f$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the values of $$f$$ at the endpoints of the interval.</item>
      <item>The largest of the values from Steps 1 and 2 is the absolute maximum value; the smallest of these values is the absolute minimum value.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function {f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1} {- \frac{1}{2} \leqslant x \leqslant 4} Solution Since f is continuous on \left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2},4} \right\rbrack , we can...
body_xml: Example 8 Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $${f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1} {- \frac{1}{2} \leqslant x \leqslant 4}$$ Solution Since $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2},4} \right\rbrack$$ , we can use the Closed Interval Method. Example 7(a) we found the critical numbers $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 2$$ . Notice that each of these critical numbers lies in the interval $$\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2},4} \right\rbrack$$ . The values of $$f$$ at these critical numbers are $${f(0) = 1} {f(2) = - 3}$$ The values of $$f$$ at the endpoints of the interval are $${f\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{8}} {f(4) = 17}$$ Comparing these four numbers, we see that the absolute maximum value is $$f(4) = 17$$ and the absolute minimum value is $$f(2) = - 3$$ . In this example the absolute maximum occurs at an endpoint, whereas the absolute minimum occurs at a critical number. The graph of $$f$$ is sketched in Figure 15.

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 (a) Use a calculator or computer to estimate the absolute minimum and maximum values of the function {f(x) = x - 2\sin x},{0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi} . (b) Use calculus to find the exact minimum and maximum values....
body_xml:
<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Use a calculator or computer to estimate the absolute minimum and maximum values of the function $${f(x) = x - 2\sin x},{0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi}$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Use calculus to find the exact minimum and maximum values.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Figure 16 shows a graph of $$f$$ in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 1,8} \right\rbrack$$ . The absolute maximum value is about $$6.97$$ and it occurs when $$x \approx 5.24$$ . Similarly, the absolute minimum value is about $$- 0.68$$ and it occurs when $$x \approx 1.05$$ . It is possible to get more accurate numerical estimates, but for exact values we must use calculus. Figure 16 Details A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from 0 to 2 pi and the vertical axis is displayed from negative 1 to 8. The curve begins at the origin, goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant, concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (pi/3, negative 0.6), then goes up and to the right through the approximate point (1.9, 0), becoming concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (5 pi/3, 6.97), and then goes down and to the right, exits the viewing window at approximately (2 pi, 6.4).</item>
      <item>(b) The function $$f(x) = x - 2\sin x$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 - 2\cos x$$ , we have $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$$ and this occurs when $$x = \pi \slash 3$$ or $$5\pi \slash 3$$ . The values of $$f$$ at these critical numbers are $$f\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{\pi}{3} - 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3} \approx - 0.684853$$ and $$f\left( {5\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{5\pi}{3} - 2\sin\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{5\pi}{3} + \sqrt{3} \approx 6.968039$$ The values of $$f$$ at the endpoints are $$f(0) = 0 f\left( {2\pi} \right) = 2\pi \approx 6.28$$ Comparing these four numbers and using the Closed Interval Method, we see that the absolute minimum value is $$f\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right) = \pi \slash 3 - \sqrt{3}$$ and the absolute maximum value is $$f\left( {5\pi \slash 3} \right) = 5\pi \slash 3 + \sqrt{3}$$ . The values from part (a) serve as a check on our work.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed on April 24, 1990, by the space shuttle Discovery. A model for the velocity of the shuttle during this mission, from liftoff at t = 0 until the solid rocket boosters were...
body_xml: Example 10 The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed on April 24, 1990, by the space shuttle Discovery. A model for the velocity of the shuttle during this mission, from liftoff at $$t = 0$$ until the solid rocket boosters were jettisoned at $$t = 126{seconds}$$ , is given by $$\upsilon(t) = 0.001302t^{3} - 0.09029t^{2} + 23.61t - 3.083$$ (in feet per second). Using this model, estimate the absolute maximum and minimum values of the acceleration of the shuttle between liftoff and the jettisoning of the boosters. Solution We are asked for the extreme values not of the given velocity function, but rather of the acceleration function. So we first need to differentiate to find the acceleration: $$\begin{array}{l} {{a(t)} = {\upsilon^{\prime}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}{({0.001302t^{3} - 0.09029t^{2} + 23.61t - 3.083})}}} \\ {\phantom{a(t)} = {0.003906t^{2} - 0.18058t + 23.61}} \end{array}$$ We now apply the Closed Interval Method to the continuous function $$a$$ on the interval $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 126$$ . Its derivative is $$a^{\prime}(t) = 0.007812t - 0.18058$$ The only critical number occurs when $$a^{\prime}(t) = 0$$ : $$t_{1} = \frac{0.18058}{0.007812} \approx 23.12$$ Evaluating $$a(t)$$ at the critical number and at the endpoints, we have $${a(0) = 23.61} {a\left( t_{1} \right) \approx 21.52} {a(126) \approx 62.87}$$ So the maximum acceleration is about $$62.87{{ft} \slash s}^{2}$$ and the minimum acceleration is about $$21.52{{ft} \slash s}^{2}$$ .

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let’s apply Rolle’s Theorem to the position function s = f(t) of a moving object. If the object is in the same place at two different instants t = a and t = b , then f(a) = f(b) . Rolle’s Theorem says that there is...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let’s apply Rolle’s Theorem to the position function $$s = f(t)$$ of a moving object. If the object is in the same place at two different instants $$t = a$$ and $$t = b$$ , then $$f(a) = f(b)$$ . Rolle’s Theorem says that there is some instant of time $$t = c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ when $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ ; that is, the velocity is $$0$$ . (In particular, you can see that this is true when a ball is thrown directly upward.)</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Prove that the equation x^{3} + x - 1 = 0 has exactly one real solution. Solution First we use the Intermediate Value Theorem (2.5.10) to show that a solution exists. Let f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1 . Then f(0) = - 1 < 0 and...
body_xml: Example 2 Prove that the equation $$x^{3} + x - 1 = 0$$ has exactly one real solution. Solution First we use the Intermediate Value Theorem (2.5.10) to show that a solution exists. Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1$$ . Then $$f(0) = - 1 < 0$$ and $$f(1) = 1 > 0$$ . Since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is continuous, so the Intermediate Value Theorem states that there is a number $$c$$ between $$0$$ and $$1$$ such that $$f(c) = 0$$ . Thus the given equation has a solution. To show that the equation has no other real solution, we use Rolle’s Theorem and argue by contradiction. Suppose that it had two solutions $$a$$ and $$b$$ . Then $$f(a) = 0 = f(b)$$ and, since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is differentiable on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Thus, by Rolle’s Theorem, there is a number $$c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ such that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ . But $${f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} + 1 \geqslant 1} {{for all}x}$$ (since $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ ) so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ can never be $$0$$ . This gives a contradiction. Therefore the equation can’t have two real solutions. Figure 2 shows a graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1$$ discussed in Example 2. Rolle’s Theorem shows that, no matter how much we enlarge the viewing rectangle, we can never find a second $$x$$ -intercept.

title: The Mean Value Theorem
snippet: The Mean Value Theorem: The Mean Value Theorem Let f be a function that satisfies the following hypotheses: f is continuous on the closed interval \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack . f is differentiable on the open interval \left( {a,b}...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The Mean Value Theorem" title="The Mean Value Theorem">
    <heading level="4">The Mean Value Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function that satisfies the following hypotheses:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f$$ is continuous on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .</item>
      <item>$$f$$ is differentiable on the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Then there is a number $$c$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or, equivalently,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(b) - f(a) = f^{\prime}(c)(b - a)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The Mean Value Theorem is an example of what is called an existence theorem. Like the Intermediate Value Theorem, the Extreme Value Theorem, and Rolle’s Theorem, it guarantees that there exists a number with a certain property, but it doesn’t tell us how to find the number.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 To illustrate the Mean Value Theorem with a specific function, let’s consider f(x) = x^{3} - x , a = 0 , b = 2 . Since f is a polynomial, it is continuous and differentiable for all x , so it is certainly continuous on...
body_xml: Example 3 To illustrate the Mean Value Theorem with a specific function, let’s consider $$f(x) = x^{3} - x$$ , $$a = 0$$ , $$b = 2$$ . Since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is continuous and differentiable for all $$x$$ , so it is certainly continuous on $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ and differentiable on $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ . Therefore, by the Mean Value Theorem, there is a number $$c$$ in $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ such that $$f(2) - f(0) = f^{\prime}(c)\left( {2 - 0} \right)$$ Now $$f(2) = 6$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 1$$ , so the above equation becomes $$6 = {({3c^{ 2} - 1})}2 = 6c^{ 2} - 2$$ which gives $$c^{ 2} = \frac{4}{3}$$ , that is, $$c = \pm 2 \slash \sqrt{3}$$ . But $$c$$ must lie in $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ , so $$c = 2 \slash \sqrt{3}$$ . Figure 6 illustrates this calculation: The tangent line at this value of $$c$$ is parallel to the secant line $$OB$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 If an object moves in a straight line with position function s = f(t) , then the average velocity between t = a and t = b is \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} and the velocity at t = c is f^{\prime}(c) . Thus the Mean Value...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>If an object moves in a straight line with position function $$s = f(t)$$ , then the average velocity between $$t = a$$ and $$t = b$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and the velocity at $$t = c$$ is $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ . Thus the Mean Value Theorem (in the form of Equation 1) tells us that at some time $$t = c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ the instantaneous velocity $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ is equal to that average velocity. For instance, if a car traveled $$180$$ km in $$2$$ hours, then the speedometer must have read $$90{km} \slash h$$ at least once.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In general, the Mean Value Theorem can be interpreted as saying that there is a number at which the instantaneous rate of change is equal to the average rate of change over an interval.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Suppose that f(0) = - 3 and f^{\prime}(x) \leqslant 5 for all values of x . How large can f(2) possibly be? Solution We are given that f is differentiable (and therefore continuous) everywhere. In particular, we can...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that $$f(0) = - 3$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) \leqslant 5$$ for all values of $$x$$ . How large can $$f(2)$$ possibly be?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We are given that $$f$$ is differentiable (and therefore continuous) everywhere. In particular, we can apply the Mean Value Theorem on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ . There exists a number $$c$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(2) - f(0) = f^{\prime}(c)\left( {2 - 0} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(2) = f(0) + 2f^{\prime}(c) = - 3 + 2f^{\prime}(c)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We are given that $$f^{\prime}(x) \leqslant 5$$ for all $$x$$ , so in particular we know that $$f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant 5$$ . Multiplying both sides of this inequality by $$2$$ , we have $$2f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant 10$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(2) = - 3 + 2f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant - 3 + 10 = 7$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The largest possible value for $$f(2)$$ is $$7$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Theorem
snippet: Theorem: Theorem If f^{\prime}(x) = 0 for all x in an interval \left( {a,b} \right) , then f is constant on \left( {a,b} \right) .
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem" title="Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ for all $$x$$ in an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is constant on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Corollary
snippet: Corollary: Corollary If f^{\prime}(x) = g^{\prime}(x) for all x in an interval \left( {a,b} \right) , then f - g is constant on \left( {a,b} \right) ; that is, f(x) = g(x) + c where c is a constant.
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Corollary" title="Corollary">
    <heading level="4">Corollary</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f^{\prime}(x) = g^{\prime}(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f - g$$ is constant on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ ; that is, $$f(x) = g(x) + c$$ where $$c$$ is a constant.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Prove the identity \tan^{- 1}x + \cot^{- 1}x = \pi \slash 2 . Solution Although calculus isn’t needed to prove this identity, the proof using calculus is quite simple. If f(x) = \tan^{- 1}x + \cot^{- 1}x , then...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Prove the identity $$\tan^{- 1}x + \cot^{- 1}x = \pi \slash 2$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Although calculus isn’t needed to prove this identity, the proof using calculus is quite simple. If $$f(x) = \tan^{- 1}x + \cot^{- 1}x$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}} - \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>for all values of $$x$$ . Therefore $$f(x) = C$$ , a constant. To determine the value of $$C$$ , we put $$x = 1$$ [because we can evaluate $$f(1)$$ exactly]. Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C = f(1) = \tan^{- 1}1 + \cot^{- 1}1 = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$\tan^{- 1}x + \cot^{- 1}x = \pi \slash 2$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find where the function f(x) = 3x^{4} - 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 5 is increasing and where it is decreasing. Solution We start by differentiating f : f^{\prime}(x) = 12x^{3} - 12x^{2} - 24x = 12x\left( {x - 2} \right)\left(...
body_xml:
Example 1 Find where the function $$f(x) = 3x^{4} - 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 5$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing. Solution We start by differentiating $$f$$ : $$f^{\prime}(x) = 12x^{3} - 12x^{2} - 24x = 12x\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ To use the I/D Test we have to know where $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ and where $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . To solve these inequalities we first find where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , namely at $$x = 0,2,{and} - 1$$ . These are the critical numbers of $$f$$ , and they divide the domain into four intervals (see the number line Figure 2). Within each interval, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ must be always positive or always negative. (See Examples 3 and 4 in Appendix A.) We can determine which is the case for each interval from the signs of the three factors of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , namely, $$12x$$ , $$x - 2$$ , and $$x + 1$$ as shown in the following chart. A plus sign indicates that the given expression is positive, and a minus sign indicates that it is negative. The last column of the chart gives the conclusion based on the I/D Test. For instance, $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$0 < x < 2$$ , so $$f$$ is decreasing on $$(0,2)$$ . (It would also be true to say that $$f$$ is decreasing on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ .) Interval $$12x$$ $$x - 2$$ $$x + 1$$ $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ $$f$$ $$x < - 1$$ − − − − decreasing on $$( - \infty, - 1)$$ $$- 1 < x < 0$$ − − + + increasing on $$( - 1,0)$$ $$0 < x < 2$$ + − + − decreasing on $$(0,2)$$ $$x > 2$$ + + + + increasing on $$(2,\infty)$$
The graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 3 confirms the information in the chart.

title: The First Derivative Test
snippet: The First Derivative Test: The First Derivative Test Suppose that c is a critical number of a continuous function f . (a) If f^{\prime} changes from positive to negative at c , then f has a local maximum at c . (b) If f^{\prime} changes...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The First Derivative Test" title="The First Derivative Test">
    <heading level="4">The First Derivative Test</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that $$c$$ is a critical number of a continuous function $$f$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ .</item>
      <item>(c) If $$f^{\prime}$$ is positive to the left and right of $$c$$ , or negative to the left and right of $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has no local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<example number="2">

    <paragraph>Solution From the chart in the solution to Example 1 we see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$- 1$$ , so $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ is a local minimum value by the First Derivative Test. Similarly, $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$2$$ , so $$f(2) = - 27$$ is also a local minimum value. As noted previously, $$f(0) = 5$$ is a local maximum value because $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ .</paragraph>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the local maximum and minimum values of the function {g(x) = x + 2\sin x} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi} Solution As in Example 1, we start by finding the critical numbers. The derivative is g^{\prime}(x) = 1 +...
body_xml:
Example 3 Find the local maximum and minimum values of the function $${g(x) = x + 2\sin x} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi}$$ Solution As in Example 1, we start by finding the critical numbers. The derivative is $$g^{\prime}(x) = 1 + 2\cos x$$ so $$g^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\cos x = - \frac{1}{2}$$ . The solutions of this equation are $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and $$4\pi \slash 3$$ . Because $$g$$ is differentiable everywhere, the only critical numbers are $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and $$4\pi \slash 3$$ . We split the domain into intervals according to the critical numbers. Within each interval, $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ is either always positive or always negative and so we analyze $$g$$ in the following chart. Interval $$g^{\prime}(x) = 1 + 2\cos x$$ $$g$$ $$0 < x < 2\pi \slash 3$$ + increasing on $$\left( {0,2\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ $$2\pi \slash 3 < x < 4\pi \slash 3$$ − decreasing on $$\left( {2\pi \slash 3,4\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ $$4\pi \slash 3 < x < 2\pi$$ + increasing on $$\left( {4\pi \slash 3,2\pi} \right)$$
The $$+$$ signs in the chart come from the fact that $$g^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$\cos x > - \frac{1}{2}$$ . From the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ , this is true in the indicated intervals. Alternatively, we can choose a test value within each interval and check the sign of $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ using that value. Because $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$2\pi \slash 3$$ , the First Derivative Test tells us that there is a local maximum at $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and the local maximum value is $$g\left( {2\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3} + 2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3} + 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \sqrt{3} \approx 3.83$$ Likewise, $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$4\pi \slash 3$$ and so $$g\left( {4\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\left( {- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right) = \frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3} \approx 2.46$$ is a local minimum value. The graph of $$g$$ in Figure 5 supports our conclusion.

snippet: Definition: Definition If the graph of f lies above all of its tangents on an interval I , then f is called concave upward on I . If the graph of f lies below all of its tangents on I , then f is called concave downward on I .

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Figure 9 shows a population graph for honeybees raised in an apiary. How does the rate of population growth change over time? When is this rate highest? Over what intervals is P concave upward or concave downward?...
body_xml: Example 4 Figure 9 shows a population graph for honeybees raised in an apiary. How does the rate of population growth change over time? When is this rate highest? Over what intervals is $$P$$ concave upward or concave downward? Solution By looking at the slope of the curve as $$t$$ increases, we see that the rate of growth of the population is initially very small, then gets larger until it reaches a maximum at about $$t = 12$$ weeks, and decreases as the population begins to level off. As the population approaches its maximum value of about $$75,000$$ (called the carrying capacity), the rate of growth, $$P^{\prime}(t)$$ , approaches $$0$$ . The curve appears to be concave upward on $$(0,12)$$ and concave downward on $$(12,18)$$ .

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Sketch a possible graph of a function f that satisfies the following conditions: (i) f^{\prime}(x) > 0 on \left( {- \infty,1} \right) , f^{\prime}(x) < 0 on \left( {1,\infty} \right) (ii) f^{''}(x) > 0 on \left( {-...
body_xml: Example 5 Sketch a possible graph of a function $$f$$ that satisfies the following conditions: (i) $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right)$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ (ii) $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ , $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- 2,2} \right)$$ (iii) $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = - 2$$ , $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = 0$$ Solution Condition (i) tells us that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ . Condition (ii) says that $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ , and concave downward on $$\left( {- 2,2} \right)$$ . From Condition (iii) we know that the graph of $$f$$ has two horizontal asymptotes: $$y = - 2$$ (to the left) and $$y = 0$$ (to the right). We first draw the horizontal asymptote $$y = - 2$$ as a dashed line (see Figure 10). We then draw the graph of $$f$$ approaching this asymptote at the far left, increasing to its maximum point at $$x = 1$$ , and decreasing toward the $$x$$ -axis at the far right. We also make sure that the graph has inflection points when $$x = - 2$$ and $$2$$ . Notice that we made the curve bend upward for $$x < - 2$$ and $$x > 2$$ , and bend downward when $$x$$ is between $$- 2$$ and $$2$$ .

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Discuss the curve y = x^{4} - 4x^{3} with respect to concavity, points of inflection, and local maxima and minima. Solution If f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3} , then \begin{array}{rll} {f^{\prime}(x)} & = & {4x^{3} - 12x^{2} =...
body_xml:
Example 6 Discuss the curve $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ with respect to concavity, points of inflection, and local maxima and minima. Solution If $$f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ , then $$\begin{array}{rll} {f^{\prime}(x)} & = & {4x^{3} - 12x^{2} = 4x^{2}\left( {x - 3} \right)} \\ {f^{''}(x)} & = & {12x^{2} - 24x = 12x\left( {x - 2} \right)} \end{array}$$ To find the critical numbers we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and obtain $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 3$$ . (Note that $$f^{\prime}$$ is a polynomial and hence defined everywhere.) To use the Second Derivative Test we evaluate $$f^{''}$$ at these critical numbers: $${f^{''}(0) = 0} {f^{''}(3) = 36 > 0}$$ Since $$f^{\prime}(3) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(3) > 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test tells us that $$f(3) = - 27$$ is a local minimum. Because $$f^{''}(0) = 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test gives no information about the critical number $$0$$ . But since $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and also for $$0 < x < 3$$ , the First Derivative Test tells us that $$f$$ does not have a local maximum or minimum at $$0$$ . Since $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 0$$ or $$2$$ , we divide the real line into intervals with these numbers as endpoints and complete the following chart. Interval $$f^{''}(x) = 12x\left( {x - 2} \right)$$ Concavity $$({- \infty,0})$$ + upward $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ − downward $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ + upward
The point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave upward to concave downward there. Also $$\left( {2, - 16} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave downward to concave upward there. The graph of $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ in Figure 12 supports our conclusions.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Sketch the graph of the function f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{1 \slash 3} . Solution First note that the domain of f is \mathbb{R} . Calculation of the first two derivatives gives {f^{\prime}(x) =...
body_xml:
Example 7 Sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{1 \slash 3}$$ . Solution First note that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Calculation of the first two derivatives gives $${f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{4 - x}{x^{1 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{2 \slash 3}}} {f^{''}(x) = \frac{- 8}{x^{4 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{5 \slash 3}}}$$ Use the differentiation rules to check these calculations. Since $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 4$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 6$$ , the critical numbers are $$0$$ , $$4$$ , and $$6$$ . Interval $$4 - x$$ $$x^{1 \slash 3}$$ $$\left( {6 - x} \right)^{2 \slash 3}$$ $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ $$f$$ $$x < 0$$ + − + − decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ $$0 < x < 4$$ + + + + increasing on $$\left( {0,4} \right)$$ $$4 < x < 6$$ − + + − decreasing on $$\left( {4,6} \right)$$ $$x > 6$$ − + + − decreasing on $$\left( {6,\infty} \right)$$
To find the local extreme values we use the First Derivative Test. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local minimum. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$4$$ , $$f(4) = 2^{5 \slash 3}$$ is a local maximum. The sign of $$f^{\prime}$$ does not change at $$6$$ , so there is no minimum or maximum there. (The Second Derivative Test could be used at $$4$$ but not at $$0$$ or $$6$$ because $$f^{''}$$ does not exist at either of these numbers.) Looking at the expression for $$f^{''}(x)$$ and noting that $$x^{4 \slash 3} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we have $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and for $$0 < x < 6$$ and $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for $$x > 6$$ . So $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,6} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {6,\infty} \right)$$ , and the only inflection point is $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ . Using all of the information we gathered about $$f$$ from its first and second derivatives, we sketch the graph in Figure 13. Note that the curve has vertical tangents at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ because $$\left. |{f^{\prime}(x)|}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and as $$\left. x\rightarrow 6 \right.$$ . Try reproducing the graph in Figure 13 with a graphing calculator or computer. Some machines produce the complete graph, some produce only the portion to the right of the $$y$$ -axis, and some produce only the portion between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 6$$ . For an explanation, see Example 7 in Graphing Calculators and Computers at www.stewartcalculus.com.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Use the first and second derivatives of f(x) = e^{1 \slash x} , together with asymptotes, to sketch its graph. Solution Notice that the domain of f is \left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0 \right\} , so we check for vertical...
body_xml: Example 8 Use the first and second derivatives of $$f(x) = e^{1 \slash x}$$ , together with asymptotes, to sketch its graph. Solution Notice that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0 \right\}$$ , so we check for vertical asymptotes by computing the left and right limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , we know that $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}e^{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}e^{ t} = \infty$$ and this shows that $$x = 0$$ is a vertical asymptote. As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ , we have $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}e^{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}e^{ t} = 0$$ As $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and so $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow \pm \infty}e^{1 \slash x} = e^{0} = 1$$ This shows that $$y = 1$$ is a horizontal asymptote (to both the left and right). Now let’s compute the derivative. The Chain Rule gives $$f^{\prime}(x) = - \frac{e^{1 \slash x}}{x^{2}}$$ Since $$e^{1 \slash x} > 0$$ and $$x^{2} > 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ , we have $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ . Thus $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . There is no critical number, so the function has no local maximum or minimum. The second derivative is $$f^{''}(x) = - \frac{x^{2}e^{1 \slash x}{({- 1 \slash x^{2}})} - e^{1 \slash x}{({2x})}}{x^{4}} = \frac{e^{1 \slash x}{({2x + 1})}}{x^{4}}$$ Since $$e^{1 \slash x} > 0$$ and $$x^{4} > 0$$ , we have $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > - \frac{1}{2}$$ $$\left( {x \neq 0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ when $$x < - \frac{1}{2}$$ . So the curve is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - \frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . The inflection point is $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},e^{- 2}} \right)$$ . To sketch the graph of $$f$$ we first draw the horizontal asymptote $$y = 1$$ (as a dashed line), together with the parts of the curve near the asymptotes in a preliminary sketch [Figure 14(a)]. These parts reflect the information concerning limits and the fact that $$f$$ is decreasing on both $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . Notice that we have indicated that $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ even though $$f(0)$$ does not exist. In Figure 14(b) we finish the sketch by incorporating the information concerning concavity and the inflection point. In Figure 14(c) we check our work with a computer.

title: L’Hospital’s Rule
snippet: L’Hospital’s Rule: L’Hospital’s Rule Suppose f and g are differentiable and g^{\prime}(x) \neq 0 on an open interval I that contains a (except possibly at a ). Suppose that \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = 0 and \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow...
body_xml: L’Hospital’s Rule Suppose $$f$$ and $$g$$ are differentiable and $$g^{\prime}(x) \neq 0$$ on an open interval $$I$$ that contains $$a$$ (except possibly at $$a$$ ). Suppose that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = 0$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = 0$$ or that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = \pm \infty$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = \pm \infty$$ (In other words, we have an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ .) Then $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$$ if the limit on the right side exists (or is $$\infty$$ or $$- \infty$$ ). Figure 1 suggests visually why l’Hospital’s Rule might be true. The first graph shows two differentiable functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ , each of which approaches $$0$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ . If we were to zoom in toward the point $$\left( {a,0} \right)$$ , the graphs would start to look almost linear. But if the functions actually were linear, as in the second graph, then their ratio would be $$\frac{m_{1}\left( {x - a} \right)}{m_{2}\left( {x - a} \right)} = \frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}$$ which is the ratio of their derivatives. This suggests that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1} . Solution Since \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\ln x = \ln 1 = 0 and \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\left( {x - 1} \right) = 0 the limit is an indeterminate form of type...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\ln x = \ln 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\left( {x - 1} \right) = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>the limit is an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ , so we can apply l’Hospital’s Rule:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\ln x} \right)}{\frac{d}{dx}\left( {x - 1} \right)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{1 \slash x}{1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{1}{x} = 1} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that when using l’Hospital’s Rule we differentiate the numerator and denominator separately. We do not use the Quotient Rule.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Calculate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{x^{2}} . Solution We have \lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}e^{ x} = \infty and \lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{2} = \infty , so the limit is an indeterminate form of type...
body_xml: Example 2 Calculate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{x^{2}}$$ . Solution We have $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}e^{ x} = \infty$$ and $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}x^{2} = \infty$$ , so the limit is an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ , and l’Hospital’s Rule gives $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}{(e^{ x})}}{\frac{d}{dx}{(x^{2})}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{2x}$$ Since $$\left. e^{ x}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. 2x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , the limit on the right side is also indeterminate. A second application of l’Hospital’s Rule gives $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{2x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e^{ x}}{2} = \infty$$ The graph of the function of Example 2 is shown in Figure 2. We have noticed previously that exponential functions grow far more rapidly than power functions, so the result of Example 2 is not unexpected. See also Exercise 75.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Calculate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}} . Solution Since \left. \ln x\rightarrow\infty \right. and \left. \sqrt{x}\rightarrow\infty \right. as \left. x\rightarrow\infty \right. , l’Hospital’s...
body_xml: Example 3 Calculate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}}$$ . Solution Since $$\left. \ln x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. \sqrt{x}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , l’Hospital’s Rule applies: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1 \slash x}{\frac{1}{2}x^{- 1 \slash 2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1 \slash x}{1 \slash {({2\sqrt{x}})}}$$ Notice that the limit on the right side is now indeterminate of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ . But instead of applying l’Hospital’s Rule a second time as we did in Example 2, we simplify the expression and see that a second application is unnecessary: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1 \slash x}{1 \slash {({2\sqrt{x}})}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2}{\sqrt{x^{}}} = 0$$ The graph of the function of Example 3 is shown in Figure 3. We have discussed previously the slow growth of logarithms, so it isn’t surprising that this ratio approaches $$0$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . See also Exercise 76.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x - x}{x^{3}} . (See Exercise 2.2.48.) Solution Noting that both \left. \tan x - x\rightarrow 0 \right. and \left. x^{3}\rightarrow 0 \right. as \left. x\rightarrow 0 \right....
body_xml: Example 4 Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x - x}{x^{3}}$$ . (See Exercise 2.2.48.) Solution Noting that both $$\left. \tan x - x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and $$\left. x^{3}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we use l’Hospital’s Rule: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x - x}{x^{3}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sec^{2}x - 1}{3x^{2}}$$ Since the limit on the right side is still indeterminate of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ , we apply l’Hospital’s Rule again: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sec^{2}x - 1}{3x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{2\sec^{2}x\tan x}{6x}$$ Because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\sec^{2}x = 1$$ , we simplify the calculation by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{2\sec^{2}x\tan x}{6x} = \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sec^{2}x \cdot \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x}{x} = \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x}{x}$$ We can evaluate this last limit either by using l’Hospital’s Rule a third time or by writing $$\tan x$$ as $$\left( {\sin x} \right) \slash \left( {\cos x} \right)$$ and making use of our knowledge of trigonometric limits. Putting together all the steps, we get $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x - x}{x^{3}}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sec^{2}x - 1}{3x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{2\sec^{2}x\tan x}{6x}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x - x}{x^{3}}} = {\frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan x}{x} = \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sec^{2}x}{1} = \frac{1}{3}}} \end{array}$$ The graph in Figure 4 gives visual confirmation of the result of Example 4. If we were to zoom in too far, however, we would get an inaccurate graph because $$\tan x$$ is close to $$x$$ when $$x$$ is small. See Exercise 2.2.48(d).

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi^{-}}\frac{\sin x}{1 - \cos x} . Solution If we blindly attempted to use l’Hospital’s Rule, we might think that an equivalent limit is \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi^{-}}\frac{\cos...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi^{-}}\frac{\sin x}{1 - \cos x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If we blindly attempted to use l’Hospital’s Rule, we might think that an equivalent limit is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi^{-}}\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = - \infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is wrong! Although the numerator $$\left. \sin x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\pi^{-} \right.$$ , notice that the denominator $$\left( {1 - \cos x} \right)$$ does not approach $$0$$ , so l’Hospital’s Rule can’t be applied here.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The required limit can, in fact, be found by direct substitution because the function is continuous at $$\pi$$ and the denominator is nonzero there:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\pi^{-}}\frac{\sin x}{1 - \cos x} = \frac{\sin\pi}{1 - \cos\pi} = \frac{0}{1 - \left( {- 1} \right)} = 0$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Evaluate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x . Solution The given limit is indeterminate because, as \left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right. , the first factor (x) approaches 0 while the second factor \left( {\ln x}...
body_xml: Example 6 Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x$$ . Solution The given limit is indeterminate because, as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , the first factor $$(x)$$ approaches $$0$$ while the second factor $$\left( {\ln x} \right)$$ approaches $$- \infty$$ . Writing $$x = 1 \slash \left( {1 \slash x} \right)$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , so l’Hospital’s Rule gives $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{\ln x}{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1 \slash x}{- 1 \slash x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {- x} \right) = 0$$ Figure 5 shows the graph of the function in Example 6. Notice that the function is undefined at $$x = 0$$ ; the graph approaches the origin but never quite reaches it.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Compute \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\left( {\frac{1}{\ln x} - \frac{1}{x - 1}} \right) . Solution First notice that \left. 1 \slash \left( {\ln x} \right)\rightarrow\infty \right. and \left. 1 \slash \left( {x - 1}...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Compute $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\left( {\frac{1}{\ln x} - \frac{1}{x - 1}} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution First notice that $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {\ln x} \right)\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 1^{+} \right.$$ , so the limit is indeterminate of type $$\infty - \infty$$ . Here we can start with a common denominator:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\left( {\frac{1}{\ln x} - \frac{1}{x - 1}} \right) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x - 1 - \ln x}{(x - 1)\ln x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Both numerator and denominator have a limit of $$0$$ , so l’Hospital’s Rule applies, giving</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x - 1 - \ln x}{\left( {x - 1} \right)\ln x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{1 - \frac{1}{x}}{\left( {x - 1} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \ln x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x - 1}{x - 1 + x\ln x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Again we have an indeterminate limit of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ , so we apply l’Hospital’s Rule a second time:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x - 1}{x - 1 + x\ln x}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{1}{1 + x \cdot \frac{1}{x} + \ln x}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x - 1}{x - 1 + x\ln x}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{1}{2 + \ln x} = \frac{1}{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Calculate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {e^{ x} - x} \right) . Solution This is an indeterminate difference because both e^{ x} and x approach infinity. We would expect the limit to be infinity because \left....
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Calculate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( {e^{ x} - x} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution This is an indeterminate difference because both $$e^{ x}$$ and $$x$$ approach infinity. We would expect the limit to be infinity because $$\left. e^{ x}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ much faster than $$x$$ . But we can verify this by factoring out $$x$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{ x} - x = x\left( {\frac{e^{ x}}{x} - 1} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The term $$\left. e^{ x} \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ by l’Hospital’s Rule and so we now have a product in which both factors grow large:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}(e^{ x} - x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack {x\left( {\frac{e^{ x}}{x} - 1} \right)} \right\rbrack = \infty$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Calculate \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)^{\cot x} . Solution First notice that as \left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right. , we have \left. 1 + \sin 4x\rightarrow 1 \right. and \left. \cot...
body_xml:
<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Calculate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)^{\cot x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution First notice that as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , we have $$\left. 1 + \sin 4x\rightarrow 1 \right.$$ and $$\left. \cot x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , so the given limit is indeterminate (type $$1^{\infty}$$ ). Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)^{\cot x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\ln y = \ln{\lbrack\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)^{\cot x}\rbrack} = \cot x\ln\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right) = \frac{\ln\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)}{\tan x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so l’Hospital’s Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\ln y = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{\ln\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)}{\tan x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{\frac{4\cos 4x}{1 + \sin 4x}}{\sec^{2}x} = 4$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So far we have computed the limit of $$\ln y$$ , but what we want is the limit of $$y$$ . To find this we use the fact that $$y = e^{\ln y}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {1 + \sin 4x} \right)^{\cot x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}y = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}e^{\ln y} = e^{4}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Find \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{x} . Solution Notice that this limit is indeterminate since 0^{x} = 0 for any x > 0 but x^{0} = 1 for any x \neq 0 . (Recall that 0^{0} is undefined.) We could proceed as in...
body_xml: Example 10 Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{x}$$ . Solution Notice that this limit is indeterminate since $$0^{x} = 0$$ for any $$x > 0$$ but $$x^{0} = 1$$ for any $$x \neq 0$$ . (Recall that $$0^{0}$$ is undefined.) We could proceed as in Example 9 or by writing the function as an exponential: $$x^{x} = {(e^{\ln x})}^{x} = e^{ x\ln x}$$ In Example 6 we used l’Hospital’s Rule to show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x = 0$$ Therefore $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}e^{ x\ln x} = e^{0} = 1$$ The graph of the function $$y = x^{x}$$ , $$x > 0$$ , is shown in Figure 6. Notice that although $$0^{0}$$ is not defined, the values of the function approach $$1$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ . This confirms the result of Example 10.

<note type="theorem" source_type="L’Hospital" title="L’Hospital">
    <heading level="4">L’Hospital</heading>
    <paragraph>L’Hospital’s Rule is named after a French nobleman, the Marquis de l’Hospital (1661–1704), but was discovered by a Swiss mathematician, John Bernoulli (1667–1748). You might sometimes see l’Hospital spelled as l’Hôpital, but he spelled his own name l’Hospital, as was common in the 17th century. See Exercise 85 for the example that the Marquis used to illustrate his rule. See the project for further historical details.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Use the guidelines to sketch the curve y = \frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1} . Domain The domain is {\{{x{|{x^{2} - 1 \neq 0}}}\}} = \left\{ {x{|{x \neq \pm 1}}} \right\} = \left( {- \infty, - 1} \right) \cup \left( {- 1,1}...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the guidelines to sketch the curve $$y = \frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Domain The domain is $${\{{x{|{x^{2} - 1 \neq 0}}}\}} = \left\{ {x{|{x \neq \pm 1}}} \right\} = \left( {- \infty, - 1} \right) \cup \left( {- 1,1} \right) \cup \left( {1,\infty} \right)$$</item>
      <item>Intercepts The $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts are both $$0$$ .</item>
      <item>Symmetry Since $$f( - x) = f(x)$$ , the function $$f$$ is even. The curve is symmetric about the $$y$$ -axis.</item>
      <item>Asymptotes $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow \pm \infty}\frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow \pm \infty}\frac{2}{1 - 1/x^{2}} = 2$$ Therefore the line $$y = 2$$ is a horizontal asymptote (at both the left and right). Since the denominator is $$0$$ when $$x = \pm 1$$ , we compute the following limits: $$\begin{array}{rclrcl} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}} & = & \infty & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}\frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}}} & = & {- \infty} \\ {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1^{+}}\frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}} & = & {- \infty} & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1^{-}}\frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}}} & = & \infty \end{array}$$ Therefore the lines $$x = 1$$ and $$x = - 1$$ are vertical asymptotes. This information about limits and asymptotes enables us to draw the preliminary sketch in Figure 5, showing the parts of the curve near the asymptotes. Figure 5 Details Two dashed vertical lines and a dashed horizontal line are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The dashed horizontal line y = 2 runs from the second quadrant to the first quadrant, crossing the y axis at (0, 2). A dashed vertical line x = negative 1 is drawn from the second quadrant to the third quadrant, crossing the x axis at (negative 1, 0). Another dashed vertical line x = 1 is drawn from the first quadrant to the fourth quadrant, crossing the x axis at (1, 0). Preliminary sketch</item>
      <item>Intervals of Increase or Decrease $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{({x^{2} - 1})({4x}) - 2x^{2} \cdot 2x}{{({x^{2} - 1})}^{2}} = \frac{- 4x}{{({x^{2} - 1})}^{2}}$$ Since $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x < 0\left( {x \neq - 1} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x > 0\left( {x \neq 1} \right)$$ , $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Local Maximum or Minimum Values The only critical number is $$x = 0$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local maximum by the First Derivative Test.</item>
      <item>Concavity and Points of Inflection $$f^{''}(x) = \frac{{({x^{2} - 1})}^{2}({- 4}) + 4x \cdot 2({x^{2} - 1})2x}{{({x^{2} - 1})}^{4}} = \frac{12x^{2} + 4}{{({x^{2} - 1})}^{3}}$$ Since $$12x^{2} + 4 > 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we have $$\left. f^{''}(x) > 0 \Leftrightarrow x^{2} - 1 > 0 \Leftrightarrow |x| > 1 \right.$$ and $$\left. f^{''}(x) < 0 \Leftrightarrow |x| < 1 \right.$$ . Thus the curve is concave upward on the intervals $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ . It has no point of inflection because $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ are not in the domain of $$f$$ .</item>
      <item>Sketch the Curve Using the information in E–G, we finish the sketch in Figure 6. Figure 6 Details Three dashed lines and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. A dashed horizontal line y = 2 runs from the second quadrant to the first quadrant, crossing the y axis at (0, 2). A dashed vertical line x = negative 1 is drawn from the second quadrant to the third quadrant, crossing the x axis at (negative 1, 0). Another dashed vertical line x = 1 is drawn from the first quadrant to the fourth quadrant, crossing the x axis at (1, 0). The curve has three parts. The first part lies entirely in the second quadrant, above the dashed horizontal line y = 2 and to the left of x = negative 1. It enters from the left above the line y = 2, gradually goes up and to the right, concave up, then goes up and to the right, approaches x = negative 1, and exits the viewing window to the left of it at the top. The second part resembles an inverted U-shaped curve and lies between x = negative 1 and x = 1. It enters from the bottom to the right of x = negative 1, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at (0, 0), then goes down and to the right, veering toward x = 1, approaches it as the curve falls steeply to the right. The third part lies entirely in the first quadrant, above the dashed horizontal line and to the right of x = 1. It enters at the top to the right of x = 1, goes down and to the right, concave up, veers toward the dashed horizontal line, and exits near its right extreme. Finished sketch of $$y = \frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>We have shown the curve approaching its horizontal asymptote from above in Figure 5. This is confirmed by the intervals of increase and decrease.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Sketch the graph of f(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x + 1}} . Domain The domain is \left\{ {x{|{x + 1 > 0}}} \right\} = \left\{ {x{|{x > - 1}}} \right\} = \left( {- 1,\infty} \right) . Intercepts The x - and y -intercepts...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x + 1}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Domain The domain is $$\left\{ {x{|{x + 1 > 0}}} \right\} = \left\{ {x{|{x > - 1}}} \right\} = \left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Intercepts The $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts are both $$0$$ .</item>
      <item>Symmetry None</item>
      <item>Asymptotes Since $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x + 1}} = \infty$$ there is no horizontal asymptote. Since $$\left. \sqrt{x + 1}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow - 1^{+} \right.$$ and $$f(x)$$ is always positive, we have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - 1^{+}}\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x + 1}} = \infty$$ and so the line $$x = - 1$$ is a vertical asymptote.</item>
      <item>Intervals of Increase or Decrease $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x + 1}(2x) - x^{2} \cdot 1/(2\sqrt{x + 1})}{x + 1} = \frac{3x^{2} + 4x}{2{(x + 1)}^{3/2}} = \frac{x(3x + 4)}{2{(x + 1)}^{3/2}}$$ We see that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 0$$ (notice that $$- \frac{4}{3}$$ is not in the domain of $$f$$ ), so the only critical number is $$0$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$- 1 < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > 0$$ , $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and increasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Local Maximum or Minimum Values Since $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local (and absolute) minimum by the First Derivative Test.</item>
      <item>Concavity and Points of Inflection $$f^{''}(x) = \frac{2{({x + 1})}^{3/2}{({6x + 4})} - {({3x^{2} + 4x})}3{({x + 1})}^{1/2}}{4{({x + 1})}^{3}} = \frac{3x^{2} + 8x + 8}{4{({x + 1})}^{5/2}}$$ Note that the denominator is always positive. The numerator is the quadratic $$3x^{2} + 8x + 8$$ , which is always positive because its discriminant is $$b^{2} - 4ac = - 32$$ , which is negative, and the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is positive. Thus $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , which means that $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ and there is no point of inflection.</item>
      <item>Sketch the Curve The curve is sketched in Figure 7. Figure 7 Details A dashed vertical line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The dashed vertical line labeled x = negative 1 is drawn from the second quadrant to the third quadrant, crossing the x axis at (negative 1, 0). The curve y = x^2/(sqrt(x + 1)) enters the second quadrant at the top, very close to the right of x = negative 1, goes down and to the right, veering away from it, concave up, reaches its low point at the origin, and then goes gradually up and to the right, exiting the viewing window at the top right.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Sketch the graph of f(x) = xe^{ x} . Domain The domain is \mathbb{R} . Intercepts The x - and y -intercepts are both 0 . Symmetry None Asymptotes Because both x and e^{ x} become large as \left. x\rightarrow\infty...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = xe^{ x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Domain The domain is $$\mathbb{R}$$ .</item>
      <item>Intercepts The $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts are both $$0$$ .</item>
      <item>Symmetry None</item>
      <item>Asymptotes Because both $$x$$ and $$e^{ x}$$ become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , we have $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}xe^{ x} = \infty$$ . As $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , however, $$\left. e^{ x}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and so we have an indeterminate product that requires the use of l’Hospital’s Rule: $${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}}_{}xe^{ x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{x}{e^{- x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{- e^{- x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {- e^{ x}} \right) = 0$$ Thus the $$x$$ -axis is a horizontal asymptote.</item>
      <item>Intervals of Increase or Decrease $$f^{\prime}(x) = xe^{ x} + e^{ x} = (x + 1)e^{ x}$$ Since $$e^{ x}$$ is always positive, we see that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x + 1 > 0$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x + 1 < 0$$ . So $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Local Maximum or Minimum Values Because $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$x = - 1$$ , $$f( - 1) = {- e}^{- 1} \approx - 0.37$$ is a local (and absolute) minimum.</item>
      <item>Concavity and Points of Inflection $$f^{''}(x) = (x + 1)e^{ x} + e^{ x} = (x + 2)e^{ x}$$ Since $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ if $$x > - 2$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ if $$x < - 2$$ , $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- 2,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ . The inflection point is $$( - 2, - 2e^{- 2}) \approx ( - 2, - 0.27)$$ .</item>
      <item>Sketch the Curve We use this information to sketch the curve in Figure 8. Figure 8 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve y = x e^x enters the third quadrant very close to and below the x axis, goes down and to the right, initially concave down, then becomes concave up at approximately x = negative 2, reaches the labeled low point at (negative 1, negative 1/e), then goes up and to the right through the origin, and extends into the first quadrant.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Sketch the graph of f(x) = \frac{\cos x}{2 + \sin x} . Domain The domain is \mathbb{R} . Intercepts The y -intercept is f(0) = \frac{1}{2} . The x -intercepts occur when \cos x = 0 , that is, x = \left( {\pi/2} \right)...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{\cos x}{2 + \sin x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Domain The domain is $$\mathbb{R}$$ .</item>
      <item>Intercepts The $$y$$ -intercept is $$f(0) = \frac{1}{2}$$ . The $$x$$ -intercepts occur when $$\cos x = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \left( {\pi/2} \right) + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer.</item>
      <item>Symmetry $$f$$ is neither even nor odd, but $$f(x + 2\pi) = f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ and so $$f$$ is periodic and has period $$2\pi$$ . Thus, in what follows, we need to consider only $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ and then extend the curve by translation in part H.</item>
      <item>Asymptotes None</item>
      <item>Intervals of Increase or Decrease $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)\left( {- \sin x} \right) - \cos x\left( {\cos x} \right)}{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{2}} = - \frac{2\sin x + 1}{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{2}}$$ The denominator is always positive, so $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$\left. 2\sin x + 1 < 0\Leftrightarrow\sin x < - \frac{1}{2}\Leftrightarrow 7\pi/6 < x < 11\pi/6 \right.$$ . So $$f$$ is increasing on $$(7\pi/6,11\pi/6)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {0,7\pi/6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {11\pi/6,2\pi} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Local Maximum or Minimum Values From part E and the First Derivative Test, we see that the local minimum value is $$f(7\pi/6) = - 1/\sqrt{3}$$ and the local maximum value is $$f(11\pi/6) = 1/\sqrt{3}$$ .</item>
      <item>Concavity and Points of Inflection If we use the Quotient Rule again and simplify, we get $$f^{''}(x) = - \frac{2\cos x\left( {1 - \sin x} \right)}{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{3}}$$ Because $$\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{3} > 0$$ and $$1 - \sin x \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we know that $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$\cos x < 0$$ , that is, $$\pi/2 < x < 3\pi/2$$ . So $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {\pi/2,3\pi/2} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {0,\pi/2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {3\pi/2,2\pi} \right)$$ . The inflection points are $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ and $$(3\pi/2,0)$$ .</item>
      <item>Sketch the Curve The graph of the function restricted to $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ is shown in Figure 9. Then we extend it, using periodicity, to arrive at the graph in Figure 10. Figure 9 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 2 pi in increments of pi/2 units. The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 1/2. The curve begins at the point (0, 1/2), goes down and to the right through (pi/2, 0), concave up, reaches the labeled low point at (7 pi/6, negative 1/sqrt(3)), then goes up and to the right through (3 pi/2, 0), now concave down, reaches the labeled high point at (11pi/6, 1/sqrt(3)), and then goes down and to the right. Figure 10 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane such that it increases and decreases with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each maximum and minimum. The x axis is displayed from negative 3 pi/2 to 7 pi/2 in increments of pi/2 units. The curve enters the second quadrant near the x axis, goes down and to the right through (negative 3 pi/2, 0), concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (negative 5 pi/6, negative 0.6), then goes steeply up and to the right through (negative pi/2, 0), now concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (negative pi/6, 0.6). It then goes gradually down and to the right by crossing the y axis at (0, 1/2), then crosses the x axis at (pi/2, 0), becoming concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (7 pi/6, negative 0.6), then goes steeply up and to the right through (3 pi/2, 0), reaches its high point at approximately (11 pi/6, 0.6), then goes gradually down and to the right through (5 pi/2, 0). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds rightward.</item>
    </list>
  </example>
