<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the properties of integrals to evaluate $$\int_{0}^{1}{(4 + 3x^{2})\mathit{dx}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Using Properties 2 and 3 of integrals, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{0}^{1}{(4 + 3x^{2})\mathit{dx} = {\int_{0}^{1}{4\mathit{dx} + {\int_{0}^{1}{3x^{2}}}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{4\mathit{dx} + 3{\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}}\mathit{dx}}}}$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph>and we found in Example 5.1.2 that $${\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}}\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{3}$$ . So</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{0}^{1}{(4 + 3x^{2})}}\mathit{dx}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{4\mathit{dx} + 3{\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}}\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{1}{(4 + 3x^{2})}}\mathit{dx}} = {4 + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 5}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

      <item>8. If $$m \leqslant f(x) \leqslant M$$ for $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , then $$m(b - a) \leqslant {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\mathit{dx} \leqslant M(b - a)}}$$</item>

<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Property 8 to estimate $${\int_{0}^{1}e^{- x^{2}}}\mathit{dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Because $$f(x) = e^{- x^{2}}$$ is a decreasing function on $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ , its absolute maximum value is $$M = f(0) = 1$$ and its absolute minimum value is $$m = f(1) = e^{- 1}$$ . Thus, by Property 8,</paragraph>

title: Riemann
snippet: Riemann: Riemann Bernhard Riemann received his Ph.D. under the direction of the legendary Gauss at the University of Göttingen and remained there to teach. Gauss, who was not in the habit of praising other mathematicians, spoke of...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Riemann" title="Riemann">
    <heading level="4">Riemann</heading>
    <paragraph>Bernhard Riemann received his Ph.D. under the direction of the legendary Gauss at the University of Göttingen and remained there to teach. Gauss, who was not in the habit of praising other mathematicians, spoke of Riemann’s “creative, active, truly mathematical mind and gloriously fertile originality.” The definition (2) of an integral that we use is due to Riemann. He also made major contributions to the theory of functions of a complex variable, mathematical physics, number theory, and the foundations of geometry. Riemann’s broad concept of space and geometry turned out to be the right setting, $$50$$ years later, for Einstein’s general relativity theory. Riemann’s health was poor throughout his life, and he died of tuberculosis at the age of 39.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 If f is the function whose graph is shown in Figure 2 and g(x) = {\int_{o}^{x}f}(t)\mathit{dt} , find the values of g(0) , g(1) , g(2) , g(3) , g(4) , and g(5) . Then sketch a rough graph of g . Solution First we...
body_xml: Example 1 If $$f$$ is the function whose graph is shown in Figure 2 and $$g(x) = {\int_{o}^{x}f}(t)\mathit{dt}$$ , find the values of $$g(0)$$ , $$g(1)$$ , $$g(2)$$ , $$g(3)$$ , $$g(4)$$ , and $$g(5)$$ . Then sketch a rough graph of $$g$$ . Solution First we notice that $$g(0) = {\int_{0}^{0}f}(t)\mathit{dt} = 0$$ . From Figure 3 we see that $$g(1)$$ is the area of a triangle: $$g(1) = {\int_{0}^{1}f}(t)\mathit{dt} = \frac{1}{2}(1 \cdot 2) = 1$$ To find $$g(2)$$ we add to $$g(1)$$ the area of a rectangle: $$g(2) = {\int_{0}^{2}f}(t)\mathit{dt} = {\int_{0}^{1}f}(t)\mathit{dt} + {\int_{1}^{2}f}(t)\mathit{dt} = 1 + (1 \cdot 2) = 3$$ We estimate that the area under $$f$$ from $$2$$ to $$3$$ is about $$1.3$$ , so $$g(3) = g(2) + {\int_{2}^{3}f}(t)\mathit{dt} \approx 3 + 1.3 = 4.3$$ For $$t > 3$$ , $$f(t)$$ is negative and so we start subtracting areas: $$\begin{array}{l} {{g(4)} = {g(3)} + {\int_{3}^{4}{f(t)\mathit{dt} \approx 4.3 + \left( {- 1.3} \right) = 3.0}}} \\ {{g(5)} = {g(4)} + {\int_{4}^{5}{f(t)\mathit{dt} \approx 3 + \left( {- 1.3} \right) = 1.7}}} \end{array}$$ We use these values to sketch the graph of $$g$$ in Figure 4. Notice that, because $$f(t)$$ is positive for $$t < 3$$ , we keep adding area for $$t < 3$$ and so $$g$$ is increasing up to $$x = 3$$ , where it attains a maximum value. For $$x > 3$$ , $$g$$ decreases because $$f(t)$$ is negative.

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1" title="The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1">
    <heading level="4">The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , then the function $$g$$ defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$g(x) = {\int_{a}^{x}{f(t)\mathit{dt} a \leqslant x \leqslant b}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and differentiable on $$(a,b)$$ , and $$g^{\prime}(x) = f(x)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We abbreviate the name of this theorem as FTC1. In words, it says that the derivative of a definite integral with respect to its upper limit is the integrand evaluated at the upper limit.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Although a formula of the form g(x) = \int_{a}^{x}f(t)\mathit{dt} may seem like a strange way of defining a function, books on physics, chemistry, and statistics are full of such functions. For instance, the Fresnel...
body_xml: Example 3 Although a formula of the form $$g(x) = \int_{a}^{x}f(t)\mathit{dt}$$ may seem like a strange way of defining a function, books on physics, chemistry, and statistics are full of such functions. For instance, the Fresnel function $$S{(x)} = {\int_{0}^{x}\sin}{({\pi t^{2} \slash 2})}\mathit{dt}$$ is named after the French physicist Augustin Fresnel (1788–1827), who is famous for his works in optics. This function first appeared in Fresnel’s theory of the diffraction of light waves, but more recently it has been applied to the design of highways. Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem tells us how to differentiate the Fresnel function: $$S^{\prime}{(x)} = \sin{({\pi x^{2} \slash 2})}$$ This means that we can apply all the methods of differential calculus to analyze $$S$$ (see Exercise 81). Figure 7 shows the graphs of $$f(x) = \sin\left( {\pi x^{2} \slash 2} \right)$$ and the Fresnel function $$S{(x)} = {\int_{0}^{x}f}(t)\mathit{dt}$$ . A computer was used to graph $$S$$ by computing the value of this integral for many values of $$x$$ . It does indeed look as if $$S(x)$$ is the area under the graph of $$f$$ from $$0$$ to $$x$$ [until $$x \approx 1.4$$ when $$S(x)$$ becomes a difference of areas]. Figure 8 shows a larger part of the graph of $$S$$ . If we now start with the graph of $$S$$ in Figure 7 and think about what its derivative should look like, it seems reasonable that $$S^{\prime}(x) = f(x)$$ . [For instance, $$S$$ is increasing when $$f(x) > 0$$ and decreasing when $$f(x) < 0$$ .] So this gives a visual confirmation of Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

    <paragraph>Find $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{\int_{1}^{x^{4}}\sec}t\mathit{dt}$$ .</paragraph>

<note type="theorem" source_type="The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2" title="The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2">
    <heading level="4">The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{a}^{b}f}(x)\mathit{dx} = F(b) - F(a)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$F$$ is any antiderivative of $$f$$ , that is, a function $$F$$ such that $$F^{\prime} = f$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We abbreviate this theorem as FTC2.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate the integral {\int_{1}^{3}e^{ x}}\mathit{dx} . Solution The function f(x) = e^{ x} is continuous everywhere and we know that an antiderivative is F(x) = e^{ x} , so Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem gives...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate the integral $${\int_{1}^{3}e^{ x}}\mathit{dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The function $$f(x) = e^{ x}$$ is continuous everywhere and we know that an antiderivative is $$F(x) = e^{ x}$$ , so Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{1}^{3}e^{ x}}\mathit{dx} = F(3) - F(1) = e^{ 3} - e$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that FTC2 says we can use any antiderivative $$F$$ of $$f$$ . So we may as well use the simplest one, namely $$F(x) = e^{ x}$$ , instead of $$e^{ x} + 7$$ or $$e^{ x} + C$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Compare the calculation in Example 5 with the much harder one in Example 5.2.4.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the area under the parabola y = x^{2} from 0 to 1 . Solution An antiderivative of f(x) = x^{2} is F(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{3} . The required area A is found using Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem: A =...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the area under the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ from $$0$$ to $$1$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution An antiderivative of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ is $$F(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{3}$$ . The required area $$A$$ is found using Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A = {\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}}\mathit{dx} = \left. \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1^{3}}{3} - \frac{0^{3}}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In applying the Fundamental Theorem we use a particular antiderivative $$F$$ of $$f$$ . It is not necessary to use the most general antiderivative.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="7">

    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{3}^{6}\frac{\mathit{dx}}{x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The given integral is another way of writing</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{3}^{6}{\frac{1}{x}}}\mathit{dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>An antiderivative of $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ is $$F(x) = \ln|x|$$ and, because $$3 \leqslant x \leqslant 6$$ , we can write $$F(x) = \ln x$$ . So</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${{\int_{3}^{6}{\frac{1}{x}}}\mathit{dx} = \ln x\rbrack_{3}^{6} = \ln 6 - \ln 3}{= \ln\frac{6}{3} = \ln 2}$$</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 8 Find the area under the cosine curve from $$0$$ to $$b$$ , where $$0 \leqslant b \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ . Solution Since an antiderivative of $$f(x) = \cos x$$ is $$F(x) = \sin x$$ , we have $$A = {\int_{0}^{b}\cos}x\mathit{dx} = \sin x\rbrack_{0}^{b} = \sin b - \sin 0 = \sin b$$ In particular, taking $$b = \pi \slash 2$$ , we have proved that the area under the cosine curve from $$0$$ to $$\pi \slash 2$$ is $$\sin\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right) = 1$$ . (See Figure 9.)

    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{3}{{({x^{3} - 6x})}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{x^{4}}{4} - 6\left. \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{3}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{3}{{({x^{3} - 6x})}\mathit{dx}}} = \left( {\frac{1}{4} \cdot 3^{4} - 3 \cdot 3^{2}} \right) - \left( {\frac{1}{4} \cdot 0^{4} - 3 \cdot 0^{2}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{3}{{({x^{3} - 6x})}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{81}{4} - 27 - 0 + 0 = - 6.75} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Compare this calculation with Example 5.2.3.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find \int_{0}^{2}\left( 2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1} \right)\mathit{dx} and interpret the result in terms of areas. Solution The Fundamental Theorem gives \begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x +...
body_xml: Example 4 Find $$\int_{0}^{2}\left( 2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1} \right)\mathit{dx}$$ and interpret the result in terms of areas. Solution The Fundamental Theorem gives $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}\mathit{dx} = 2\frac{x^{4}}{4} - 6\frac{x^{2}}{2} + \left. {3\tan^{- 1}x} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{2}x^{4} - 3x^{2} + 3\tan^{- 1}x\rbrack_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{2}{(2^{4})} - 3{(2^{2})} + 3\tan^{- 1}2 - 0} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1}} \right)}\mathit{dx}} = - 4 + 3\tan^{- 1}2} \end{array}$$ This is the exact value of the integral. If a decimal approximation is desired, we can use a calculator to approximate $$\tan^{- 1}2$$ . Doing so, we get $$\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2x^{3} - 6x + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 1}} \right)\mathit{dx} \approx - 0.67855$$ Figure 2 shows the graph of the integrand in Example 4. We know from Section 5.2 that the value of the integral can be interpreted as a net area: the sum of the areas labeled with a plus sign minus the area labeled with a minus sign.

<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{1}^{9}\frac{2t^{2} + t^{2}\sqrt{t} - 1}{t^{2}}\mathit{dt}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution First we need to write the integrand in a simpler form by carrying out the division:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{9}\frac{2t^{2} + t^{2}\sqrt{t} - 1}{t^{2}}}\mathit{dt} = \int_{1}^{9}{({2 + t^{1 \slash 2} - t^{- 2}})}\mathit{dt}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{1}^{9}\frac{2t^{2} + t^{2}\sqrt{t} - 1}{t^{2}}}\mathit{dt}} = 2t + \frac{t^{3 \slash 2}}{\frac{3}{2}} - \left. \frac{t^{- 1}}{- 1} \right\rbrack_{1}^{9} = 2t + \frac{2}{3}t^{3 \slash 2} + \left. \frac{1}{t} \right\rbrack_{1}^{9}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{1}^{9}\frac{2t^{2} + t^{2}\sqrt{t} - 1}{t^{2}}}\mathit{dt}} = \left( {2 \cdot 9 + \frac{2}{3} \cdot 9^{3 \slash 2} + \frac{1}{9}} \right) - \left( {2 \cdot 1 + \frac{2}{3} \cdot 1^{3 \slash 2} + \frac{1}{1}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{1}^{9}\frac{2t^{2} + t^{2}\sqrt{t} - 1}{t^{2}}}\mathit{dt}} = 18 + 18 + \frac{1}{9} - 2 - \frac{2}{3} - 1 = 32\frac{4}{9}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 A particle moves along a line so that its velocity at time t is \upsilon(t) = t^{2} - t - 6 (measured in meters per second). (a) Find the displacement of the particle during the time period 1 \leqslant t \leqslant 4 ....
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>A particle moves along a line so that its velocity at time $$t$$ is $$\upsilon(t) = t^{2} - t - 6$$ (measured in meters per second).</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Find the displacement of the particle during the time period $$1 \leqslant t \leqslant 4$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Find the distance traveled during this time period.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) By Equation 2, the displacement is $$\begin{array}{l} {{s{(4)} - s{(1)}} = {\int_{1}^{4}{\upsilon{(t)}\mathit{dt} =}}\int_{1}^{4}{({t^{2} - t - 6})}\mathit{dt}} \\ {\phantom{s{(4)} - s{(1)}} = \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{3}}{3} - \frac{t^{2}}{2} - 6t}\rbrack_{1}^{4} = - \frac{9}{2} \right.} \end{array}$$ This means that the particle moved $$4.5$$ m toward the left.</item>
      <item>(b) Note that $$\upsilon(t) = t^{2} - t - 6 = \left( {t - 3} \right)\left( {t + 2} \right)$$ and so $$\upsilon(t) \leqslant 0$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,3} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\upsilon(t) \geqslant 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {3,4} \right\rbrack$$ . Thus, from Equation 3, the distance traveled is $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{4}{\left| {\upsilon{(t)}} \right|\mathit{dt}}} = {\int_{1}^{3}{\left\lbrack {- \upsilon{(t)}} \right\rbrack\mathit{dt} +}}{\int_{3}^{4}{\upsilon{(t)}\mathit{dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\left| {\upsilon{(t)}} \right|\mathit{dt}}} = {\int_{1}^{3}{{({- t^{2} + t + 6})}\mathit{dt} +}}{\int_{3}^{4}{{({t^{2} - t - 6})}\mathit{dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\left| {\upsilon{(t)}} \right|\mathit{dt}}} = \left\lbrack {- \frac{t^{3}}{3} + \frac{t^{2}}{2} + 6t} \right\rbrack_{1}^{3} + \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{3}}{3} - \frac{t^{2}}{2} - 6t} \right\rbrack_{3}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\left| {\upsilon{(t)}} \right|\mathit{dt}}} = \frac{61}{6} \approx 10.17m} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>To integrate the absolute value of $$v(t)$$ , we use Property 5 of integrals from Section 5.2 to split the integral into two parts, one where $$v(t) \leqslant 0$$ and one where $$v(t) \geqslant 0$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

unit_title: Indefinite Integrals and the Net Change Theorem
title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Figure 4 shows the power consumption in the city of San Francisco for a day in September ( P is measured in megawatts; t is measured in hours starting at midnight). Estimate the energy used on that day. Solution Power...
body_xml: Example 7 Figure 4 shows the power consumption in the city of San Francisco for a day in September ( $$P$$ is measured in megawatts; $$t$$ is measured in hours starting at midnight). Estimate the energy used on that day. Solution Power is the rate of change of energy: $$P(t) = E^{\prime}(t)$$ . So, by the Net Change Theorem, $$\int_{0}^{24}{P(t)\mathit{dt} = {\int_{0}^{24}{E^{\prime}(t)\mathit{dt}}} = E(24) - E(0)}$$ is the total amount of energy used on that day. We approximate the value of the integral using the Midpoint Rule with $$12$$ subintervals and $$\Delta t = 2$$ : $$\begin{array}{lcl} {\int_{0}^{24}{{P(t)}\mathit{dt}}} & \approx & {\left\lbrack {P(1) + P(3) + P(5) + \cdots P(21) + P(23)} \right\rbrack\Delta t} \\ & \approx & \left( 440 + 400 + 420 + 620 + 790 + 840 + 850 \right. \\ & & {\left. + 840 + 810 + 690 + 670 + 550 \right)(2)} \\ & = & 15,840 \end{array}$$ The energy used was approximately $$15,840$$ megawatt-hours.

snippet: A Note on Units: A Note on Units How did we know what units to use for energy in Example 7? The integral \int_{0}^{24}{P(t)\mathit{dt}} is defined as the limit of sums of terms of the form P\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t . Now P\left(...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="A Note on Units" title="A Note on Units">
    <heading level="4">A Note on Units</heading>
    <paragraph>How did we know what units to use for energy in Example 7? The integral $$\int_{0}^{24}{P(t)\mathit{dt}}$$ is defined as the limit of sums of terms of the form $$P\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t$$ . Now $$P\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)$$ is measured in megawatts and $$\Delta t$$ is measured in hours, so their product is measured in megawatt-hours. The same is true of the limit. In general, the unit of measurement for $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ is the product of the unit for $$f(x)$$ and the unit for $$x$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1 Let $$u = 2x + 1$$ . Then $$\mathit{du} = 2\mathit{dx}$$ , so $$\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\mathit{du}$$ . Thus the Substitution Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int\sqrt{u}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\mathit{du} = \frac{1}{2}{\int{u^{1 \slash 2}\mathit{du}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{u^{3 \slash 2}}{3 \slash 2} + C = \frac{1}{3}u^{3 \slash 2} + C} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {2x + 1} \right)^{3 \slash 2} + C} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2 Another possible substitution is $$u = \sqrt{2x + 1}$$ . Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{du} = \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\sqrt{2x + 1}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>

    <paragraph>(Or observe that $$u^{2} = 2x + 1$$ , so $$2u\mathit{du} = 2\mathit{dx}$$ .) Therefore</paragraph>

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals" title="The Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals">
    <heading level="4">The Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$g^{\prime}$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$f$$ is continuous on the range of $$u = g(x)$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{a}^{b}{f{({g{(x)}})}g^{\prime}{(x)}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{g{(a)}}^{g{(b)}}{f(u)\mathit{du}}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This rule says that when using a substitution in a definite integral, we must put everything in terms of the new variable $$u$$ , not only $$x$$ and $$\mathit{dx}$$ but also the limits of integration. The new limits of integration are the values of $$u$$ that correspond to $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="7">

    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}$$ using (6).</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Using the substitution from Solution 1 of Example 2, we have $$u = 2x + 1$$ and $$\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\mathit{du}$$ . To find the new limits of integration we note that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${when}x = 0,u = 2(0) + 1 = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${when}x = 4,u = 2(4) + 1 = 9$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{1}^{9}{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u}\mathit{du}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3}u^{3 \slash 2}\rbrack_{1}^{9}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{3}{({9^{3 \slash 2} - 1^{3 \slash 2}})} = \frac{26}{3}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Observe that when using (6) we do not return to the variable $$x$$ after integrating. We simply evaluate the expression in $$u$$ between the appropriate values of $$u$$ .</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 9 Evaluate $$\int_{1}^{e}{\frac{\ln x}{x}\mathit{dx}}$$ . Solution We let $$u = \ln x$$ because its differential $$\mathit{du} = (1 \slash x)\mathit{dx}$$ occurs in the integral. When $$x = 1$$ , $$u = \ln 1 = 0$$ ; when $$x = e$$ , $$u = \ln e = 1$$ . Thus $${\int_{1}^{e}{\frac{\ln x}{x}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{u\mathit{du}}} = \left. \frac{u^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{2}$$ Because the function $$f(x) = \left( \ln x \right) \slash x$$ in Example 9 is positive for $$x > 1$$ , the integral represents the area of the shaded region in Figure 2.

      <item>(a) If $$f$$ is even $$\left\lbrack {f( - x) = f(x)} \right\rbrack$$ , then $${\int_{- a}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx} = 2}}{\int_{0}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}}$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) If $$f$$ is odd $$\left\lbrack {f( - x) = - f(x)} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$\int_{- a}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx} = 0}$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the area of the region bounded above by y = e^{ x} , bounded below by y = x , and bounded on the sides by x = 0 and x = 1 . Solution The region is shown in Figure 4. The upper boundary curve is y = e^{ x} and the...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the area of the region bounded above by $$y = e^{ x}$$ , bounded below by $$y = x$$ , and bounded on the sides by $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region is shown in Figure 4. The upper boundary curve is $$y = e^{ x}$$ and the lower boundary curve is $$y = x$$ . So we use the area formula (2) with $$f(x) = e^{ x}$$ , $$g(x) = x$$ , $$a = 0$$ , and $$b = 1$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{1}{({e^{ x} - x})dx = e^{ x} - \frac{1}{2}x^{2}\rbrack_{0}^{1}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {e - \frac{1}{2} - 1 = e - 1.5}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabolas y = x^{2} and y = 2x - x^{2} . Solution We first find the points of intersection of the parabolas by solving their equations simultaneously. This gives x^{2} = 2x -...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabolas $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$y = 2x - x^{2}$$ . Solution We first find the points of intersection of the parabolas by solving their equations simultaneously. This gives $$x^{2} = 2x - x^{2}$$ , or $$2x^{2} - 2x = 0$$ . Thus $$2x\left( {x - 1} \right) = 0$$ , so $$x = 0$$ or $$1$$ . The points of intersection are $$(0,0)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ . We see from Figure 6 that the top and bottom boundaries are $$y_{T} = 2x - x^{2}$$ and $$y_{B} = x^{2}$$ The area of a typical rectangle is $${({y_{T} - y_{B}})}\Delta x = {\left( {2x - x^{2} - x^{2}} \right)}\Delta x = \left( {\left. 2x - 2x^{2} \right)\Delta x} \right.$$ and the region lies between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ . So the total area is $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {2x - 2x^{2}} \right)dx = 2}}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {x - x^{2}} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = 2\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = 2\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}} \right) = \frac{1}{3}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the approximate area of the region bounded by the curves y = x \slash \sqrt{x^{2} + 1} and y = x^{4} - x . Solution If we were to try to find the exact intersection points, we would have to solve the equation...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the approximate area of the region bounded by the curves $$y = x \slash \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ and $$y = x^{4} - x$$ . Solution If we were to try to find the exact intersection points, we would have to solve the equation $$\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} = x^{4} - x$$ This looks like a very difficult equation to solve exactly (in fact, it’s impossible), so instead we graph the two curves using a computer (see Figure 7). One intersection point is the origin, and we find that the other occurs when $$x \approx 1.18$$ . So an approximation to the area between the curves is $$A \approx {\int_{0}^{1.18}{{\left\lbrack {\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} - {({x^{4} - x})}} \right\rbrack}dx}}$$ To integrate the first term we use the substitution $$u = x^{2} + 1$$ . Then $$du = 2xdx$$ , and when $$x = 1.18$$ , we have $$u \approx 2.39$$ ; when $$x = 0$$ , $$u = 1$$ . So $$\begin{array}{l} {A \approx {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{1}^{2.39}{\frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} - {\int_{0}^{1.18}{{({x^{4} - x})}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. \sqrt{u} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2.39} - \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1.18}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\sqrt{2.39} - 1 - \frac{(1.18)^{5}}{5} + \frac{(1.18)^{2}}{2}}} \\ {\phantom{A} \approx 0.785} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the area of the region bounded by the curves y = \sin x , y = \cos x , x = 0 , and x = \pi \slash 2 . Solution The points of intersection occur when \sin x = \cos x , that is, when x = \pi \slash 4 (since 0...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the area of the region bounded by the curves $$y = \sin x$$ , $$y = \cos x$$ , $$x = 0$$ , and $$x = \pi \slash 2$$ . Solution The points of intersection occur when $$\sin x = \cos x$$ , that is, when $$x = \pi \slash 4$$ (since $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ ). The region is sketched in Figure 9. Observe that $$\cos x \geqslant \sin x$$ when $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 4$$ but $$\sin x \geqslant \cos x$$ when $$\pi \slash 4 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ . Therefore the required area is $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left| \cos x - \sin x \middle| dx = A_{1} + A_{2} \right.}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{{({\cos x - \sin x})}dx + {\int_{\pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({\sin x - \cos x})}dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\left\lbrack {\sin x + \cos x} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 4} + \left\lbrack {- \cos x - \sin x} \right\rbrack_{\pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 2}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 0 - 1} \right) + \left( {- 0 - 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {2\sqrt{2} - 2}} \end{array}$$ In this particular example we could have saved some work by noticing that the region is symmetric about $$x = \pi \slash 4$$ and so $$A = 2A_{1} = 2{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{{({\cos x - \sin x})}dx}}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the area enclosed by the line y = x - 1 and the parabola y^{2} = 2x + 6 . Solution By solving the two equations simultaneously we find that the points of intersection are \left( {- 1, - 2} \right) and \left( {5,4}...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the area enclosed by the line $$y = x - 1$$ and the parabola $$y^{2} = 2x + 6$$ . Solution By solving the two equations simultaneously we find that the points of intersection are $$\left( {- 1, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {5,4} \right)$$ . We solve the equation of the parabola for $$x$$ and notice from Figure 12 that the left and right boundary curves are $$x_{L} = \frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3$$ and $$x_{R} = y + 1$$ We must integrate between the appropriate $$y$$ -values, $$y = - 2$$ and $$y = 4$$ . Thus $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {{\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {x_{R} - x_{L}} \right)}dy}} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\left\lbrack {\left( {y + 1} \right) - \left( {\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3} \right)} \right\rbrack dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {- \frac{1}{2}y^{2} + y + 4} \right)}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. {- \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{y^{3}}{3} \right) + \frac{y^{2}}{2} + 4y} \right\rbrack_{- 2}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {- \frac{1}{6}(64) + 8 + 16 - \left( {\frac{4}{3} + 2 - 8} \right) = 18}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the area of the region enclosed by the curves y = 1/x , y = x , and y = \frac{1}{4}x , using x as the variable of integration and y as the variable of integration. Solution The region is graphed in Figure 14. If...
body_xml: Example 6 Find the area of the region enclosed by the curves $$y = 1/x$$ , $$y = x$$ , and $$y = \frac{1}{4}x$$ , using $$x$$ as the variable of integration and $$y$$ as the variable of integration. Solution The region is graphed in Figure 14. If we integrate with respect to $$x$$ , we must split the region into two parts because the top boundary consists of two separate curves, as shown in Figure 15(a). We compute the area as $$\begin{array}{l} {A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \int_{0}^{1}(x - \frac{1}{4}x)\mathit{dx} + \int_{1}^{2}\left( \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{4}x \right)\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left\lbrack \frac{3}{8}x^{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} + \left\lbrack \ln x - \frac{1}{8}x^{2} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \ln 2} \end{array}$$ If we integrate with respect to $$y$$ , we also need to divide the region into two parts because the right boundary consists of two separate curves, as shown in Figure 15(b). We compute the area as $$\begin{array}{l} {A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \int_{0}^{1/2}(4y - y)\mathit{dy} + \int_{1/2}^{1}\left( \frac{1}{y} - y \right)\mathit{dy}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left\lbrack \frac{3}{2}y^{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1/2} + \left\lbrack \ln y - \frac{1}{2}y^{2} \right\rbrack_{1/2}^{1} = \ln 2} \end{array}$$ Figure 15 Details Two lines, a curve, a shaded region, and a line segment are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1 and the y axis is displayed from 0 to 1 in increments of 1. The first line, y = x, enters from the bottom left, rises upward to the right passing through the origin, and exits at the top right. The second line, y = 1/4 x, enter from the bottom left and also passes through the origin but slopes upward to the right more gradually than y = x, and exits at the right of the viewing window. The curve y = 1/x, enters from the top, goes down to the right, concaves up, descending more gradually as it proceeds to the right, crossing the line y = x at (1, 1) and the line y = 1/4 x at (2, 0.5), and exits at the bottom right. The region is bound by the curve and the two lines are shaded. A vertical dashed line segment rises upward from the tick mark 1 on the x axis, meets the second line, and rises further upward as a solid line until the intersection point of the curve and the first line, y = x. The area to the left of the solid line segment is shaded darker and labeled A_1. The area to the right of the line segment is labeled A_2. Two lines, a curve, a shaded region, and a line segment are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1 and the y axis is displayed from 0 to 1 in increments of 1/2. The first line, y = x, enters from the bottom left, rises upward to the right passing through the origin, and exits at the top right. The second line, y = 1/4 x, enter from the bottom left and also passes through the origin but slopes upward to the right more gradually than y = x, and exits at the right of the viewing window. The curve y = 1/x, enters from the top, goes down to the right, concaves up, descending more gradually as it proceeds to the right, crossing the line y = x at (1, 1) and the line y = 1/4 x at (2, 0.5), and exits at the bottom right. The region is bound by the curve and the two lines are shaded. A horizontal dashed line segment runs rightward from the tick mark 1/2 on the y axis, meets the first line, and continues rightward as a solid line until the intersection point of the curve and the second line. The area below the solid line segment is shaded darker and labeled A_1. The area above the line segment is labeled A_2.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Figure 16 shows velocity curves for two cars, A and B, that start side by side and move along the same road. What does the area between the curves represent? Use the Midpoint Rule to estimate it. Solution We know from...
body_xml:
Example 7 Figure 16 shows velocity curves for two cars, A and B, that start side by side and move along the same road. What does the area between the curves represent? Use the Midpoint Rule to estimate it. Solution We know from Section 5.4 that the area under the velocity curve $$A$$ represents the distance traveled by car A during the first $$16$$ seconds. Similarly, the area under curve $$B$$ is the distance traveled by car B during that time period. So the area between these curves, which is the difference of the areas under the curves, is the distance between the cars after $$16$$ seconds. We read the velocities from the graph and convert them to feet per second $$({1{mi} \slash h = \frac{5280}{3600}{ft} \slash s})$$ . $$t$$ 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 $$v_{A}$$ 0 34 54 67 76 84 89 92 95 $$v_{B}$$ 0 21 34 44 51 56 60 63 65 $$v_{A} - v_{B}$$ 0 13 20 23 25 28 29 29 30
We use the Midpoint Rule with $$n = 4$$ intervals, so that $$\Delta t = 4$$ . The midpoints of the intervals are $${\overline{t}}_{1} = 2$$ , $${\overline{t}}_{2} = 6$$ , $${\overline{t}}_{3} = 10$$ , and $${\overline{t}}_{4} = 14$$ . We estimate the distance between the cars after $$16$$ seconds as follows: $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{0}^{16}{\left( {\upsilon_{A} - \upsilon_{B}} \right)}dt \approx \Delta t\left\lbrack {13 + 23 + 28 + 29} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{16}{\left( {\upsilon_{A} - \upsilon_{B}} \right)}dt} = 4(93) = 372{ft}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Figure 17 is an example of a pathogenesis curve for a measles infection. It shows how the disease develops in an individual with no immunity after the measles virus spreads to the bloodstream from the respiratory...
body_xml: Example 8 Figure 17 is an example of a pathogenesis curve for a measles infection. It shows how the disease develops in an individual with no immunity after the measles virus spreads to the bloodstream from the respiratory tract. The patient becomes infectious to others once the concentration of infected cells becomes great enough and remains infectious until the immune system manages to prevent further transmission. However, symptoms don’t develop until the “amount of infection” reaches a particular threshold. The amount of infection needed to develop symptoms depends on both the concentration of infected cells and time, and corresponds to the area under the pathogenesis curve until symptoms appear. (See Exercise 5.1.15.) (a) The pathogenesis curve in Figure 17 has been modeled by $$f(t) = - t\left( {t - 21} \right)\left( {t + 1} \right)$$ . If infectiousness begins on day $$t_{1} = 10$$ and ends on day $$t_{2} = 18$$ , what are the corresponding concentration levels of infected cells? (b) The level of infectiousness for an infected person is the area between $$N = f(t)$$ and the line through the points $$P_{1}\left( {t_{1},f\left( t_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$P_{2}\left( {t_{2},f\left( t_{2} \right)} \right)$$ , measured in $$({cells} \slash {mL}) \cdot {days}$$ . (See Figure 18.) Compute the level of infectiousness for this particular patient. Solution (a) Infectiousness begins when the concentration reaches $$f(10) = 1210{cells} \slash {mL}$$ and ends when the concentration reduces to $$f(18) = 1026{cells} \slash {mL}$$ . (b) The line through $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ has slope $$\frac{1026 - 1210}{18 - 10} = - \frac{184}{8} = - 23$$ and equation $$\left. N - 1210 = - 23\left( {t - 10} \right)\Leftrightarrow N = - 23t + 1440 \right.$$ . The area between $$f$$ and this line is $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{10}^{18}{\lbrack{f{(t)} - {({- 23t + 1440})}}\rbrack}dt} = {\int_{10}^{18}({- t^{3} + 20t^{2} + 21t + 23t - 1440)dt}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{10}^{18}{\lbrack{f{(t)} - {({- 23t + 1440})}}\rbrack}dt} = {\int_{10}^{18}({- t^{3} + 20t^{2} + 44t - 1440})dt}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{10}^{18}{\lbrack{f{(t)} - {({- 23t + 1440})}}\rbrack}dt} = \left\lbrack {- \frac{t^{4}}{4} + 20\frac{t^{3}}{3} + 44\frac{t^{2}}{2} - 1440t} \right\rbrack_{10}^{18}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{10}^{18}{\lbrack{f{(t)} - {({- 23t + 1440})}}\rbrack}dt} = {- 6156 - \left( {- 8033\frac{1}{3}} \right) \approx 1877}} \end{array}$$ Thus the level of infectiousness for this patient is about $$1877({cells} \slash {mL}) \cdot {days}$$ .

title: Definition of Volume
snippet: Definition of Volume: Definition of Volume Let S be a solid that lies between x = a and x = b . If the cross-sectional area of S in the plane P_{x} , through x and perpendicular to the x -axis, is A(x) , where A is a continuous function,...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Definition of Volume" title="Definition of Volume">
    <heading level="4">Definition of Volume</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$S$$ be a solid that lies between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ . If the cross-sectional area of $$S$$ in the plane $$P_{x}$$ , through $$x$$ and perpendicular to the $$x$$ -axis, is $$A(x)$$ , where $$A$$ is a continuous function, then the volume of $$S$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$V = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}A}(x_{i}^{\ast})\Delta x = {\int_{a}^{b}A}(x)dx$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Show that the volume of a sphere of radius r is V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} . Solution If we place the sphere so that its center is at the origin, then the plane P_{x} intersects the sphere in a circle whose radius (from...
body_xml: Example 1 Show that the volume of a sphere of radius $$r$$ is $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$ . Solution If we place the sphere so that its center is at the origin, then the plane $$P_{x}$$ intersects the sphere in a circle whose radius (from the Pythagorean Theorem) is $$y = \sqrt{r^{2} - x^{2}}$$ . (See Figure 4.) So the cross-sectional area is $$A(x) = \pi y^{2} = \pi(r^{2} - x^{2})$$ Using the definition of volume with $$a = - r$$ and $$b = r$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{- r}^{r}A(x)dx = \int_{- r}^{r}\pi(r^{2} - x^{2})dx} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi{\int_{0}^{r}{(r^{2} - x^{2})dx}}} \left( \text{The integrand is even.} \right)} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {r^{2}x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{r} = 2\pi\left( {r^{3} - \frac{r^{3}}{3}} \right) = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the x -axis the region under the curve y = \sqrt{x} from 0 to 1 . Illustrate the definition of volume by sketching a typical approximating cylinder. Solution The...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the $$x$$ -axis the region under the curve $$y = \sqrt{x}$$ from $$0$$ to $$1$$ . Illustrate the definition of volume by sketching a typical approximating cylinder. Solution The region is shown in Figure 6(a) given below. If we rotate about the $$x$$ -axis, we get the solid shown in Figure 6(b). When we slice through the point $$x$$ , we get a disk with radius $$\sqrt{x}$$ . The area of this cross-section is $$A(x) = \pi{(\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{︸}}{\sqrt{x}})}^{2} = \pi x$$ and the volume of the approximating cylinder (a disk with thickness $$\Delta x$$ ) is $$A(x)\Delta x = \pi x\Delta x$$ The solid lies between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ , so its volume is $$V = \int_{0}^{1}A(x)dx = \int_{0}^{1}\pi xdx = \pi\frac{x^{2}}{2}\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}$$ Did we get a reasonable answer in Example 2? As a check on our work, let’s replace the given region by a square with base $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ and height $$1$$ . If we rotate this square, we get a cylinder with radius $$1$$ , height $$1$$ , and volume $$\pi \cdot 1^{2} \cdot 1 = \pi$$ . We computed that the given solid has half this volume. That seems about right.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by y = x^{3} , y = 8 , and x = 0 about the y -axis. Solution The region is shown in Figure 7(a) and the resulting solid is shown in Figure 7(b)....
body_xml: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $$y = x^{3}$$ , $$y = 8$$ , and $$x = 0$$ about the $$y$$ -axis. Solution The region is shown in Figure 7(a) and the resulting solid is shown in Figure 7(b). Because the region is rotated about the $$y$$ -axis, it makes sense to slice the solid perpendicular to the $$y$$ -axis (obtaining circular cross-sections) and therefore to integrate with respect to $$y$$ . If we slice at height $$y$$ , we get a circular disk with radius $$x$$ , where $$x = \sqrt[3]{y}$$ . So the area of a cross-section through $$y$$ is $$A(y) = \pi{(\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{︸}}{x})}^{2} = \pi{(\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{︸}}{\sqrt[3]{y}})}^{2} = \pi y^{2/3}$$ and the volume of the approximating cylinder pictured in Figure 7(b) is $$A(y)\Delta y = \pi y^{2/3}\Delta y$$ Since the solid lies between $$y = 0$$ and $$y = 8$$ , its volume is $$V = \int_{0}^{8}A(y)dy = \int_{0}^{8}\pi y^{2/3}dy = \pi\left\lbrack {\frac{3}{5}y^{5/3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{8} = \frac{96\pi}{5}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 The region \mathcal{R} enclosed by the curves y = x and y = x^{2} is rotated about the x -axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid. Solution The curves y = x and y = x^{2} intersect at the points (0,0) and \left(...
body_xml: Example 4 The region $$\mathcal{R}$$ enclosed by the curves $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^{2}$$ is rotated about the $$x$$ -axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid. Solution The curves $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^{2}$$ intersect at the points $$(0,0)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ . The region between them, the solid of rotation, and a cross-section perpendicular to the $$x$$ -axis are shown in Figure 8. A cross-section in the plane $$P_{x}$$ has the shape of a washer (an annular ring) with inner radius $$x^{2}$$ and outer radius $$x$$ [see Figure 8(c)], so we find the cross-sectional area by subtracting the area of the inner circle from the area of the outer circle: $${A(x) = {\pi(\underset{\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{ \text{outer} }}{︸}}{x})}}^{2} - \pi{(\underset{\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{ \text{inner} }}{︸}}{x^{2}})}^{2} = \pi(x^{2} - x^{4})$$ Therefore we have $$\begin{array}{l} {v = {\int_{0}^{1}{A(x)dx}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\pi(x^{2} - x^{4})}}dx} \\ {\phantom{v} = \pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{5}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{2\pi}{15}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region in Example 4 about the line y = 2 . Solution The solid and a cross-section are shown in Figure 9. Again the cross-section is a washer, but this time the...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region in Example 4 about the line $$y = 2$$ . Solution The solid and a cross-section are shown in Figure 9. Again the cross-section is a washer, but this time the inner radius is $$2 - x$$ and the outer radius is $$2 - x^{2}$$ . The cross-sectional area is $${A(x) = {\pi(\underset{\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{ \text{outer} }}{︸}}{2 - x^{2}})}}^{2} - \pi{(\underset{\underset{\underset{ \text{radius} }{ \text{inner} }}{︸}}{2 - x})}^{2}$$ and so the volume of $$S$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{0}^{1}A{(x)}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\pi\int_{0}^{1}{{\lbrack{{({2 - x^{2}})}^{2} - {({2 - x})}^{2}}\rbrack}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\pi\int_{0}^{1}{({x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4x})}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - 5\frac{x^{3}}{3} + 4\frac{x^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{8\pi}{15}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region in Example 4 about the line x = - 1 . Solution Figure 11 shows a horizontal cross-section. It is a washer with inner radius 1 + y and outer radius 1 +...
body_xml: Example 6 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region in Example 4 about the line $$x = - 1$$ . Solution Figure 11 shows a horizontal cross-section. It is a washer with inner radius $$1 + y$$ and outer radius $$1 + \sqrt{y}$$ , so the cross-sectional area is $$\begin{array}{l} {{A(y)} = {\pi({outer radius})^{2} - \pi({inner radius})^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{A(y)} = {\pi{({1 + \sqrt{y}})}^{2} - \pi\left( {1 + y} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$ The volume is $$\begin{matrix} {V = {\int_{0}^{1}A(y)dy = \pi\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\left( {1 + \sqrt{y}} \right)^{2} - \left( {1 + y} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack dy}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \pi\int_{0}^{1}\left( {2\sqrt{y} - y - y^{2}} \right)dy = \pi\left\lbrack {\frac{4y^{3/2}}{3} - \frac{y^{2}}{2} - \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}} \end{matrix}$$

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Figure 12 shows a solid with a circular base of radius 1 . Parallel cross-sections perpendicular to the base are equilateral triangles. Find the volume of the solid. SolutionLet’s take the circle to be x^{2} + y^{2} =...
body_xml: Example 7 Figure 12 shows a solid with a circular base of radius $$1$$ . Parallel cross-sections perpendicular to the base are equilateral triangles. Find the volume of the solid. SolutionLet’s take the circle to be $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . The solid, its base, and a typical cross-section at a distance $$x$$ from the origin are shown in Figure 13. Since $$B$$ lies on the circle, we have $$y = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ and so the base of the triangle $$ABC$$ is $$\left| {AB} \right| = 2y = 2\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ . Since the triangle is equilateral, we see from Figure 13(c) that its height is $$\sqrt{3}y = \sqrt{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ . The cross-sectional area is therefore $$A(x) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \cdot \sqrt{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} = \sqrt{3}({1 - x^{2}})$$ and the volume of the solid is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{- 1}^{1}A(x)dx = \int_{- 1}^{1}\sqrt{3}({1 - x^{2}})dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{3}({1 - x^{2}})dx = 2\sqrt{3}\left\lbrack {x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find the volume of a pyramid whose base is a square with side L and whose height is h . Solution We place the origin O at the vertex of the pyramid and the x -axis along its central axis as in Figure 14. Any plane...
body_xml: Example 8 Find the volume of a pyramid whose base is a square with side $$L$$ and whose height is $$h$$ . Solution We place the origin $$O$$ at the vertex of the pyramid and the $$x$$ -axis along its central axis as in Figure 14. Any plane $$P_{x}$$ that passes through $$x$$ and is perpendicular to the $$x$$ -axis intersects the pyramid in a square with side of length $$s$$ , say. We can express $$s$$ in terms of $$x$$ by observing from the similar triangles in Figure 15 that $$\frac{x}{h} = \frac{s/2}{L/2} = \frac{s}{L}$$ and so $$s = Lx/h$$ . [Another method is to observe that the line $$OP$$ has slope $$L/(2h)$$ and so its equation is $$y = Lx/(2h)$$ .] Therefore the cross-sectional area is $$A(x) = s^{2} = \frac{L^{2}}{h^{2}}x^{2}$$ The pyramid lies between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = h$$ , so its volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{0}^{h}A(x)dx = \int_{0}^{h}{\frac{L^{2}}{h^{2}}x^{2}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \frac{L^{2}}{h^{2}}\left. \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{h} = \frac{L^{2}h}{3}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 A wedge is cut out of a circular cylinder of radius 4 by two planes. One plane is perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder. The other intersects the first at an angle of 30^{{^\circ}} along a diameter of the cylinder....
body_xml: Example 9 A wedge is cut out of a circular cylinder of radius 4 by two planes. One plane is perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder. The other intersects the first at an angle of $$30^{{^\circ}}$$ along a diameter of the cylinder. Find the volume of the wedge. Solution If we place the $$x$$ -axis along the diameter where the planes meet, then the base of the solid is a semicircle with equation $$y = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$$ , $$- 4 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$$ . A cross-section perpendicular to the $$x$$ -axis at a distance $$x$$ from the origin is a triangle $$\mathit{ABC}$$ , as shown in Figure 17, whose base is $$y = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$$ and whose height is $$\left| {BC} \right| = y\tan 30^{{^\circ}} = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}/\sqrt{3}$$ . So the cross-sectional area is $$\begin{array}{l} {A(x) = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{16 - x^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{16 - x^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{A(x)} = \frac{16 - x^{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}} \end{array}$$ and the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{- 4}^{4}{A(x)dx =}}{\int_{- 4}^{4}\frac{16 - x^{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}}dx} \\ {\phantom{V} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{\int_{0}^{4}{(16 - x^{2})dx =}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left\lbrack {16x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{128}{3\sqrt{3}}} \end{array}$$ For another method see Exercise 77.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the y -axis the region bounded by y = 2x^{2} - x^{3} and y = 0 . Solution From the sketch in Figure 6 we see that a typical shell has radius x , circumference...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the $$y$$ -axis the region bounded by $$y = 2x^{2} - x^{3}$$ and $$y = 0$$ . Solution From the sketch in Figure 6 we see that a typical shell has radius $$x$$ , circumference $$2\pi x$$ , and height $$f(x) = 2x^{2} - x^{3}$$ . So, by the shell method, the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{0}^{2}{\underset{circumference}{\underset{︸}{\left( {2\pi x} \right)}}\underset{height}{\underset{︸}{({2x^{2} - x^{3}})}}\underset{thickness}{\underset{︸}{dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi{\int_{0}^{2}{{({2x^{3} - x^{4}})}dx = 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}x^{4} - \frac{1}{5}x^{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left( {8 - \frac{32}{5}} \right) = \frac{16}{5}\pi}} \end{array}$$ It can be verified that the shell method gives the same answer as slicing.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the y -axis the region between y = x and y = x^{2} . Solution The region and a typical shell are shown in Figure 8. We see that the shell has radius x ,...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the $$y$$ -axis the region between $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^{2}$$ . Solution The region and a typical shell are shown in Figure 8. We see that the shell has radius $$x$$ , circumference $$2\pi x$$ , and height $$x - x^{2}$$ . So the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{0}^{1}{{({2\pi x})}{({x - x^{2}})}dx = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{1}{{({x^{2} - x^{3}})}dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{6}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use cylindrical shells to find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the x -axis the region under the curve y = \sqrt{x^{}} from 0 to 1 . Solution This problem was solved using disks in Example 6.2.2. To...
body_xml: Example 3 Use cylindrical shells to find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the $$x$$ -axis the region under the curve $$y = \sqrt{x^{}}$$ from $$0$$ to $$1$$ . Solution This problem was solved using disks in Example 6.2.2. To use shells we relabel the curve $$y = \sqrt{x^{}}$$ (in the figure in that example) as $$x = y^{2}$$ in Figure 9. For rotation about the $$x$$ -axis we see that a typical shell has radius $$y$$ , circumference $$2\pi y$$ , and height $$1 - y^{2}$$ . So the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {{\int_{0}^{1}{{({2\pi y})}{({1 - y^{2}})}dy}} = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{1}{{({y - y^{3}})}dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2}}{2} - \frac{y^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}}} \end{array}$$ In this problem the disk method was simpler.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by y = x - x^{2} and y = 0 about the line x = 2 . Solution Figure 10 shows the region and a cylindrical shell formed by rotation about the line x = 2...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $$y = x - x^{2}$$ and $$y = 0$$ about the line $$x = 2$$ . Solution Figure 10 shows the region and a cylindrical shell formed by rotation about the line $$x = 2$$ . It has radius $$2 - x$$ , circumference $$2\pi\left( {2 - x} \right)$$ , and height $$x - x^{2}$$ . The volume of the given solid is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\int_{0}^{1}{2\pi{({2 - x})}{({x - x^{2}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi{\int_{0}^{1}{{({x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 2x})}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{4}}{4} - x^{3} + x^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Figure 11 shows the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves y = x^{2} and y = 2x . A solid is formed by rotating the region about the line x = - 1 . Find the volume of the solid using x as the variable of...
body_xml: Example 5 Figure 11 shows the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$y = 2x$$ . A solid is formed by rotating the region about the line $$x = - 1$$ . Find the volume of the solid using $$x$$ as the variable of integration and $$y$$ as the variable of integration. Solution The solid is shown in Figure 12(a). To find the volume using $$x$$ as the variable of integration, we draw the sample rectangle vertically, as in Figure 12(b). Rotating the region about the line $$x = - 1$$ produces cylindrical shells, so the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{0}^{2}2\pi(x + 1)(2x - x^{2})\mathit{dx} = 2\pi\int_{0}^{2}(x^{2} + 2x - x^{3})\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + x^{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{16\pi}{3}}} \end{array}$$ To find the volume using y as the variable of integration, we draw the sample rectangle horizontally as in Figure 12(c). Rotating the region about the line produces washer-shaped cross-sections, so the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack \pi\left( \sqrt{y} + 1 \right)^{2} - \pi\left( \frac{1}{2}y + 1 \right)^{2} \right\rbrack\mathit{dy} = \pi\int_{0}^{4}\left( 2\sqrt{y} - \frac{1}{4}y^{2} \right)\mathit{dy}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \pi\left\lbrack \frac{4}{3}y^{3/2} - \frac{1}{12}y^{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{16\pi}{3}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 (a) How much work is done in lifting a 1.2 -kg book off the floor to put it on a desk that is 0.7 m high? Use the fact that the acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.8m \slash s^{2} . (b) How much work is done in...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="3">Example 1</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) How much work is done in lifting a $$1.2$$ -kg book off the floor to put it on a desk that is $$0.7$$ m high? Use the fact that the acceleration due to gravity is $$g = 9.8m \slash s^{2}$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) How much work is done in lifting a $$20$$ -lb weight $$6$$ ft off the ground?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The force exerted is equal and opposite to that exerted by gravity, so Equation 1 gives $$F = mg = (1.2)(9.8) = 11.76N$$ and then Equation 2 gives the work done as $$W = Fd = \left( {11.76N} \right)\left( {0.7m} \right) \approx 8.2J$$</item>
      <item>(b) Here the force is given as $$F = 20$$ lb, so the work done is $$W = Fd = \left( {20{lb}} \right)\left( {6{ft}} \right) = 120{ft-lb}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Notice that in part (b), unlike part (a), we did not have to multiply by $$g$$ because we were given the weight (which is a force) and not the mass of the object.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 When a particle is located a distance x feet from the origin, a force of x^{2} + 2x pounds acts on it. How much work is done in moving it from x = 1 to x = 3 ? Solution {W = \int_{1}^{3}{({x^{2} + 2x})}}dx = \left....
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="3">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>When a particle is located a distance $$x$$ feet from the origin, a force of $$x^{2} + 2x$$ pounds acts on it. How much work is done in moving it from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 3$$ ?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${W = \int_{1}^{3}{({x^{2} + 2x})}}dx = \left. \frac{x^{3}}{3}{+ x^{2}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{3} = \frac{50}{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The work done is $$16\frac{2}{3}$$ ft-lb.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 A force of 40 N is required to hold a spring that has been stretched from its natural length of 10 cm to a length of 15 cm. How much work is done in stretching the spring from 15 cm to 18 cm? Solution According to...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="3">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>A force of $$40$$ N is required to hold a spring that has been stretched from its natural length of $$10$$ cm to a length of $$15$$ cm. How much work is done in stretching the spring from $$15$$ cm to $$18$$ cm?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution According to Hooke’s Law, the force required to hold the spring stretched $$x$$ meters beyond its natural length is $$f(x) = kx$$ . When the spring is stretched from $$10$$ cm to $$15$$ cm, the amount stretched is $$5{cm} = 0.05m$$ . This means that $$f(0.05) = 40$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$0.05k = 40 k = \frac{40}{0.05} = 800$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$f(x) = 800x$$ and the work done in stretching the spring from $$15$$ cm to $$18$$ cm is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\int_{0.05}^{0.08}{800x}dx = 800\left. \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0.05}^{0.08}}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {400{\lbrack{{(0.08)}^{2} - {(0.05)}^{2}}\rbrack} = 1.56J}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 A 200 -lb cable is 100 ft long and hangs vertically from the top of a tall building. How much work is required to lift the cable to the top of the building? How much work is required to pull up only 20 feet of the...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="3">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>A $$200$$ -lb cable is $$100$$ ft long and hangs vertically from the top of a tall building.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>How much work is required to lift the cable to the top of the building?</item>
      <item>How much work is required to pull up only $$20$$ feet of the cable?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>One method is to use an argument similar to the one that led to Definition 4. [For another method, see Exercise 14(b).] Let’s place the origin at the top of the building and the $$x$$ -axis pointing downward as in Figure 2. We divide the cable into small parts with length $$\Delta x$$ . If $$x_{i}^{*}$$ is a point in the $$i$$ th such interval, then all points in the interval are lifted by approximately the same amount, namely $$x_{i}^{*}$$ . The cable weighs $$2$$ pounds per foot, so the weight of the $$i$$ th part is $$\left( 2{lb} \slash {ft})(\Delta x{ft}) = 2\Delta x{lb} \right.$$ . Thus the work done on the $$i$$ th part, in foot-pounds, is $$\underset{force}{\underset{︸}{\left( 2\Delta x \right)}} \cdot \underset{distance}{\underset{︸}{x_{i}^{*}}} = 2x_{i}^{*}\Delta x$$ Figure 2 Details A two-dimensional rendering of a building is drawn alongside a vertical axis labeled x. The positive x axis runs vertically downward and has three tick marks labeled 0, x_i^* and 100, with x_i^8 lying below 0 and 100 lying below x_i^*. The top of the building is directly across x = 0. A cable hangs from the top of the building until directly across x = 100. From the top of the building, a tick cable runs vertically downward until x = 100. The tick mark x_i^*corresponds to a small interval Delta x is marked on the cable. We get the total work done by adding all these approximations and letting the number of parts become large (so $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ ): $$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{2x_{i}^{*}\Delta x = \int_{0}^{100}{2x}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {\left. x^{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{100} = 10,000{ft-lb}}} \end{array}$$ If we had placed the origin at the bottom of the cable and the $$x$$ -axis upward, we would have gotten $$W = \int_{0}^{100}2(100 - x)dx$$ which gives the same answer.</item>
      <item>The work required to move the top $$20$$ ft of cable to the top of the building is computed in the same manner as part (a): $$W_{1} = {\int_{0}^{20}{2x}dx = x^{2}\rbrack_{0}^{20}} = 400{ft-lb}$$ Every part of the lower $$80$$ ft of cable moves the same distance, namely $$20$$ ft, so the work done is $$W_{2} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \underset{\underset{distance}{︸}}{20} \cdot \underset{\underset{force}{︸}}{{2\Delta x}} \right) = \int_{20}^{100}40\mathit{dx} = 3200{ft-lb}$$ (Alternatively, we can observe that the lower $$80$$ ft of cable weighs $$80 \cdot 2 = 160{lb}$$ and moves uniformly $$20$$ ft, so the work done is $$160 \cdot 20 = 3200{ft-lb}$$ .) The total work done is $$W_{1} + W_{2} = 400 + 3200 = 3600{ft-lb}$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 A tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with height 10 m and base radius 4 m. It is filled with water to a height of 8 m. Find the work required to empty the tank by pumping all of the water to the top of the...
body_xml: Example 5 A tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with height $$10$$ m and base radius $$4$$ m. It is filled with water to a height of $$8$$ m. Find the work required to empty the tank by pumping all of the water to the top of the tank. (The density of water is $$1000{kg} \slash m^{3}$$ .) Solution Let’s measure depths from the top of the tank by introducing a vertical coordinate line as in Figure 3. The water extends from a depth of $$2$$ m to a depth of $$10$$ m and so we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {2,10} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and choose $$x_{i}^{*}$$ in the $$i$$ th subinterval. This divides the water into $$n$$ layers. The $$i$$ th layer is approximated by a circular cylinder with radius $$r_{i}$$ and height $$\Delta x$$ . We can compute $$r_{i}$$ from similar triangles, using Figure 4, as follows: $$\frac{r_{i}}{10 - x_{i}^{*}} = \frac{4}{10} r_{i} = \frac{2}{5}\left( {10 - x_{i}^{*}} \right)$$ Thus an approximation to the volume of the $$i$$ th layer of water is $$V_{i} \approx \pi r_{i}^{2}\Delta x = \frac{4\pi}{25}\left( {10 - x_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}\Delta x$$ and so its mass is $$\begin{array}{lcl} m_{i} & = & {{density} \times {volume}} \\ & \approx & {1000 \cdot \frac{4\pi}{25}{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x = 160\pi{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x} \end{array}$$ The force required to raise this layer must overcome the force of gravity and so $$\begin{array}{l} {F_{i} = m_{i}g \approx (9.8)160\pi{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x} \\ {\phantom{F_{i}} = 1568\pi{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x} \end{array}$$ Each particle in the layer must travel a distance upward of approximately $$x_{i}^{*}$$ . The work $$W_{i}$$ done to raise this layer to the top is approximately the product of the force $$F_{i}$$ and the distance $$x_{i}^{*}$$ : $$W_{i} \approx F_{i}x_{i}^{*} \approx 1568\pi x_{i}^{*}\left( {10 - x_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}\Delta x$$ To find the total work done in emptying the entire tank, we add the contributions of each of the $$n$$ layers and then take the limit as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}1568}\pi x_{i}^{*}{({10 - x_{i}^{*}})}^{2}\Delta x = \int_{2}^{10}1568}\pi x{({10 - x})}^{2}dx} \\ {\phantom{W} = {1568\pi\int_{2}^{10}{({100x - 20x^{2} + x^{3}})}}dx = 1568\pi\left\lbrack {50x^{2} - \frac{20x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{2}^{10}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {1568\pi\left( \frac{2048}{3} \right) \approx 3.4 \times 10^{6}J}} \end{array}$$

<example number="1">
    <heading level="3">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the average value of the function $${f(x)} = 1 + x^{2}$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>With $$a = - 1$$ and $$b = 2$$ we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{avg} = \frac{1}{b - a}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} = \frac{1}{2 - \left( {- 1} \right)}{\int_{- 1}^{2}{{({1 + x^{2}})}dx = \frac{1}{3}\left\lbrack {x + \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{- 1}^{2} = 2}}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="theorem" source_type="The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals" title="The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals">
    <heading level="3">The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then there exists a number $$c$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ such that</paragraph>

    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{a}^{b}{{f(x)}dx = {f(c)}\left( {b - a} \right)}$$</paragraph>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Since {f(x)} = 1 + x^{2} is continuous on the interval \left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack , the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals says there is a number c in \left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack such that \int_{-...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="3">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Since $${f(x)} = 1 + x^{2}$$ is continuous on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack$$ , the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals says there is a number $$c$$ in $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{- 1}^{2}{{({1 + x^{2}})}dx = {f(c)}\left\lbrack {2 - \left( {- 1} \right)} \right\rbrack}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In this particular case we can find $$c$$ explicitly. From Example 1 we know that $$f_{avg} = 2$$ , so the value of $$c$$ satisfies</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f(c)} = f_{avg} = 2$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$1 + c^{ 2} = 2$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$c^{ 2} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So in this case there happen to be two numbers $$c = \pm 1$$ in the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack$$ that work in the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Show that the average velocity of a car over a time interval \left\lbrack {t_{1},t_{2}} \right\rbrack is the same as the average of its velocities during the trip. Solution If s(t) is the displacement of the car at...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="3">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that the average velocity of a car over a time interval $$\left\lbrack {t_{1},t_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ is the same as the average of its velocities during the trip.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$s(t)$$ is the displacement of the car at time $$t$$ , then, by definition, the average velocity of the car over the interval is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>On the other hand, the average value of the velocity function on the interval is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\upsilon_{avg} = {\frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}{\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}{\upsilon{(t)}dt = \frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}{\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}{s^{\prime}{(t)}dt}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon_{ave}} = {\frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}\left\lbrack {s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)} \right\rbrack \left( \text{by the Net Change Theorem} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon_{ave}} = {\frac{s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}} = {average velocity}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\int{x\sin xdx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Using Formula 1 Suppose we choose $$f(x) = x$$ and $$g^{\prime}(x) = \sin x$$ . Then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1$$ and $$g(x) = - \cos x$$ . (For $$g$$ we can choose any antiderivative of $$g^{\prime}$$ .) Thus, using Formula 1, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{x\sin xdx}} = {f(x)g(x) - {\int{g(x)f^{\prime}(x)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\sin xdx}} = {x\left( {- \cos x} \right) - {\int{\left( {- \cos x} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\sin xdx}} = {- x\cos x + {\int{\cos xdx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\sin xdx}} = {- x\cos x + \sin x + C}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It’s wise to check the answer by differentiating it. If we do so, we get $$x\sin x$$ , as expected.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Using Formula 2 Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${u = x} {dv = \sin xdx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${du = dx} {v = - \cos x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and so</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It is helpful to use the pattern:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclrcl} u & = & {\boxed{ }} & { dv} & = & {\boxed{ }} \\ {du} & = & {\boxed{ }} & { v} & = & {\boxed{ }} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>
