body_xml: Example 7 A wagon is pulled a distance of $$100$$ m along a horizontal path by a constant force of $$70$$ N. The handle of the wagon is held at an angle of $$35^{{^\circ}}$$ above the horizontal. Find the work done by the force. Solution If $$\mathbf{F}$$ and $$\mathbf{D}$$ are the force and displacement vectors, as pictured in Figure 7, then the work done is $$\begin{array}{l} {W = {\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D} = \left| \mathbf{F} \right|\left| \mathbf{D} \right|\cos 35^{{^\circ}}}} \\ {\phantom{W} = {(70)(100)\cos 35^{{^\circ}} \approx 5734N \cdot m = 5734J}} \end{array}$$

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find a vector perpendicular to the plane that passes through the points $$P(1,4,6)$$ , $$Q( - 2,5, - 1)$$ , and $$R(1, - 1,1)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ is perpendicular to both $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ and is therefore perpendicular to the plane through $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ . We know from (12.2.1) that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} & = & {\left( {- 2 - 1} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {5 - 4} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {- 1 - 6} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}} & = & {\left( {1 - 1} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {- 1 - 4} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {1 - 6} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 5\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We compute the cross product of these vectors:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {- 3} & 1 & {- 7} \\ 0 & {- 5} & {- 5} \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}} = {\left( {- 5 - 35} \right)\mathbf{i} - \left( {15 - 0} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {15 - 0} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 40\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j} + 15\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So the vector $$\langle{- 40, - 15,15}\rangle$$ is perpendicular to the given plane. Any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector, such as $$\langle{- 8, - 3,3}\rangle$$ , is also perpendicular to the plane.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="4">

title: Properties of the Cross Product
snippet: Properties of the Cross Product: Properties of the Cross Product If \mathbf{a} , \mathbf{b} , and \mathbf{c} are vectors and c is a scalar, then \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = - \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} \left( {c\mathbf{a}} \right)...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Properties of the Cross Product" title="Properties of the Cross Product">
    <heading level="4">Properties of the Cross Product</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ are vectors and $$c$$ is a scalar, then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = - \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}$$</item>
      <item>$$\left( {c\mathbf{a}} \right) \times \mathbf{b} = c\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) = \mathbf{a} \times \left( {c\mathbf{b}} \right)$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{a} \times \left( {\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}} \right) = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}$$</item>
      <item>$$\left( {\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} \right) \times \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right) = \left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{c}$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{a} \times \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right) = \left( {\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}} \right){\mathbf{b}} - \left( {\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \right){\mathbf{c}}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the scalar triple product to show that the vectors $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{1,4, - 7}\rangle}$$ , $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{2, - 1,4}\rangle}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c} = {\langle{0, - 9,18}\rangle}$$ are coplanar.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We use Equation 13 to compute their scalar triple product:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 4 & {- 7} \\ 2 & {- 1} & 4 \\ 0 & {- 9} & 18 \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {1\left| \begin{array}{cr} {- 1} & 4 \\ {- 9} & 18 \end{array} \right| - 4\left| \begin{array}{cr} 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 18 \end{array} \right| - 7\left| \begin{array}{lc} 2 & {- 1} \\ 0 & {- 9} \end{array} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {1(18) - 4(36) - 7\left( {- 18} \right) = 0}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, by (14), the volume of the parallelepiped determined by $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ is $$0$$ . This means that $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ are coplanar.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 A bolt is tightened by applying a 40 -N force to a 0.25 -m wrench, as shown in Figure 5. Find the magnitude of the torque about the center of the bolt. Solution The magnitude of the torque vector is \begin{array}{l}...
body_xml: Example 6 A bolt is tightened by applying a $$40$$ -N force to a $$0.25$$ -m wrench, as shown in Figure 5. Find the magnitude of the torque about the center of the bolt. Solution The magnitude of the torque vector is $$\begin{array}{l} {\left| \mathbf{\tau} \right| = \left| {\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}} \right| = \left| \mathbf{r} \right|\left| \mathbf{F} \right|\sin 75^{{^\circ}} = (0.25)(40)\sin 75^{{^\circ}}} \\ {\phantom{\left| \mathbf{\tau} \right|} = {10\sin 75^{{^\circ}} \approx 9.66N \cdot m}} \end{array}$$ If the bolt is right-threaded, then the torque vector itself is $$\mathbf{\tau} = \left| \mathbf{\tau} \right|\mathbf{n} \approx 9.66\mathbf{n}$$ where $$\mathbf{n}$$ is a unit vector directed down into the page (by the right-hand rule).

<note type="theorem" source_type="Hamilton" title="Hamilton">

    <paragraph>The cross product was invented by the Irish mathematician Sir William Rowan Hamilton (1805–1865), who had created a precursor of vectors, called quaternions. When he was five years old Hamilton could read Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. At age eight he added French and Italian and at ten he could read Arabic and Sanskrit. At the age of 21, while still an undergraduate at Trinity College in Dublin, Hamilton was appointed Professor of Astronomy at the university and Royal Astronomer of Ireland!</paragraph>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 (a) Find a vector equation and parametric equations for the line that passes through the point \left( {5,1,3} \right) and is parallel to the vector \mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k} . (b) Find two other points on...
body_xml: Example 1 (a) Find a vector equation and parametric equations for the line that passes through the point $$\left( {5,1,3} \right)$$ and is parallel to the vector $$\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}$$ . (b) Find two other points on the line. Solution (a) Here $$\mathbf{r}_{0} = {\langle{5,1,3}\rangle} = 5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}$$ , so the vector equation (1) becomes $$\mathbf{r} = \left( {5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}} \right) + t\left( {\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}} \right)$$ or $$\mathbf{r} = \left( {5 + t} \right){\mathbf{i}} + \left( {1 + 4t} \right){\mathbf{j}} + \left( {3 - 2t} \right){\mathbf{k}}$$ Parametric equations are $${x = 5 + t} {y = 1 + 4t} {z = 3 - 2t}$$ (b) Choosing the parameter value $$t = 1$$ gives $$x = 6$$ , $$y = 5$$ , and $$z = 1$$ , so $$\left( {6,5,1} \right)$$ is a point on the line. Similarly, $$t = - 1$$ gives the point $$\left( {4, - 3,5} \right)$$ . Figure 3 shows the line $$L$$ in Example 1 and its relation to the given point and to the vector that gives its direction.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 (a) Find parametric equations and symmetric equations of the line that passes through the points A\left( {2,4, - 3} \right) and B\left( {3, - 1,1} \right) . (b) At what point does this line intersect the \mathit{xy}...
body_xml: Example 2 (a) Find parametric equations and symmetric equations of the line that passes through the points $$A\left( {2,4, - 3} \right)$$ and $$B\left( {3, - 1,1} \right)$$ . (b) At what point does this line intersect the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane? Solution (a) We are not explicitly given a vector parallel to the line, but we observe that the vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ with representation $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{AB}}$$ is parallel to the line and $$\mathbf{v} = {\langle{3 - 2, - 1 - 4,1 - \left( {- 3} \right)}\rangle} = {\langle{1, - 5,4}\rangle}$$ Thus direction numbers are $$a = 1$$ , $$b = - 5$$ , and $$c = 4$$ . Taking the point $$\left( {2,4, - 3} \right)$$ as $$P_{0}$$ , we see that parametric equations (2) are $${x = 2 + t} {y = 4 - 5t} {z = - 3 + 4t}$$ and symmetric equations (3) are $$\frac{x - 2}{1} = \frac{y - 4}{- 5} = \frac{z + 3}{4}$$ (b) The line intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane when $$z = 0$$ . From the parametric equations we have $$z = - 3 + 4t = 0$$ , which gives $$t = \frac{3}{4}$$ . Using this value of $$t$$ , we get $$x = 2 + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{11}{4}$$ and $$y = 4 - 5\left( \frac{3}{4} \right) = \frac{1}{4}$$ . Thus the line intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane at the point $$\left( {\frac{11}{4},\frac{1}{4},0} \right)$$ . Alternatively, we can put $$z = 0$$ in the symmetric equations and obtain $$\frac{x - 2}{1} = \frac{y - 4}{- 5} = \frac{3}{4}$$ which again gives $$x = \frac{11}{4}$$ and $$y = \frac{1}{4}$$ . Figure 4 shows the line $$L$$ in Example 2 and the point $$P$$ where it intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Show that the lines L_{1} and L_{2} with parametric equations \begin{array}{clll} {{L_{1}:} } & {{x = 1 + t} } & {{y = - 2 + 3t} } & {{z = 4 - t} } \\ {{L_{2}:} } & {{x = 2s} } & {{y = 3 + s} } & {z = - 3 + 4s}...
body_xml: Example 3 Show that the lines $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ with parametric equations $$\begin{array}{clll} {{L_{1}:} } & {{x = 1 + t} } & {{y = - 2 + 3t} } & {{z = 4 - t} } \\ {{L_{2}:} } & {{x = 2s} } & {{y = 3 + s} } & {z = - 3 + 4s} \end{array}$$ are skew lines; that is, they do not intersect and are not parallel (and therefore do not lie in the same plane). Solution The lines are not parallel because the corresponding direction vectors $$\langle{1,3, - 1}\rangle$$ and $$\langle{2,1,4}\rangle$$ are not parallel. (Their components are not proportional.) If $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ had a point of intersection, there would be values of $$t$$ and $$s$$ such that $$\begin{array}{rlrcl} 1 & + & t & = & {2s} \\ {- 2} & + & {3t} & = & {3 + s} \\ 4 & - & t & = & {- 3 + 4s} \end{array}$$ But if we solve the first two equations, we get $$t = \frac{11}{5}$$ and $$s = \frac{8}{5}$$ , and these values don’t satisfy the third equation. Therefore there are no values of $$t$$ and $$s$$ that satisfy the three equations, so $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ do not intersect. Thus $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ are skew lines. The lines $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ in Example 3, shown in Figure 5, are skew lines.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find an equation of the plane through the point \left( {2,4, - 1} \right) with normal vector \mathbf{n} = {\langle{2,3,4}\rangle} . Find the intercepts and sketch the plane. Solution Putting a = 2 , b = 3 , c = 4 ,...
body_xml: Example 4 Find an equation of the plane through the point $$\left( {2,4, - 1} \right)$$ with normal vector $$\mathbf{n} = {\langle{2,3,4}\rangle}$$ . Find the intercepts and sketch the plane. Solution Putting $$a = 2$$ , $$b = 3$$ , $$c = 4$$ , $$x_{0} = 2$$ , $$y_{0} = 4$$ , and $$z_{0} = - 1$$ in Equation 7, we see that an equation of the plane is $$2\left( {x - 2} \right) + 3\left( {y - 4} \right) + 4\left( {z + 1} \right) = 0$$ or $$2x + 3y + 4z = 12$$ To find the $$x$$ -intercept we set $$y = z = 0$$ in this equation and obtain $$x = 6$$ . Similarly, the $$y$$ -intercept is $$4$$ and the $$z$$ -intercept is $$3$$ . This enables us to sketch the portion of the plane that lies in the first octant (see Figure 7).

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find an equation of the plane that passes through the points P\left( {1,3,2} \right) , Q\left( {3, - 1,6} \right) , and R\left( {5,2,0} \right) . Solution The vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} corresponding to...
body_xml: Example 5 Find an equation of the plane that passes through the points $$P\left( {1,3,2} \right)$$ , $$Q\left( {3, - 1,6} \right)$$ , and $$R\left( {5,2,0} \right)$$ . Solution The vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ corresponding to $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ are $${\mathbf{a} = {\langle{2, - 4,4}\rangle}} {\mathbf{b} = {\langle{4, - 1, - 2}\rangle}}$$ Since both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ lie in the plane, their cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is orthogonal to the plane and can be taken as the normal vector. Thus $$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left| \begin{array}{crr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & {- 4} & 4 \\ 4 & {- 1} & {- 2} \end{array} \right| = 12\mathbf{i} + 20\mathbf{j} + 14\mathbf{k}$$ With the point $$P\left( {1,3,2} \right)$$ and the normal vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ , an equation of the plane is $$12\left( {x - 1} \right) + 20\left( {y - 3} \right) + 14\left( {z - 2} \right) = 0$$ or $$6x + 10y + 7z = 50$$ Figure 8 shows the portion of the plane in Example 5 that is enclosed by triangle $$PQR$$ .

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the point at which the line with parametric equations x = 2 + 3t , y = - 4t , z = 5 + t intersects the plane 4x + 5y - 2z = 18 . Solution We substitute the expressions for x , y , and z from the parametric...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the point at which the line with parametric equations $$x = 2 + 3t$$ , $$y = - 4t$$ , $$z = 5 + t$$ intersects the plane $$4x + 5y - 2z = 18$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We substitute the expressions for $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ from the parametric equations into the equation of the plane:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$4\left( {2 + 3t} \right) + 5\left( {- 4t} \right) - 2\left( {5 + t} \right) = 18$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This simplifies to $$- 10t = 20$$ , so $$t = - 2$$ . Therefore the point of intersection occurs when the parameter value is $$t = - 2$$ . Then $$x = 2 + 3\left( {- 2} \right) = - 4$$ , $$y = - 4\left( {- 2} \right) = 8$$ , $$z = 5 - 2 = 3$$ and so the point of intersection is $$\left( {- 4,8,3} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 (a) Find the angle between the planes x + y + z = 1 and x - 2y + 3z = 1 . (b) Find symmetric equations for the line of intersection L of these two planes. Figure 10 shows the planes in Example 7 and their line of...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Find the angle between the planes $$x + y + z = 1$$ and $$x - 2y + 3z = 1$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) Find symmetric equations for the line of intersection $$L$$ of these two planes. Figure 10 shows the planes in Example 7 and their line of intersection $$L$$ . Figure 10 Details Two planes and a line graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The axes are along three sides of a rectangular box. The x axis is along the right side of the base and is displayed from negative 2 to 2, from back to front, in increments of 1. The y axis is along the front side of the base and is displayed from negative 3 to 3, from left to right, in increments of 1. The z axis is along the front side of the left face and is displayed from negative 6 to 6, from bottom to top, in increments of 1. The first plane, labeled x + y + z = 1 resembles a square with its top right corner at the back left corner of the top face of the rectangular box and the bottom left corner of the plane lies at the bottom right corner of the front face. The second plane, labeled x minus 2 y + 3 z = 1, slopes gradually downward to the left from the right face of the rectangular box. The two planes intersect at approximately the middle of the box and the line of their intersection is labeled L. The line begins approximately at the middle of the front face, slopes upward to the back and slightly to the right, and ends at the top right of the back face.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The normal vectors of these planes are $${\mathbf{n}_{1} = {\langle{1,1,1}\rangle}} {\mathbf{n}_{2} = {\langle{1, - 2,3}\rangle}}$$ and so, if $$\theta$$ is the angle between the planes, Corollary 12.3.6 gives $$\begin{array}{ccl} {\cos\theta} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{n}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{n}_{2}}{\left| \mathbf{n}_{1} \right|\left| \mathbf{n}_{2} \right|} = \frac{1(1) + 1\left( {- 2} \right) + 1(3)}{\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1}\sqrt{1 + 4 + 9}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{42}}} \\ \theta & = & {\cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{42}} \right) \approx 72^{{^\circ}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>(b) We first need to find a point on $$L$$ . For instance, we can find the point where the line intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane by setting $$z = 0$$ in the equations of both planes. This gives the equations $$x + y = 1$$ and $$x - 2y = 1$$ , whose solution is $$x = 1$$ , $$y = 0$$ . So the point $$(1,0,0)$$ lies on $$L$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Now we observe that, since $$L$$ lies in both planes, it is perpendicular to both of the normal vectors. Thus a vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ parallel to $$L$$ is given by the cross product</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{n}_{1} \times \mathbf{n}_{2} = \left| \begin{array}{crr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & {- 2} & 3 \end{array} \right| = 5\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and so the symmetric equations of $$L$$ can be written as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x - 1}{5} = \frac{y}{- 2} = \frac{z}{- 3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Another way to find the line of intersection is to solve the equations of the planes for two of the variables in terms of the third, which can be taken as the parameter.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find the distance between the parallel planes 10x + 2y - 2z = 5 and 5x + y - z = 1 . Solution First we note that the planes are parallel because their normal vectors \langle{10,2, - 2}\rangle and \langle{5,1, -...
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the distance between the parallel planes $$10x + 2y - 2z = 5$$ and $$5x + y - z = 1$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution First we note that the planes are parallel because their normal vectors $$\langle{10,2, - 2}\rangle$$ and $$\langle{5,1, - 1}\rangle$$ are parallel. To find the distance $$D$$ between the planes, we choose any point on one plane and calculate its distance to the other plane. In particular, if we put $$y = z = 0$$ in the equation of the first plane, we get $$10x = 5$$ and so $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},0,0} \right)$$ is a point in this plane. By Formula 9, the distance between $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},0,0} \right)$$ and the plane $$5x + y - z - 1 = 0$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D = \frac{\left| {5\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) + 1(0) - 1(0) - 1} \right|}{\sqrt{5^{2} + 1^{2} + \left( {- 1} \right)^{2}}} = \frac{\frac{3}{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So the distance between the planes is $$\sqrt{3} \slash 6$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 In Example 3 we showed that the lines \begin{array}{clll} {{L_{1}:} } & {{x = 1 + t} } & {{y = - 2 + 3t} } & {{z = 4 - t} } \\ {{L_{2}:} } & {{x = 2s} } & {{y = 3 + s} } & {{z = - 3 + 4s} } \end{array} are skew. Find...
body_xml: Example 9 In Example 3 we showed that the lines $$\begin{array}{clll} {{L_{1}:} } & {{x = 1 + t} } & {{y = - 2 + 3t} } & {{z = 4 - t} } \\ {{L_{2}:} } & {{x = 2s} } & {{y = 3 + s} } & {{z = - 3 + 4s} } \end{array}$$ are skew. Find the distance between them. Solution Since the two lines $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ are skew, they can be viewed as lying on two parallel planes $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ . The distance between $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ is the same as the distance between $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ , which can be computed as in Example 8. The common normal vector to both planes must be orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = {\langle{1,3, - 1}\rangle}$$ (the direction of $$L_{1}$$ ) and $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = {\langle{2,1,4}\rangle}$$ (the direction of $$L_{2}$$ ). So a normal vector is $$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{v}_{1} \times \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left| \begin{array}{crr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 3 & {- 1} \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \end{array} \right| = 13\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}$$ If we put $$s = 0$$ in the equations of $$L_{2}$$ , we get the point $$\left( {0,3, - 3} \right)$$ on $$L_{2}$$ and so an equation for $$P_{2}$$ is $$13\left( {x - 0} \right) - 6\left( {y - 3} \right) - 5\left( {z + 3} \right) = 0$$ or $$13x - 6y - 5z + 3 = 0$$ If we now set $$t = 0$$ in the equations for $$L_{1}$$ , we get the point $$\left( {1, - 2,4} \right)$$ on $$P_{1}$$ . So the distance between $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ is the same as the distance from $$\left( {1, - 2,4} \right)$$ to $$13x - 6y - 5z + 3 = 0$$ . By Formula 9, this distance is $$D = \frac{\left| {13(1) - 6\left( {- 2} \right) - 5(4) + 3} \right|}{\sqrt{13^{2} + \left( {- 6} \right)^{2} + \left( {- 5} \right)^{2}}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{230}} \approx 0.53$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Sketch the graph of the surface z = x^{2} . Solution Notice that the equation of the graph, z = x^{2} , doesn’t involve y . This means that any vertical plane with equation y = k (parallel to the \mathit{xz} -plane)...
body_xml: Example 1 Sketch the graph of the surface $$z = x^{2}$$ . Solution Notice that the equation of the graph, $$z = x^{2}$$ , doesn’t involve $$y$$ . This means that any vertical plane with equation $$y = k$$ (parallel to the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane) intersects the graph in a curve with equation $$z = x^{2}$$ . So these vertical traces are parabolas. Figure 1 shows how the graph is formed by taking the parabola $$z = x^{2}$$ in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane and moving it in the direction of the $$y$$ -axis. The graph is a surface, called a parabolic cylinder, made up of infinitely many shifted copies of the same parabola. Here the rulings of the cylinder are parallel to the $$y$$ -axis.

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Identify and sketch the surfaces.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$</item>
      <item>(b) $$y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Since $$z$$ is missing and the equations $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$z = k$$ represent a circle with radius $$1$$ in the plane $$z = k$$ , the surface $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ is a circular cylinder whose axis is the $$z$$ -axis. (See Figure 2. We first encountered this surface in Example 12.1.2.) Here the rulings are vertical lines. Figure 2 Details A three dimensional rendering of a cylinder is graphed in the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The cylinder has its center at the origin and it's top and bottom surfaces are parallel to the x y plane. Vertical lines are drawn on the outer surface of the cylinder, such that they are parallel to the z axis. $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$</item>
      <item>(b) In this case $$x$$ is missing and the surface is a circular cylinder whose axis is the $$x$$ -axis. (See Figure 3.) It is obtained by taking the circle $$y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ , $$x = 0$$ in the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane and moving it parallel to the $$x$$ -axis. Figure 3 Details A three dimensional rendering of a cylinder is graphed in the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The cylinder has its center at the origin and it's top and bottom surfaces are parallel to the y z plane. Lines are drawn on the outer surface of the cylinder, such that they are parallel to the x axis. $$y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use traces to sketch the quadric surface with equation x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{9} + \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1 Solution By substituting z = 0 , we find that the trace in the \mathit{xy} -plane is x^{2} + y^{2} \slash 9 = 1 ,...
body_xml: Example 3 Use traces to sketch the quadric surface with equation $$x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{9} + \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1$$ Solution By substituting $$z = 0$$ , we find that the trace in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is $$x^{2} + y^{2} \slash 9 = 1$$ , which we recognize as an equation of an ellipse. In general, the horizontal trace in the plane $$z = k$$ is $${x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{9} = 1 - \frac{k^{2}}{4}} {z = k}$$ which is an ellipse, provided that $$k^{2} < 4$$ , that is, $$- 2 < k < 2$$ . (If $$\left| k \middle| = 2 \right.$$ , the trace consists of a single point, and the trace is empty for $$\left| k \middle| > 2 \right.$$ .) Similarly, vertical traces parallel to the $$\mathit{yz}$$ - and $$\mathit{xz}$$ -planes are also ellipses: $$\begin{array}{cll} {{\frac{y^{2}}{9} + \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1 - k^{2}} } & {{x = k} } & \left( {{if} - 1 < k < 1} \right) \\ {{x^{2} + \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1 - \frac{k^{2}}{9}} } & {{y = k} } & \left( {{if} - 3 < k < 3} \right) \end{array}$$ Figure 4 shows how drawing some traces indicates the shape of the surface. It’s called an ellipsoid because all of its traces are ellipses. Notice that it is symmetric with respect to each coordinate plane; this is because its equation involves only even powers of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Use traces to sketch the surface z = 4x^{2} + y^{2} . Solution If we put x = 0 , we get z = y^{2} , so the \mathit{yz} -plane intersects the surface in a parabola. If we put x = k (a constant), we get z = y^{2} +...
body_xml: Example 4 Use traces to sketch the surface $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ . Solution If we put $$x = 0$$ , we get $$z = y^{2}$$ , so the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane intersects the surface in a parabola. If we put $$x = k$$ (a constant), we get $$z = y^{2} + 4k^{2}$$ . This means that if we slice the graph with any plane parallel to the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane, we obtain a parabola that opens upward. Similarly, if $$y = k$$ , the trace is $$z = 4x^{2} + k^{2}$$ , which is again a parabola that opens upward. If we put $$z = k$$ , we get the horizontal traces $$4x^{2} + y^{2} = k$$ , which we recognize as a family of ellipses $$(k > 0)$$ . Knowing the shapes of the traces, we can sketch the graph in Figure 5. Because of the elliptical and parabolic traces, the quadric surface $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is called an elliptic paraboloid.

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Sketch the surface z = y^{2} - x^{2} . Solution The traces in the vertical planes x = k are the parabolas z = y^{2} - k^{2} , which open upward. The traces in y = k are the parabolas z = - x^{2} + k^{2} , which open...
body_xml: Example 5 Sketch the surface $$z = y^{2} - x^{2}$$ . Solution The traces in the vertical planes $$x = k$$ are the parabolas $$z = y^{2} - k^{2}$$ , which open upward. The traces in $$y = k$$ are the parabolas $$z = - x^{2} + k^{2}$$ , which open downward. The horizontal traces are $$y^{2} - x^{2} = k$$ , a family of hyperbolas. We draw the families of traces in Figure 6, and we show how the traces appear when placed in their correct planes in Figure 7. In Figure 8 we fit together the traces from Figure 7 to form the surface $$z = y^{2} - x^{2}$$ , a hyperbolic paraboloid. Notice that the shape of the surface near the origin resembles that of a saddle. This surface will be investigated further in Section 14.7 when we discuss saddle points.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Sketch the surface \frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} - \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1 . Solution The trace in any horizontal plane z = k is the ellipse \frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} = 1 + \frac{k^{2}}{4} z = k but the traces in the \mathit{xz} -...
body_xml: Example 6 Sketch the surface $$\frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} - \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1$$ . Solution The trace in any horizontal plane $$z = k$$ is the ellipse $$\frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} = 1 + \frac{k^{2}}{4} z = k$$ but the traces in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ - and $$\mathit{yz}$$ -planes are the hyperbolas $${\frac{x^{2}}{4} - \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1} {y = 0}$$ and $${y^{2} - \frac{z^{2}}{4} = 1} {x = 0}$$ This surface is called a hyperboloid of one sheet and is sketched in Figure 9.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Identify and sketch the surface 4x^{2} - y^{2} + 2z^{2} + 4 = 0 . Solution Dividing by - 4 , we first put the equation in standard form: - x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{4} - \frac{z^{2}}{2} = 1 Comparing this equation with...
body_xml: Example 7 Identify and sketch the surface $$4x^{2} - y^{2} + 2z^{2} + 4 = 0$$ . Solution Dividing by $$- 4$$ , we first put the equation in standard form: $$- x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{4} - \frac{z^{2}}{2} = 1$$ Comparing this equation with Table 1, we see that it represents a hyperboloid of two sheets, the only difference being that in this case the axis of the hyperboloid is the $$y$$ -axis. The traces in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ - and $$\mathit{yz}$$ -planes are the hyperbolas $$- x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1 z = 0$$ and $$\frac{y^{2}}{4} - \frac{z^{2}}{2} = 1 x = 0$$ The surface has no trace in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, but traces in the vertical planes $$y = k$$ for $$|k| > 2$$ are the ellipses $${x^{2} + \frac{z^{2}}{2} = \frac{k^{2}}{4} - 1} {y = k}$$ which can be written as $${\frac{x^{2}}{\frac{k^{2}}{4} - 1} + \frac{z^{2}}{2\left( {\frac{k^{2}}{4} - 1} \right)} = 1} {y = k}$$ These traces are used to make the sketch in Figure 10.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Classify the quadric surface x^{2} + 2z^{2} - 6x - y + 10 = 0 . Solution By completing the square we rewrite the equation as y - 1 = \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + 2z^{2} Comparing this equation with Table 1, we see that...
body_xml: Example 8 Classify the quadric surface $$x^{2} + 2z^{2} - 6x - y + 10 = 0$$ . Solution By completing the square we rewrite the equation as $$y - 1 = \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + 2z^{2}$$ Comparing this equation with Table 1, we see that it represents an elliptic paraboloid. Here, however, the axis of the paraboloid is parallel to the $$y$$ -axis, and it has been shifted so that its vertex is the point $$\left( {3,1,0} \right)$$ . The traces in the plane $$y = k\left( {k > 1} \right)$$ are the ellipses $${\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + 2z^{2} = k - 1} {y = k}$$ The trace in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the parabola with equation $$y = 1 + \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}$$ , $$z = 0$$ . The paraboloid is sketched in Figure 11.

<example number="1">

    <paragraph>If</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r}(t) = {\langle{t^{3},\ln(3 - t),\sqrt{t}}\rangle}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>then the component functions are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f(t) = t^{3}} {g(t) = \ln\left( {3 - t}) \right.} {h(t) = \sqrt{t}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>By our usual convention, the domain of $$\mathbf{r}$$ consists of all values of $$t$$ for which the expression for $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ is defined. The expressions $$t^{3}$$ , $$\ln\left( {3 - t}) \right.$$ , and $$\sqrt{t}$$ are all defined when $$3 - t > 0$$ and $$t \geqslant 0$$ . Therefore the domain of $$\mathbf{r}$$ is the interval $$\lbrack 0,3)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{r}(t) , where \mathbf{r}{(t)} = {({1 + t^{3}})}\mathbf{i} + te^{- t}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\sin t}{t}\mathbf{k} . Solution According to Definition 1, the limit of \mathbf{r} is the...
body_xml: Example 2 Find $$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{r}(t)$$ , where $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = {({1 + t^{3}})}\mathbf{i} + te^{- t}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\sin t}{t}\mathbf{k}$$ . Solution According to Definition 1, the limit of $$\mathbf{r}$$ is the vector whose components are the limits of the component functions of $$\mathbf{r}$$ : $$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\mathbf{r}(t)$$ $$=$$ $$\left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}(1 + t^{3})} \right\rbrack\mathbf{i} + \left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}te^{- t}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{j} + \left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin t}{t}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{k}$$ $$=$$ $$\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{k}$$ (by Equation 3.3.5 )

    <paragraph math="block">$${x = 1 + t} {y = 2 + 5t} {z = - 1 + 6t}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which we recognize from Equations 12.5.2 as parametric equations of a line passing through the point $$\left( {1,2, - 1}) \right.$$ and parallel to the vector $$\langle{1,5,6}\rangle$$ . Alternatively, we could observe that the function can be written as $$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_{0} + t\mathbf{v}$$ , where $$\mathbf{r}_{0} = {\langle{1,2, - 1}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = {\langle{1,5,6}\rangle}$$ , and this is the vector equation of a line as given by Equation 12.5.1.</paragraph>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Sketch the curve whose vector equation is \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} Solution The parametric equations for this curve are {x = \cos t} {y = \sin t} {z = t} Since x^{2} + y^{2} =...
body_xml: Example 4 Sketch the curve whose vector equation is $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k}$$ Solution The parametric equations for this curve are $${x = \cos t} {y = \sin t} {z = t}$$ Since $$x^{2} + y^{2} = \cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t = 1$$ for all values of $$t$$ , the curve must lie on the circular cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . The point $$\left( {x,y,z}) \right.$$ lies directly above the point $$\left( {x,y,0}) \right.$$ , which moves counterclockwise around the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane. (The projection of the curve onto the $$xy$$ -plane has vector equation $$\mathbf{r}(t) = {\langle{\cos t,\sin t,0}\rangle}$$ . See Example 10.1.2.) Since $$z = t$$ , the curve spirals upward around the cylinder as $$t$$ increases. The curve, shown in Figure 2, is called a helix.

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find a vector equation and parametric equations for the line segment that joins the point P\left( {1,3, - 2}) \right. to the point Q\left( {2, - 1,3}) \right. . Solution In Section 12.5 we found a vector equation for...
body_xml: Example 5 Find a vector equation and parametric equations for the line segment that joins the point $$P\left( {1,3, - 2}) \right.$$ to the point $$Q\left( {2, - 1,3}) \right.$$ . Solution In Section 12.5 we found a vector equation for the line segment that joins the tip of the vector $$\mathbf{r}_{0}$$ to the tip of the vector $$\mathbf{r}_{1}$$ : $${\mathbf{r}(t) = \left( {1 - t}) \right.\mathbf{r}_{0} + t\mathbf{r}_{1}} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1}$$ (See Equation 12.5.4.) Here we take $$\mathbf{r}_{0} = {\langle{1,3, - 2}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}_{1} = {\langle{2, - 1,3}\rangle}$$ to obtain a vector equation of the line segment from $$P$$ to $$Q$$ : $${\mathbf{r}(t) = \left( {1 - t}) \right.{\langle{1,3, - 2}\rangle} + t{\langle{2, - 1,3}\rangle}} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1}$$ or $${\mathbf{r}(t) = {\langle{1 + t,3 - 4t, - 2 + 5t}\rangle}} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1}$$ The corresponding parametric equations are $${x = 1 + t} {y = 3 - 4t} {z = - 2 + 5t} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1}$$ Figure 4 shows the line segment $$PQ$$ in Example 5.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find a vector function that represents the curve of intersection of the cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 and the plane y + z = 2 . Solution Figure 5 shows how the plane and the cylinder intersect, and Figure 6 shows the...
body_xml: Example 6 Find a vector function that represents the curve of intersection of the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and the plane $$y + z = 2$$ . Solution Figure 5 shows how the plane and the cylinder intersect, and Figure 6 shows the curve of intersection $$C$$ , which is an ellipse. The projection of $$C$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$z = 0$$ . So we know from Example 10.1.2 that we can write $${x = \cos t} {y = \sin t} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi}$$ From the equation of the plane, we have $$z = 2 - y = 2 - \sin t$$ So we can write parametric equations for $$C$$ as $${x = \cos t} {y = \sin t} {z = 2 - \sin t} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi}$$ The corresponding vector equation is $${\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + \left( {2 - \sin t}) \right.\mathbf{k}} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi}$$ This equation is called a parametrization of the curve $$C$$ . The arrows in Figure 6 indicate the direction in which $$C$$ is traced as the parameter $$t$$ increases.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Find parametric equations for the curve of intersection of the paraboloid 4y = x^{2} + z^{2} and the plane y = x . Solution Because any point on the curve C of intersection satisfies the equations of both surfaces, we...
body_xml: Example 7 Find parametric equations for the curve of intersection of the paraboloid $$4y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and the plane $$y = x$$ . Solution Because any point on the curve $$C$$ of intersection satisfies the equations of both surfaces, we can substitute $$y = x$$ into the equation of the paraboloid, giving $$4x = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ . Completing the square in $$x$$ gives $$(x - 2)^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ , so $$C$$ must be contained in the circular cylinder $$(x - 2)^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ , and the projection of $$C$$ onto the $$xz$$ -plane is the circle $$(x - 2)^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ , $$y = 0$$ [with center $$\left( {2,0,0} \right)$$ and radius $$2$$ ]. From Example 10.1.4, we can write $$x = 2 + 2\cos t$$ , $$z = 2\sin t$$ , $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ , and because $$y = x$$ , parametric equations for $$C$$ are $${x = 2 + 2\cos t} {y = 2 + 2\cos t} {z = 2\sin t} {0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi}$$ Figure 7 shows the surfaces of Example 7 and their curve of intersection.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Use a calculator or computer to draw the curve with vector equation \mathbf{r}(t) = {\langle{t,t^{2},t^{3}}\rangle} . This curve is called a twisted cubic. Solution We start by plotting the curve with parametric...
body_xml: Example 8 Use a calculator or computer to draw the curve with vector equation $$\mathbf{r}(t) = {\langle{t,t^{2},t^{3}}\rangle}$$ . This curve is called a twisted cubic. Solution We start by plotting the curve with parametric equations $$x = t$$ , $$y = t^{2}$$ , $$z = t^{3}$$ for $$- 2 \leqslant t \leqslant 2$$ . The result is shown in Figure 10(a), but it’s hard to see the true nature of the curve from that graph alone. Some three-dimensional graphing software allows the user to enclose a curve or surface in a box instead of displaying the coordinate axes. When we look at the same curve in a box in Figure 10(b), we have a much clearer picture of the curve. We can see that it climbs from a lower corner of the box to the upper corner nearest us, and it twists as it climbs. We get an even better idea of the curve when we view it from different vantage points. Part (c) shows the result of rotating the box to give another viewpoint. Parts (d), (e), and (f) show the views we get when we look directly at a face of the box. In particular, part (d) shows the view from directly above the box. It is the projection of the curve onto the $$xy$$ -plane, namely, the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ . Part (e) shows the projection onto the $$xz$$ -plane, the cubic curve $$z = x^{3}$$ . It’s now obvious why the given curve is called a twisted cubic.

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <list type="unordered">

    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) According to Theorem 2, we differentiate each component of $$\mathbf{r}$$ : $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} = 3t^{2}\mathbf{i} + {({1 - t})}e^{- t}\mathbf{j} + 2\cos 2t\mathbf{k}$$</item>
      <item>(b) Since $$\mathbf{r}{(0)} = \mathbf{i}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(0)} = \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$$ , the unit tangent vector at the point $$({1,0,0})$$ is $$\mathbf{T}{(0)} = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(0)}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(0)}} \right|} = \frac{\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{1 + 4}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\mathbf{j} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\mathbf{k}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 2 For the curve $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = \sqrt{t}\mathbf{i} + {({2 - t})}\mathbf{j}$$ , find $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}$$ and sketch the position vector $$\mathbf{r}{(1)}$$ and the tangent vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(1)}$$ . Solution We have $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(1)} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}$$ The curve is a plane curve and elimination of the parameter from the equations $$x = \sqrt{t}$$ , $$y = 2 - t$$ gives $$y = 2 - x^{2}$$ , $$x \geqslant 0$$ . In Figure 2 we draw the position vector $$\mathbf{r}{(1)} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$$ starting at the origin and the tangent vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(1)}$$ starting at the corresponding point $$({1,1})$$ . Notice from Figure 2 that the tangent vector points in the direction of increasing $$t$$ . (See Exercise 60.)

body_xml: Example 3 Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the helix with parametric equations $${x = 2\cos t} {y = \sin t} {z = t}$$ at the point $$({0,1,\pi \slash 2})$$ . Solution The vector equation of the helix is $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = {\langle{2\cos t,\sin t,t}\rangle}$$ , so $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} = {\langle{- 2\sin t,\cos t,1}\rangle}$$ The parameter value corresponding to the point $$({0,1,\pi \slash 2})$$ is $$t = \pi \slash 2$$ , so the tangent vector there is $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{({\pi \slash 2})} = {\langle{- 2,0,1}\rangle}$$ . The tangent line is the line through $$({0,1,\pi \slash 2})$$ parallel to the vector $$\langle{- 2,0,1}\rangle$$ , so by Equations 12.5.2 its parametric equations are $${x = - 2t} {y = 1} {z = \frac{\pi}{2} + t}$$ The helix and the tangent line in Example 3 are shown in Figure 3.

title: Theorem
snippet: Theorem: Theorem Suppose \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} are differentiable vector functions, c is a scalar, and f is a real-valued function. Then \frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} + \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack =...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem" title="Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are differentiable vector functions, $$c$$ is a scalar, and $$f$$ is a real-valued function. Then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} + \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)} + \mathbf{v}^{\prime}{(t)}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {c\mathbf{u}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = c\mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {f{(t)}\mathbf{u}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = f^{\prime}{(t)}\mathbf{u}{(t)} + f{(t)}\mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)} + \mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}^{\prime}{(t)}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \times \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)} \times \mathbf{v}{(t)} + \mathbf{u}{(t)} \times \mathbf{v}^{\prime}{(t)}$$</item>
      <item>$${\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{({f{(t)}})}} \right\rbrack = f^{\prime}{(t)}\mathbf{u}^{\prime}{({f{(t)}})}} {({Chain Rule})}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Proof of Formula 4
snippet: Proof of Formula 4: Proof of Formula 4 Let {\mathbf{u}{(t)} = {\langle{f_{1}{(t)},f_{2}{(t)},f_{3}{(t)}}\rangle}} {\mathbf{v}{(t)} = {\langle{g_{1}{(t)},g_{2}{(t)},g_{3}{(t)}}\rangle}} Then \mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)} =...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Proof of Formula 4" title="Proof of Formula 4">
    <heading level="4">Proof of Formula 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\mathbf{u}{(t)} = {\langle{f_{1}{(t)},f_{2}{(t)},f_{3}{(t)}}\rangle}} {\mathbf{v}{(t)} = {\langle{g_{1}{(t)},g_{2}{(t)},g_{3}{(t)}}\rangle}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)} = f_{1}{(t)}g_{1}{(t)} + f_{2}{(t)}g_{2}{(t)} + f_{3}{(t)}g_{3}{(t)} = \underset{\mathbf{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}f_{\mathbf{i}}{(t)}g_{\mathbf{i}}{(t)}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so the ordinary Product Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack = \frac{d}{dt}\underset{\mathit{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}f_{\mathit{i}}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}{(t)} = \underset{\mathit{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {f_{\mathit{i}}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}{(t)}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack} = \underset{\mathit{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}\left\lbrack {f_{\mathit{i}}^{\prime}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}{(t)} + f_{\mathit{i}}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack} = \underset{\mathit{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}f_{\mathit{i}}^{\prime}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}{(t)} + \underset{\mathit{i}=1}{\overset{3}{\sum}}f_{\mathit{i}}{(t)}g_{\mathit{i}}^{\prime}{(t)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right\rbrack} = \mathbf{u}^{\prime}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}{(t)} + \mathbf{u}{(t)} \cdot \mathbf{v}^{\prime}{(t)}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the length of the arc of the circular helix with vector equation \mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} from the point ({1,0,0}) to the point ({1,0,2\pi}) . Solution Since...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the length of the arc of the circular helix with vector equation $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k}$$ from the point $$({1,0,0})$$ to the point $$({1,0,2\pi})$$ . Solution Since $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} = - \sin t\mathbf{i} + \cos t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$ , we have $$|\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)| = \sqrt{{( - \sin t)}^{2} + \cos^{2}t + 1} = \sqrt{2}$$ The arc from $$({1,0,0})$$ to $$({1,0,2\pi})$$ is described by the parameter interval $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ and so, from Formula 3, we have $$L = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right|dt = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{2}dt = 2\sqrt{2}\pi$$ Figure 2 shows the arc of the helix whose length is computed in Example 1.

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Reparametrize the helix \mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} with respect to arc length measured from ({1,0,0}) in the direction of increasing t . Solution The initial point ({1,0,0})...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Reparametrize the helix $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k}$$ with respect to arc length measured from $$({1,0,0})$$ in the direction of increasing $$t$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The initial point $$({1,0,0})$$ corresponds to the parameter value $$t = 0$$ . From Example 1 we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{ds}{dt} = \left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right| = \sqrt{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$s = s{(t)} = \int_{o}^{t}\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(u)}} \right|du = \int_{o}^{t}\sqrt{2}du = \sqrt{2}t$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore $$t = s \slash \sqrt{2}$$ and the required reparametrization is obtained by substituting for $$t$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r}{({t{(s)}})} = \cos{({s \slash \sqrt{2}})}\mathbf{i} + \sin{({s \slash \sqrt{2}})}\mathbf{j} + {({s \slash \sqrt{2}})}\mathbf{k}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition The curvature of a curve is \kappa = \left| \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} \right| where \mathbf{T} is the unit tangent vector.
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>The curvature of a curve is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa = \left| \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} \right|$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$\mathbf{T}$$ is the unit tangent vector.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Show that the curvature of a circle of radius a is 1 \slash a . Solution We can take the circle to have center the origin, and then a parametrization is \mathbf{r}{(t)} = a\cos t\mathbf{i} + a\sin t\mathbf{j} Therefore...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that the curvature of a circle of radius $$a$$ is $$1 \slash a$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We can take the circle to have center the origin, and then a parametrization is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = a\cos t\mathbf{i} + a\sin t\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} = - a\sin t\mathbf{i} + a\cos t\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right| = a$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{T}{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right|} = - \sin t\mathbf{i} + \cos t\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{T}^{\prime}{(t)} = - \cos t\mathbf{i} - \sin t\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This gives $$\left| {\mathbf{T}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right| = 1$$ , so using Formula 9, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa{(t)} = \frac{\left| {\mathbf{T}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right|}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right|} = \frac{1}{a}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the curvature of the twisted cubic \mathbf{r}{(t)} = {\langle{t,t^{2},t^{3}}\rangle} at a general point and at ({0,0,0}) . Solution We first compute the required ingredients: \begin{array}{rcl}...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the curvature of the twisted cubic $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = {\langle{t,t^{2},t^{3}}\rangle}$$ at a general point and at $$({0,0,0})$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We first compute the required ingredients:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} & = & {{\langle 1,2t,3t^{2}\rangle} {\mathbf{r}^{''}(t)} = {\langle 0,2,6t\rangle}} \\ \left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \right| & = & \sqrt{1 + 4t^{2} + 9t^{4}} \\ {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \times \mathbf{r}^{''}(t)} & = & \left| \begin{array}{lll} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & {2t} & {3t^{2}} \\ 0 & 2 & {6t} \end{array} \middle| = 6t^{2}\mathbf{i} - 6t\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} \right. \\ \left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \times \mathbf{r}^{''}(t) \right| & = & {\sqrt{36t^{4} + 36t^{2} + 4} = 2\sqrt{9t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Theorem 10 then gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa{(t)} = \frac{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} \times \mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)}} \right|}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}} \right|^{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{1 + 9t^{2} + 9t^{4}}}{{({1 + 4t^{2} + 9t^{4}})}^{3 \slash 2}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At the origin, where $$t = 0$$ , the curvature is $$\kappa{(0)} = 2$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the curvature of the parabola y = x^{2} at the points ({0,0}) , ({1,1}) , and ({2,4}) . Solution Since y^{\prime} = 2x and y^{''} = 2 , Formula 11 gives \kappa{(x)} = \frac{\left| y^{''} \right|}{{\lbrack{1 +...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the curvature of the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the points $$({0,0})$$ , $$({1,1})$$ , and $$({2,4})$$ . Solution Since $$y^{\prime} = 2x$$ and $$y^{''} = 2$$ , Formula 11 gives $$\kappa{(x)} = \frac{\left| y^{''} \right|}{{\lbrack{1 + {(y^{\prime})}^{2}}\rbrack}^{3 \slash 2}} = \frac{2}{{({1 + 4x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}$$ The curvature at $$({0,0})$$ is $$\kappa{(0)} = 2$$ . At $$({1,1})$$ it is $$\kappa{(1)} = 2 \slash 5^{3 \slash 2} \approx 0.18$$ . At $$({2,4})$$ it is $$\kappa{(2)} = 2 \slash 17^{3 \slash 2} \approx 0.03$$ . Observe from the expression for $$\kappa{(x)}$$ or the graph of $$\kappa$$ in Figure 5 that $$\left. \kappa{(x)}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ . This corresponds to the fact that the parabola appears to become nearly straight as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ .

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the unit normal and binormal vectors for the circular helix \mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} Solution We first compute the ingredients needed for the unit normal vector:...
body_xml: Example 6 Find the unit normal and binormal vectors for the circular helix $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k}$$ Solution We first compute the ingredients needed for the unit normal vector: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} & = & {{- \sin t\mathbf{i} + \cos t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}} \left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \right| = \sqrt{2}} \\ {\mathbf{T}(t)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}{|\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}( - \sin t\mathbf{i} + \cos t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})} \\ {\mathbf{T}^{\prime}(t)} & = & {{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}( - \cos t\mathbf{i} - \sin t\mathbf{j})} \left| \mathbf{T}^{\prime}(t) \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \\ {\mathbf{N}(t)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{T}^{\prime}(t)}{\left| \mathbf{T}^{\prime}(t) \right|} = - \cos t\mathbf{i} - \sin t\mathbf{j} = \langle - \cos t, - \sin t,0\rangle} \end{array}$$ This shows that the unit normal vector at any point on the helix is horizontal and points toward the $$z$$ -axis. The binormal vector is $$\left. \mathbf{B}{(t)} = \mathbf{T}{(t)} \times \mathbf{N}{(t)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \middle| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {- \sin t} & {\cos t} & 1 \\ {- \cos t} & {- \sin t} & 0 \end{matrix} \middle| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\langle{\sin t, - \cos t,1}\rangle} \right.$$ Figure 7 illustrates Example 6 by showing the vectors $$\mathbf{T}$$ , $$\mathbf{N}$$ , and $$\mathbf{B}$$ at two locations on the helix. In general, the vectors $$\mathbf{T}$$ , $$\mathbf{N}$$ , and $$\mathbf{B}$$ , starting at the various points on a curve, form a set of orthogonal vectors, called the $$\mathbf{TNB}$$ frame, that moves along the curve as $$t$$ varies. This $$\mathbf{TNB}$$ frame plays an important role in the branch of mathematics known as differential geometry and in its applications to the motion of spacecraft.

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Find the unit tangent, unit normal, and binormal vectors and the curvature for the curve \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t,\sqrt{2}\ln t,1/t\rangle at the point (1,0,1) . Solution We start by finding \mathbf{T} and...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the unit tangent, unit normal, and binormal vectors and the curvature for the curve $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t,\sqrt{2}\ln t,1/t\rangle$$ at the point $$(1,0,1)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We start by finding $$\mathbf{T}$$ and $$\mathbf{T}^{'}$$ as functions of $$t$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{r}^{'}(t)} & = & {\langle 1,\sqrt{2}/t, - 1/t^{2}\rangle} \\ \left| \mathbf{r}^{'}(t) \right| & = & {\sqrt{1 + \frac{2}{t^{2}} + \frac{1}{t^{4}}} = \frac{1}{t^{2}}\sqrt{t^{4} + 2t^{2} + 1}} \\ \phantom{\left| r^{'}(t) \right|} & = & {\frac{1}{t^{2}}\sqrt{{(t^{2} + 1)}^{2}} = \frac{1}{t^{2}}(t^{2} + 1) {( \text{because} t^{2} + 1 > 0)}} \\ {\mathbf{T}(t)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{r}^{'}(\mathbf{t})}{\left| \mathbf{r}^{'}(t) \right|} = \frac{t^{2}}{(t^{2} + 1)}\langle 1,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}, - \frac{1}{t^{2}}\rangle = \frac{1}{(t^{2} + 1)}\langle t^{2},\sqrt{2}t, - 1\rangle} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We use formula 3 of Theorem 13.2.3 to differentiate $$\mathbf{T}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{T}^{'}(t) = \frac{- 2t}{{(t^{2} + 1)}^{2}}\langle t^{2},\sqrt{2t}, - 1\rangle + \frac{1}{(t^{2} + 1)}\langle 2t,\sqrt{2},0\rangle$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The point $$(1,0,1)$$ corresponds to $$t = 1$$ , so we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{T}(1)} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\langle 1,\sqrt{2}, - 1\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{T}^{'}(1)} & = & {- \frac{1}{2}\langle 1,\sqrt{2}, - 1\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\langle 2,\sqrt{2},0\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle 1,0,1\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{N}(1)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{T}^{'}(1)}{\left| \mathbf{T}^{'}(1) \right|} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\langle 1,0,1\rangle}{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1 + 0 + 1}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle 1,0,1\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{B}(1)} & = & {\mathbf{T}(1) \times \mathbf{N}(1) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\langle\sqrt{2}, - 2, - \sqrt{2}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle 1, - \sqrt{2}, - 1\rangle} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and, by formula 9, the curvature is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa(1) = \frac{\mathbf{T}^{'}(1)}{\mathbf{r}^{'}(1)} = \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We could also use Theorem 10 to compute $$\kappa(1)$$ ; you can check that we get the same answer.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find equations of the normal plane and osculating plane of the helix in Example 6 at the point P{({0,1,\pi \slash 2})} . Solution The point P corresponds to t = \pi \slash 2 and the normal plane there has normal vector...
body_xml: Example 8 Find equations of the normal plane and osculating plane of the helix in Example 6 at the point $$P{({0,1,\pi \slash 2})}$$ . Solution The point $$P$$ corresponds to $$t = \pi \slash 2$$ and the normal plane there has normal vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{({\pi \slash 2})} = {\langle{- 1,0,1}\rangle}$$ , so an equation of the normal plane is $$- 1{({x - 0})} + 0{({y - 1})} + 1\left( {z - \frac{\pi}{2}} \right) = 0$$ or $$z = x + \frac{\pi}{2}$$ The osculating plane at $$P$$ contains the vectors $$\mathbf{T}$$ and $$\mathbf{N}$$ , so a vector normal to the osculating plane is $$\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{B}$$ . From Example 6 we have $${\mathbf{B}{(t)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\langle{\sin t, - \cos t,1}\rangle}} {\mathbf{B}\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \langle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rangle}$$ The vector $$\langle{1,0,1}\rangle$$ , is parallel to $$\mathbf{B}(\pi/2)$$ (so also normal to the osculating plane). Thus an equation of the osculating plane is $$1{({x - 0})} + 0{({y - 1})} + 1\left( {z - \frac{\pi}{2}} \right) = 0$$ or $$z = - x + \frac{\pi}{2}$$ Figure 10 shows the helix and the osculating plane in Example 8.

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Find and graph the osculating circle of the parabola y = x^{2} at the origin. Solution From Example 5, the curvature of the parabola at the origin is \kappa{(0)} = 2 . So the radius of the osculating circle there is 1...
body_xml: Example 9 Find and graph the osculating circle of the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the origin. Solution From Example 5, the curvature of the parabola at the origin is $$\kappa{(0)} = 2$$ . So the radius of the osculating circle there is $$1 \slash \kappa = \frac{1}{2}$$ . Moving this distance in the direction of $$\mathbf{N} = \langle 0,1\rangle$$ (the tangent vector is horizontal at the origin so the normal vector is vertical) leads us to the center of curvature at $$\left( {0,\frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ , so an equation of the circle of curvature is $$x^{2} + \left( {y - \frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}$$ This circle is graphed in Figure 11.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The position vector of an object moving in a plane is given by \mathbf{r}(t) = t^{3}\mathbf{i} + t^{2}\mathbf{j} . Find its velocity, speed, and acceleration when t = 1 and illustrate geometrically. Solution The...
body_xml: Example 1 The position vector of an object moving in a plane is given by $$\mathbf{r}(t) = t^{3}\mathbf{i} + t^{2}\mathbf{j}$$ . Find its velocity, speed, and acceleration when $$t = 1$$ and illustrate geometrically. Solution The velocity and acceleration at time $$t$$ are $${\mathbf{v}(t)} = {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}\mathbf{i} + 2t\mathbf{j}} {\mathbf{a}(t)} = {\mathbf{r}^{''}(t) = 6t\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}}$$ and the speed is $$\left| \mathbf{v}(t) \right| = {\sqrt{{(3t^{2})}^{2} + {(2t)}^{2}} = \sqrt{9t^{4} + 4t^{2}}}$$ When $$t = 1$$ , we have $${\mathbf{v}(1)} = {3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}} {\mathbf{a}(1)} = {6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}} \left| \mathbf{v}(1) \right| = \sqrt{13}$$ These velocity and acceleration vectors are shown in Figure 2.

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed of a particle with position vector \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^{2},e^{ t},te^{ t}\rangle . Solution \begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{v}(t)} & = & {{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = \langle...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed of a particle with position vector $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^{2},e^{ t},te^{ t}\rangle$$ . Solution $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{v}(t)} & = & {{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = \langle 2t},e^{ t},(1 + t)e^{ t}\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{a}(t)} & = & {{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}(t) = \langle 2},e^{ t},(2 + t)e^{ t}\rangle} \\ \left| \mathbf{v}(t) \right| & = & \sqrt{4t^{2} + e^{2t} + {(1 + t)}^{2}e^{2t}} \end{array}$$ Figure 3 shows the path of the particle in Example 2 with the velocity and acceleration vectors when $$t = 1$$ .

unit_title: Motion in Space: Velocity and Acceleration
title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 A moving particle starts at an initial position \mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 1,0,0\rangle with initial velocity \mathbf{v}(0) = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} . Its acceleration is \mathbf{a}(t) = 4t\mathbf{i} +...
body_xml: Example 3 A moving particle starts at an initial position $$\mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 1,0,0\rangle$$ with initial velocity $$\mathbf{v}(0) = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$ . Its acceleration is $$\mathbf{a}(t) = 4t\mathbf{i} + 6t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$ . Find its velocity and position at time $$t$$ . Solution Since $$\mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{v}^{\prime}(t)$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{v}(t) = \int\mathbf{a}(t)dt = \int(4t\mathbf{i} + 6t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})dt} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{v}(t)} = 2t^{2}\mathbf{i} + 3t^{2}\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} + C} \end{array}$$ To determine the value of the constant vector $$\mathbf{C}$$ , we use the fact that $$\mathbf{v}(0) = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$ . The preceding equation gives $$\mathbf{v}(0) = \mathbf{C}$$ , so $$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$ and $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{v}(t) = 2t^{2}\mathbf{i} + 3t^{2}\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{v}(t)} = (2t^{2} + 1)\mathbf{i} + (3t^{2} - 1)\mathbf{j} + (t + 1)\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$ Since $$\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}(t) = \int\mathbf{v}(t)dt} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}(t)} = \int\lbrack(2t^{2} + 1)\mathbf{i} + (3t^{2} - 1)\mathbf{j} + (t + 1)\mathbf{k}\rbrack dt} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}(t)} = \left( \frac{2}{3}t^{3} + t \right)\mathbf{i} + (t^{3} - t)\mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{1}{2}t^{2} + t \right)\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{D}} \end{array}$$ Putting $$t = 0$$ , we find that $$\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{i}$$ , so the position at time $$t$$ is given by $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \left( \frac{2}{3}t^{3} + t + 1 \right)\mathbf{i} + (t^{3} - t)\mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{1}{2}t^{2} + t \right)\mathbf{k}$$ The expression for $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ that we obtained in Example 3 was used to plot the path of the particle in Figure 4 for $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 3$$ .

unit_title: Motion in Space: Velocity and Acceleration
title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 An object with mass m that moves in a circular path with constant angular speed \omega has position vector \mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos\omega t\mathbf{i} + a\sin\omega t\mathbf{j} . Find the force acting on the object and...
body_xml: Example 4 An object with mass $$m$$ that moves in a circular path with constant angular speed $$\omega$$ has position vector $$\mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos\omega t\mathbf{i} + a\sin\omega t\mathbf{j}$$ . Find the force acting on the object and show that it is directed toward the origin. Solution To find the force, we first need to know the acceleration: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{v}(t)} & = & {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = - a\omega\sin\omega t\mathbf{i} + a\omega\cos\omega t\mathbf{j}} \\ {\mathbf{a}(t)} & = & {\mathbf{v}^{\prime}(t) = - a\omega^{2}\cos\omega t\mathbf{i} - a\omega^{2}\sin\omega t\mathbf{j}} \end{array}$$ Therefore Newton’s Second Law gives the force as $$\mathbf{F}(t) = m\mathbf{a}(t) = - m\omega^{2}(a\cos\omega t\mathbf{i} + a\sin\omega t\mathbf{j})$$ Notice that $$\mathbf{F}(t) = - m\omega^{2}\mathbf{r}(t)$$ . This shows that the force acts in the direction opposite to the radius vector $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ and therefore points toward the origin (see Figure 5). Such a force is called a centripetal (center-seeking) force. The object moving with position $$P$$ has angular speed $$\omega = d\theta \slash dt$$ , where $$\theta$$ is the angle shown in Figure 5.

unit_title: Motion in Space: Velocity and Acceleration
title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 A projectile is fired with angle of elevation \alpha and initial velocity \mathbf{v}_{0} . (See Figure 6.) Assuming that air resistance is negligible and the only external force is due to gravity, find the position...
body_xml: Example 5 A projectile is fired with angle of elevation $$\alpha$$ and initial velocity $$\mathbf{v}_{0}$$ . (See Figure 6.) Assuming that air resistance is negligible and the only external force is due to gravity, find the position function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ of the projectile. What value of $$\alpha$$ maximizes the range (the horizontal distance traveled)? Solution We set up the axes so that the projectile starts at the origin. Since the force due to gravity acts downward, we have $$F = m\mathbf{a} = - mg\mathbf{j}$$ where $$\left. g = \middle| \mathbf{a} \middle| \approx 9.8m \slash s^{2} \right.$$ . Thus $$\mathbf{a} = - g\mathbf{j}$$ Since $$\mathbf{v}^{\prime}(t) = \mathbf{a}$$ , we have $$\mathbf{v}(t) = - gt\mathbf{j} + C$$ where $$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{v}(0) = \mathbf{v}_{0}$$ . Therefore $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = \mathbf{v}(t) = - gt\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{v}_{0}$$ Integrating again, we obtain $$\mathbf{r}(t) = - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{v}_{0} + D$$ But $$\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{r}(0) = 0$$ , so the position vector of the projectile is given by $$\mathbf{r}(t) = - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{v}_{0}$$ If we write $$\left| \mathbf{v}_{0} \middle| = v_{0} \right.$$ (the initial speed of the projectile), then $$\mathbf{v}_{0} = v_{0}\cos\alpha\mathbf{i} + v_{0}\sin\alpha\mathbf{j}$$ and Equation 3 becomes $$\mathbf{r}(t) = (v_{0}\cos\alpha)t\mathbf{i} + \left\lbrack (v_{0}\sin\alpha)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2} \right\rbrack\mathbf{j}$$ The parametric equations of the trajectory are therefore $${x = (v_{0}\cos\alpha)t} {y = (v_{0}\sin\alpha)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}}$$ The horizontal distance $$d$$ is the value of $$x$$ when $$y = 0$$ . Setting $$y = 0$$ , we obtain $$t = 0$$ or $$t = (2v_{0}\sin\alpha) \slash g$$ . This second value of $$t$$ then gives $$d = x = (v_{0}\cos\alpha)\frac{2v_{0}\sin\alpha}{g} = \frac{v_{0}^{2}(2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha)}{g} = \frac{v_{0}^{2}\sin 2\alpha}{g}$$ Clearly, $$d$$ has its maximum value when $$\sin 2\alpha = 1$$ , that is, $$\alpha = 45^{{^\circ}}$$ . If you eliminate $$t$$ from Equations 4, you will see that $$y$$ is a quadratic function of $$x$$ . So the path of the projectile is part of a parabola.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 A projectile is fired with initial speed 150m \slash s and angle of elevation 30^{{^\circ}} from a position 10 m above ground level. Where does the projectile hit the ground, and with what speed? Solution If we place...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>A projectile is fired with initial speed $$150m \slash s$$ and angle of elevation $$30^{{^\circ}}$$ from a position $$10$$ m above ground level. Where does the projectile hit the ground, and with what speed?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we place the origin at ground level, then the initial position of the projectile is $$(0,10)$$ and so we need to adjust Equations 4 by adding $$10$$ to the expression for $$y$$ . With $$v_{0} = 150m \slash s$$ , $$\alpha = 30^{{^\circ}}$$ , and $$g = 9.8m \slash s^{2}$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} x & = & {150\cos(30^{{^\circ}})t = 75\sqrt{3}t} \\ y & = & {10 + 150\sin(30^{{^\circ}})t - \frac{1}{2}(9.8)t^{2} = 10 + 75t - 4.9t^{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Impact occurs when $$y = 0$$ , that is, $$4.9t^{2} - 75t - 10 = 0$$ . Using the quadratic formula to solve this equation (and taking only the positive value of $$t$$ ), we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t = \frac{75 + \sqrt{5625 + 196}}{9.8} \approx 15.44$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then $$x \approx 75\sqrt{3}(15.44) \approx 2006$$ , so the projectile hits the ground about $$2006$$ m away.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The velocity of the projectile is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = 75\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + (75 - 9.8t)\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So its speed at impact is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| \mathbf{v}(15.44) \right| = {\sqrt{{(75\sqrt{3})}^{2} + {(75 - 9.8 \cdot 15.44)}^{2}} \approx 151m \slash s}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 A particle moves with position function \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^{2},t^{2},t^{3}\rangle . Find the tangential and normal components of acceleration. Solution \begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{r}(t)} & = & {t^{2}\mathbf{i} +...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>A particle moves with position function $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^{2},t^{2},t^{3}\rangle$$ . Find the tangential and normal components of acceleration.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{r}(t)} & = & {t^{2}\mathbf{i} + t^{2}\mathbf{j} + t^{3}\mathbf{k}} \\ {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} & = & {2t\mathbf{i} + 2t\mathbf{j} + 3t^{2}\mathbf{k}} \\ {\mathbf{r}^{''}(t)} & = & {2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 6t\mathbf{k}} \\ \left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \right| & = & \sqrt{8t^{2} + 9t^{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore Equation 9 gives the tangential component as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{T} = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{''}(t)}{\left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \right|} = \frac{8t + 18t^{3}}{\sqrt{8t^{2} + 9t^{4}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)} \times \mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {2t} & {2t} & {3t^{2}} \\ 2 & 2 & {6t} \end{array} \right| = 6t^{2}\mathbf{i} - 6t^{2}\mathbf{j}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Equation 10 gives the normal component as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{N} = \frac{\left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \times \mathbf{r}^{''}(t) \right|}{\left| \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \right|} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}t^{2}}{\sqrt{8t^{2} + 9t^{4}}}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A function $$\mathbf{f}$$ of two variables is a rule that assigns to each ordered pair of real numbers $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in a set $$D$$ a unique real number denoted by $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . The set $$D$$ is the domain of $$f$$ and its range is the set of values that $$f$$ takes on, that is, $$\left\{ {f\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| \right.\left( {x,y} \right) \in D} \right\}$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 For each of the following functions, evaluate f\left( {3,2} \right) and find and sketch the domain. (a) f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{x + y + 1}}{x - 1} (b) f{({x,y})} = x\ln{({y^{2} - x})} Solution (a) f\left(...
body_xml: Example 1 For each of the following functions, evaluate $$f\left( {3,2} \right)$$ and find and sketch the domain. (a) $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{x + y + 1}}{x - 1}$$ (b) $$f{({x,y})} = x\ln{({y^{2} - x})}$$ Solution (a) $$f\left( {3,2} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{3 + 2 + 1}}{3 - 1} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}$$ The expression for $$f$$ makes sense if the denominator is not $$0$$ and the quantity under the square root sign is nonnegative. So the domain of $$f$$ is $$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x + y + 1 \geqslant 0,x \neq 1 \right\}$$ The inequality $$x + y + 1 \geqslant 0$$ , or $$y \geqslant - x - 1$$ , describes the points that lie on or above the line $$y = - x - 1$$ , while $$x \neq 1$$ means that the points on the line $$x = 1$$ must be excluded from the domain (see Figure 2). (b) $$f{({3,2})} = 3\ln{({2^{2} - 3})} = 3\ln 1 = 0$$ Since $$\ln{({y^{2} - x})}$$ is defined only when $$y^{2} - x > 0$$ , that is, $$x < y^{2}$$ , the domain of $$f$$ is $$D = \left\{ {({x,y})} \middle| x < y^{2} \right\}$$ . This is the set of points to the left of the parabola $$x = y^{2}$$ . (See Figure 3.)

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the domain and range of g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} . Solution The domain of g is D = {\{{{({x,y})}\left| {9 - x^{2} - y^{2} \geqslant 0}\} \right. = \left. \{{({x,y})} \right|x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the domain and range of $$g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ . Solution The domain of $$g$$ is $$D = {\{{{({x,y})}\left| {9 - x^{2} - y^{2} \geqslant 0}\} \right. = \left. \{{({x,y})} \right|x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 9}\}}$$ which is the disk with center $$({0,0})$$ and radius $$3$$ . (See Figure 4.) The range of $$g$$ is $$\{{z|z = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}},{({x,y})} \in D}\}$$ Since $$z$$ is a positive square root, $$z \geqslant 0$$ . Also, because $$9 - x^{2} - y^{2} \leqslant 9$$ , we have $$\sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} \leqslant 3$$ So the range is $$\left\{ z \middle| 0 \leqslant z \leqslant 3 \right\} = \left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack$$

snippet: Example 3: Example 3 In regions with severe winter weather, the wind-chill index is often used to describe the apparent severity of the cold. This index W is a subjective temperature that depends on the actual temperature T and the wind...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>In regions with severe winter weather, the wind-chill index is often used to describe the apparent severity of the cold. This index $$W$$ is a subjective temperature that depends on the actual temperature $$T$$ and the wind speed $$\upsilon$$ . So $$W$$ is a function of $$T$$ and $$\upsilon$$ , and we can write $$W = f{({T,\upsilon})}$$ . Table 1 records values of $$W$$ compiled by the US National Weather Service and the Meteorological Service of Canada.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For instance, the table shows that if the actual temperature is $$- 5^{{^\circ}}C$$ and the wind speed is $$50{km}/h$$ , then subjectively it would feel as cold as a temperature of about $$- 15^{{^\circ}}C$$ with no wind. So</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({- 5,50})} = - 15$$</paragraph>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="The Wind-Chill Index" title="The Wind-Chill Index">
      <heading level="4">The Wind-Chill Index</heading>
      <paragraph>The wind-chill index measures how cold it feels when it’s windy. It is based on a model of how fast a human face loses heat. It was developed through clinical trials in which volunteers were exposed to a variety of temperatures and wind speeds in a refrigerated wind tunnel.</paragraph>
    </note>
  </example>
