snippet: Example 4: Example 4 In 1928 Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas published a study in which they modeled the growth of the American economy during the period 1899–1922. They considered a simplified view of the economy in which production output...
body_xml:
Example 4 In 1928 Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas published a study in which they modeled the growth of the American economy during the period 1899–1922. They considered a simplified view of the economy in which production output is determined by the amount of labor involved and the amount of capital invested. While many other factors affect economic performance, this model proved to be remarkably accurate. The function Cobb and Douglas used to model production was of the form $$P{({L,K})} = bL^{\alpha}K^{1 - \alpha}$$ where $$P$$ is the total production (the monetary value of all goods produced in a year), $$L$$ is the amount of labor (the total number of person-hours worked in a year), and $$K$$ is the amount of capital invested (the monetary worth of all machinery, equipment, and buildings). In the Discovery Project following Section 14.3 we will show how the form of Equation 1 follows from certain economic assumptions. Cobb and Douglas used economic data published by the government to obtain Table 2. They took the year 1899 as a baseline and $$P$$ , $$L$$ , and $$K$$ for 1899 were each assigned the value $$100$$ . The values for other years were expressed as percentages of the 1899 values. Table 2 Year $$P$$ $$L$$ $$K$$ 1899 100 100 100 1900 101 105 107 1901 112 110 114 1902 122 117 122 1903 124 121 131 1904 122 121 138 1905 143 125 149 1906 152 134 163 1907 151 140 176 1908 126 123 185 1909 155 143 198 1910 159 147 208 1911 153 148 216 1912 177 155 226 1913 184 156 236 1914 169 152 244 1915 189 156 266 1916 225 183 298 1917 227 198 335 1918 223 201 366 1919 218 196 387 1920 231 194 407 1921 179 146 417 1922 240 161 431
Cobb and Douglas used the method of least squares to fit the data of Table 2 to the function $$P{({L,K})} = 1.01L^{0.75}K^{0.25}$$ (See Exercise 81 for the details.) If we use the model given by the function in Equation 2 to compute the production in the years 1910 and 1920, we get the values $$\begin{matrix} {{P(147,208)} = {1.01{(147)}^{0.75}{(208)}^{0.25} \approx 161.9}} \\ {{P(194,407)} = {1.01{(194)}^{0.75}{(407)}^{0.25} \approx 235.8}} \end{matrix}$$ which are quite close to the actual values, $$159$$ and $$231$$ . The production function (1) has subsequently been used in many settings, ranging from individual firms to global economics. It has become known as the Cobb-Douglas production function. Its domain is $$\left\{ {({L,K})} \middle| L \geqslant 0,K \geqslant 0 \right\}$$ because $$L$$ and $$K$$ represent labor and capital and are therefore never negative.

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition If f is a function of two variables with domain D , then the graph of f is the set of all points ({x,y,z}) in {\mathbb{R}}^{3} such that z = f{({x,y})} and ({x,y}) is in D .
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ is a function of two variables with domain $$D$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is the set of all points $$({x,y,z})$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ such that $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ and $$({x,y})$$ is in $$D$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Sketch the graph of the function f{({x,y})} = 6 - 3x - 2y . Solution The graph of f has the equation z = 6 - 3x - 2y , or 3x + 2y + z = 6 , which represents a plane. To graph the plane we first find the intercepts....
body_xml: Example 5 Sketch the graph of the function $$f{({x,y})} = 6 - 3x - 2y$$ . Solution The graph of $$f$$ has the equation $$z = 6 - 3x - 2y$$ , or $$3x + 2y + z = 6$$ , which represents a plane. To graph the plane we first find the intercepts. Putting $$y = z = 0$$ in the equation, we get $$x = 2$$ as the $$x$$ -intercept. Similarly, the $$y$$ -intercept is $$3$$ and the $$z$$ -intercept is $$6$$ . This helps us sketch the portion of the graph that lies in the first octant in Figure 6.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Sketch the graph of g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} . Solution In Example 2 we found that the domain of g is the disk with center (0,0) and radius 3 . The graph of g has equation z = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} . We...
body_xml: Example 6 Sketch the graph of $$g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ . Solution In Example 2 we found that the domain of $$g$$ is the disk with center $$(0,0)$$ and radius $$3$$ . The graph of $$g$$ has equation $$z = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ . We square both sides of this equation to obtain $$z^{2} = 9 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ , or $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 9$$ , which we recognize as an equation of the sphere with center the origin and radius $$3$$ . But, since $$z \geqslant 0$$ , the graph of $$g$$ is just the top half of this sphere (see Figure 7).

title: Example 7

body_xml: Example 7 Use a computer to draw the graph of the Cobb-Douglas production function $$P{({L,K})} = 1.01L^{0.75}K^{0.25}$$ . Solution Figure 8 shows the graph of $$P$$ for values of the labor $$L$$ and capital $$K$$ that lie between $$0$$ and $$300$$ . The computer has drawn the surface by plotting vertical traces. We see from these traces that the value of the production $$P$$ increases as either $$L$$ or $$K$$ increases, as expected.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Find the domain and range and sketch the graph of h{({x,y})} = 4x^{2} + y^{2} . Solution Notice that h{({x,y})} is defined for all possible ordered pairs of real numbers ({x,y}) , so the domain is {\mathbb{R}}^{2} ,...
body_xml: Example 8 Find the domain and range and sketch the graph of $$h{({x,y})} = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ . Solution Notice that $$h{({x,y})}$$ is defined for all possible ordered pairs of real numbers $$({x,y})$$ , so the domain is $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , the entire $$xy$$ -plane. The range of $$h$$ is the set $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ of all nonnegative real numbers. [Notice that $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ and $$y^{2} \geqslant 0$$ , so $$h{({x,y})} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ and $$y$$ .] The graph of $$h$$ has the equation $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ , which is the elliptic paraboloid that we sketched in Example 12.6.4. Horizontal traces are ellipses and vertical traces are parabolas (see Figure 9).

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition The level curves of a function f of two variables are the curves with equations f{({x,y})} = k , where k is a constant (in the range of f ).

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>The level curves of a function $$f$$ of two variables are the curves with equations $$f{({x,y})} = k$$ , where $$k$$ is a constant (in the range of $$f$$ ).</paragraph>
  </note>

Solution The point $$(1,3)$$ lies partway between the level curves with $$z$$ -values $$70$$ and $$80$$ . We estimate that $$f{({1,3})} \approx 73$$ Similarly, we estimate that $$f{({4,5})} \approx 56$$

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Sketch the level curves of the function f{({x,y})} = 6 - 3x - 2y for the values k = - 6,0,6,12 . Solution The level curves are 6 - 3x - 2y = k or 3x + 2y + {({k - 6})} = 0 This is a family of lines with slope -...
body_xml: Example 10 Sketch the level curves of the function $$f{({x,y})} = 6 - 3x - 2y$$ for the values $$k = - 6,0,6,12$$ . Solution The level curves are $$6 - 3x - 2y = k$$ or $$3x + 2y + {({k - 6})} = 0$$ This is a family of lines with slope $$- \frac{3}{2}$$ . The four particular level curves with $$k = - 6,0,6, \text{and} 12$$ are $$3x + 2y - 12 = 0$$ , $$3x + 2y - 6 = 0$$ , $$3x + 2y = 0$$ , and $$3x + 2y + 6 = 0$$ . They are sketched in Figure 16. For equally spaced values of $$k$$ the level curves are equally spaced parallel lines because the graph of $$f$$ is a plane (see Figure 6).

title: Example 11
snippet: Example 11: Example 11 Sketch the level curves of the function g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} for k = 0,1,2,3 Solution The level curves are \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} = k or x^{2} + y^{2} = 9 - k^{2} This is a family of concentric...
body_xml: Example 11 Sketch the level curves of the function $$g{({x,y})} = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ for $$k = 0,1,2,3$$ Solution The level curves are $$\sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} = k$$ or $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9 - k^{2}$$ This is a family of concentric circles with center $$({0,0})$$ and radius $$\sqrt{9 - k^{2}}$$ . The cases $$k = 0,1,2,3$$ are shown in Figure 17. Try to visualize these level curves lifted up to form a surface and compare with the graph of $$g$$ (a hemisphere) in Figure 7.

title: Example 12
snippet: Example 12: Example 12 Sketch some level curves of the function h{({x,y})} = 4x^{2} + y^{2} + 1 . Solution The level curves are 4x^{2} + y^{2} + 1 = k or \frac{x^{2}}{\frac{1}{4}{({k - 1})}} + \frac{y^{2}}{k - 1} = 1 which, for k > 1 ,...
body_xml: Example 12 Sketch some level curves of the function $$h{({x,y})} = 4x^{2} + y^{2} + 1$$ . Solution The level curves are $$4x^{2} + y^{2} + 1 = k$$ or $$\frac{x^{2}}{\frac{1}{4}{({k - 1})}} + \frac{y^{2}}{k - 1} = 1$$ which, for $$k > 1$$ , describes a family of ellipses with semiaxes $$\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{k - 1}$$ and $$\sqrt{k - 1}$$ . Figure 18(a) shows a contour map of $$h$$ drawn by a computer. Figure 18(b) shows these level curves lifted up to the graph of $$h$$ (an elliptic paraboloid) where they become horizontal traces. We see from Figure 18 how the graph of $$h$$ is put together from the level curves.

body_xml: Example 13 Plot level curves for the Cobb-Douglas production function of Example 4. Solution In Figure 19 we use a computer to draw a contour plot for the Cobb-Douglas production function $$P{({L,K})} = 1.01L^{0.75}K^{0.25}$$ Level curves are labeled with the value of the production $$P$$ . For instance, the level curve labeled $$140$$ shows all values of the labor $$L$$ and capital investment $$K$$ that result in a production of $$P = 140$$ . We see that, for a fixed value of $$P$$ , as $$L$$ increases $$K$$ decreases, and vice versa.

<example number="14">
    <heading level="4">Example 14</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the domain of $$f$$ if</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({x,y,z})} = \ln{({z - y})} + xy\sin z$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The expression for $$f{({x,y,z})}$$ is defined as long as $$z - y > 0$$ , so the domain of $$f$$ is</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 15 Find the level surfaces of the function $$f{({x,y,z})} = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}$$ Solution The level surfaces are $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = k$$ , where $$k \geqslant 0$$ . These form a family of concentric spheres with radius $$\sqrt{k}$$ . (See Figure 21.) Thus, as $$({x,y,z})$$ varies over any sphere with center $$O$$ , the value of $$f{({x,y,z})}$$ remains fixed.

body_xml: Example 16 Describe the level surfaces of the function $$f{({x,y,z})} = x^{2} - y - z^{2}$$ Solution The level surfaces are $$x^{2} - y - z^{2} = k$$ , or $$y = x^{2} - z^{2} - k$$ , a family of hyperbolic paraboloids. Figure 22 shows the level surfaces for $$k = 0$$ and $$k = \pm 5$$ .

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition Let f be a function of two variables whose domain D includes points arbitrarily close to ({a,b}) . Then we say that the limit of f{({x,y})} as ({x,y}) approaches (a,b) is L and we write...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="4">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function of two variables whose domain $$D$$ includes points arbitrarily close to $$({a,b})$$ . Then we say that the limit of $$f{({x,y})}$$ as $$({x,y})$$ approaches $$(a,b)$$ is $$L$$ and we write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}f(x,y) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every number $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there is a corresponding number $$\delta > 0$$ such that if</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${({x,y})} \in D$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$0 < \sqrt{{({x - a})}^{2} + {({y - b})}^{2}} < \delta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {f{({x,y})} - L} \right| < \varepsilon$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Show that \lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{x^{2} - y^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{2}} does not exist. Solution Let f{({x,y})} = {({x^{2} - y^{2}})} \slash {({x^{2} + y^{2}})} . First let’s approach ({0,0}) along the...
body_xml: Example 1 Show that $$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{x^{2} - y^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ does not exist. Solution Let $$f{({x,y})} = {({x^{2} - y^{2}})} \slash {({x^{2} + y^{2}})}$$ . First let’s approach $$({0,0})$$ along the $$x$$ -axis. On this path $$y = 0$$ for every point $$({x,y})$$ , so the function becomes $$f{({x,0})} = x^{2} \slash x^{2} = 1$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ and thus $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow 1 \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.{along the}x˗{axis}$$ We now approach along the $$y$$ -axis by putting $$x = 0$$ . Then $$f{({0,y})} = \frac{- y^{2}}{y^{2}} = - 1$$ for all $$y \neq 0$$ , so $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow - 1 \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.{along the}y˗{axis}$$ (See Figure 4.) Since $$f$$ has two different limits as $$({x,y})$$ approaches $$({0,0})$$ along two different lines, the given limit does not exist. (This confirms the conjecture we made on the basis of numerical evidence at the beginning of this section.)

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 If f{({x,y})} = \frac{xy}{x^{2} + y^{2}} , does \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim}f{({x,y})} exist? Solution If y = 0 , then f{({x,0})} = 0 \slash x^{2} = 0 . Therefore \left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow 0...
body_xml: Example 2 If $$f{({x,y})} = \frac{xy}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ , does $$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim}f{({x,y})}$$ exist? Solution If $$y = 0$$ , then $$f{({x,0})} = 0 \slash x^{2} = 0$$ . Therefore $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow 0 \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right. \text{along the} x \text{-axis}$$ If $$x = 0$$ , then $$f{({0,y})} = 0 \slash y^{2} = 0$$ , so $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow 0 \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.{along the}y \text{-axis}$$ Although we have obtained identical limits along the two axes, that does not show that the given limit is $$0$$ . Let’s now approach $$({0,0})$$ along another line, say $$y = x$$ . For all $$x \neq 0$$ , $$f{({x,x})} = \frac{x^{2}}{x^{2} + x^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}$$ Therefore $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2} \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}{along}y = x \right.$$ (See Figure 5.) Since we have obtained different limits along different paths, the given limit does not exist.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 If f{({x,y})} = \frac{xy^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{4}} , does \lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}f(x,y) exist? Solution With the solution of Example 2 in mind, let’s try to save time by letting \left....
body_xml: Example 3 If $$f{({x,y})} = \frac{xy^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{4}}$$ , does $$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}f(x,y)$$ exist? Solution With the solution of Example 2 in mind, let’s try to save time by letting $$\left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.$$ along any line through the origin. If the line is not the $$y$$ -axis, then $$y = mx$$ , where $$m$$ is the slope, and $$f{({x,y})} = f{({x,mx})} = \frac{x{({mx})}^{2}}{x^{2} + {({mx})}^{4}} = \frac{m^{2}x^{3}}{x^{2} + m^{4}x^{4}} = \frac{m^{2}x}{1 + m^{4}x^{2}}$$ So $$\left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow 0 \right. {as} \left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}{along}y = mx \right.$$ We get the same result as $$\left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.$$ along the line $$x = 0$$ . Thus $$f$$ has the same limiting value along every line through the origin. But that does not show that the given limit is $$0$$ , for if we now let $$\left. {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.$$ along the parabola $$x = y^{2}$$ , we have $$f{({x,y})} = f{({y^{2},y})} = \frac{y^{2} \cdot y^{2}}{{(y^{2})}^{2} + y^{4}} = \frac{y^{4}}{2y^{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$$ so $$\left. \left. f{({x,y})}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2} \right. {as} {({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}{along}x = y^{2} \right.$$ Since different paths lead to different limiting values, the given limit does not exist. Figure 7 shows the graph of the function in Example 3. Notice the ridge above the parabola $$x = y^{2}$$ .

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow(1,2)}{({x^{2}y^{3} - x^{3}y^{2} + 3x + 2y})}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Since $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2}y^{3} - x^{3}y^{2} + 3x + 2y$$ is a polynomial, we can find the limit by direct substitution:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow(1,2)}{({x^{2}y^{3} - x^{3}y^{2} + 3x + 2y})} = 1^{2} \cdot 2^{3} - 1^{3} \cdot 2^{2} + 3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 = 11$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate \lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow( - 2,3)}\frac{x^{2}y + 1}{x^{3}y^{2} - 2x} if it exists. Solution The function f(x,y) = (x^{2}y + 1)/(x^{3}y^{2} - 2x) is a rational function and the point ( - 2 , 3 ) is in its...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow( - 2,3)}\frac{x^{2}y + 1}{x^{3}y^{2} - 2x}$$ if it exists.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The function $$f(x,y) = (x^{2}y + 1)/(x^{3}y^{2} - 2x)$$ is a rational function and the point ( $$- 2$$ , $$3$$ ) is in its domain (the denominator is not $$0$$ there), so we can evaluate the limit by direct substitution:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{(x,y)\rightarrow( - 2,3)}\frac{x^{2}y + 1}{x^{3}y^{2} - 2x} = \frac{( - 2)^{2}(3) + 1}{( - 2)^{3}(3)^{2} - 2( - 2)} = - \frac{13}{68}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find \lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} if it exists. Solution 1 As in Example 3, we could show that the limit along any line through the origin is 0 . This doesn’t prove that the...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ if it exists.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 1 As in Example 3, we could show that the limit along any line through the origin is $$0$$ . This doesn’t prove that the given limit is $$0$$ , but the limits along the parabolas $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$x = y^{2}$$ also turn out to be $$0$$ , so we begin to suspect that the limit does exist and is equal to $$0$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Let $$\varepsilon > 0$$ . We want to find $$\delta > 0$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${if} {0 < \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} < \delta} {then} {\left| {\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>that is, $${if} {0 < \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} < \delta} {then} {\frac{3x^{2}|y|}{x^{2} + y^{2}} < \varepsilon}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>But $$x^{2} \leqslant x^{2} + y^{2}$$ since $$y^{2} \geqslant 0$$ , so $$x^{2} \slash {({x^{2} + y^{2}})} \leqslant 1$$ and therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{3x^{2}|y|}{x^{2} + y^{2}} \leqslant 3|y| = 3\sqrt{y^{2}} \leqslant 3\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus if we choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash 3$$ and let $$0 < \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} < \delta$$ , then by (5) we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} - 0} \middle| \right. \leqslant 3\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} < 3\delta = 3\left( \frac{\varepsilon}{3} \right) = \varepsilon$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Hence, by Definition 1,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution 2 As in Solution 1,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| \frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} \middle| = \frac{3x^{2}|y|}{x^{2} + y^{2}} \leq 3|y| \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$- 3|y| \leq \frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} \leq 3|y|$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now $$\left| y \middle| \rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. y\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ so $$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}( - 3|y|) = 0$$ and $$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}(3|y|) = 0$$ (using Limit Law 3). Thus, by the Squeeze Theorem,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} = 0$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Definition

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">

    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ of two variables is called continuous at $$({a,b})$$ if</paragraph>

    <paragraph>We say that $$f$$ is continuous on $$D$$ if $$f$$ is continuous at every point $$({a,b})$$ in $$D$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 9 Let $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} & {{if}(x,y) \neq (0,0)} \\ 0 & {{if}(x,y) = (0,0)} \end{cases}$$ We know $$f$$ is continuous for $${({x,y})} \neq {({0,0})}$$ since it is equal to a rational function there. Also, from Example 6, we have $$\lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}f{({x,y})} = \lim\limits_{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}\frac{3x^{2}y}{x^{2} + y^{2}} = 0 = f{({0,0})}$$ Therefore $$f$$ is continuous at $$({0,0})$$ , and so it is continuous on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . Figure 8 shows the graph of the continuous function in Example 9.

body_xml: Example 10 Where is the function $$h{({x,y})} = e^{- (x^{2} + y^{2})}$$ continuous? Solution The function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is a polynomial and thus is continuous on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . Because the function $$g{(t)} = e^{- t}$$ is continuous for all values of $$t$$ , the composite function $$h{({x,y})} = g{({f{({x,y})}})} = e^{- (x^{2} + y^{2})}$$ is continuous on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . The function $$h$$ is graphed in Figure 9.

body_xml: Example 11 Where is the function $$h{({x,y})} = \arctan{({y \slash x})}$$ continuous? Solution The function $$f{({x,y})} = y \slash x$$ is a rational function and therefore continuous except on the line $$x = 0$$ . The function $$g{(t)} = \arctan t$$ is continuous everywhere. So the composite function $$g{({f{({x,y})}})} = \arctan{({y \slash x})} = h{({x,y})}$$ is continuous except where $$x = 0$$ . The graph in Figure 10 shows the break in the graph of $$h$$ above the $$y$$ -axis.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 If f{({x,y})} = x^{3} + x^{2}y^{3} - 2y^{2} , find f_{x}{({2,1})} and f_{y}{({2,1})} . Solution Holding y constant and differentiating with respect to x , we get f_{x}{({x,y})} = 3x^{2} + 2xy^{3} and so f_{x}{({2,1})}...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f{({x,y})} = x^{3} + x^{2}y^{3} - 2y^{2}$$ , find $$f_{x}{({2,1})}$$ and $$f_{y}{({2,1})}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Holding $$y$$ constant and differentiating with respect to $$x$$ , we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x}{({x,y})} = 3x^{2} + 2xy^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x}{({2,1})} = 3 \cdot 2^{2} + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1^{3} = 16$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Holding $$x$$ constant and differentiating with respect to $$y$$ , we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lllll} {f_{y}{({x,y})}} & = & {3x^{2}y^{2} - 4y} & & \\ {f_{y}{({2,1})}} & = & {3 \cdot 2^{2} \cdot 1^{2} - 4 \cdot 1} & = & 8 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 If f{({x,y})} = \sin\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) , calculate \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} . Solution Using the Chain Rule for functions of one variable, we have \begin{array}{l}...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f{({x,y})} = \sin\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right)$$ , calculate $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$ and $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using the Chain Rule for functions of one variable, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = {\cos\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) = \cos\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{1 + y}}} \\ {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = {\cos\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) = - \cos\left( \frac{x}{1 + y} \right) \cdot \frac{x}{(1 + y)^{2}}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3

body_xml: Example 3 If $$f{({x,y})} = 4 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ , find $$f_{x}{({1,1})}$$ and $$f_{y}{({1,1})}$$ and interpret these numbers as slopes. Solution We have $$\begin{array}{rclrcl} {f_{x}(x,y)} & = & {{- 2x} } & {f_{y}(x,y)} & = & {- 4y} \\ {f_{x}(1,1)} & = & {{- 2} } & {f_{y}(1,1)} & = & {- 4} \end{array}$$ The graph of $$f$$ is the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ and the vertical plane $$y = 1$$ intersects it in the parabola $$z = 2 - x^{2}$$ , $$y = 1$$ . (As in the preceding discussion, we label it $$C_{1}$$ in Figure 2.) The slope of the tangent line to this parabola at the point $$({1,1,1})$$ is $$f_{x}{({1,1})} = - 2$$ . (Notice that the tangent line slopes downward in the positive $$x$$ -direction.) Similarly, the curve $$C_{2}$$ in which the plane $$x = 1$$ intersects the paraboloid is the parabola $$z = 3 - 2y^{2}$$ , $$x = 1$$ , and the slope of the tangent line at $$({1,1,1})$$ is $$f_{y}{({1,1})} = - 4$$ . (See Figure 3.)

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 In Exercise 14.1.39 we defined the body mass index (BMI) of a person as B{({m,h})} = \frac{m}{h^{2}} Calculate the partial derivatives of B for a young man with m = 64{kg} and h = 1.68m and interpret them. Solution...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>In Exercise 14.1.39 we defined the body mass index (BMI) of a person as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$B{({m,h})} = \frac{m}{h^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Calculate the partial derivatives of $$B$$ for a young man with $$m = 64{kg}$$ and $$h = 1.68m$$ and interpret them.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Regarding $$h$$ as a constant, we see that the partial derivative with respect to $$m$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial B}{\partial m}{({m,h})} = \frac{\partial}{\partial m}\left( \frac{m}{h^{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{h^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial B}{\partial m}{({64,1.68})} = \frac{1}{{(1.68)}^{2}} \approx 0.35{({{kg}/m^{2}})}/{kg}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is the rate at which the man’s BMI increases with respect to his weight when he weighs $$64$$ kg and his height is $$1.68$$ m. So if his weight increases by a small amount, one kilogram for instance, and his height remains unchanged, then his BMI will increase from $$B(64,1.68) \approx 22.68$$ by about $$0.35$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now we regard $$m$$ as a constant. The partial derivative with respect to $$h$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\frac{\partial B}{\partial h}(m,h)} = {\frac{\partial}{\partial h}\left( \frac{m}{h^{2}} \right) = m\left( - \frac{2}{h^{3}} \right) = - \frac{2m}{h^{3}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\frac{\partial B}{\partial h}(64,1.68)} = {- \frac{2 \cdot 64}{{(1.68)}^{3}} \approx - 27({kg}/m^{2})/m}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is the rate at which the man’s BMI increases with respect to his height when he weighs $$64$$ kg and his height is $$1.68$$ m. So if the man is still growing and his weight stays unchanged while his height increases by a small amount, say $$1$$ cm, then his BMI will decrease by about $$27{(0.01)} = 0.27$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find \partial z/\partial x and \partial z/\partial y if z is defined implicitly as a function of x and y by the equation x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} + 6xyz + 4 = 0 Then evaluate these partial derivatives at the point ( -...
body_xml: Example 5 Find $$\partial z/\partial x$$ and $$\partial z/\partial y$$ if $$z$$ is defined implicitly as a function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ by the equation $$x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} + 6xyz + 4 = 0$$ Then evaluate these partial derivatives at the point $$( - 1,1,2)$$ Solution To find $$\partial z/\partial x$$ , we differentiate implicitly with respect to $$x$$ , being careful to treat $$y$$ as a constant and $$z$$ as a function (of $$x$$ ): $$3x^{2} + 3z^{2}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + 6yz + 6xy\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 0$$ Solving this equation for $$\partial z/\partial x$$ , we obtain $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = - \frac{x^{2} + 2yz}{z^{2} + 2xy}$$ Similarly, implicit differentiation with respect to $$y$$ gives $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = - \frac{y^{2} + 2xz}{z^{2} + 2xy}$$ Notice that the point $$( - 1,1,2)$$ satisfies the equation $$x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} + 6xyz + 4 = 0$$ so it lies on the surface. At this point $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = - \frac{{( - 1)}^{2} + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2}{2^{2} + 2( - 1) \cdot 1} = - \frac{5}{2}$$ and $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = - \frac{1^{2} + 2( - 1) \cdot 2}{2^{2} + 2( - 1) \cdot 1} = \frac{3}{2}$$ Some software can plot surfaces defined by implicit equations in three variables. Figure 4 shows such a plot of the surface defined by the equation in Example 5.

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Show that the function u{({x,y})} = e^{ x}\sin y is a solution of Laplace’s equation. Solution We first compute the needed second-order partial derivatives: \begin{matrix} u_{x} & = & {e^{ x}\sin y} & { u_{y}} & = &...
body_xml:
<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that the function $$u{({x,y})} = e^{ x}\sin y$$ is a solution of Laplace’s equation.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We first compute the needed second-order partial derivatives:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} u_{x} & = & {e^{ x}\sin y} & { u_{y}} & = & {e^{ x}\cos y} \\ u_{xx} & = & {e^{ x}\sin y} & { u_{yy}} & = & {- e^{ x}\sin y} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u_{xx} + u_{yy} = e^{ x}\sin y - e^{ x}\sin y = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore $$u$$ satisfies Laplace’s equation.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="10">

    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclrcl} u_{x} & = & {\cos{({x - at})}} & { u_{t}} & = & {- a\cos(x - at)} \\ u_{xx} & = & {- \sin{({x - at})}} & { u_{tt}} & = & {- a^{2}\sin{({x - at})} = a^{2}u_{xx}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 2 Show that $$f{({x,y})} = xe^{ xy}$$ is differentiable at $$(1,0)$$ and find its linearization there. Then use it to approximate $$f{({1.1, - 0.1})}$$ . Solution The partial derivatives are $$\begin{array}{lcllcl} {f_{x}(x,y)} & = & {e^{ xy} + xye^{ xy}} & { {f_{y}(x,y)}} & = & {x^{2}e^{ xy}} \\ {f_{x}(1,0)} & = & 1 & { {f_{y}(1,0)}} & = & 1 \end{array}$$ Both $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ are continuous functions, so $$f$$ is differentiable by Theorem 8. The linearization is $$\begin{array}{l} {L{({x,y})} = f{({1,0})} + f_{x}{({1,0})}{({x - 1})} + f_{y}{({1,0})}{({y - 0})}} \\ {\phantom{L{({x,y})}} = 1 + 1{({x - 1})} + 1 \cdot y = x + y} \end{array}$$ The corresponding linear approximation is $$xe^{ xy} \approx x + y$$ so $$f{({1.1, - 0.1})} \approx 1.1 - 0.1 = 1$$ Compare this with the actual value of $$f{({1.1, - 0.1})} = 1.1e^{- 0.11} \approx 0.98542$$ . Figure 5 shows the graphs of the function $$f$$ and its linearization $$L$$ in Example 2.

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>At the beginning of Section 14.3 we discussed the heat index (perceived temperature) $$I$$ as a function of the actual temperature $$T$$ and the relative humidity $$H$$ and gave the following table of values from the National Weather Service.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Find a linear approximation for the heat index $$I = f{({T,H})}$$ when $$T$$ is near $$96^{{^\circ}}F$$ and $$H$$ is near $$70{div}$$ . Use it to estimate the heat index when the actual temperature is $$97^{{^\circ}}F$$ and the relative humidity is $$72{div}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We read from the table that $$f{({96,70})} = 125$$ . At the beginning of Section 14.3 we used the tabular values to estimate that $$f_{T}{({96,70})} \approx 3.75$$ and $$f_{H}{({96,70})} \approx 0.9$$ . So the linear approximation is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {f{({T,H})} \approx f{({96,70})} + f_{T}{({96,70})}{({T - 96})} + f_{H}{({96,70})}{({H - 70})}} \\ {\phantom{f{({T,H})}} \approx 125 + 3.75{({T - 96})} + 0.9{({H - 70})}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In particular,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({97,72})} \approx 125 + 3.75{(1)} + 0.9{(2)} = 130.55$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, when $$T = 97^{{^\circ}}F$$ and $$H = 72{div}$$ , the heat index is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$I \approx 131^{{^\circ}}F$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 (a) If z = f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 3xy - y^{2} , find the differential dz . (b) If x changes from 2 to 2.05 and y changes from 3 to 2.96 , compare the values of \Delta z and dz . Solution (a) Definition 10 gives dz =...
body_xml: Example 4 (a) If $$z = f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 3xy - y^{2}$$ , find the differential $$dz$$ . (b) If $$x$$ changes from $$2$$ to $$2.05$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$3$$ to $$2.96$$ , compare the values of $$\Delta z$$ and $$dz$$ . Solution (a) Definition 10 gives $$dz = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}dy = {({2x + 3y})}dx + {({3x - 2y})}dy$$ (b) Putting $$x = 2$$ , $$dx = \Delta x = 0.05$$ , $$y = 3$$ , and $$dy = \Delta y = - 0.04$$ , we get $$dz = \left\lbrack {2{(2)} + 3{(3)}} \right\rbrack 0.05 + \left\lbrack {3{(2)} - 2{(3)}} \right\rbrack{({- 0.04})} = 0.65$$ The increment of $$z$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta z = f{({2.05,2.96})} - f{({2,3})}} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z} = {\lbrack{{(2.05)}^{2} + 3{(2.05)}{(2.96)} - {(2.96)}^{2}}\rbrack} - \left\lbrack {2^{2} + 3{(2)}{(3)} - 3^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z} = 0.6449} \end{array}$$ Notice that $$\Delta z \approx dz$$ but $$dz$$ is easier to compute. In Example 4, $$dz$$ is close to $$\Delta z$$ because the tangent plane is a good approximation to the surface $$z = x^{2} + 3xy - y^{2}$$ near $$(2,3,13)$$ . (See Figure 8.)

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 The base radius and height of a right circular cone are measured as 10 cm and 25 cm, respectively, with a possible error in measurement of as much as \varepsilon cm in each. (a) Use differentials to estimate the...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>The base radius and height of a right circular cone are measured as $$10$$ cm and $$25$$ cm, respectively, with a possible error in measurement of as much as $$\varepsilon$$ cm in each.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Use differentials to estimate the maximum error in the calculated volume of the cone.</item>
      <item>(b) What is the estimated maximum error in volume if the radius and height are measured with errors up to $$0.1$$ cm?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The volume $$V$$ of a cone with base radius $$r$$ and height $$h$$ is $$V = \pi r^{2}h \slash 3$$ . So the differential of $$V$$ is $$dV = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}dr + \frac{\partial V}{\partial h}dh = \frac{2\pi rh}{3}dr + \frac{\pi r^{2}}{3}dh$$ Since each error is at most $$\varepsilon$$ cm, we have $$\left| {\Delta r} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , $$\left| {\Delta h} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ . To estimate the largest error in the volume, we take the largest error in the measurement of $$r$$ and of $$h$$ . Therefore we take $$\mathit{dr} = \varepsilon$$ and $$\mathit{dh} = \varepsilon$$ along with $$r = 10$$ , $$h = 25$$ . This gives $$\Delta V \approx \mathit{dV} = \frac{500\pi}{3}\varepsilon + \frac{100\pi}{3}\varepsilon = 200\pi\varepsilon$$ Thus the maximum error in the calculated volume is about $$200\pi\varepsilon{cm}^{3}$$ .</item>
      <item>(b) If the largest error in each measurement is $$\varepsilon = 0.1{cm}$$ , then $$\mathit{dV} = 200\pi(0.1) \approx 63$$ , so the estimated maximum error in volume is about $$63{cm}^{3}$$ . (Note that since the measured volume of the cone is $$V = \pi{(10)}^{2}(25)/3 \approx 2618$$ , this is a relative error of $$63/2618 \approx 0.024 \text{or} 2.4\%$$ .)</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 The dimensions of a rectangular box are measured to be 75 cm, 60 cm, and 40 cm, and each measurement is correct to within \varepsilon cm. (a) Use differentials to estimate the largest possible error when the volume of...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>The dimensions of a rectangular box are measured to be $$75$$ cm, $$60$$ cm, and $$40$$ cm, and each measurement is correct to within $$\varepsilon$$ cm.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Use differentials to estimate the largest possible error when the volume of the box is calculated from these measurements.</item>
      <item>(b) What is the estimated maximum error in the calculated volume if the measured dimensions are correct to within $$0.2$$ cm?</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) If the dimensions of the box are $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , then its volume is $$V = xyz$$ and so $$dV = \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}dz = yzdx + xzdy + xydz$$ We are given that $$\left| {\Delta x} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , $$\left| {\Delta y} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , and $$\left| {\Delta z} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ . To estimate the largest error in the volume, we therefore use $$dx = \varepsilon$$ , $$dy = \varepsilon$$ , and $$dz = \varepsilon$$ together with $$x = 75$$ , $$y = 60$$ , and $$z = 40$$ : $$\Delta V \approx dV = {(60)}{(40)}\varepsilon + {(75)}{(40)}\varepsilon + {(75)}{(60)}\varepsilon = 9900\varepsilon$$ Thus the maximum error in the calculated volume is about $$9900$$ times larger than the error in each measurement taken.</item>
      <item>(b) If the largest error in each measurement is $$\varepsilon = 0.2{cm}$$ , then $$\mathit{dV} = 9900(0.2) = 1980$$ , so an error of only $$0.2$$ cm in measuring each dimension could lead to an error of approximately $$1980{cm}^{3}$$ in the calculated volume. (This may seem like a large error, but you can verify that it’s only about $$1\%$$ of the volume of the box.)</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$z = x^{2}y + 3xy^{4}$$ , where $$x = \sin 2t$$ and $$y = \cos t$$ , find $$dz/dt$$ when $$t = 0$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The Chain Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dz}{dt}}{= {({2xy + 3y^{4}})}{({2\cos 2t})} + {({x^{2} + 12xy^{3}})}{({- \sin t})}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It’s not necessary to substitute the expressions for $$x$$ and $$y$$ in terms of $$t$$ . We simply observe that when $$t = 0$$ , we have $$x = \sin 0 = 0$$ and $$y = \cos 0 = 1$$ . Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dz}{dt}|_{t = 0} = (0 + 3)(2\cos 0) + (0 + 0)( - \sin 0) = 6$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 The pressure P (in kilopascals), volume V (in liters), and temperature T (in kelvins) of a mole of an ideal gas are related by the equation PV = 8.31T . Find the rate at which the pressure is changing when the...

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>The pressure $$P$$ (in kilopascals), volume $$V$$ (in liters), and temperature $$T$$ (in kelvins) of a mole of an ideal gas are related by the equation $$PV = 8.31T$$ . Find the rate at which the pressure is changing when the temperature is $$300$$ K and increasing at a rate of $$0.1K/s$$ and the volume is $$100$$ L and increasing at a rate of $$0.2L/s$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution If $$t$$ represents the time elapsed in seconds, then at the given instant we have $$T = 300$$ , $$dT/dt = 0.1$$ , $$V = 100$$ , $$dV/dt = 0.2$$ . Since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$P = 8.31\frac{T}{V}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>the Chain Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dP}{dt} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\frac{dT}{dt} + \frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{8.31}{V}\frac{dT}{dt} - \frac{8.31T}{V^{2}}\frac{dV}{dt}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dP}{dt}}{= \frac{8.31}{100}{(0.1)} - \frac{8.31{(300)}}{100^{2}}{(0.2)} = - 0.04155}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The pressure is decreasing at a rate of about $$0.042{kPa}/s$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$z = e^{ x}\sin y$$ , where $$x = st^{2}$$ and $$y = s^{2}t$$ , find $$\partial z/\partial s$$ and $$\partial z/\partial t$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Applying Case 2 of the Chain Rule, we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} = (e^{ x}\sin{y)(t}^{2}) + (e^{ x}\cos y)(2st)} \\ {{\frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}} = (e^{ x}\sin y)(2st) + (e^{ x}\cos y)(s^{2})} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we wish, we can now express $$\partial z/\partial s$$ and $$\partial z/\partial t$$ solely in terms of $$s$$ and $$t$$ by substituting $$x = st^{2}$$ , $$y = s^{2}t$$ , to get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = t^{2}e^{ st^{2}}\sin{({s^{2}t})} + 2ste^{ st^{2}}\cos{({s^{2}t})}} \\ {\frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = 2ste^{ st^{2}}\sin{({s^{2}t})} + s^{2}e^{ st^{2}}\cos{({s^{2}t})}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

Although we haven’t written the derivatives on the branches, it’s understood that if a branch leads from $$y$$ to $$u$$ , then the partial derivative for that branch is $$\partial y/\partial u$$ . With the aid of the tree diagram, we can now write the required expressions: $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial w}{\partial u} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial u} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial t}\frac{\partial t}{\partial u}} \\ {\frac{\partial w}{\partial\upsilon} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial\upsilon} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial t}\frac{\partial t}{\partial\upsilon}} \end{array}$$

<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$g{({s,t})} = f{({s^{2} - t^{2},t^{2} - s^{2}})}$$ and $$f$$ is differentiable, show that $$g$$ satisfies the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t\frac{\partial g}{\partial s} + s\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Let $$x = s^{2} - t^{2}$$ and $$y = t^{2} - s^{2}$$ . Then $$g{({s,t})} = f{({x,y})}$$ and the Chain Rule gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial g}{\partial s} & = & {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(2s) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}( - 2s)} \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} & = & {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}( - 2t) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(2t)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$t\frac{\partial g}{\partial s} + s\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \left( {2st\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} - 2st\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} \right) + \left( {- 2st\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + 2st\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} \right) = 0$$</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 7 If $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ has continuous second-order partial derivatives and $$x = r^{2} + s^{2}$$ and $$y = 2rs$$ , find expressions for $$\partial z/\partial r$$ and $$\partial^{2}z/\partial r^{2}$$ . Solution (a) The Chain Rule gives $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}{({2r})} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}{({2s})}$$ (b) Applying the Product Rule to the expression in part (a), we get $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial r^{2}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( {2r\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + 2s\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial r^{2}}} = 2\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + 2r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right) + 2s\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)} \end{array}$$ But, using the Chain Rule again (see Figure 5), we have $$\begin{array}{lllll} {\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)\frac{\partial y}{\partial r}} & = & {\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x^{2}}(2r) + \frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x}(2s)} \\ {\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)\frac{\partial y}{\partial r}} & = & {\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y}(2r) + \frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y^{2}}(2s)} \end{array}$$ Putting these expressions into Equation 4 and using the equality of the mixed second-order derivatives, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial r^{2}} = 2\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + 2r\left( {2r\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x^{2}} + 2s\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x}} \right) + 2s\left( {2r\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y} + 2s\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y^{2}}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial r^{2}}}{= 2\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + 4r^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x^{2}} + 8rs\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y} + 4s^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y^{2}}}} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Example 1 Use the weather map in Figure 1 to estimate the value of the directional derivative of the temperature function at Reno in the southeasterly direction. Solution We start by drawing a line through Reno toward the southeast [in the direction of $$\mathbf{u} = (\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \slash \sqrt{2}$$ ; see Figure 4]. We approximate the directional derivative $$D_{u}T$$ by the average rate of change of the temperature between the points where this line intersects the isothermals $$T = 50$$ and $$T = 60$$ . The temperature at the point southeast of Reno is $$T = 60^{{^\circ}}F$$ and the temperature at the point northwest of Reno is $$T = 50^{{^\circ}}F$$ . The distance between these points looks to be about $$75$$ miles. So the rate of change of the temperature in the southeasterly direction is $$D_{\mathbf{u}}T \approx \frac{60 - 50}{75} = \frac{10}{75} \approx 0.13^{{^\circ}}F \slash {mi}$$

<example number="6">

    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) We first compute the gradient vector: $$\begin{array}{lll} {\nabla f(x,y)} & = & {\langle f_{x},f_{y}\rangle = \langle e^{ y},xe^{ y}\rangle} \\ {\nabla f(2,0)} & = & {\langle 1,2\rangle} \end{array}$$ The unit vector in the direction of $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = \langle - \frac{3}{2},2\rangle$$ is $$\mathbf{u} = {\langle{- \frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}}\rangle}$$ , so the rate of change of $$f$$ in the direction from $$P$$ to $$Q$$ is $${D_{u}f\left( {2,0} \right) = \nabla f\left( {2,0} \right) \cdot \mathbf{u} = {\langle{1,2}\rangle} \cdot {\langle{- \frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}}\rangle}} = 1$$</item>
      <item>(b) According to Theorem 15, $$f$$ increases fastest in the direction of the gradient vector $$\nabla f{({2,0})} = {\langle{1,2}\rangle}$$ . The maximum rate of change is $$\left| {\nabla f{({2,0})}} \right| = \left| {\langle{1,2}\rangle} \right| = \sqrt{5}$$</item>

snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Suppose that the temperature at a point ({x,y,z}) in space is given by T{({x,y,z})} = 80 \slash {({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})} , where T is measured in degrees Celsius and x , y , z in meters. In which direction...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that the temperature at a point $$({x,y,z})$$ in space is given by $$T{({x,y,z})} = 80 \slash {({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})}$$ , where $$T$$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $$x$$ , $$y$$ , $$z$$ in meters. In which direction does the temperature increase fastest at the point $$({1,1, - 2})$$ ? What is the maximum rate of increase?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The gradient of $$T$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\nabla T = \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial T}{\partial z}\mathbf{k}} \\ {\phantom{\nabla T}{= - \frac{160x}{{({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})}^{2}}\mathbf{i} - \frac{320y}{{({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})}^{2}}\mathbf{j} - \frac{480z}{{({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})}^{2}}\mathbf{k}}} \\ {\phantom{\nabla T}{= \frac{160}{{({1 + x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 3z^{2}})}^{2}}{({- x\mathbf{i} - 2y\mathbf{j} - 3z\mathbf{k}})}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At the point $$({1,1, - 2})$$ the gradient vector is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\nabla T{({1,1, - 2})} = \frac{160}{256}{({- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}})} = \frac{5}{8}{({- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}})}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>By Theorem 15 the temperature increases fastest in the direction of the gradient vector $$\nabla T{({1,1, - 2})} = \frac{5}{8}{({- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}})}$$ or, equivalently, in the direction of $$- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}$$ or the unit vector $${({- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}})} \slash \sqrt{41}$$ . The maximum rate of increase is the length of the gradient vector:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {\nabla T{({1,1, - 2})}} \right| = \frac{5}{8}\left| {- \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}} \right| = \frac{5}{8}\sqrt{41}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore the maximum rate of increase of temperature is $$\frac{5}{8}\sqrt{41} \approx 4{}_{}^{} \slash m$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="8">

    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} + \frac{z^{2}}{9} = 3$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph>Then Equation 19 gives the equation of the tangent plane at $$({- 2,1, - 3})$$ as</paragraph>

<example number="9">

    <paragraph>Solution The surface $$z = 2x^{2} + y^{2}$$ or, equivalently, $$2x^{2} + y^{2} - z = 0$$ is a level surface (with $$k = 0$$ ) of the function</paragraph>

    <paragraph>By Equation 19 the equation of the tangent plane at $$(1,1,3)$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$4(x - 1) + 2(y - 1) - (z - 3) = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which simplifies to $$z = 4x + 2y - 3$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Compare the solution to Example 9 to the one in Example 14.4.1.</paragraph>

[This means that $$f{({x,y})} \leqslant f{({a,b})}$$ for all points $$({x,y})$$ in some disk with center $$({a,b})$$ .] The number $$f{({a,b})}$$ is called a local maximum value. Then $$f_{x}(x,y) = 2x - 2 f_{y}(x,y) = 2y - 6$$ These partial derivatives are equal to $$0$$ when $$x = 1$$ and $$y = 3$$ , so the only critical point is $$({1,3})$$ . Therefore $$f{({1,3})} = 4$$ is a local minimum, and in fact it is the absolute minimum of $$f$$ . This can be confirmed geometrically from the graph of $$f$$ , which is the elliptic paraboloid with vertex $$({1,3,4})$$ shown in Figure 2.

    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the extreme values of $$f{({x,y})} = y^{2} - x^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$f_{x} = - 2x$$ and $$f_{y} = 2y$$ , the only critical point is $$({0,0})$$ . Notice that for points on the $$x$$ -axis we have $$y = 0$$ , so $$f{({x,y})} = - x^{2} < 0$$ (if $$x \neq 0$$ ). However, for points on the $$y$$ -axis we have $$x = 0$$ , so $$f{({x,y})} = y^{2} > 0$$ (if $$y \neq 0$$ ). Thus every disk with center $$({0,0})$$ contains points where $$f$$ takes on positive values as well as points where $$f$$ takes on negative values. Therefore $$f{({0,0})} = 0$$ can’t be an extreme value for $$f$$ , so $$f$$ has no extreme value.</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="theorem" source_type="Second Derivatives Test" title="Second Derivatives Test">
    <heading level="4">Second Derivatives Test</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose the second partial derivatives of $$f$$ are continuous on a disk with center $$({a,b})$$ , and suppose that $$f_{x}{({a,b})} = 0$$ and $$f_{y}{({a,b})} = 0$$ [so $$({a,b})$$ is a critical point of $$f$$ ]. Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D = D{({a,b})} = f_{xx}{({a,b})}f_{yy}{({a,b})} - \left\lbrack {f_{xy}{({a,b})}} \right\rbrack^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) If $$D > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}{({a,b})} > 0$$ , then $$f{({a,b})}$$ is a local minimum.</item>
      <item>(b) If $$D > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}{({a,b})} < 0$$ , then $$f{({a,b})}$$ is a local maximum.</item>
      <item>(c) If $$D < 0$$ , then $$f{({a,b})}$$ is a saddle point of $$f$$ .</item>
    </list>

snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the local maximum and minimum values and saddle points of f{({x,y})} = x^{4} + y^{4} - 4xy + 1 . Solution We first find the partial derivatives: f_{x} = 4x^{3} - 4y f_{y} = 4y^{3} - 4x Since these partial...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the local maximum and minimum values and saddle points of $$f{({x,y})} = x^{4} + y^{4} - 4xy + 1$$ . Solution We first find the partial derivatives: $$f_{x} = 4x^{3} - 4y f_{y} = 4y^{3} - 4x$$ Since these partial derivatives exist everywhere, the critical points occur where both partial derivatives are zero: $$x^{3} - y = 0$$ and $$y^{3} - x = 0$$ To solve these equations we substitute $$y = x^{3}$$ from the first equation into the second one. This gives $$0 = x^{9} - x = x{({x^{8} - 1})} = x{({x^{4} - 1})}{({x^{4} + 1})} = x{({x^{2} - 1})}{({x^{2} + 1})}{({x^{4} + 1})}$$ so there are three real solutions: $$x = 0$$ , $$1$$ , $$- 1$$ . The three critical points are $$({0,0})$$ , $$({1,1})$$ , and $$({- 1, - 1})$$ . Next we calculate the second partial derivatives and $$D(x,y)$$ : $$f_{xx} = 12x^{2} f_{xy} = - 4 f_{yy} = 12y^{2}$$ $$D{({x,y})} = f_{xx}f_{yy} - {(f_{xy})}^{2} = 144x^{2}y^{2} - 16$$ Since $$D{({0,0})} = - 16 < 0$$ , it follows from case (c) of the Second Derivatives Test that the origin is a saddle point. Since $$D{({1,1})} = 128 > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}{({1,1})} = 12 > 0$$ , we see from case (a) of the test that $$f{({1,1})} = - 1$$ is a local minimum. This means that $$- 1$$ is a local minimum value, and it occurs at the point $$(1,1)$$ . Similarly, we have $$D{({- 1, - 1})} = 128 > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}{({- 1, - 1})} = 12 > 0$$ , so $$f{({- 1, - 1})} = - 1$$ is also a local minimum. The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure 4.

title: Example 4

body_xml:
Example 4 Find and classify the critical points of the function $$f{({x,y})} = 10x^{2}y - 5x^{2} - 4y^{2} - x^{4} - 2y^{4}$$ Also find the highest point on the graph of $$f$$ . Solution The first-order partial derivatives are $${f_{x} = 20xy - 10x - 4x^{3}} {f_{y} = 10x^{2} - 8y - 8y^{3}}$$ So to find the critical points we need to solve the equations $$2x{({10y - 5 - 2x^{2}})} = 0$$ $$5x^{2} - 4y - 4y^{3} = 0$$ From Equation 4 we see that either $$x = 0$$ or $$10y - 5 - 2x^{2} = 0$$ In the first case $$(x = 0)$$ , Equation 5 becomes $$- 4y{({1 + y^{2}})} = 0$$ , so $$y = 0$$ and we have the critical point $$({0,0})$$ . In the second case $$({10y - 5 - 2x^{2} = 0})$$ , we get $$x^{2} = 5y - 2.5$$ and, putting this in Equation 5, we have $$25y - 12.5 - 4y - 4y^{3} = 0$$ or, equivalently, $$4y^{3} - 21y + 12.5 = 0$$ Using a graphing calculator or computer to solve this equation numerically, we obtain $$y \approx - 2.5452 y \approx 0.6468 y \approx 1.8984$$ (Alternatively, we could graph the function $$g{(y)} = 4y^{3} - 21y + 12.5$$ as in Figure 6, and find the intercepts.) From Equation 6, the corresponding $$x$$ -values are given by $$x = \pm \sqrt{5y - 2.5}$$ If $$y \approx - 2.5452$$ , then $$x$$ has no corresponding real values. If $$y \approx 0.6468$$ , then $$x \approx \pm 0.8567$$ . If $$y \approx 1.8984$$ , then $$x \approx \pm 2.6442$$ . So we have a total of five critical points, which are analyzed in the following chart. All quantities are rounded to two decimal places. Critical point Value of $$f$$ $$f_{xx}$$ $$D$$ Conclusion $$({0,0})$$ 0.00 $$- 10.00$$ 80.00 local maximum $$({\pm 2.64,1.90})$$ 8.50 $$- 55.93$$ 2488.72 local maximum $$({\pm 0.86,0.65})$$ $$- 1.48$$ $$- 5.87$$ $$- 187.64$$ saddle point
Figures 7 and 8 give two views of the graph of $$f$$ and we see that the surface opens downward. [This can also be seen from the expression for $$f{({x,y})}$$ : the dominant terms are $$- x^{4} - 2y^{4}$$ when $$|x|$$ and $$|y|$$ are large.] Comparing the values of $$f$$ at its local maximum points, we see that the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ is $$f{({\pm 2.64,1.90})} \approx 8.50$$ . In other words, the highest points on the graph of $$f$$ are $$({\pm 2.64,1.90,8.50})$$ .

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the shortest distance from the point ({1,0, - 2}) to the plane x + 2y + z = 4 . Solution The distance from any point ({x,y,z}) to the point ({1,0, - 2}) is d = \sqrt{{({x - 1})}^{2} + y^{2} + {({z + 2})}^{2}} but...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the shortest distance from the point $$({1,0, - 2})$$ to the plane $$x + 2y + z = 4$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The distance from any point $$({x,y,z})$$ to the point $$({1,0, - 2})$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$d = \sqrt{{({x - 1})}^{2} + y^{2} + {({z + 2})}^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>but if $$({x,y,z})$$ lies on the plane $$x + 2y + z = 4$$ , then $$z = 4 - x - 2y$$ and so we have $$d = \sqrt{{({x - 1})}^{2} + y^{2} + {({6 - x - 2y})}^{2}}$$ . We can minimize $$d$$ by minimizing the simpler expression</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$d^{2} = f{({x,y})} = {({x - 1})}^{2} + y^{2} + {({6 - x - 2y})}^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>By solving the equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x} = 2{({x - 1})} - 2{({6 - x - 2y})} = 4x + 4y - 14 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{y} = 2y - 4{({6 - x - 2y})} = 4x + 10y - 24 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we find that the only critical point is $$\left( {\frac{11}{6},\frac{5}{3}} \right)$$ . Since $$f_{xx} = 4$$ , $$f_{xy} = 4$$ , and $$f_{yy} = 10$$ , we have $$D{({x,y})} = f_{xx}f_{yy} - {(f_{xy})}^{2} = 24 > 0$$ and $$f_{xx} > 0$$ , so by the Second Derivatives Test $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$\left( {\frac{11}{6},\frac{5}{3}} \right)$$ . Intuitively, we can see that this local minimum is actually an absolute minimum because there must be a point on the given plane that is closest to $$({1,0, - 2})$$ . If $$x = \frac{11}{6}$$ and $$y = \frac{5}{3}$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${d = \sqrt{{({x - 1})}^{2} + y^{2} + {({6 - x - 2y})}^{2}} =}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{5}{6} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{5}{3} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{5}{6} \right)^{2}} = \frac{5}{6}\sqrt{6}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The shortest distance from $$({1,0, - 2})$$ to the plane $$x + 2y + z = 4$$ is $$\frac{5}{6}\sqrt{6}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Example 5 could also be solved using vectors. Compare with the methods of Section 12.5.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 A rectangular box without a lid is to be made from 12m^{2} of cardboard. Find the maximum volume of such a box. Solution Let the length, width, and height of the box (in meters) be x , y , and z , as shown in Figure...
body_xml: Example 6 A rectangular box without a lid is to be made from $$12m^{2}$$ of cardboard. Find the maximum volume of such a box. Solution Let the length, width, and height of the box (in meters) be $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , as shown in Figure 10. Then the volume of the box is $$V = xyz$$ We can express $$V$$ as a function of just two variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ by using the fact that the area of the four sides and the bottom of the box is $$2xz + 2yz + xy = 12$$ Solving this equation for $$z$$ , we get $$z = {({12 - xy})} \slash \left\lbrack {2{({x + y})}} \right\rbrack$$ , so the expression for $$V$$ becomes $$V = xy\frac{12 - xy}{2{({x + y})}} = \frac{12xy - x^{2}y^{2}}{2{({x + y})}}$$ We compute the partial derivatives: $${\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = \frac{y^{2}{({12 - 2xy - x^{2}})}}{2{({x + y})}^{2}}}{\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = \frac{x^{2}{({12 - 2xy - y^{2}})}}{2{({x + y})}^{2}}}$$ If $$V$$ is a maximum, then $$\partial V \slash \partial x = \partial V \slash \partial y = 0$$ , but $$x = 0$$ or $$y = 0$$ gives $$V = 0$$ . It remains to solve the equations $${12 - 2xy - x^{2} = 0}{12 - 2xy - y^{2} = 0}$$ These imply that $$x^{2} = y^{2}$$ and so $$x = y$$ . (Note that $$x$$ and $$y$$ must both be nonnegative in this problem.) If we put $$x = y$$ in either equation we get $$12 - 3x^{2} = 0$$ , which gives $$x = 2$$ , $$y = 2$$ , and $$z = {({12 - 2 \cdot 2})} \slash \left\lbrack {2{({2 + 2})}} \right\rbrack = 1$$ . We could use the Second Derivatives Test to show that this gives a local maximum of $$V$$ , or we could simply argue from the physical nature of this problem that there must be an absolute maximum volume, which has to occur at a critical point of $$V$$ , so it must occur when $$x = 2$$ , $$y = 2$$ , $$z = 1$$ . Then $$V = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 4$$ , so the maximum volume of the box is $$4m^{3}$$ .

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">

    <paragraph>Let $$(a,b)$$ be a point in the domain $$D$$ of a function $$f$$ of two variables. Then $$f(a,b)$$ is the</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">

snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function f{({x,y})} = x^{2} - 2xy + 2y on the rectangle D = \left\{ {({x,y})} \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\} . Solution Since f...
body_xml: Example 7 Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} - 2xy + 2y$$ on the rectangle $$D = \left\{ {({x,y})} \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ . Solution Since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is continuous on the closed, bounded rectangle $$D$$ , so Theorem 8 tells us there is both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum. According to step 1 in (9), we first find the critical points. These occur when $$\begin{array}{l} {f_{x} = 2x - 2y = 0} \\ {f_{y} = - 2x + 2 = 0} \end{array}$$ so the only critical point is $$({1,1})$$ . This point is in $$D$$ and the value of $$f$$ there is $$f{({1,1})} = 1$$ . In step 2 we look at the values of $$f$$ on the boundary of $$D$$ , which consists of the four line segments $$L_{1}$$ , $$L_{2}$$ , $$L_{3}$$ , $$L_{4}$$ shown in Figure 12. On $$L_{1}$$ we have $$y = 0$$ and $${f{({x,0})} = x^{2}} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3}$$ This is an increasing function of $$x$$ , so its minimum value is $$f{({0,0})} = 0$$ and its maximum value is $$f{({3,0})} = 9$$ . On $$L_{2}$$ we have $$x = 3$$ and $${f{({3,y})} = 9 - 4y} {0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2}$$ This is a decreasing function of $$y$$ , so its maximum value is $$f{({3,0})} = 9$$ and its minimum value is $$f{({3,2})} = 1$$ . On $$L_{3}$$ we have $$y = 2$$ and $${f{({x,2})} = x^{2} - 4x + 4} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3}$$ By the methods of Chapter 4, or simply by observing that $$f{({x,2})} = {({x - 2})}^{2}$$ , we see that the minimum value of this function is $$f{({2,2})} = 0$$ and the maximum value is $$f{({0,2})} = 4$$ . Finally, on $$L_{4}$$ we have $$x = 0$$ and $${f{({0,y})} = 2y} {0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2}$$ with maximum value $$f{({0,2})} = 4$$ and minimum value $$f{({0,0})} = 0$$ . Thus, on the boundary, the minimum value of $$f$$ is $$0$$ and the maximum is $$9$$ . In step 3 we compare these values with the value $$f{({1,1})} = 1$$ at the critical point and conclude that the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ is $$f{({3,0})} = 9$$ and the absolute minimum value is $$f{({0,0})} = f{({2,2})} = 0$$ . Figure 13 shows the graph of $$f$$ .

<note type="procedure" source_type="Method of Lagrange Multipliers" title="Method of Lagrange Multipliers">

    <paragraph>To find the maximum and minimum values of $$f{({x,y,z})}$$ subject to the constraint $$g{({x,y,z})} = k$$ [assuming that these extreme values exist and $$\nabla g \neq 0$$ on the surface $$g{({x,y,z})} = k$$ ]:</paragraph>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the extreme values of the function f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 2y^{2} on the circle x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 . Solution We are asked for the extreme values of f subject to the constraint g{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 . Using...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the extreme values of the function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ on the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Solution We are asked for the extreme values of $$f$$ subject to the constraint $$g{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Using Lagrange multipliers, we solve the equations $$\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$$ and $$g{({x,y})} = 1$$ , which can be written as $${f_{x} = \lambda g_{x}} {f_{y} = \lambda g_{y}} {g{({x,y})} = 1}$$ or as $$2x = 2x\lambda$$ $$4y = 2y\lambda$$ $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ From (2) we have $$2x(1 - \lambda) = 0$$ , so $$x = 0$$ or $$\lambda = 1$$ . If $$x = 0$$ , then (4) gives $$y = \pm 1$$ . If $$\lambda = 1$$ , then $$y = 0$$ from (3), so then (4) gives $$x = \pm 1$$ . Therefore $$f$$ has possible extreme values at the points $$({0,1})$$ , $$({0, - 1})$$ , $$({1,0})$$ , and $$({- 1,0})$$ . Evaluating $$f$$ at these four points, we find that $${f{({0,1})} = 2} {f{({0, - 1})} = 2} {f{({1,0})} = 1} {f{({- 1,0})} = 1}$$ Therefore the maximum value of $$f$$ on the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ is $$f{({0, \pm 1})} = 2$$ and the minimum value is $$f{({\pm 1,0})} = 1$$ . In geometric terms, these correspond to the highest and lowest points on the curve $$C$$ in Figure 2, where $$C$$ consists of those points on the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ that are directly above the constraint circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Figure 3 shows a contour map of $$f$$ . The extreme values of $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ correspond to the level curves of $$f$$ that just touch the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Our next illustration of Lagrange’s method is to reconsider the problem given in Example 14.7.6.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 A rectangular box without a lid is to be made from 12m^{2} of cardboard. Find the maximum volume of such a box. Solution As in Example 14.7.6, we let x , y , and z be the length, width, and height, respectively, of the...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>A rectangular box without a lid is to be made from $$12m^{2}$$ of cardboard. Find the maximum volume of such a box.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution As in Example 14.7.6, we let $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ be the length, width, and height, respectively, of the box in meters. Then we wish to maximize</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$V = xyz$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>subject to the constraint</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$g{({x,y,z})} = 2xz + 2yz + xy = 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, we look for values of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , $$z$$ , and $$\lambda$$ such that $$\nabla V = \lambda\nabla g$$ and $$g{({x,y,z})} = 12$$ . This gives the equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} V_{x} & = & {\lambda g_{x}} \\ V_{y} & = & {\lambda g_{y}} \\ V_{z} & = & {\lambda g_{z}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2xz + 2yz + xy = 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which become</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{yz} = \lambda(2z + y)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{xz} = \lambda(2z + x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{xy} = \lambda(2x + 2y)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2\mathit{xz} + 2\mathit{yz} + \mathit{xy} = 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>There are no general rules for solving systems of equations. Sometimes some ingenuity is required. In the present example you might notice that if we multiply (5) by $$x$$ , (6) by $$y$$ , and (7) by $$z$$ , then the left sides of these equations will be identical. Doing this, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{xyz} = \lambda(2xz + xy)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{xyz} = \lambda(2yz + xy)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{xyz} = \lambda(2xz + 2yz)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Another method for solving the system of equations (5, 6, 7, and 8) is to solve each of Equations 5, 6, and 7 for $$\lambda$$ and then to equate the resulting expressions.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In general $$\lambda$$ can be $$0$$ , but here we observe that $$\mathbf{\lambda} \neq 0$$ because $$\mathbf{\lambda} = 0$$ would imply $$yz = xz = xy = 0$$ from (5), (6), and (7) and this would contradict (8). Therefore, from (9) and (10), we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2xz + xy = 2yz + xy$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which gives $$xz = yz$$ . But $$z \neq 0$$ (since $$z = 0$$ would give $$V = 0$$ ), so $$x = y$$ . From (10) and (11) we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2yz + xy = 2xz + 2yz$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which gives $$2xz = xy$$ and so (since $$x \neq 0$$ ) $$y = 2z$$ . If we now put $$x = y = 2z$$ in (8), we get</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$4z^{2} + 4z^{2} + 4z^{2} = 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ are all positive, we therefore have $$z = 1$$ and so $$x = 2$$ and $$y = 2$$ . Thus we have only one point where $$f$$ may have an extreme value; how do we know if this point corresponds to a maximum or minimum? As in Example 14.7.6, we argue that there must be a maximum volume, which must occur at the point we found.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the points on the sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4 that are closest to and farthest from the point ({3,1, - 1}) . Solution The distance from a point ({x,y,z}) to the point ({3,1, - 1}) is d = \sqrt{{({x - 3})}^{2}...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the points on the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ that are closest to and farthest from the point $$({3,1, - 1})$$ . Solution The distance from a point $$({x,y,z})$$ to the point $$({3,1, - 1})$$ is $$d = \sqrt{{({x - 3})}^{2} + {({y - 1})}^{2} + {({z + 1})}^{2}}$$ but the algebra is simpler if we instead maximize and minimize the square of the distance: $$d^{2} = f{({x,y,z})} = {({x - 3})}^{2} + {({y - 1})}^{2} + {({z + 1})}^{2}$$ The constraint is that the point $$({x,y,z})$$ lies on the sphere, that is, $$g{({x,y,z})} = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ According to the method of Lagrange multipliers, we solve $$\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$$ , $$g = 4$$ . This gives $$2(x - 3) = 2x\lambda$$ $$2(y - 1) = 2y\lambda$$ $$2(z + 1) = 2z\lambda$$ $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ The simplest way to solve these equations is to solve for $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ in terms of $$\lambda$$ from (12), (13), and (14), and then substitute these values into (15). From (12) we have $$\left. x - 3 = x\lambda \Rightarrow x{({1 - \lambda})} = 3 \Rightarrow x = \frac{3}{1 - \lambda} \right.$$ [Note that $$1 - \lambda \neq 0$$ because $$\lambda = 1$$ is impossible from (12).] Similarly, (13) and (14) give $$y = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda} z = - \frac{1}{1 - \lambda}$$ Therefore, from (15), we have $$\frac{3^{2}}{{({1 - \lambda})}^{2}} + \frac{1^{2}}{{({1 - \lambda})}^{2}} + \frac{{({- 1})}^{2}}{{({1 - \lambda})}^{2}} = 4$$ which gives $${({1 - \lambda})}^{2} = \frac{11}{4}$$ , $$1 - \lambda = \pm \sqrt{11}/2$$ , so $$\lambda = 1 \pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{2}$$ These values of $$\lambda$$ then give the corresponding points $$({x,y,z})$$ : $$\left( {\frac{6}{\sqrt{11}},{\frac{2}{\sqrt{11}}, - \left. \frac{2}{\sqrt{11}} \right)}} \right.$$ and $$\left( \left. - {\frac{6}{\sqrt{11}}, - \frac{2}{\sqrt{11}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{11}}} \right) \right.$$ It’s easy to see that $$f$$ has a smaller value at the first of these points, so the closest point is $$({6/\sqrt{11},2/\sqrt{11}, - 2/\sqrt{11}})$$ and the farthest is $$({- 6/\sqrt{11}, - 2/\sqrt{11},2/\sqrt{11}})$$ . Figure 4 shows the sphere and the nearest point $$P$$ in Example 3. Can you see how to find the coordinates of $$P$$ without using calculus?

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the extreme values of f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 2y^{2} on the disk D = \{(x,y)|x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1\} . Solution According to the procedure in (14.7.9), we compare the values of f at the critical points in D with...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the extreme values of $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ on the disk $$D = \{(x,y)|x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1\}$$ . Solution According to the procedure in (14.7.9), we compare the values of $$f$$ at the critical points in $$D$$ with the extreme values of $$f$$ on the boundary of $$D$$ . Since $$f_{x} = 2x$$ and $$f_{y} = 4y$$ , the only critical point is $$({0,0})$$ . We compare the value of $$f$$ at that point with the extreme values on the boundary that we found in Example 1 using Lagrange multipliers: $${f{({0,0})} = 0} {f{({\pm 1,0})} = 1} {f{({0, \pm 1})} = 2}$$ Therefore the maximum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ is $$f{({0, \pm 1})} = 2$$ and the minimum value is $$f{({0,0})} = 0$$ . Figure 5 shows the portion of the graph of $$f$$ above the disk $$D$$ . You can see that the highest point on the surface occurs at $$({0, \pm 1})$$ and the lowest point is at the origin. Figure 6 shows a contour map of $$f$$ superimposed on the disk $$D$$ .

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the maximum value of the function f{({x,y,z})} = x + 2y + 3z on the curve of intersection of the plane x - y + z = 1 and the cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 . Solution We maximize the function f{({x,y,z})} = x + 2y +...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the maximum value of the function $$f{({x,y,z})} = x + 2y + 3z$$ on the curve of intersection of the plane $$x - y + z = 1$$ and the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Solution We maximize the function $$f{({x,y,z})} = x + 2y + 3z$$ subject to the constraints $$g{({x,y,z})} = x - y + z = 1$$ and $$h{({x,y,z})} = x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . The Lagrange condition is $$\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g + \mu\nabla h$$ , so we solve the equations $$1 = \lambda + 2x\mu$$ $$2 = - \lambda + 2y\mu$$ $$3 = \lambda$$ $$x - y + z = 1$$ $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ Putting $$\lambda = 3$$ [from (19)] in (17), we get $$2x\mu = - 2$$ , so $$x = - 1/\mu$$ . Similarly, (18) gives $$y = 5/{({2\mu})}$$ . Substitution in (21) then gives $$\frac{1}{\mu^{2}} + \frac{25}{4\mu^{2}} = 1$$ and so $$\mu^{2} = \frac{29}{4}$$ , $$\mu = \pm \sqrt{29}/2$$ . Then $$x = \mp 2/\sqrt{29}$$ , $$y = \pm 5/\sqrt{29}$$ , and, from (20), $$z = 1 - x + y = 1 \pm 7/\sqrt{29}$$ . The corresponding values of $$f$$ are $$\mp \frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} + 2\left( {\pm \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}} \right) + 3\left( {1 \pm \frac{7}{\sqrt{29}}} \right) = 3 \pm \sqrt{29}$$ Therefore the maximum value of $$f$$ on the given curve is $$3 + \sqrt{29}$$ . The cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ intersects the plane $$x - y + z = 1$$ in an ellipse (Figure 8). Example 5 asks for the maximum value of $$f$$ when $$({x,y,z})$$ is restricted to lie on the ellipse.

body_xml: Example 1 Estimate the volume of the solid that lies above the square $$R = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ and below the elliptic paraboloid $$z = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ . Divide $$R$$ into four equal squares and choose the sample point to be the upper right corner of each square $$R_{ij}$$ . Sketch the solid and the approximating rectangular boxes. Solution The squares are shown in Figure 6. The paraboloid is the graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ and the area of each square is $$\Delta A = 1$$ . Approximating the volume by the Riemann sum with $$m = n = 2$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {V \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{2}f}{\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{V} = f{\left( {1,1} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {1,2} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {2,1} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {2,2} \right)}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{V} = 13(1) + 7(1) + 10(1) + 4(1) = 34} \end{array}$$ This is the volume of the approximating rectangular boxes shown in Figure 7.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 If R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1, - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\} , evaluate the integral {\iint\limits_{R}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dA Solution It would be very difficult to...
body_xml: Example 2 If $$R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1, - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ , evaluate the integral $${\iint\limits_{R}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dA$$ Solution It would be very difficult to evaluate this integral directly from Definition 5 but, because $$\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \geqslant 0$$ , we can compute the integral by interpreting it as a volume. If $$z = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ , then $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ and $$z \geqslant 0$$ , so the given double integral represents the volume of the solid $$S$$ that lies below the circular cylinder $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ and above the rectangle $$R$$ . (See Figure 9.) The volume of $$S$$ is the area of a semicircle with radius $$1$$ times the length of the cylinder. Thus $${\iint\limits_{R}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dA = \frac{1}{2}\pi{(1)}^{2} \times 4 = 2\pi$$

<note type="procedure" source_type="Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals" title="Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals">
