title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use the Midpoint Rule with m = n = 2 to estimate the value of the integral {\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA , where {R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y...
body_xml: Example 3 Use the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 2$$ to estimate the value of the integral $${\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA$$ , where $${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ . Solution In using the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 2$$ , we evaluate $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x - 3y^{2}$$ at the centers of the four subrectangles shown in Figure 10. So $${\overline{x}}_{1} = \frac{1}{2}$$ , $${\overline{x}}_{2} = \frac{3}{2}$$ , $${\overline{y}}_{1} = \frac{5}{4}$$ , and $${\overline{y}}_{2} = \frac{7}{4}$$ . The area of each subrectangle is $$\Delta A = \frac{1}{2}$$ . Thus $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{2}f}{({{\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j}})}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} = f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{1},{\overline{y}}_{1}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{1},{\overline{y}}_{2}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{2},{\overline{y}}_{1}} \right)}\Delta A + f{({{\overline{x}}_{2},{\overline{y}}_{2}})}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= f{\left( {\frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{1}{2},\frac{7}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{4}} \right)}\Delta A}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= \left( {- \frac{67}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{139}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{51}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{123}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= - \frac{95}{8} = - 11.875}} \end{array}$$ Thus we have $${\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA \approx - 11.875$$

body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate the iterated integrals.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $${\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{1}^{2}x^{2}}}ydydx$$</item>
      <item>(b) $${\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{3}x^{2}}}ydxdy$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Regarding $$x$$ as a constant, we obtain $$\int_{1}^{2}{x^{2}ydy = \left\lbrack x^{2}\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{y = 1}^{y = 2} = x^{2}\left( \frac{2^{2}}{2} \right) - x^{2}\left( \frac{1^{2}}{2} \right) = \frac{3}{2}x^{2}}$$ Thus the function $$A$$ in the preceding discussion is given by $$A(x) = \frac{3}{2}x^{2}$$ in this example. We now integrate this function of $$x$$ from $$0$$ to $$3$$ : $$\int_{0}^{3}\int_{1}^{2}x^{2}ydydx = {\int_{0}^{3}\left\lbrack {\int_{1}^{2}{x^{2}ydy}} \right\rbrack}dx = \int_{0}^{3}\frac{3}{2}x^{2}dx = \frac{x^{3}}{2}\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{27}{2}$$</item>
      <item>(b) Here we first integrate with respect to $$x$$ , regarding $$y$$ as a constant: $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydxdy = \int_{1}^{2}\left\lbrack \int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydx \right\rbrack dy = \int_{1}^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{3}}{3}y \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 3}dy} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydxdy}\left. = {\int_{1}^{2}{9ydy = 9\frac{y^{2}}{2}}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \frac{27}{2}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Fubini’s Theorem
snippet: Fubini’s Theorem: Fubini’s Theorem If f is continuous on the rectangle {R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b \right.},\left. c \leqslant y \leqslant d \right\} then {\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA =...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Fubini’s Theorem" title="Fubini’s Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Fubini’s Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f$$ is continuous on the rectangle</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b \right.},\left. c \leqslant y \leqslant d \right\}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{f(x,y)dydx}}}}} = {\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x,y)dxdy}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>More generally, this is true if we assume that $$f$$ is bounded on $$R$$ , $$f$$ is discontinuous only on a finite number of smooth curves, and the iterated integrals exist.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Theorem 10 is named after the Italian mathematician Guido Fubini (1879–1943), who proved a very general version of this theorem in 1907. But the version for continuous functions was known to the French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy almost a century earlier.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate the double integral {\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA , where {R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\} . (Compare with Example 3.)...
body_xml: Example 5 Evaluate the double integral $${\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA$$ , where $${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ . (Compare with Example 3.) Solution 1 Fubini’s Theorem gives $$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{1}^{2}{(x - 3y^{2})}}}dydx = {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {xy - y^{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 1}^{y = 2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} = \left. {\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {x - 7} \right)}}dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 7x \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = - 12} \end{array}$$ Solution 2 Again applying Fubini’s Theorem, but this time integrating with respect to $$x$$ first, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})dA = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{2}{(x - 3y^{2})dxdy}}}}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - 3xy^{2}} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 2}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})dA}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{(2 - 6y^{2})dy = \left. {2y - 2y^{3}} \right\rbrack}}_{1}^{2} = - 12} \end{array}$$ Notice the negative answer in Example 5; nothing is wrong with that. The function f is not a positive function, so its integral doesn’t represent a volume. From Figure 13 we see that $$f$$ is always negative on $$R$$ , so the value of the integral is the negative of the volume that lies above the graph of $$f$$ and below $$R$$ .

body_xml: Example 6 Evaluate $${\iint_{R}y}\sin{\left( {xy} \right)}dA$$ , where $$R = \left\lbrack {1,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . Solution If we first integrate with respect to $$x$$ , we get $$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{1}^{2}{y\sin(xy)dxdy}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}} = {{\int_{0}^{\pi}{y\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{y}\cos(xy)} \right\rbrack_{x = 1}^{x = 2}}}dy}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}}{= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{( - \cos 2y + \cos y)dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}}{= - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2y + \sin y\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = 0}} \end{array}$$ For a function $$f$$ that takes on both positive and negative values, $$\iint_{R}{f(x,y)dA}$$ is a difference of volumes: $$V_{1} - V_{2}$$ , where $$V_{1}$$ is the volume above $$R$$ and below the graph of $$f$$ , and $$V_{2}$$ is the volume below $$R$$ and above the graph. The fact that the integral in Example 6 is $$0$$ means that these two volumes $$V_{1}$$ and $$V_{2}$$ are equal. (See Figure 14.)

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Find the volume of the solid S that is bounded by the elliptic paraboloid x^{2} + 2y^{2} + z = 16 , the planes x = 2 and y = 2 , and the three coordinate planes. Solution We first observe that S is the solid that lies...
body_xml: Example 7 Find the volume of the solid $$S$$ that is bounded by the elliptic paraboloid $$x^{2} + 2y^{2} + z = 16$$ , the planes $$x = 2$$ and $$y = 2$$ , and the three coordinate planes. Solution We first observe that $$S$$ is the solid that lies under the surface $$z = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ and above the square $$R = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ . (See Figure 15.) This solid was considered in Example 1, but we are now in a position to evaluate the double integral using Fubini’s Theorem. Therefore $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{R}{({16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}})}dA = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{2}{({16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}})}dxdy} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {16x - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - 2y^{2}x} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 2}dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{{\left( {\frac{88}{3} - 4y^{2}} \right)}dy = \left\lbrack {\frac{88}{3}y - \frac{4}{3}y^{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = 48}}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 if R = \left\lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \right. , then, by Equation 11, \begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}{\sin x\cos ydA = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sin xdx{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash...
body_xml: Example 8 if $$R = \left\lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \right.$$ , then, by Equation 11, $$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}{\sin x\cos ydA = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sin xdx{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\cos ydy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{\sin x\cos ydA}}{= \left\lbrack - \cos x \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack \sin y \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1}} \end{array}$$ The function $$f(x,y) = \sin x\cos y$$ in Example 8 is positive on $$R$$ , so the integral represents the volume of the solid that lies above $$R$$ and below the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 16.

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 The contour map in Figure 18 shows the snowfall, in inches, that fell on the state of Colorado on December 20 and 21, 2006. (The state is in the shape of a rectangle that measures 388 mi west to east and 276 mi south...
body_xml: Example 9 The contour map in Figure 18 shows the snowfall, in inches, that fell on the state of Colorado on December 20 and 21, 2006. (The state is in the shape of a rectangle that measures $$388$$ mi west to east and $$276$$ mi south to north.) Use the contour map to estimate the average snowfall for the entire state of Colorado on those days. Solution Let’s place the origin at the southwest corner of the state. Then $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 388$$ , $$0 \leqslant y \leqslant 276$$ , and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is the snowfall, in inches, at a location $$x$$ miles to the east and $$y$$ miles to the north of the origin. If $$R$$ is the rectangle that represents Colorado, then the average snowfall for the state on December 20–21 was $$f_{avg} = \frac{1}{A(R)}{\iint\limits_{R}{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA}}$$ where $$A(R) = 388 \cdot 276$$ . To estimate the value of this double integral, let’s use the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 4$$ . In other words, we divide $$R$$ into $$16$$ subrectangles of equal size, as in Figure 19. The area of each subrectangle is $$\Delta A = \frac{1}{16}(388)(276) = 6693{mi}^{2}$$ Using the contour map to estimate the value of $$f$$ at the center of each subrectangle, we get $$\begin{matrix} {\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{4}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{4}f({\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j})\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} \approx {\Delta A}\lbrack 0 + 15 + 8 + 7 + 2 + 25 + 18.5 + 11 +} \\ { 4.5 + 28 + 17 + 13.5 + 12 + 15 + 17.5 + 13\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} = (6693)(207)} \end{matrix}$$ Therefore $$f_{avg} \approx \frac{(6693)(207)}{(388)(276)} \approx 12.9$$ On December 20–21, 2006, Colorado received an average of approximately $$13$$ inches of snow.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Evaluate \iint_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}} , where D is the region bounded by the parabolas y = 2x^{2} and y = 1 + x^{2} . Solution The parabolas intersect when 2x^{2} = 1 + x^{2} , that is, x^{2} = 1 , so x = \pm 1 . We...
body_xml: Example 1 Evaluate $$\iint_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the region bounded by the parabolas $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ . Solution The parabolas intersect when $$2x^{2} = 1 + x^{2}$$ , that is, $$x^{2} = 1$$ , so $$x = \pm 1$$ . We note that the region $$D$$ , sketched in Figure 8, is a type I region but not a type II region and we can write $$D = \left\{ (x,y) \middle| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,2x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 1 + x^{2} \right\}$$ Since the lower boundary is $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and the upper boundary is $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ , Equation 3 gives $$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{2x^{2}}^{1 + x^{2}}{(x + 2y)dydx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2x^{2}}^{y = 1 + x^{2}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\lbrack x(1 + x^{2}) + {(1 + x^{2})}^{2} - x(2x^{2}) - {(2x^{2})}^{2}\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{( - 3x^{4} - x^{3} + 2x^{2} + x + 1)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = \left. - 3\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{4}}{4} + 2\frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right\rbrack_{- 1}^{1} = \frac{32}{15}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid that lies under the paraboloid z = x^{2} + y^{2} and above the region D in the xy -plane bounded by the line y = 2x and the parabola y = x^{2} . Solution 1 From Figure 9 we see that D is a...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the volume of the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and above the region $$D$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane bounded by the line $$y = 2x$$ and the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ . Solution 1 From Figure 9 we see that $$D$$ is a type I region and $$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2,x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 2x \right\}$$ Therefore the volume under $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and above $$D$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}d}}A = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{x^{2}}^{2x}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {x^{2}y + \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = x^{2}}^{y = 2x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}\left\lbrack {x^{2}(2x) + \frac{(2x)^{3}}{3} - x^{2}x^{2} - \frac{\left( x^{2} \right)^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}\left( {- \frac{x^{6}}{3} - x^{4} + \frac{14x^{3}}{3}} \right)}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\left. - \frac{x^{7}}{21} - \frac{x^{5}}{5} + \frac{7x^{4}}{6} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{216}{35}}} \end{array}$$ Solution 2 From Figure 10 we see that $$D$$ can also be written as a type II region: $$D = {\{{{(x,y)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 4,\frac{1}{2}y \leqslant x \leqslant \sqrt{y}}\}}}$$ Therefore another expression for $$V$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}d}}A = {\int_{0}^{4}{{\int_{\frac{1}{2}y}^{\sqrt{y}}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dxdy}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + y^{2}x} \right\rbrack_{x = \frac{1}{2}y}^{x = \sqrt{y}}dy = {\int_{0}^{4}\left( {\frac{y^{3 \slash 2}}{3} + y^{5 \slash 2} - \frac{y^{3}}{24} - \frac{y^{3}}{2}} \right)}dy}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \left. \frac{2}{15}y^{5 \slash 2} + \frac{2}{7}y^{7 \slash 2} - \frac{13}{96}y^{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{216}{35}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate \iint\limits_{D}{xy\mathit{dA}} , where D is the region bounded by the line y = x - 1 and the parabola y^{2} = 2x + 6 . Solution The region D is shown in Figure 12. Again D is both type I and type II, but the...
body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate $$\iint\limits_{D}{xy\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the region bounded by the line $$y = x - 1$$ and the parabola $$y^{2} = 2x + 6$$ . Solution The region $$D$$ is shown in Figure 12. Again $$D$$ is both type I and type II, but the description of $$D$$ as a type I region is more complicated because the lower boundary consists of two parts. Therefore we prefer to express $$D$$ as a type II region: $$D = {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)| - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 4,\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3 \leqslant x \leqslant y + 1}\}}$$ Then (4) gives $$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\int_{\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3}^{y + 1}{\mathit{xy}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2}y} \right\rbrack_{x = \frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3}^{x = y + 1}dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- 2}^{4}{y\left\lbrack {\left( {y + 1} \right)^{2} - \left( {\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {- \frac{y^{5}}{4} + 4y^{3} + 2y^{2} - 8y} \right)}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {- \frac{y^{6}}{24} + y^{4} + 2\frac{y^{3}}{3} - 4y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{- 2}^{4} = 36} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the planes x + 2y + z = 2 , x = 2y , x = 0 , and z = 0 . Solution In a question such as this, it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one of the three-dimensional solid and another...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the planes $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , $$x = 2y$$ , $$x = 0$$ , and $$z = 0$$ . Solution In a question such as this, it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one of the three-dimensional solid and another of the plane region $$D$$ over which it lies. Figure 13 shows the tetrahedron $$T$$ bounded by the coordinate planes $$x = 0$$ , $$z = 0$$ , the vertical plane $$x = 2y$$ , and the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ . Since the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ intersects the $$xy$$ -plane (whose equation is $$z = 0$$ ) in the line $$x + 2y = 2$$ , we see that $$T$$ lies above the triangular region $$D$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane bounded by the lines $$x = 2y$$ , $$x + 2y = 2$$ , and $$x = 0$$ . (See Figure 14.) The plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ can be written as $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ , so the required volume lies under the graph of the function $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ and above $$D = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,x \slash 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 - x \slash 2} \right.}\}}}$$ Therefore $$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)\mathit{dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x \slash 2}^{1 - x \slash 2}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {2y - xy - y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = x \slash 2}^{y = 1 - x \slash 2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {2 - x - x\left( {1 - \frac{x}{2}} \right) - \left( {1 - \frac{x}{2}} \right)^{2} - x + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x^{2}}{4}} \right\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{{({x^{2} - 2x + 1})}dx = \left. \frac{x^{3}}{3} - x^{2} + x \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate the iterated integral \int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}dydx}} . Solution If we try to evaluate the integral as it stands, we are faced with the task of first evaluating \int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy} . But it’s...
body_xml: Example 5 Evaluate the iterated integral $$\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}dydx}}$$ . Solution If we try to evaluate the integral as it stands, we are faced with the task of first evaluating $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ . But it’s impossible to do so in finite terms since $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ is not an elementary function. (See the end of Section 7.5.) So we must change the order of integration. This is accomplished by first expressing the given iterated integral as a double integral. Using (3) backward, we have $$\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dA}}}}}$$ where $$D = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,x \leqslant y \leqslant 1} \right.}\}}}$$ We sketch this region $$D$$ in Figure 15. Then from Figure 16 we see that an alternative description of $$D$$ is $$D = \left\{ \left. {\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant x \leqslant y} \right.} \right\} \right.$$ This enables us to use (4) to express the double integral as an iterated integral in the reverse order: $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dA}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{y}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {x\sin{(y^{2})}} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = y}dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{y\sin{(y^{2})}dy = \left. {- \frac{1}{2}\cos{(y^{2})}} \right\rbrack}}_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 1} \right)} \end{array}$$

snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Use Property 10 to estimate the integral \iint_{D}{e^{\sin x\cos y}\mathit{dA}} , where D is the disk with center the origin and radius 2 . Solution Since - 1 \leqslant \sin x \leqslant 1 and - 1 \leqslant \cos y...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Property 10 to estimate the integral $$\iint_{D}{e^{\sin x\cos y}\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the disk with center the origin and radius $$2$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Since $$- 1 \leqslant \sin x \leqslant 1$$ and $$- 1 \leqslant \cos y \leqslant 1$$ , we have $$- 1 \leqslant \sin x\cos y \leqslant 1$$ and, because the natural exponential function is increasing, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$e^{- 1} \leqslant e^{\sin x\cos y} \leqslant e^{1} = e$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus, using $$m = e^{- 1} = 1 \slash e$$ , $$M = e$$ , and $$A(D) = \pi(2)^{2}$$ in Property 10, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{4\pi}{e} \leqslant {\iint\limits_{D}{e^{\sin x\cos y}\mathit{dA} \leqslant 4\pi e}}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Evaluate \iint_{R}{({3x + 4y^{2}})}\mathit{dA} , where R is the region in the upper half-plane bounded by the circles x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 and x^{2} + y^{2} = 4 . Solution The region R can be described as R = {\{{{\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\iint_{R}{({3x + 4y^{2}})}\mathit{dA}$$ , where $$R$$ is the region in the upper half-plane bounded by the circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The region $$R$$ can be described as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$R = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right){|{y \geqslant 0,1 \leqslant x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 4}}}\}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It is the half-ring shown in Figure 2(b), and in polar coordinates it is given by $$1 \leqslant r \leqslant 2$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . Therefore, by Formula 2,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}\lbrack 3(r\cos\theta) + 4{(r\sin\theta)}^{2}\rbrack rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}(3r^{2}\cos\theta + 4r^{3}\sin^{2}\theta)drd\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack r^{3}\cos\theta + r^{4}\sin^{2}\theta \right\rbrack_{r = 1}^{r = 2}d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi}(7\cos\theta + 15\sin^{2}\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\lbrack 7\cos\theta + \frac{15}{2}(1 - \cos 2\theta)\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \left. {7\sin\theta + \frac{15\theta}{2} - \frac{15}{4}\sin 2\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = \frac{15\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Here we use the trigonometric identity</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {1 - \cos 2\theta} \right)}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>See Section 7.2 for advice on integrating trigonometric functions.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Evaluate the double integral \int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}(x^{2} + y^{2})\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} Solution This iterated integral is a double integral over the region R shown in Figure 6 and described by R =...
body_xml: Example 2 Evaluate the double integral $$\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}(x^{2} + y^{2})\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$ Solution This iterated integral is a double integral over the region $$R$$ shown in Figure 6 and described by $$R = \{(x,y)| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\}$$ The region is a half-disk, so it is more simply described in polar coordinates: $$R = \{(r,\theta)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1\}$$ Therefore we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}(x^{2} + y^{2})\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(r^{2})r\mathit{dr}\mathit{d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{r = 0}^{r = 1}\mathit{d\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\pi}\mathit{d\theta} = \frac{\pi}{4}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid bounded by the plane z = 0 and the paraboloid z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2} . Solution If we put z = 0 in the equation of the paraboloid, we get x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 . This means that the plane...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid bounded by the plane $$z = 0$$ and the paraboloid $$z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ . Solution If we put $$z = 0$$ in the equation of the paraboloid, we get $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . This means that the plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , so the solid lies under the paraboloid and above the circular disk $$D$$ given by $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1$$ [see Figures 7 and 2(a)]. In polar coordinates $$D$$ is given by $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Since $$1 - x^{2} - y^{2} = 1 - r^{2}$$ , the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{D}(1 - x^{2} - y^{2})dA = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(1 - r^{2})rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{1}(r - r^{3})dr = 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{r^{2}}{2} - \frac{r^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Use a double integral to find the area enclosed by one loop of the four-leaved rose r = \cos 2\theta . Solution From the sketch of the curve in Figure 9, we see that a loop is given by the region D = \left\{ \left....
body_xml: Example 4 Use a double integral to find the area enclosed by one loop of the four-leaved rose $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ . Solution From the sketch of the curve in Figure 9, we see that a loop is given by the region $$D = \left\{ \left. {\left( {r,\theta} \right)\left. \middle| {- \pi \slash 4 \leqslant \theta \leqslant} \right.\pi \slash 4,0 \leqslant r \leqslant \cos 2\theta} \right\} \right.$$ So the area is $$\begin{array}{l} {{A(D)} = \iint\limits_{D}\mathit{dA} = \int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\int_{0}^{\cos 2\theta}rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{A(D)} = \int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}r^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\cos 2\theta}d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\cos^{2}2\theta d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A(D)} = \frac{1}{4}\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}(1 + \cos 4\theta)d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {\theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 4\theta} \right\rbrack_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4} = \frac{\pi}{8}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the volume of the solid that lies under the paraboloid z = x^{2} + y^{2} , above the xy -plane, and inside the cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x . Solution The solid lies above the disk D whose boundary circle has...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the volume of the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ , above the $$xy$$ -plane, and inside the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x$$ . Solution The solid lies above the disk $$D$$ whose boundary circle has equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x$$ or, after completing the square, $$(x - 1)^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ (See Figures 10 and 11.) In polar coordinates we have $$x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}$$ and $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , so the boundary circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x$$ becomes $$r^{2} = 2r\cos\theta$$ , or $$r = 2\cos\theta$$ . Thus the disk $$D$$ is given by $$D = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| - \pi \slash 2 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \slash 2,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2\cos\theta \right\}$$ and, by Formula 3, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{D}({x^{2} + y^{2}})\mathit{dA} = \int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\int_{0}^{2\cos\theta}r^{2}rdrd\theta = \int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\cos\theta}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 4\int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\cos^{4}\theta d\theta = 8\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\cos^{4}\theta d\theta = 8\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left( \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2} \right)^{2}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 2\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack {1 + 2\cos 2\theta + \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 4\theta} \right)} \right\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 2\left\lbrack {\frac{3}{2}\theta + \sin 2\theta + \frac{1}{8}\sin 4\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2} = 2\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \frac{3\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Charge is distributed over the triangular region D in Figure 3 so that the charge density at \left( {x,y} \right) is \sigma\left( {x,y} \right) = xy , measured in coulombs per square meter (C \slash m^{2}) . Find the...
body_xml: Example 1 Charge is distributed over the triangular region $$D$$ in Figure 3 so that the charge density at $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$\sigma\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ , measured in coulombs per square meter $$(C \slash m^{2})$$ . Find the total charge. Solution From Equation 2 and Figure 3 we have $$\begin{array}{l} {Q = {\iint\limits_{D}\sigma}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{1 - x}^{1}{xy}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 1 - x}^{y = 1}dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x}{2}{\lbrack{1^{2} - \left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}}\rbrack}}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({2x^{2} - x^{3}})dx}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{2x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{5}{24}}} \end{array}$$ Thus the total charge is $$\frac{5}{24}C$$ .

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the mass and center of mass of a triangular lamina with vertices \left( {0,0} \right) , \left( {1,0} \right) , and \left( {0,2} \right) if the density function is \rho\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + 3x + y . Solution...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the mass and center of mass of a triangular lamina with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ if the density function is $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + 3x + y$$ . Solution The triangle is shown in Figure 5. (Note that the equation of the upper boundary is $$y = 2 - 2x$$ .) The mass of the lamina is $$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}\left( {1 + 3x + y} \right)}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {y + 3xy + \frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{m} = 4{\int_{0}^{1}{({1 - x^{2}})}}dx = 4\left\lbrack {x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{8}{3}} \end{array}$$ Then the formulas in (5) give $$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{x} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({x + 3x^{2} + xy})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + 3x^{2}y + x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({x - x^{3}})}}dx = \frac{3}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{3}{8}} \\ {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({y + 3xy + y^{2}})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2}}{2} + 3x\frac{y^{2}}{2} + \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx = \frac{1}{4}{\int_{0}^{1}{({7 - 9x - 3x^{2} + 5x^{3}})}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {7x - 9\frac{x^{2}}{2} - x^{3} + 5\frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{11}{16}} \end{array}$$ The center of mass is at the point $$\left( {\frac{3}{8},\frac{11}{16}} \right)$$ .

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 The density at any point on a semicircular lamina is proportional to the distance from the center of the circle. Find the center of mass of the lamina. Solution Let’s place the lamina as the upper half of the circle...
body_xml: Example 3 The density at any point on a semicircular lamina is proportional to the distance from the center of the circle. Find the center of mass of the lamina. Solution Let’s place the lamina as the upper half of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ . (See Figure 6.) Then the distance from a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to the center of the circle (the origin) is $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ . Therefore the density function is $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ where $$K$$ is some constant. Both the density function and the shape of the lamina suggest that we convert to polar coordinates. Then $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = r$$ and the region $$D$$ is given by $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . Thus the mass of the lamina is $$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}\rho}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}}dA} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta = K{\int_{0}^{\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{a}{r^{2}dr}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = K\pi\left. \frac{r^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{K\pi a^{3}}{3}} \end{array}$$ Both the lamina and the density function are symmetric with respect to the $$y$$ -axis, so the center of mass must lie on the $$y$$ -axis, that is, $$\overline{x} = 0$$ . The $$y$$ -coordinate is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = \frac{3}{K\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{r\sin\theta\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin\theta d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}}dr =}}\frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\left\lbrack {- \cos\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\frac{2a^{4}}{4} = \frac{3a}{2\pi}} \end{array}$$ Therefore the center of mass is located at the point $$\left( {0,3a \slash \left( {2\pi} \right)} \right)$$ . Compare the location of the center of mass in Example 3 with Example 8.3.4, where we found that the center of mass of a lamina with the same shape but uniform density is located at the point $$\left( {0,4a \slash \left( {3\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the moments of inertia I_{x} , I_{y} , and I_{0} of a homogeneous disk D with density \rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \rho , center the origin, and radius a . Solution The boundary of D is the circle x^{2} + y^{2} =...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the moments of inertia $$I_{x}$$ , $$I_{y}$$ , and $$I_{0}$$ of a homogeneous disk $$D$$ with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \rho$$ , center the origin, and radius $$a$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution The boundary of $$D$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ and in polar coordinates $$D$$ is described by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ . By Formula 6,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{x} = {\iint\limits_{D}{y^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\sin\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin^{2}\theta}d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2\theta})d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \frac{\rho}{2}\left\lbrack \theta - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Similarly, Formula 7 gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{y} = {\iint\limits_{D}{x^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\cos\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{y}} = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)d\theta\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(From the symmetry of the problem, it is expected that $$I_{x} = I_{y}$$ .) We could use Formula 8 to compute $$I_{0}$$ directly, or use</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$I_{0} = I_{x} + I_{y} = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4} + \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4} = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{2}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the radius of gyration about the $$x$$ -axis of the disk in Example 4.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution As noted, the mass of the disk is $$m = \rho\pi a^{2}$$ , so from Equations 10 we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\overset{=}{y}}^{2} = \frac{I_{x}}{m} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\pi\rho a^{4}}{\rho\pi a^{2}} = \frac{a^{2}}{4}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore the radius of gyration about the $$x$$ -axis is $$\overset{=}{y} = \frac{1}{2}a$$ , which is half the radius of the disk.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 If the joint density function for X and Y is given by f\left( {x,y} \right) = \begin{cases} {C\left( {x + 2y} \right)} & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 10,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 10} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases} find...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>If the joint density function for $$X$$ and $$Y$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \begin{cases} {C\left( {x + 2y} \right)} & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 10,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 10} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>find the value of the constant $$C$$ . Then find $$P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We find the value of $$C$$ by ensuring that the double integral of $$f$$ over $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ is equal to $$1$$ . Because $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ outside the rectangle $$\left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}} = {\int_{0}^{10}{\int_{0}^{10}{C\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx = C{\int_{0}^{10}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 10}}}}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = C{\int_{0}^{10}{{\left( {10x + 100} \right)}dx = 1500C}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore $$1500C = 1$$ and so $$C = \frac{1}{1500}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now we can compute the probability that $$X$$ is at most $$7$$ and $$Y$$ is at least $$2$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right) = {\int_{- \infty}^{7}{\int_{2}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = {\int_{0}^{7}{\int_{2}^{10}{\frac{1}{1500}\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2}^{y = 10}dx = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}{\left( {8x + 96} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{868}{1500} \approx 0.5787} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 The manager of a movie theater determines that the average time moviegoers wait in line to buy a ticket for a film is 10 minutes and the average time they wait to buy popcorn is 5 minutes. Assuming that the waiting...
body_xml: Example 7 The manager of a movie theater determines that the average time moviegoers wait in line to buy a ticket for a film is $$10$$ minutes and the average time they wait to buy popcorn is $$5$$ minutes. Assuming that the waiting times are independent, find the probability that a moviegoer waits a total of less than $$20$$ minutes before taking his or her seat. Solution Assuming that both the waiting time $$X$$ for the ticket purchase and the waiting time $$Y$$ in the refreshment line are modeled by exponential probability density functions, we can write the individual density functions as $$f_{1}(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & {{if}x < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{10}e^{- x \slash 10}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \end{array} f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}y < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{5}e^{- y \slash 5}} & {{if}y \geqslant 0} \end{cases} \right.$$ Since $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are independent, the joint density function is the product: $$f(x,y) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} {\frac{1}{50}{e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0,y \geqslant 0} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$ We are asked for the probability that $$X + Y < 20$$ : $$P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = P\left( {\left( {X,Y} \right) \in D} \right)$$ where $$D$$ is the triangular region shown in Figure 8. Thus $$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = {\int_{0}^{20}{\int_{0}^{20 - x}{\frac{1}{50}e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = \frac{1}{50}\int_{0}^{20}\left\lbrack {e^{- x \slash 10}\left( {- 5} \right)e^{- y \slash 5}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 20 - x}dx} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{e^{- x \slash 10}{({1 - e^{{({x - 20})} \slash 5}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{{({e^{- x \slash 10} - e^{- 4}e^{ x \slash 10}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = 1 + e^{- 4} - 2e^{- 2} \approx 0.7476} \end{array}$$ This means that about $$75\%$$ of the moviegoers wait less than $$20$$ minutes before taking their seats.

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 A factory produces (cylindrically shaped) roller bearings that are sold as having diameter 4.0 cm and length 6.0 cm. In fact, the diameters X are normally distributed with mean 4.0 cm and standard deviation 0.01 cm...
body_xml: Example 8 A factory produces (cylindrically shaped) roller bearings that are sold as having diameter $$4.0$$ cm and length $$6.0$$ cm. In fact, the diameters $$X$$ are normally distributed with mean $$4.0$$ cm and standard deviation $$0.01$$ cm while the lengths $$Y$$ are normally distributed with mean $$6.0$$ cm and standard deviation $$0.01$$ cm. Assuming that $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are independent, write the joint density function and graph it. Find the probability that a bearing randomly chosen from the production line has either length or diameter that differs from the mean by more than $$0.02$$ cm. Solution We are given that $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are normally distributed with $$\mu_{1} = 4.0$$ , $$\mu_{2} = 6.0$$ , and $$\sigma_{1} = \sigma_{2} = 0.01$$ . So the individual density functions for $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are $${f_{1}{(x)} = \frac{1}{0.01\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{- {({x - 4})}^{2} \slash 0.0002}} {f_{2}(y) = \frac{1}{0.01\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{- {({y - 6})}^{2} \slash 0.0002}}$$ Since $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are independent, the joint density function is the product: $$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( {x,y} \right) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)} \\ {\phantom{f\left( {x,y} \right)} = \frac{1}{0.0002\pi}e^{- {({x - 4})}^{2} \slash 0.0002}e^{- {({y - 6})}^{2} \slash 0.0002}} \\ {\phantom{f\left( {x,y} \right)} = \frac{5000}{\pi}e^{- 5000{\lbrack{{({x - 4})}^{2} + {({y - 6})}^{2}}\rbrack}}} \end{array}$$ A graph of this function is shown in Figure 9. Let’s first calculate the probability that both $$X$$ and $$Y$$ differ from their means by less than $$0.02$$ cm. Using a calculator or computer to estimate the integral, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {3.98 < X < 4.02,5.98 < Y < 6.02} \right) = {\int_{3.98}^{4.02}{\int_{5.98}^{6.02}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {3.98 < X < 4.02,5.98 < Y < 6.02} \right)} = \frac{5000}{\pi}{\int_{3.98}^{4.02}{\int_{5.98}^{6.02}{e^{- 5000{\lbrack{{({x - 4})}^{2} + {({y - 6})}^{2}}\rbrack}}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {3.98 < X < 4.02,5.98 < Y < 6.02} \right)} \approx 0.91} \end{array}$$ Then the probability that either $$X$$ or $$Y$$ differs from its mean by more than $$0.02$$ cm is approximately $$1 - 0.91 = 0.09$$

body_xml: Example 1 Find the surface area of the part of the surface $$z = x^{2} + 2y + 2$$ that lies above the triangular region $$T$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ . Solution The region $$T$$ is shown in Figure 3 and is described by $$T = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \right\}$$ Using Formula 2 with $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + 2y + 2$$ , we get $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{T}{\sqrt{\left( {2x} \right)^{2} + (2)^{2} + 1}dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\sqrt{4x^{2} + 5}dydx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{0}^{1}{x\sqrt{4x^{2} + 5}}}dx = \frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{2}{3}\left. {({4x^{2} + 5})}^{3 \slash 2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{12}{({27 - 5\sqrt{5}})}} \end{array}$$ Figure 4 shows the portion of the surface whose area we have just computed.

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the area of the part of the paraboloid z = x^{2} + y^{2} that lies under the plane z = 9 . Solution The plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle x^{2} + y^{2} = 9 , z = 9 . Therefore the given surface lies...
body_xml: Example 2 Find the area of the part of the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ that lies under the plane $$z = 9$$ . Solution The plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ , $$z = 9$$ . Therefore the given surface lies above the disk $$D$$ with center the origin and radius $$3$$ . (See Figure 5.) Using Formula 3, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}}dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( {2x} \right)^{2} + \left( {2y} \right)^{2}}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + 4{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dA}}} \end{array}$$ Converting to polar coordinates, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{3}{\sqrt{1 + 4r^{2}}rdrd\theta =}}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{3}{\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{1 + 4r^{2}}\left( {8r} \right)dr}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. {2\pi{\left( \frac{1}{8} \right)}\frac{2}{3}{({1 + 4r^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{\pi}{6}{({37\sqrt{37} - 1})}} \end{array}$$

    <paragraph>Evaluate the triple integral $${\iiint_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$B$$ is the rectangular box given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$B = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1, - 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 3 \right\}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution We could use any of the six possible orders of integration. If we choose to integrate with respect to $$x$$ , then $$y$$ , and then $$z$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{xyz^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz} =}}}}{\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}yz^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 1}}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}{\frac{yz^{2}}{2}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz} =}}}{\int_{0}^{3}{\left\lbrack \frac{y^{2}z^{2}}{4} \right\rbrack_{y = - 1}^{y = 2}\mathit{dz}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}\frac{3z^{2}}{4}}\mathit{dz} = \left. \frac{z^{3}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{27}{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Evaluate \iiint_{E}{z\mathit{dV}} , where E is the solid in the first octant bounded by the surface z = 12xy and the planes y = x , x = 1 . Solution When we set up a triple integral it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one...
body_xml: Example 2 Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}$$ , where $$E$$ is the solid in the first octant bounded by the surface $$z = 12xy$$ and the planes $$y = x$$ , $$x = 1$$ . Solution When we set up a triple integral it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one of the solid region $$E$$ (Figure 5) and, for a type 1 region, one of its projection $$D$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane (Figure 6). The lower boundary of the solid $$E$$ is the plane $$z = 0$$ and the upper boundary is the surface $$z = 12xy$$ , so we use $$u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ and $$u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right) = 12xy$$ in Formula 7. Notice that the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane is the triangular region shown in Figure 6, and we have $$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 12xy} \right\}$$ This description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region enables us to evaluate the integral as follows: $$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\int_{0}^{12xy}{z\mathit{dz}}}}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}\left\lbrack \frac{z^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack}}_{z = 0}^{z = 12xy}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\left( {12xy} \right)^{2}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = 72}}}{\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x}x^{2}y^{2}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}} = {72{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {x^{2}\frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = x}\mathit{dx}} = 24\int_{0}^{1}x^{5}\mathit{dx} = 24\left\lbrack \frac{x^{6}}{6} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 1} = 4}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate \iiint_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}} , where E is the region bounded by the paraboloid y = x^{2} + z^{2} and the plane y = 4 . Solution The solid E is shown in Figure 10. If we regard it as a type 1...
body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}$$ , where $$E$$ is the region bounded by the paraboloid $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and the plane $$y = 4$$ . Solution The solid $$E$$ is shown in Figure 10. If we regard it as a type 1 region, then we need to consider its projection $$D_{1}$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, which is the parabolic region shown in Figures 10 and 11. (The trace of $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ in the plane $$z = 0$$ is the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ .) From $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ we obtain $$z = \pm \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ , so the lower boundary surface of $$E$$ is $$z = - \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ and the upper surface is $$z = \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ . Therefore the description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region is $$E = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| - 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2,x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 4, - \sqrt{y - x^{2}} \leqslant z \leqslant \sqrt{y - x^{2}} \right\}$$ and so we obtain $${\iiint\limits_{E}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{x^{2}}^{4}{\int_{- \sqrt{y - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{y - x^{2}}}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$ Although this expression is correct, it is extremely difficult to evaluate. So let’s instead consider $$E$$ as a region of a different type. If we regard $$E$$ as a type 3 region, then we need to consider its projection $$D_{3}$$ onto the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, which is the disk $$x^{2} + z^{2} \leqslant 4$$ shown in Figures 12 and 13. (The trace of $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ in the plane $$y = 4$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ .) Then the left boundary of $$E$$ is the paraboloid $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and the right boundary is the plane $$y = 4$$ , so taking $$u_{1}\left( {x,z} \right) = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and $$u_{2}\left( {x,z} \right) = 4$$ in Equation 11, we have $${\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV} =}}{\iint\limits_{D_{3}}\left\lbrack {\int_{x^{2} + z^{2}}^{4}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dy}}} \right\rbrack}\mathit{dA} = {\iint\limits_{D_{3}}{({4 - x^{2} - z^{2}})}}\sqrt{x^{2} - z^{2}}\mathit{dA}$$ Although this integral could be written as $$\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{{({4 - x^{2} - z^{2}})}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}}}$$ it’s easier to convert to polar coordinates in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$z = r\sin\theta$$ . This gives $$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}} = {\iint\limits_{D_{3}}{{({4 - x^{2} - z^{2}})}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{2}{{({4 - r^{2}})}rr\mathit{dr}d\theta =}}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{2}{{({4r^{2} - r^{4}})}\mathit{dr}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{4r^{3}}{3} - \frac{r^{5}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{128\pi}{15}}} \end{array}$$ The most difficult step in evaluating a triple integral is setting up an expression for the region of integration (such as Equation 9 in Example 2). Remember that the limits of integration in the inner integral contain at most two variables, the limits of integration in the middle integral contain at most one variable, and the limits of integration in the outer integral must be constants.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Express the iterated integral {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x^{2}}{\int_{0}^{y}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} as a triple integral and then rewrite it as an iterated integral in the following...
body_xml: Example 4 Express the iterated integral $${\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x^{2}}{\int_{0}^{y}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$ as a triple integral and then rewrite it as an iterated integral in the following orders. (a) Integrate first with respect to $$x$$ , then $$z$$ , and then $$y$$ . (b) Integrate first with respect to $$y$$ , then $$x$$ , and then $$z$$ . Solution We can write $${\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x^{2}}{\int_{0}^{y}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$ where $$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2},0 \leqslant z \leqslant y} \right\}$$ . From this description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region we see that $$E$$ lies between the lower surface $$z = 0$$ and the upper surface $$z = y$$ , and its projection onto the $$xy$$ -plane is $$\left\{ {\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}} \right\}$$ , as shown in Figures 14 and 15. So $$E$$ is the solid enclosed by the planes $$z = 0$$ , $$x = 1$$ , $$y = z$$ and the parabolic cylinder $$y = x^{2}$$ (or $$x = \sqrt{y}$$ ). Using Figure 14 as a guide, we can write projections onto the three coordinate planes as follows (see Figure 15): $$\begin{array}{lll} {{onto the}\mathit{xy}{-plane}: D_{1}} & = & {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,\sqrt{y} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}} \\ {{onto the}\mathit{yz}{-plane}: D_{2}} & = & {\{{\left( {y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant y}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,z \leqslant y \leqslant 1}\}} \\ {{onto the}\mathit{xz}{-plane}: D_{3}} & = & {\{{\left( {x,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant x^{2}}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {x,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,\sqrt{z} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}} \end{array}$$ (a) In order to integrate first with respect to $$x$$ , then $$z$$ , and then $$y$$ , we need to consider $$E$$ as a type 2 region where the back boundary is the surface $$x = \sqrt{y}$$ and the front boundary is the plane $$x = 1$$ ; the projection onto the $$yz$$ -plane is $$D_{2}$$ . We describe $$E$$ by $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant y,\sqrt{y} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}}$$ and then $${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{y}{\int_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}f}}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}$$ (b) In order to integrate first with respect to $$y$$ , then $$x$$ , and then $$z$$ , we need to consider $$E$$ as a type 3 region where the left boundary is the plane $$y = z$$ and the right boundary is the surface $$y = x^{2}$$ . The projection onto the $$xz$$ -plane is $$D_{3}$$ and $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,\sqrt{z} \leqslant x \leqslant 1,z \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}}\}}$$ and then $${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int_{z}^{x^{2}}f}}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dz}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Use a triple integral to find the volume of the tetrahedron T bounded by the planes x + 2y + z = 2 , x = 2y , x = 0 , and z = 0 . Solution The tetrahedron T and its projection D onto the \mathit{xy} -plane are shown in...
body_xml: Example 5 Use a triple integral to find the volume of the tetrahedron $$T$$ bounded by the planes $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , $$x = 2y$$ , $$x = 0$$ , and $$z = 0$$ . Solution The tetrahedron $$T$$ and its projection $$D$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane are shown in Figures 16 and 17. The lower boundary of $$T$$ is the plane $$z = 0$$ and the upper boundary is the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , that is, $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ . Therefore we have $$\begin{array}{l} {V(T) = {\iiint\limits_{T}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x/2}^{1 - x/2}{\int_{0}^{2 - x - 2y}{dzdydx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V(T)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x \slash 2}^{1 - x \slash 2}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{3}}}}} \end{array}$$ by the same calculation as in Example 15.2.4. (Notice that it is not necessary to use triple integrals to compute volumes. They simply give an alternative method for setting up the calculation.)

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the center of mass of a solid of constant density that is bounded by the parabolic cylinder x = y^{2} and the planes x = z , z = 0 , and x = 1 . Solution The solid E and its projection onto the \mathit{xy} -plane...
body_xml: Example 6 Find the center of mass of a solid of constant density that is bounded by the parabolic cylinder $$x = y^{2}$$ and the planes $$x = z$$ , $$z = 0$$ , and $$x = 1$$ . Solution The solid $$E$$ and its projection onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane are shown in Figure 19. The lower and upper surfaces of $$E$$ are the planes $$z = 0$$ and $$z = x$$ , so we describe $$E$$ as a type 1 region: $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right){|{- 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,y^{2} \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant x}}}\}}$$ Then, if the density is $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \rho$$ , the mass is $$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iiint\limits_{E}{\rho\mathit{dV} = \int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{y^{2}}^{1}\int_{0}^{x}\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = \rho\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{y^{2}}^{1}x\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack}_{x = y^{2}}^{x = 1}\mathit{dy}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\frac{\rho}{2}{\int_{- 1}^{1}{({1 - y^{4}})}}\mathit{dy} = \rho{\int_{0}^{1}{({1 - y^{4}})}}\mathit{dy}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\rho\left\lbrack {y - \frac{y^{5}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4\rho}{5}}} \end{array}$$ Because of the symmetry of $$E$$ and $$\rho$$ about the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, we can immediately say that $$M_{\mathit{xz}} = 0$$ and therefore $$\overline{y} = 0$$ . The other moments are $$\begin{array}{l} {M_{\mathit{yz}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{x\rho\mathit{dV}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{x\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{yz}}} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{x^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} = \rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\left\lbrack \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{x = y^{2}}^{x = 1}\mathit{dy}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{yz}}} = {\frac{2\rho}{3}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({1 - y^{6}})}\mathit{dy}}} = \frac{2\rho}{3}\left\lbrack {y - \frac{y^{7}}{7}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4\rho}{7}}} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {M_{\mathit{xy}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{z\rho\mathit{dV}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{z\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{xy}}} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\left\lbrack \frac{z^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{z = 0}^{z = x}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} = \frac{\rho}{2}{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{x^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{xy}}} = {\frac{\rho}{3}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({1 - y^{6}})}\mathit{dy} = \frac{2\rho}{7}}}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore the center of mass is $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y},\overline{z}} \right) = \left( {\frac{M_{\mathit{yz}}}{m},\frac{M_{\mathit{xz}}}{m},\frac{M_{\mathit{xy}}}{m}} \right) = \left( {\frac{5}{7},0,\frac{5}{14}} \right)$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 (a) Plot the point with cylindrical coordinates \left( {2,2\pi/3,1} \right) and find its rectangular coordinates. (b) Find cylindrical coordinates of the point with rectangular coordinates \left( {3, - 3, - 7} \right)...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) Plot the point with cylindrical coordinates $$\left( {2,2\pi/3,1} \right)$$ and find its rectangular coordinates.</item>
      <item>(b) Find cylindrical coordinates of the point with rectangular coordinates $$\left( {3, - 3, - 7} \right)$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Solution</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) The point with cylindrical coordinates $$\left( {2,2\pi/3,1} \right)$$ is plotted in Figure 3. From Equations 1, its rectangular coordinates are $$\begin{array}{l} {x = 2\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = - 1} \\ {y = 2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = \sqrt{3}} \\ {z = 1} \end{array}$$ Figure 3 Details Two line segments and a point are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first line segment lies in the second quadrant of the x y plane, begins at the origin, and slopes upward to the right at an angle 2 pi/3 from the x axis, and is labeled 2. The second line segment is vertical, begins from the point the first line segment ends, runs parallel to the z axis until a point labeled (2, 2 pi/3, 1), and is labeled 1. So the point is $$({- 1,\sqrt{3},1})$$ in rectangular coordinates.</item>
      <item>(b) From Equations 2 and noting that $$\theta$$ is in quadrant IV of the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, we have $$\begin{array}{rll} r & = & {\sqrt{3^{2} + {({- 3})}^{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}} \\ {\tan\theta} & = & {{\frac{- 3}{3} = - 1} {so} {\theta = \frac{7\pi}{4} + 2n\pi}} \\ z & = & {- 7} \end{array}$$ Therefore one set of cylindrical coordinates is $$({3\sqrt{2},7\pi/4, - 7})$$ . Another is $$({3\sqrt{2}, - \pi/4, - 7})$$ . As with polar coordinates, there are infinitely many choices.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Describe the surface whose equation in cylindrical coordinates is z = r . Solution The equation says that the z -value, or height, of each point on the surface is the same as r , the distance from the point to the z...
body_xml: Example 2 Describe the surface whose equation in cylindrical coordinates is $$z = r$$ . Solution The equation says that the $$z$$ -value, or height, of each point on the surface is the same as $$r$$ , the distance from the point to the $$z$$ -axis. Because $$\theta$$ doesn’t appear, it can vary. So any horizontal trace in the plane $$z = k{\left( {k > 0} \right)}$$ is a circle of radius $$k$$ . These traces suggest that the surface is a cone. This prediction can be confirmed by converting the equation into rectangular coordinates. From the first equation in (2) we have $$z^{2} = r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ We recognize the equation $$z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ (by comparison with Table 1 in Section 12.6) as being a circular cone whose axis is the $$z$$ -axis (see Figure 7).

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate \iiint_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV} , where E is the solid that lies under the paraboloid z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2} and above the \mathit{xy} -plane (see Figure 10). Solution Because E is symmetric about the z -axis, we...
body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$E$$ is the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ and above the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane (see Figure 10). Solution Because $$E$$ is symmetric about the $$z$$ -axis, we use cylindrical coordinates. In addition, cylindrical coordinates are appropriate because the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2} = 4 - (x^{2} + y^{2})$$ is easily expressed in cylindrical coordinates as $$z = 4 - r^{2}$$ . The paraboloid intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane in the circle $$r^{2} = 4$$ or, equivalently, $$r = 2$$ , so the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the disk $$r \leqslant 2$$ . Thus the region $$E$$ is given by $$\left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 4 - r^{2}} \right\}$$ and from Formula 4 we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{4 - r^{2}}\left( r\cos\theta \right)^{2}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}(r^{3}\cos^{2}\theta)\rbrack(4 - r^{2})\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos^{2}\theta d\theta\int_{0}^{2}(4r^{3} - r^{5})\mathit{dr}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack \theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack r^{4} - \frac{1}{6}r^{6} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}(2\pi)(16 - \frac{32}{3}) = \frac{16}{3}\pi} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 A solid E lies within the cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 to the right of the \mathit{xy} -plane, below the plane z = 4 , and above the paraboloid z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2} . (See Figure 12.) The density at any point is...
body_xml: Example 4 A solid $$E$$ lies within the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ to the right of the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, below the plane $$z = 4$$ , and above the paraboloid $$z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ . (See Figure 12.) The density at any point is proportional to its distance from the axis of the cylinder. Find the mass of $$E$$ . Solution In cylindrical coordinates the cylinder is $$r = 1$$ and the paraboloid is $$z = 1 - r^{2}$$ , so we can write $$E = \left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1,1 - r^{2} \leqslant z \leqslant 4} \right\}$$ Since the density at $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is proportional to the distance from the $$z$$ -axis, the density function is $$⍴({x,y,z}) = K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = Kr$$ where $$K$$ is the proportionality constant. Therefore, from Formula 15.6.13, the mass of $$E$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iiint\limits_{E}{K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{1 - r^{2}}^{4}{{({Kr})}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{Kr^{2}{\lbrack{4 - {({1 - r^{2}})}}\rbrack}\mathit{dr}d\theta = K{\int_{0}^{\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{1}{{({3r^{2} + r^{4}})}\mathit{dr}}}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\pi K\left\lbrack r^{3} + \frac{r^{5}}{5} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{6\pi K}{5}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate {\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} . Solution This iterated integral is a triple integral over...
body_xml: Example 5 Evaluate $${\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$ . Solution This iterated integral is a triple integral over the solid region $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)| - 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2, - \sqrt{4 - x^{2}} \leqslant y \leqslant \sqrt{4 - x^{2}},\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} \leqslant z \leqslant 2}\}}$$ and the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 4$$ . The lower surface of $$E$$ is the cone $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and its upper surface is the plane $$z = 2$$ . (See Figure 13.) This region has a much simpler description in cylindrical coordinates: $$E = \left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,r \leqslant z \leqslant 2} \right\}$$ Therefore we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dV} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{r}^{2}{r^{2}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta}}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{2}{r^{3}{({2 - r})}\mathit{dr}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{- \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}{\int_{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{2}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} = 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}r^{4} - \frac{1}{5}r^{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{16}{5}\pi} \end{array}$$

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The point \left( {2,\pi \slash 4,\pi \slash 3} \right) is given in spherical coordinates. Plot the point and find its rectangular coordinates. Solution We plot the point in Figure 6. From Equations 1 we have...
body_xml: Example 1 The point $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 4,\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ is given in spherical coordinates. Plot the point and find its rectangular coordinates. Solution We plot the point in Figure 6. From Equations 1 we have $$\begin{array}{l} {x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}} \\ {y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}} \\ {z = \rho\cos\phi = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 2\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = 1} \end{array}$$ Thus the point $$({2,\pi \slash 4,\pi \slash 3})$$ is $$({\sqrt{3 \slash 2},\sqrt{3 \slash 2},1})$$ in rectangular coordinates.

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 The point ({0,2\sqrt{3}, - 2}) is given in rectangular coordinates. Find spherical coordinates for this point. Solution From Equation 2 we have \rho = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} = \sqrt{0 + 12 + 4} = 4 and so...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>The point $$({0,2\sqrt{3}, - 2})$$ is given in rectangular coordinates. Find spherical coordinates for this point.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution From Equation 2 we have $$\rho = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} = \sqrt{0 + 12 + 4} = 4$$ and so Equations 1 give</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\cos\phi = \frac{z}{\rho} = \frac{- 2}{4} = - \frac{1}{2}} & { \phi = \frac{2\pi}{3}} \\ {\cos\theta = \frac{x}{\rho\sin\phi} = 0} & { \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(Note that $$\theta \neq 3\pi \slash 2$$ because $$y = 2\sqrt{3} > 0$$ .) Therefore spherical coordinates of the given point are $$\left( {4,\pi \slash 2,2\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Warning There is not universal agreement on the notation for spherical coordinates. Most books on physics reverse the meanings of $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ and use $$r$$ in place of $$\rho$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate {\iiint_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV} , where B is the unit ball: B = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} \leqslant 1}\}} Solution Since the boundary of B is a...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $${\iiint_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$B$$ is the unit ball:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$B = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} \leqslant 1}\}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solution Since the boundary of $$B$$ is a sphere, we use spherical coordinates:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$B = \left\{ {\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)|0 \leqslant \rho \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi} \right\}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In addition, spherical coordinates are appropriate because</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = \rho^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus (3) gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}e^{{(\rho^{2})}^{3 \slash 2}}\rho^{2}}{\sin\phi d\rho d\theta d\phi}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin\phi d\phi\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{1}\rho^{2}e^{\rho^{3}}d\rho}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\left\lbrack {- \cos\phi} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}{({2\pi})}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}e^{\rho^{3}}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4}{3}\pi{({e - 1})}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid that lies above the cone z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} and below the sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = z . (See Figure 9.) Solution Notice that the sphere passes...
body_xml: Example 4 Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid that lies above the cone $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and below the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = z$$ . (See Figure 9.) Solution Notice that the sphere passes through the origin and has center $$\left( {0,0,\frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ . We write the equation of the sphere in spherical coordinates as $$\rho^{2} = \rho\cos\phi$$ or $$\rho = \cos\phi$$ The equation of the cone can be written as $$\rho\cos\phi = \sqrt{\rho^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\cos^{2}\theta + \rho^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\sin^{2}\theta} = \rho\sin\phi$$ This gives $$\sin\phi = \cos\phi$$ , or $$\phi = \pi \slash 4$$ . Therefore the description of the solid $$E$$ in spherical coordinates is $$E = \left\{ {\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi \slash 4,0 \leqslant \rho \leqslant \cos\phi} \right\}$$ Figure 10 shows how $$E$$ is swept out if we integrate first with respect to $$\rho$$ , then $$\phi$$ , and then $$\theta$$ . The volume of $$E$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {{V(E)} = {{\iiint\limits_{E}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\int_{0}^{\cos\phi}{\rho^{2}\sin\phi d\rho d\phi d\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V(E)} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\sin\phi}}\left\lbrack \frac{\rho^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = \cos\phi}d\phi}} \\ {\phantom{V(E)} = {\frac{2\pi}{3}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\sin\phi\cos^{3}\phi d\phi}} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\left\lbrack {- \frac{\cos^{4}\phi}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 4} = \frac{\pi}{8}}} \end{array}$$

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 A transformation is defined by the equations {x = u^{2} - \upsilon^{2}} {y = 2u\upsilon} Find the image of the square S = \left\{ {\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)|0 \leqslant u \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 1}...
body_xml: Example 1 A transformation is defined by the equations $${x = u^{2} - \upsilon^{2}} {y = 2u\upsilon}$$ Find the image of the square $$S = \left\{ {\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)|0 \leqslant u \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 1} \right\}$$ . Solution The transformation maps the boundary of $$S$$ into the boundary of the image. So we begin by finding the images of the sides of $$S$$ . The first side, $$S_{1}$$ , is given by $${\upsilon = 0}\left( {0 \leqslant u \leqslant 1} \right)$$ . (See Figure 2.) From the given equations we have $$x = u^{2}$$ , $$y = 0$$ , and so $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$$ . Thus $$S_{1}$$ is mapped onto the line segment from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane. The second side, $$S_{2}$$ , is $${u = 1}\left( {0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 1} \right)$$ and, putting $$u = 1$$ in the given equations, we get $${x = 1 - \upsilon^{2}} {y = 2\upsilon}$$ Eliminating $$\upsilon$$ , we obtain $${x = 1 - \frac{y^{2}}{4}} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1}$$ which is part of a parabola. Similarly, $$S_{3}$$ is given by $${\upsilon = 1}\left( {0 \leqslant u \leqslant 1} \right)$$ , whose image is the parabolic arc $${x = \frac{y^{2}}{4} - 1} {- 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 0}$$ Finally, $$S_{4}$$ is given by $${u = 0}\left( {0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 1} \right)$$ whose image is $$x = - \upsilon^{2}$$ , $$y = 0$$ , that is, $$- 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 0$$ . (Notice that as we move around the square in the counterclockwise direction, we also move around the parabolic region in the counterclockwise direction.) The image of $$S$$ is the region $$R$$ (shown in Figure 2) bounded by the $$x$$ -axis and the parabolas given by Equations 4 and 5.

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">

    <paragraph>The Jacobian of the transformation $$T$$ given by $$x = g\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ and $$y = h\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial\left. ({x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} = \left. \middle| \begin{array}{ll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon} \end{array} \middle| \right. = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon} - \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The Jacobian is named after the German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi (1804–1851). Although the French mathematician Cauchy first used these special determinants involving partial derivatives, Jacobi developed them into a method for evaluating multiple integrals.</paragraph>
